# Music and Dance Practice Engineering Principles Framework

**DocID:** `MDPE` within **FPF Library**.

> A domain pattern language for creating, performing, transmitting, and deliberately developing music and dance practices and the environments that sustain them.

- **Author:** Anatoly Levenchuk, with AI-assisted development and review
- **Version designation:** 7 October 2026. To cite the text used, see [MDPE.Sources:1](#mdpesources1---edition-return).
- **Status:** Eternal alpha: a published working framework, already used in analyses and worked applications, while continuing to evolve.
- **License:** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) for original framework content; third-party material retains its own terms.
- **Publication:** [FPF Library repository](https://github.com/ailev/FPF)

Begin with the question you have about a performance, rehearsal, teaching encounter, style-development project or the environment that sustains a practice.

Search the Table of Contents by a familiar term or working question. Open the relevant pattern and compare its situation with yours. Use its method and worked cases to address your question about the performers, material, practice or supporting arrangement. Use another pattern when you need the result it supplies.

The Readme follows several performance, teaching and practice-development cases. The Architectural Reference explains their shared distinctions. For other questions, use the Table of Contents to find a method, its limits and its worked cases. Creation, rehearsal, performance, observation and development can overlap.


# Table of Contents

Search the Keywords & Search Queries column for the performance, teaching, practice or development question. Each row explains the pattern's contribution and links to its full body. The Readme offers selected starting examples; use the complete index for other working questions.

`MDPE.*` is the PatternID namespace of this framework. The numbers identify patterns across editions. The Parts group them for reading. Start with the contribution your work needs.

# Music and Dance Practice Engineering Principles Framework Readme

## Practical entries

Bring your question about performance, teaching or practice development. These selected examples show how one pattern's result changes what another method can do, where a useful branch can stop, and what changes when the conditions do. If no example fits, use the [Table of Contents](#table-of-contents) to open a pattern by its working question. Use a direct specialist method when it already supplies the needed result.

The [Architectural Reference](#music-and-dance-practice-engineering-principles-framework-architectural-reference) explains the shared language and its Music and Dance profiles. You can ask an assisting agent: “Explain this and give me your comments in the language of my work, without framework jargon.”

### MDPE-CARD-STYLE-DEVELOPMENT — Develop a new style without mistaking one showcase for a maintained practice

- **Situation:** A collective has an exciting performance and wants to invest in a recurring practice, but other participants have not yet reproduced the relation that made the showcase work.
- **Question:** Which change and next commitment are justified for the practice the collective wants to develop?
- **First useful result or blocker:** A bounded practice-development question and a supported assessment or choice of arrangement for the intended recurrence. Identify any missing participant, capability, decision authority, permission or support. Specify a representative test when its attainable contribution warrants its cost.
- **Start with:** [MDPE.8](#mdpe8---characterize-the-music-or-dance-work-methods-and-change-question) to distinguish the subjects being changed, [MDPE.1](#mdpe1---frame-a-music-or-dance-work-practice-style-or-medium-project) to frame the project, and [MDPE.21](#mdpe21---design-how-a-music-or-dance-style-is-produced-and-reproduced) when different ways to produce and reproduce the intended practice need comparison.
- **Stop or return:** Finish when the evidence supports the requested assessment, recommendation or local decision, including retention of the current arrangement. Return when an observed performance, changed participant, or support condition defeats the selected arrangement.

In the [constructed social-dance and live-music case](#mdpeapplication1---a-constructed-social-dance-and-live-music-development-decision), a rehearsed pair and a live coder have performed a successful showcase. The organizers want unfamiliar pairs to sustain partner-responsive timing in a monthly social event. MDPE.8 separates that recurring practice from the showcase and from a possible later style line. MDPE.1 bounds the present project to one twenty-minute block. MDPE.21 compares the showcase arrangement with a social-practice arrangement: the latter needs varied partners, readable timing, a host, usable sound and floor conditions, and another opportunity to practise. The organizers choose to try the second arrangement because it supports the intended social use.

Using [MDPE.22](#mdpe22---test-a-support-environment-change-for-a-music-or-dance-practice), the organizers set aside the event block for practice. They secure participants, a host, floor space and permission for the trial. [MDPE.5](#mdpe5---integrate-production-and-presentation-for-performed-music-or-dance-work) brings the music, dance, sound, and event contributions together for a pair's performance. [MDPE.12](#mdpe12---observe-and-compare-music-or-dance-performance-and-cultural-results) guides observation of eight pairs. Three sustain the intended timing. Five return to a memorized phrase after a dense accent change, and four on the far side report difficulty locating the pulse.

The organizers use [MDPE.14](#mdpe14---choose-a-response-to-conflicting-music-or-dance-results) to examine whether the musical changes and partner cue allow dancers to maintain their timing in the same performance. A longer verbal explanation would leave the sound and timing difficulty unresolved. The team compares constraining the musical changes, keeping the showcase arrangement, and maintaining separate showcase and social configurations. It selects the split. The team implements its choice with [MDPE.15](#mdpe15---make-and-test-a-local-music-or-dance-practice-change). The musician moves large accent changes away from the partner-cue interval, and the sound operator re-aims the monitor. In the later round, six pairs sustain the timing and two still need teacher cues. Both the sound and musical configuration changed, and the pairs had already practised, so these observations do not isolate either change's effect.

With [MDPE.7](#mdpe7---choose-the-next-music-or-dance-development-work), the organizers use the changed configuration and the observations to compare the larger festival slot, another transfer trial, capability development, and stopping the social branch. In this case the team chooses an unfamiliar-partner trial and keeps the current event block for a month. The showcase branch remains useful for its own audience. [MDPE.16](#mdpe16---keep-music-or-dance-alternatives-available-for-later-use) can maintain that branch when its performers, material, equipment, and permissions remain available. Another receiving group or a season-long continuation promise would require evidence for that group or interval.

### Renew a shared practice across participation, teaching and recognition

A school may teach more demanding material while its participants lose time, access or willing partners for the occasion they came to enjoy. [MDPE.25 - Renew a Shared Music or Dance Practice](#mdpe25---renew-a-shared-music-or-dance-practice) starts from that receiving participation and constructs an attainable arrangement across teaching, recognition and provision.

In its [complete Mara case](#mdpe2551---a-complete-constructed-case-the-evening-that-became-a-qualification-course), the organizers make 150 minutes of the four-hour event available for social participation, retain a bounded challenge and change an entry criterion that excluded a useful small variation. Losing the second room later reopens the timetable while the useful teaching and award distinctions remain. Finish with the supported arrangement, or explain what a proposal would still require. Use MDPE.14 alone when a bounded conflict decision is all that is needed.

### MDPE-PERFORM — Create alternatives and prepare a performing whole

- **Situation:** An attractive arrangement or movement candidate works in a rendering or isolated demonstration, but its live performer and coordination demands remain unsettled.
- **Question:** Which candidate can serve the intended performance, and does any relation need repair before we rely on it?
- **First useful result or blocker:** A comparison adequate for the intended use. It can support keeping a candidate, revising it, preserving different versions for different uses or ruling it out, or show what the available evidence cannot settle. For an open question, identify the performer, condition or observation needed to answer it.
- **Start with:** [MDPE.9](#mdpe9---generate-and-compare-music-or-dance-performance-candidates) with the intended use from [MDPE.1](#mdpe1---frame-a-music-or-dance-work-practice-style-or-medium-project). If the candidate is already selected, use its existing capability and interaction assessment where sufficient. For a consequential capability question use [MDPE.10](#mdpe10---develop-and-test-music-or-dance-performing-capability). For a question about the configuration use [MDPE.3](#mdpe3---configure-and-coordinate-a-music-or-dance-performing-whole).
- **Stop or return:** Stop when the creation or performance question is answered. A changed venue, instrument, performer, or receiving use reopens the contribution that depends on that condition.

MDPE.9's constructed music example compares three arrangements for singer, clarinet, cello, and live electronics. The antiphonal exchange requires the musicians to hear and answer one another, leave time to breathe and continue if the electronics fail. Dense spectral doubling, sparse instrumental answers, and generated responses pose different demands. A rendering can reveal limits of range and balance. A short rehearsal with these musicians can show how they breathe, follow cues, cope with latency and recover from an interruption.

Suppose that rehearsal shows that the dense version masks the answers, the sparse version preserves the desired space, and the generated responses arrive too late for the intended exchange. Those observations give grounds to reject the first candidate for this use, keep an acoustic version and return the generated responses for revision. For a further electronic trial, the musical requirement and failed timing relation guide [MDPE.3:4.7](#mdpe347---antiphonal-ensemble-cue-late-response-and-acoustic-recovery). Its constructed continuation realizes a visible readiness cue, a cutoff for the current electronic answer and an acoustic fallback, then follows their joint trial to a bounded rehearsal decision. If a performer cannot make the required response even with an adequate cue and setup, MDPE.10 addresses that capability instead.

[MDPE.11](#mdpe11---interpret-or-shape-music-or-dance-material-while-performing) concerns how musicians realize the prepared material and steer its permitted live variation. In the joint trial in MDPE.3:4.7 the musicians sustain the exchange with an acoustic answer when generation is late. Retain that fallback with the conditions under which they used it. MDPE.5 asks whether production and presentation let the intended recipients encounter the same musical relation. A successful monitor mix for the performers can still leave the audience unable to hear the answers.

If the next venue changes audibility or latency, use [MDPE.6](#mdpe6---choose-whether-and-how-to-use-a-music-or-dance-result-under-new-conditions) to decide whether the existing result can be used, revised, or branched for that venue. If the new conditions defeat the earlier assessment for this venue, identify the affected cue, sound relation or receiving use. Retain the original result at its supported scope and obtain a repair when the intended use requires it. A working acoustic branch can remain available while the electronic branch is revised. A later performance also requires available musicians and equipment.

### MDPE-TRANSFER — Move a practice to new conditions and keep it reproducible

- **Situation:** Learners can repeat a taught coordination with the teacher but cannot use it with unfamiliar partners, and a school wants to rely on the practice beyond the present class.
- **Question:** What transferred, what still depends on the teaching situation, and which result is needed for the school's next commitment?
- **First useful result or blocker:** The relations the receiving version must preserve, what the evidence establishes about that use and any missing capability, source content, partner or support that limits the answer.
- **Start with:** [MDPE.6](#mdpe6---choose-whether-and-how-to-use-a-music-or-dance-result-under-new-conditions) for the changed conditions and [MDPE.17](#mdpe17---design-and-test-transmission-of-a-music-or-dance-method) for receiving performance. Use [MDPE.23](#mdpe23---develop-and-test-music-or-dance-recognition-capability) when the uncertainty concerns recognition rather than the movement that follows.
- **Stop or return:** Keep the claim within the receiving conditions the available evidence supports. Claims about tested performance require evidence from the performance. Return a recognition problem to MDPE.23, a performance limitation to MDPE.10, or a missing support relation to MDPE.22. A broader continuation promise requires its own basis.

Suppose the teaching team wants learners to use two already taught partner-coordination variants with unfamiliar partners. MDPE.6 compares the class with that receiving use. The partners must be able to read each other’s timing and contact. Their use of teacher labels and a fixed exercise order can vary. The team can choose a receiving version of the teaching arrangement that varies those conditions while retaining the original class for learners who still need its support.

With MDPE.17, examine what the receiving dancers do, which taught method or variant they enact and what evidence shows about their use of the demonstration or lesson material. When the performance fails, MDPE.23 can separate “did not recognize the current coordination” from “recognized it but could not perform the response”. Its [constructed recognition case](#mdpe2342---a-multidance-recognition-transfer-trial) asks for a correct spoken A/B response within one agreed pulse after the cue and before the movement. The learner gives ten such responses in twelve held-out trials with unfamiliar partners and music. A second matched block adds a rapid transition from movement task A to B while retaining the same recording and partner. The next recognition cue is selected independently of that preceding sequence. Only seven of twelve responses qualify. The local ten-of-twelve entry criterion permits a subsequent supported response exercise in the first tested condition. Work on the transition limit before adding rapid switches to that exercise. These counts do not establish movement fluency. A correct recognition followed by a failed response returns to MDPE.10. If competent recognizers cannot maintain the distinction across the intended contexts, revise the distinction or receiving task before drilling it.

These results affect the receiving trial and the next teaching move. The team can use representative dance performances to identify the variant the dancers enacted. Evidence that they used the demonstration or lesson material can establish its use while leaving its causal contribution undecided. A variation introduced by the dancers can be retained when it preserves the relations needed in the new setting.

When the school asks whether another teacher can continue the practice, [MDPE.18](#mdpe18---build-usable-music-or-dance-cultural-memory-and-lineage-evidence) identifies what the lesson descriptions, recordings, and testimony can help that teacher recover and which bodily relations they omit. [MDPE.19](#mdpe19---decide-whether-a-music-or-dance-variant-can-continue-and-what-to-change) uses this evidence together with available performance and support results to assess the stated continuation promise. Existing evidence may support continuation with the current teacher while replacement remains unknown. If evidence about a replacement is needed, use any suitable existing result. Select a further test only when it can supply what is still needed and warrants the full teaching, performer, support and observation burden. A claim that replacement performance was tested must rest on that performance. The school can also propose how to prepare another teacher.

Cite the author, title and version designation shown at the beginning. Identify the wording with the permanent file link at the repository commit you used or a locator for the archived copy you consulted.

```text
Levenchuk, Anatoly. Music and Dance Practice Engineering Principles Framework.
GitHub repository: https://github.com/ailev/FPF
```

For a particular method, include its PatternID and title, for example MDPE.17 — Design and Test Transmission of a Music-or-Dance Method. For an archived copy, give a stable link or the archive name and catalogue reference that lets another reader retrieve that copy.

# Music and Dance Practice Engineering Principles Framework Architectural Reference

People and other agents can deliberately change how music or dance is performed,
taught and transmitted, or how its variants are recognized and selected. The change may concern performers,
material, tools, rehearsal, production or the venues, media, platforms and
archives that sustain a practice. Identify whether the subject is one performance,
a reusable Method, a maintained practice, the arrangement that produces a
style or an organization that holds a practice together. That distinction determines what to examine.

This framework applies systems engineering to developing and examining Music and Dance practices and
styles. FPF supplies the general distinctions among systems, agents, Methods, Work, results,
evidence, architecture and representations, as well as methods for examining change, choice,
capability and cultural evolution and for expressing them precisely. Use Systems Engineering methods
directly for questions of project scope, use, architecture, realization, configuration, consequences
or assurance. Use the Music and Dance methods and cases for the performance, transfer,
recognition, selection, practice conflicts and cultural evidence that affect work in these fields.

## MDPE.Reference:1 - A first result and a sufficient combination

Use these methods when a recurring performance or practice question requires a music or dance
contribution, or when specialist results must be used together. A composer’s material may exceed
what an ensemble can perform. A pupil may repeat a phrase fluently with a teacher and lose it with
a new partner. An event can attract an audience while the intended practice becomes harder to learn or
sustain. One pattern can supply the performance, capability, integration or decision result you
need, including an explanation of what already happened or why a proposed arrangement cannot work.

Combine the Methods by what each contributes to the question. A candidate may
require a capability the performers do not yet have. A configuration may permit
a joint trial, and an observation may affect a development choice or explain
an earlier result. The following examples show how to use those connections.

| Practice question | Contributions used together | Useful result and next branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can this material work in the intended performance? | Use the brief from `MDPE.1` or an existing brief. `MDPE.9` compares the candidates, using a performer trial when needed. `MDPE.10` addresses a limiting capability and `MDPE.3` addresses coordination. `MDPE.11` guides live interpretation or shaping. `MDPE.5` relates production and presentation to the intended performance. `MDPE.12` helps obtain or interpret the relevant comparison. | A score or construction can answer a design question. For a choice, compare the candidates against the intended use. Demonstrated capability and a suitable configuration can make a trial possible. For a claim about its performance or reception, use evidence of what happened. Reuse sufficient prior results or identify the missing contribution. One commission can finish with its own musical or dance result. |
| Will the practice remain usable with other performers or under changed conditions? | With `MDPE.6`, determine what the receiving use must preserve and what may change. `MDPE.17` helps identify what another performer enacted and what the evidence supports about the source’s contribution. Use `MDPE.10` or `MDPE.23` for an open capability or recognition question. `MDPE.18` provides memory and lineage evidence, and `MDPE.19` helps assess continuation or plan a needed reproduction test. | Existing evidence can support an adaptation or a conclusion about continuation. A trial bears on the conditions in which it took place. For a claim of later use or a successful replacement, establish the corresponding performance under those conditions. |
| Does the current or proposed arrangement support the intended style, and what change, if any, would help? | `MDPE.8` and `MDPE.1` frame the subject. `MDPE.21` compares ways to produce and reproduce the intended distinctions. `MDPE.22` addresses support, `MDPE.13` selection, and `MDPE.14` conflicts. `MDPE.15` helps test a selected change and `MDPE.16` keeps alternatives usable. Use `MDPE.20` for a forecast needed in the comparison and `MDPE.24` when the project boundary depends on which organization carries the practice or on how that organization formed. | A proposed or selected architecture, an observed local result or a supported judgement about continuation can answer the question before wider uptake is known. Use `MDPE.7` when the next work still needs to be chosen. |

The [constructed cross-pattern application](#cross-pattern-application) follows the third question through a social-dance and live-music trial. The unfamiliar
partners’ needs affect the architecture. A longer explanation would leave the sound and timing conditions unchanged. The organizers choose another transfer trial and keep the existing 20-minute
event block for a month. They defer buying the larger festival slot. The Readme gives shorter examples. The full patterns explain the methods, worked cases, limits and conditions for stopping.

Use a direct composition, choreography, teaching, engineering or operations
method when its result answers the question. Use MDPE where the music or
dance task still needs a connection between those specialist contributions.

## MDPE.Reference:2 - Several structures operate at once

During one performance a dancer may control muscular effort, execute a movement element, shape a figure,
coordinate with a partner, enact a dance style, contribute to a social event, and participate in reproducing a
practice. A musician may control an effector, produce an attack or sustained tone, shape a phrase, coordinate
with an ensemble, enact a musical style, perform for a receiving situation, and contribute to a practice at the
same time.

The following views distinguish different relations in the same performance. Use those that affect the question. Other relations may also matter.

- **Method composition.** Which smaller Methods or parts contribute to the larger Method, and how do they fit together?
- **Method unfolding.** Which result or condition enables a later move?
- **Performed Work.** Which Methods did this occurrence enact? Which other occurrences overlapped it
  or formed part of a larger bounded work, such as an event or rehearsal?
- **Capability and support.** Who can perform the actions? Who can grant any required permission or decision authority? Who or what supplies the equipment, access
  and the recurring work the performance needs?
- **Cultural evolution.** How are variants generated, performed, recognized, selected, passed on, retained,
  changed or lost across a population of practitioners?

A first–then account can express the order of actions or which result enables a later move. A list, the orientation of a
drawing, earlier training or developing the means to perform a later task does not establish a constituent
relation within ongoing work. Use `MDPE.14` when a conflict depends on a part–whole relation, scale order,
simultaneous work, a slower constraint or a representation that helps locally but compromises another result.

**Constituent actions in ongoing work.** Identify how the constituent actions enable or limit the whole performance. In a constructed dance case, the dancer can recall the figure and maintain strength and static axis control, but loses balance during rotation. The missing coordination connects muscular actions to the figure. MDPE.10 can help develop and test that capability. MDPE.17 asks whether another performer can reproduce the Method. If developing that coordination is the task, obtain the necessary instruction and practice conditions, vary the combinations and return to the whole figure. An account of the earlier rotation can use the observation already available. B.1.5.EW helps identify those connections. Use MDPE.14 if a conflict between results remains. A description can persist after a practice becomes unreproducible, and one success by a dancer does not establish retention across the population.

## MDPE.Reference:3 - Performance, recognition, selection, and continuation are different results

A detector can distinguish a signal without a listener recognizing a style. A listener can recognize a style
without selecting it. A curator or platform can select a variant without receivers being able to enact it. A
receiver can enact it once without retaining it. A score, recording, video, model, or archive can remain while
the capability and support needed for present reproduction disappear.

Use `MDPE.12` to determine what the observations support and `MDPE.23` to assess or develop recognition.
`MDPE.13` examines or designs recognition and selection arrangements. `MDPE.17` addresses receiving performance
and the source’s contribution. `MDPE.18` helps establish what can be recovered from memory or lineage evidence.
`MDPE.19` assesses continuation and helps choose a further test or change when needed and worthwhile.

The method [MDPE.25 - Renew a Shared Music or Dance Practice](#mdpe25---renew-a-shared-music-or-dance-practice) shows how these contributions can be constructed together. In its worked case, the organizers preserve time for social participation, a valued challenge and recognition while changing the timetable, teaching and selection rule. Use MDPE.14 to assess the conflict or choose a response. The people carrying out a selected change can use MDPE.15. MDPE.25 connects those contributions to the local arrangement, including learning, provision and any revision of the criterion. Use [Recover the subject](#mdpeapplication52---recover-the-subject-of-a-music-or-movement-claim) when a familiar label hides the changing object, and [Connect style, Method structure and acquisition](#mdpeapplication53---connect-style-method-structure-and-acquisition) when a recoverable description, stylistic distinction and learned performance are being confused.

## MDPE.Reference:4 - Project Work and cultural change

For example, a composition session, rehearsal, lesson, performance, release, archive reconstruction or platform
experiment is bounded Work. It may generate or enact
a Method variant, expose consequences, and influence later selection. Music or Dance culture continues across
many such Work occurrences, Agents, carriers, organizations, places, and periods. One project can influence that
culture. Its bounded result is distinct from the culture as a whole and does not by itself establish retention
across the population.

Many assignments end with a result for one project, such as a brief, composition, performance,
observation, capability judgement or comparison. A supported proposal, an assessment of a
change to practice or its environment, and a forecast may each answer a project question.
Use the continuation or cultural-development methods when the question concerns reproduction
by other participants, over further occasions or across a practitioner population.

## MDPE.Reference:5 - Conditions on a whole combination

Assess the whole combination against its intended use. Identify the performers, receiving
conditions, intended result and any conditions that have to be protected together. An
observation of a familiar pair, a recording judged by listeners and a teacher’s account of
a lesson answer different questions. To rely on them for coordination in a social dance,
establish how they bear on the participants and the conditions in which they will dance.

Check the shared resources over the period that matters. Account for preparation, coordination,
performer effort, trials and observation where needed, and the support a later occurrence
would require. Individually affordable activities can compete for the same teacher, instrument,
floor or interval. Give the local estimates and determine which activities can overlap. Use
the relevant operations method if queues, recurring load or cash flow affects the answer.

Suppose the group has 120 minutes for a shared rehearsal. Setup and warm-up require 30 minutes, each candidate
trial 20, transfer to an unfamiliar partner 20 and review of observations 20. Running three candidates
needs `30 + 3 × 20 + 20 + 20 = 130` minutes, assuming these activities use the shared interval in sequence.
Individual activities and pairs of them fit. Testing the two candidates whose comparison matters takes 110
minutes and retains the required transfer observation. These are estimates for this rehearsal. An additional
ten minutes would use all the remaining time. If setup variability, fatigue or another constraint makes
the plan infeasible or the observation inadequate, revise the plan or narrow the result promised.

For a later performance, the necessary capability, material, equipment, access and any support it requires must
be available together. A recording can preserve evidence. Losing the only available teacher may prevent the
promised reproduction. Determine whether another performer or source can supply the needed contribution.
`MDPE.16`, `MDPE.19`, `MDPE.21` and `MDPE.22` apply this comparison to their own questions. Reconsider
the combinations that rely on a changed condition and retain uses supported in their original settings.

## MDPE.Reference:6 - Shared patterns and specialized Music and Dance Methods

Music and Dance share embodied timing, variation, performance, recognition, transmission, supporting
environments and cultural change. They differ in bodily and instrumental techniques, media and
notation, social relations, training, criteria and evidence. A shared method retains the
operation that serves both. Use the relevant specialist methods for music, dance, teaching,
composition, choreography, rehearsal, production, events, platforms, robotics or machine learning.

The methods apply to social and staged dance and to acoustic, electronic and live-coded
music. Performers may be soloists, partners, ensembles or collectives, including robots
and mixed human–machine groups. Cases include classes, parties, concerts, festivals,
battles, competitions, recordings, online events, archives and short-video platforms.

[MDPE.29](#mdpe29---compose-movement-from-a-physical-relation-or-scientific-image) constructs choreography from a physical relation or scientific image. [MDPE.30](#mdpe30---construct-a-rhythmic-part-from-a-seed-phase-and-action-rule) constructs a rhythmic part from a seed, phase and action rule. The resulting choreography or part can supply candidates for MDPE.9 and can answer a commission for movement or musical material. Their cases show how a change in the relation, musical conditions or receiving use can require a revision. Use MDPE.10 for a question of capability and MDPE.3 for a question of joint performance.

## MDPE.Reference:7 - Music, Dance, and overlapping use profiles

The Music and Dance profiles identify the material, interaction, evidence and result
that matter in a particular use. They apply the specialist connections in
[A first result and a sufficient combination](#mdpereference1---a-first-result-and-a-sufficient-combination)
and the shared [combination conditions](#mdpereference5---conditions-on-a-whole-combination).
Use each source within its [limits and conditions for reconsideration](#mdpereference14---source-reliance-and-conditions-for-reconsideration).
For a narrower use, identify which conditions
change and which earlier results still hold.

### MDPE.Reference:7.1 - Music: making and realizing musical possibilities

Use the Music profile to compose, generate, realize or assess a musical idea for
its receiving situation. Identify the audible or performer-experienced distinction
that matters and which material can vary. The question may concern attack and
sustained sound, phrasing, timbre, ensemble timing, a live algorithm or a production
medium. Use `MDPE.1` or `MDPE.9` for the brief or comparison and the relevant
specialist method for composition, improvisation, arrangement, recording or coding.

Use `MDPE.10` for the capability that a musical demand requires and `MDPE.3` for relations
among performers and instruments. Use `MDPE.11` for interpretation or live shaping and
`MDPE.5` to establish whether sound, projection, venue, recording or distribution make the performance available as intended. A score, a performed
candidate, an account of what happened or a supported reason for a change can answer different
questions. With `MDPE.12`, choose listening, notation, acoustic or interaction evidence for
the question. An alignment can locate corresponding events in two variants. Timbre, bodily
effort and the listener’s experience require information that bears on those distinctions.

In live coding a performer changes running code to shape sound. For an assessment of the complete
performance, establish how the performer and system worked together in the intended set, including any recovery, using
existing evidence or a trial where needed. An algorave brings dancing, sound, a visible algorithmic
process and community conventions to the event. A seated concert may call for a different
presentation. In the constructed cross-pattern case, dense musical changes work in a showcase. In the social trial,
five of eight pairs return to a memorized phrase after a dense accent change. The team retains the showcase and tries a different social
configuration. Later audience recognition and continuation require evidence from those uses.

### MDPE.Reference:7.2 - Dance: making movement usable for its participants

Use the Dance profile to construct or assess movement for its participants and receiving use.
Partner connection, balance, transfer of weight, movement quality, space, fatigue and the relation
to music can affect both the work and its evidence. Identify the intended use. For example, a social pair may need to read
a partner, while a staged group may need to present a phrase. Use the relevant methods for choreography,
teaching, rehearsal or observation. `MDPE.3` addresses coordination, `MDPE.10` a performing
capability, and `MDPE.12` the evidence from movement, participant experience and judgement.

A drummer can sweep a **drum brush** across the head in continuous contact and make an accent audible by changing the pressure. Ed Soph’s [Foundational Brush Technique](https://www.moderndrummer.com/article/foundational-brush-technique/) describes one arrangement in which one hand sustains the sound and the other plays short notes, and another in which both hands move continuously and the drummer presses more of the brush fan against the head to accent a note. In both, distinguish the continuing movement from the event articulated within it.

In a partnered Balboa phrase, a foot can slide before it takes weight. The sound of contact, the dancer’s weight arrival and the moment the partner perceives the transfer can differ. A free-leg tap can add texture over the continuing supporting movement. If the partner treats the tap as the cue to move, it can obscure the transfer. Identify the perceived moment from evidence of the partner’s experience. A contact or pressure trace can locate contact or pressure. Its timing may coincide with the partner’s perceived transfer.

To compare free-leg articulations, take a phrase the pair can perform and hold its intended transfer time and continuing movement fixed. For the question about partner readability, use the receiving partner’s account to establish whether they recognized the transfer. Examine the pair’s response for what they did and what it shows about their ability to continue into the next movement. Reuse a relevant comparison or arrange one if needed. MDPE.9:4.3 compares candidates, MDPE.11:4.5 addresses live changes and MDPE.10 addresses performance capability. Reassess the comparison when changed partners or music alter its conditions. The analogy motivates this investigation. A particular event order or a learning benefit needs its own evidence.


Sometimes the performer must maintain a pulse while placing chosen accents. The accent can disturb the pulse, and regular movement can displace an accent. [MDPE.11:4.5.2](#mdpe11452---one-coordinating-method-two-physical-realizations) develops drum-brush and Balboa realizations of the shared coordinating method in RHY.11:4.4.1. The performer keeps the shared timing and varies preparation, articulation or correction to reduce interference. [MDPE.10:4.6](#mdpe1046---learn-to-vary-accents-over-a-continuing-pulse) develops practice with changed accents and a different reference. Use the technique of each realization, and evidence of the corresponding performance for a claim about its outcome.

[MDPE.26](#mdpe26---construct-and-change-a-partnered-movement-organization) addresses how a pair organizes its movement for the wanted quality, frees attention for partners and music, and connects a transition’s exit and entry for both participants. Its connection and fusion cases show how a difficulty in the joint action can identify a useful practice task.

[MDPE.27](#mdpe27---end-voluntary-partnered-performance) connects a voluntary decision to finish with the stopping movement, release of contact and exit. [MDPE.28](#mdpe28---receive-a-declined-invitation-and-find-an-available-next-action) addresses a declined invitation and how the person can obtain a wanted next action or identify unavailable help. Distinguish being able to take an action with support from feeling less disappointed. When a participant needs practice, derive it from the interaction or continuation that is difficult.

Use the staged-production branch to coordinate dancers, costumes, props, light, sound, venue
and presentation for a commission. The NDT case below traces a specialist choice back to the
intended performance. Use the social branch when changing partners, participation or responsive
movement matters. A camera-readable group phrase can establish what viewers could see. To rely
on it for partner transfer, establish the relevant interaction. A successful social dance
supplies evidence of the interaction that took place. A touring production still needs a
suitable configuration. Use `MDPE.6` to determine what can carry over and what needs changing.

### MDPE.Reference:7.3 - Teaching and recognition in Music and Dance

Use this profile when a question concerns what a performer can do or what a partner, listener,
teacher or recognizer can distinguish and use. Identify the relevant Music or Dance task,
conditions and permitted support. `MDPE.10` addresses performance capability and `MDPE.23`
recognition. Evidence can establish an existing capability or show a need for development. Use
`MDPE.17` when the question also concerns the contribution of a source to what recipients enact.

Suppose a learner succeeds with the teacher’s cue and fails when it disappears. That observation establishes
what happened under the two conditions. If an explanation or a teaching decision requires more, compare the
return of the familiar cue with a change in task difficulty or partner conditions. Distinguish cue-dependent
expression, missing skill, fatigue and a changed interaction by evidence appropriate to each. Use an adequate
earlier comparison or select a further one whose attainable contribution warrants its cost. The contextual-inference
sources below motivate the probe. Choosing a schedule for these dancers requires evidence of its suitability. For an exercise and feedback, a lesson method such as TOCA may be
appropriate. Attendance, teacher approval and later transfer each require evidence for the corresponding claim.

### MDPE.Reference:7.4 - Style development and continued practice

Use this profile for questions about how later performers produce variations and how their partners, listeners or other recipients recognize them.
Connect relevant performance and teaching results with recognition, selection, transmission, memory and
support. Development can build capability and the means of reproduction. The practice environment
shapes what participants encounter and select. Over time, variants can be transmitted,
recombined, retained or lost. These processes can coincide in one event and differ over longer
periods. If a change is commissioned, identify which relations the project can influence.

In `MDPE.21:4.1`, a Zouk project compares a choreography-and-showcase arrangement with one that supports
recurring partner work. The intended use is social dancing. The team selects a trial with rotating
partners and varied music, attending to readable responses, balance, recovery and refusal. Use `MDPE.13`
if the selection system rewards another result and `MDPE.22` for a difficulty sustaining a class or
event. `MDPE.18` and `MDPE.19` address memory and reproduction. The selected arrangement and trial
design answer the planning question. Evidence from later work is needed to claim wider uptake.

For a claim about recurring performance, examine the support that will be available at the required times
and use the relevant observations. With `MDPE.16`, a retained alternative needs enough support to remain
usable. A school, platform or event series can favour easily judged or camera-legible features. Use `MDPE.14`
to compare a resulting conflict and `MDPE.20` to examine competing trajectories. Obtain an additional
observation when it can answer an important open question at a justified cost. Use `MDPE.24` when persistence
and relations matter to the proposed project boundary. A commission for one work can finish with that work.

### MDPE.Reference:7.5 - Robotic, AI, and equipped performance

For robotic, AI or equipped performance, identify the intended task and the conditions
that must hold across the complete configuration. Determine who or what performs
the action, which component can change, and which development method might produce
that change. When a development decision is needed, identify who can make it. The
performer, the device being changed and the holder of that authority can differ.

In `MDPE.10:4`, Shimon’s continuation of a composition and its marimba performance are distinct from the human team’s
development choices. The Jason Barnes case distinguishes the drummer’s practice, prosthesis control and their combined
performance. For a claim about that whole, examine evidence of the musical task under the relevant combined conditions. Use
`MDPE.3` for participants and interfaces, `MDPE.10` for human practice, control learning, calibration or co-adaptation, and
`MDPE.12` to qualify the conclusion for the material and conditions examined. AI-generated movement can answer a commission
for material or a score. For a claim about interpretation or embodied performance, establish what the relevant performers did.

Choose this profile when the performer or device changes what can be assessed or developed.
A purely acoustic ensemble can use the Music profile. For transfer from robotic Music to
Dance, examine the proposed body, task, coordination and applicable evidence. Narrow the
profile when these differences affect the operation or test. A partner-Dance lesson may use
the social-Dance and teaching profiles alongside a musician’s live coding. To establish their
joint timing, use evidence that covers the relevant contributions in the same performance.

## MDPE.Reference:8 - What this publication foregrounds and leaves outside

The methods address five connected problems. They help select an engineering subject and a
style-development arrangement, create material and prepare the performing whole, perform and
make differences observable so participants can recognize and select variants, transfer and sustain a reproducible practice, and develop
the conditions in which it can continue. The last group includes practice conflicts, local
changes, alternative performances or arrangements, trajectories and the choice of further work.

The [Cross-Pattern Application](#cross-pattern-application) gives worked examples of movement exploration, a responsive duet and complete
fixed scores. They show how to connect methods under stated conditions. A complete score can answer a
composition brief. Use evidence from performance or practice for claims about realization or learning.

Use specialist methods and sources for repertoire, curriculum, performance technique, event direction, software implementation, artistic traditions and their canons, and domain history.
Take legal and safety questions to the relevant sources and authorities. The methods below identify the contribution those results can make. Systems Engineering, Human
Capability Development, Organization Change Engineering, Operations Management and Embodied Rhythmics provide their own domain methods. FPF Core, including C.39,
supplies general Method development. [External result use](#mdpereference15---external-result-use) identifies specific contributions and the conditions for using them.

## MDPE.Reference:9 - Architectural Rationale

Performance and style development often share a project. Today’s sound or movement
depends on capability, tools, selection and support. A change in production can alter
what later participants can learn or retain. Each method has its own entry so a
practitioner can start with the difficulty at hand and finish with an adequate answer.
Use the connections between methods where a question crosses their boundaries.

Music and Dance share embodied timing, variation, coordination, recognition and
transmission. A shared method is useful when both fields face a recognizable problem
and can use the same operation, result and condition for finishing the work. The profiles specify the material,
techniques, observers and evidence particular to each use. Separate frameworks
could serve readers better if recurring questions or maintenance needs diverge
enough that practitioners have to reconstruct the separate operations on each use.

Several other architectural choices are consequential for use:

| Serious alternative | Why this language uses another arrangement | When the alternative serves the reader |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct FPF and Systems Engineering, specialist methods and a guide | These sources can identify systems, choices and evidence. A music or dance project may still need a brief, a performing configuration or trial, conditions for use by a different performer, or an arrangement that reproduces the style. MDPE connects the relevant specialist results. | Use a direct result when its content and limits answer the working question. Add an MDPE contribution where a connection is still needed. |
| One broad style-engineering pattern | Configuration, recognition capability, support, local change, and continuation have different entry problems and independently useful results. Distinct patterns make each result reachable. | Use one direct Method when the present work has one coherent result and its complete move is already described. A broad chapter can explain shared reasons without absorbing the individual Methods. |
| Separate performance-engineering and style-engineering DPFs | Their frequent result exchange would make one project reconstruct connections between performance, capability, recognition, teaching, and later reproduction. | Reconsider the split when recurring uses and source changes mostly stay within one side and separate maintenance improves those uses. |
| One cross-domain Style Engineering DPF covering other cultures as well | FPF already supplies the transferable cultural-evolution distinctions. The constructive Methods and evidence for Music and Dance remain domain-specific. | Use FPF and the appropriate inquiry or domain Method for another culture. A new domain language needs its own connected practical contributions. |
| Organize the language primarily by body, phrase, performance, event, scene, and style levels | A working difficulty often crosses several simultaneous structures. Beginning from a level would hide the conflict or integration that the practitioner needs to address. | Use a scale or part-whole view inside a question that depends on that relation, particularly with `MDPE.14` or `MDPE.24`. |

Systems Engineering applies to the particular performers, equipment, production organizations,
venues, schools, archives or platforms under study. A project may need several system descriptions
to explain what a change enables. Production, recognition and transmission through these
systems can support an inquiry about cultural style. Use FPF Core’s method-development guidance when the subject
is a Method, its description, a family of Methods or support for enactment. Human capability
development, organization change and operations supply contributions where needed.
[External result use](#mdpereference15---external-result-use) identifies reliance on particular
framework editions. Establish an edition dependency from the contribution actually used.

Use `MDPE.7` to choose further development from different kinds of domain results,
and `MDPE.15` to perform or assess a selected local change. A choice can answer
the question of what to pursue before anyone plans or carries out the work. A completed or failed attempt can inform a later choice or
answer what happened. Generation, recognition, selection, transmission and
continuation each require evidence for their own claims. Connect their findings to
the cultural process or decision when the question requires that wider account.

## MDPE.Reference:10 - Shared source contributions and their limits

Systems Engineering and Method Engineering contribute ways to define a changing project
subject, use several descriptions, replace a Method and revise an architecture.
Capability-development sources connect representative work and transfer. Work-management
and organization sources address recurring support, shared resources and arrangements
that can carry out a changed practice. FPF provides the general distinctions used
to connect these contributions. The following sources provide the specialist music
and dance methods and evidence. Each pattern gives the grounds and limits for its particular use.

**Practice construction and its supporting environment.** The practitioner-authored
[Live Coding: A User's Manual](https://livecodingbook.toplap.org/book/) and
[Algorave guidelines](https://github.com/Algorave/guidelines/blob/master/README_en.md) connect live music with
performer-built tools, a visible process, event conventions and a community. `MDPE.5`, `MDPE.21` and `MDPE.22`
use these relations in a local brief. Identify the method used or proposed for the performance and use applicable information
on rehearsal, participants, capacity and costs. A manifesto can document the stated principles and a calendar
the advertised events. Evidence of performance or later cultural uptake comes from the relevant occurrences.

The [Street Tango Concept](https://tangonuevo.ru/stc7eng) describes a practitioner’s work
on technique, exercises, teaching and a proposed style. The [TOCA Method](https://tocamethod.com/?lang=en)
offers one teaching approach organized around Touch, Observation, Control and Awareness.
A teacher can assess the fit of this approach or an alternative for the learners. A
commission for one performance can finish with that performance. Use practitioner
accounts for the contribution they document. `MDPE.17` and `MDPE.18` distinguish
such evidence from grounds for disputed origins, transmission or wider recognition.

**Production as a connected result.** Kloosterman and van Kempen’s 2026
[study of an NDT Dance production](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccs.2026.100710) reconstructs choreography,
dancers’ work, costumes, props, technical rehearsal, presentation, recording and later judgement.
`MDPE.5` traces each specialist choice to what it enables in performance. `MDPE.21` and `MDPE.22`
examine recurring organizational and technical capability where needed. NDT had resources for bespoke
production and touring. For a local class or voluntary scene, establish what the intended use
requires. A less costly arrangement may be preferable if it preserves that use and the necessary contributions can still be supplied.

**Observation, representation and recognition.** [Comparative musicology](https://doi.org/10.1093/9780191872303.003.0002),
the [Global Jukebox](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0275469) and a 2026
[rhythm-aware melodic-alignment study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12673) offer different comparisons
of musical material. The alignment preprint examines variants. Use a representation that preserves
the distinctions in the question, and evidence from listeners or event decisions when those
are the subjects. Whitehead and colleagues’ [spontaneous-interactivity study](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1465595)
combines kinematic analysis, coding and interpretations by experienced participants.
Its observation and interpretation methods can be used under the conditions they cover. Its findings describe the observed cases. For audience or community recognition,
establish the recognizers, task, conditions and evidence. `MDPE.12` addresses
observation, `MDPE.23` recognition capability and `MDPE.13` the selection arrangement.

**Learning under changed conditions.** The 2021 [COIN sensorimotor study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04129-3)
and later [work on contextual cues and transition statistics](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.116281)
distinguish updating a memory from expressing it under an inferred context. `MDPE.10` and `MDPE.23` adapt
this distinction when selecting a cue or transfer probe. A return to a previously successful context can help
distinguish difficulty retrieving a response from lack of capability. Judge its applicability to a musical,
dance, broader memory or non-human case from the relevant evidence. The
[Music focus-of-attention review](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1290596) informs the choice of attentional cues for the performer and task. When
the cause remains open, ask which observations could distinguish the plausible explanations for the particular performer.

**Human, machine and combined contributions.** The [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon),
its [robotic-gesture study](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1461615), the
[Drumming Arm study](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561943) and
[JIZAI ARMS co-design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581169) distinguish a component change, the performing
configuration, capability and a development decision. `MDPE.3` and `MDPE.10` use these distinctions. The
JIZAI prototype provides evidence of the interactions examined. Claims about Dance performance or transfer
need corresponding evidence. In the 2026 [movement-model co-design study with Voguing and Dancehall dancers](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791515),
dancers’ curation and improvisation informed changes to the tool and models. Dancer-Y alone compared
three models in medium/high/low order, with self-selected music and changes to practice. These
conditions leave the isolated effect of fidelity unresolved. `MDPE.9` adapts the co-design process
to the intended performers. `MDPE.16` can retain alternatives when distinct receiving uses
warrant the cost. Assess the alternatives against the new project’s actual aims and conditions.

**Open development and cultural inquiry.** [Quality Diversity through Human Feedback](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/ding24h.html)
offers a computational method for shaping diversity from human similarity judgements. MDPE uses it to ask
which useful differences might be lost. Music or dance creation and curation need their relevant domain
methods. Yaman, Tian and Lindström’s [semantic-knowledge and innovation study](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2530750123)
gives a reason to compare knowledge-guided creation with random variation. Assess those options for the
artistic use in question. `MDPE.16` examines usable alternatives and their maintenance costs. `MDPE.20`
examines candidate mechanisms and the observations that could distinguish the trajectories they imply.

The 2024 cultural-evolution [computational-workflow](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2322887121)
and [experimental-design](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2322886121) papers contribute
target claims, model checks and design trade-offs. Use them where they help investigate
transmission, mixing, retention or the effects of an intervention. Historical reconstruction,
ethnography and direct observation offer alternatives for different evidence questions.
An account of cultural change can answer an inquiry independently or inform a
constructive decision. An improved local performance establishes a different result.

## MDPE.Reference:11 - Practical judgement, bias, and what changes next

Begin with the contribution that answers the music or dance question.
Where several results must work together, account for the effort of
obtaining relevant observations, reconciling the findings and supporting
alternatives that must remain reproducible. A settled performance can answer
a question about one event. A continuing practice may depend on teaching,
recognition and support being available again at the next occasion.

Apply these questions to the intended use. Reuse an existing answer
under conditions it covers and examine the parts that have changed.

- What must be explained, assessed or made possible, for which performers or recipients
  and under which conditions? Apply the brief and selected methods to that use.
- Which contributions are already available, which are proposed and what remains unknown? Identify
  any missing capability, configuration, observation or support on which the answer depends.
- Can the full combination meet its shared resource and interaction conditions? When narrowing
  the work, preserve the comparisons and observations on which its conclusion depends.
- What can the observation and its representation establish, what qualifies the judgement, and which
  conditions or participants does the evidence cover? Distinguish local observation, causal
  contribution, transmission and later continuation where those differences matter.
- If a change is proposed, who can decide or carry it out, and whose performance, participation or
  recurring work would it affect? Use the applicable authority and arrangements for participation, refusal or revision.
- What conclusion or work result can the recipient use now? If
  further action or reconsideration is needed, what calls for it?

Published studies, named projects, well-documented teaching and technical interventions are
easier to find than quiet social practice, oral or embodied knowledge, poorly archived variants
or the experiences of people left out of the sample. Determine what a camera, a timing measure,
a platform count or an expert judgement can establish about the task at issue. Include
participants’ experience when the question concerns it. Use `MDPE.12` for observation,
`MDPE.13` for a selection arrangement or `MDPE.18` for recoverable source and lineage evidence.

When using an NDT production result, human motor-learning study or robot performance
elsewhere, compare the relevant resources, learner, task and configuration.
Algorave guidance and TOCA teaching materials may support a brief or lesson
design. A local investment method, costs, capacity and community recognition each
need their own grounds if the question depends on them. Use adequate existing
results and identify the particular claim limited by any missing contribution.

Identify what a change affects. A new instrument or model may require an assessment of configuration or
performance. A changed teaching method may require transfer evidence, and a different selection rule
may affect which variants or capabilities receive support. A changed population or capacity can reopen
a combination while its individual methods remain usable elsewhere. Reconsider the framework boundary
when the evidence alters a recurring problem, a shared specialization or a material relation between
results. [Source use and currentness](#mdpereference14---source-reliance-and-conditions-for-reconsideration)
gives the general condition. Each method identifies the local work that can revisit its result.

## MDPE.Reference:12 - Intended use and ordinary non-use

Use MDPE for recurring engineering questions about creating, performing, developing,
transmitting, sustaining, recognizing, selecting or deliberately changing Music or Dance
practice under evolving stylistic conditions. When a direct music, dance, teaching,
rehearsal, production, event, platform, robotics, machine-learning or other specialist
method supplies the required result and its grounds, use it. Use FPF directly for a
transdisciplinary question whose answer needs no further music or dance specialization.

## MDPE.Reference:13 - PatternID and reader order

Within this framework, `MDPE.*` identifies the pattern bodies. Each PatternID gives a
stable local address. The five Parts group methods for reading and the practical entries
connect them to recurring situations. Determine working order, constituent relations
and dependencies from the work being done and the conditions that the methods describe.

## MDPE.Reference:14 - Source reliance and conditions for reconsideration

Use each pattern’s sources for the operation and conditions that they support. A citation count can establish attention, a professional endorsement its stated position, a standard its requirements, and an available artifact what its contents preserve. Current practice, effectiveness, prevalence, transmission and retention each need evidence for the corresponding claim. With sparse direct evidence, an expert estimate can support a bounded conclusion if its grounds, uncertainty and conditions for revision fit the use. Otherwise state the uncertainty. For a decision that still needs an answer, consider a narrower supported response, a worthwhile attainable inquiry or a justified stop.

Reconsider the pattern, practical entry or source use affected by a changed
source, a new specialist method, a change to a relied-on FPF contribution
or a consequential omission revealed by reader or practitioner use. Reconsider the architecture when that
evidence affects the identity, division or combination of patterns,
relations among results, problem coverage or the publication boundary.

## MDPE.Reference:15 - External result use

For a question that uses C.36.P, C.39 or E.23.CDI:4.2.1, consult the contribution from FPF Core published with this Library edition and check it against the receiving question and available inputs. These are dependencies of MDPE on Core.

For MDPE.16 and MDPE.20, the applicable assurance and currentness criteria were qualified against `FPF@2026-09-07-EA03-ASSURANCE-CURRENTNESS`. B.3.3 supplies assurance criteria, B.3.4 evidence applicability and G.11 currentness. For a different Core edition, examine any change to the criterion or premise used for that result. Retain a sufficient result where its supporting conditions still apply.

| Relied-on FPF results | Receiving use in this edition | Why this is a dependency | Reopen condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `A.1`, `A.2`, `A.2.1`, `A.3.1`, `A.3.2`, `A.15.1` and `C.2.1` | Distinguish Systems, Agents, Methods, MethodDescriptions, Work, results, assignments and epistemes across the `MDPE.*` patterns. | These distinctions determine what each method addresses, the kind of result it supplies and how its examples can be used. | Recheck the MDPE claims that rely on a changed distinction for the use in question. |
| `A.10`, `B.3.3`, `B.3.4`, `C.11`, `C.28` and `G.11` | Qualify evidence and assurance for the receiving use, compare bounded choices, distinguish observation from causal contribution and assess currentness. | MDPE.16 and MDPE.20 can rely on sufficient existing evidence of availability or a qualified forecast. Examine rights, calibration, configuration and promised-use conditions for the occasion in question. | Recheck the receiving relation when its claim, use or relied-on premise changes. Communicate the conditions governing the recipient’s use. |
| `A.22`, `C.30`, `C.32.MWA`, `C.32.MLAO` and `C.36` | Describe several architectures, identify conflicts among structures and holon positions, develop changes to reduce a conflict where needed, and distinguish cultural generation, enactment, recognition, selection, transmission, retention and loss. | `MDPE.13`, `.14`, `.17`, `.19`, `.20`, `.21`, `.22` and `.24` connect findings about these different relations. | Recheck the architectural or cultural conclusion that relies on the changed FPF distinction. |
| `E.23.CDI`, including `E.23.CDI:4.2.1` | Develop a named holder's capability and test representative transfer in `MDPE.10` and `.23`; keep the result distinct from the later performance in `MDPE.5`. In Application:5.3, reconstruct the missing connection from the receiving performance, distinguish learning from provision, and retain the help still needed. | An incomplete explanation, unavailable Method, missing learner contribution and insufficient assistance call for different work. An unsupported ability or transfer claim returns to the applicable development Method and evidence. | Recheck when the holder, receiving demand or relied-on capability result changes. |
| `C.36.P`, `C.39`, `A.2.2` and `C.2.8` | Recover the subject of a claim in Application:5.2, construct a missing way to obtain a contribution in MDPE.25, and distinguish what can be recovered about an explanation, its operations and their relations from what a learner can perform in Application:5.3. | Core supplies general claim recovery and Method development. Use relevant sources for music or dance technique and stylistic distinctions, and evidence from the performer for demonstrated capability. | Reconsider the affected construction, recovery or learning claim when its subject, receiving result or relied-on explanation changes. |
| `E.24.PUB` | Distinguish publication of a claim-bearing episteme, such as an accompanying programme note, from the performance and recording in `MDPE.5`. | For a master released for listening, use the music or distribution method. To treat audio as a claim-bearing work, establish what claims the work conveys and the applicable publication conditions. | Recheck the relied-on publication result when its edition, audience, use or availability changes. |

Systems Engineering, Human Capability Development, Organization Change Engineering, Operations Management and Embodied Rhythmics can supply domain results. Identify the result needed and check that its scope and edition fit the receiving question, that it is available and sufficiently current for the use, and that any required permission covers the proposed use. Use an adequate direct engineering, teaching, organization, operations, rhythm, music or dance result. For general Method development, use FPF Core, including C.39.

A recurring operation that remains useful after removing the music-and-dance-specific distinctions can be proposed as a Core contribution. Describe the situation, what a practitioner would do differently, the first useful result, the gap in existing Core guidance, the evidence and what would prompt reconsideration. [FPF E.4.DPF](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#e4dpf---domain-and-local-principle-frameworks-whether-and-how-to-author-and-publish) explains how to return the proposal from the domain. [FPF E.4.FPF](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#e4fpf---fpf-edition-assembly-publication-forms-carriers-and-access-routes) governs Core construction and the decision to publish. An accepted Core contribution has its own scope and grounds.

## MDPE.Reference:16 - Publication boundary

This edition includes the Readme, Table of Contents, Architectural Reference, twenty-eight
pattern bodies, shared cross-pattern methods, constructed applications, and Sources
and Edition Notes. Follow the citations for the external works used in these chapters.

For source qualifications, citation and edition information, see the [Sources and Edition Notes](#music-and-dance-practice-engineering-principles-framework-sources-and-edition-notes).

## MDPE.Reference:End


# Part I - Engineering Subject and Style-Development Architecture

## MDPE.8 - Characterize the Music-or-Dance Work, Methods, and Change Question

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance engineering entry pattern

> **Public result:** a bounded Music-or-Dance development focus identifying the work or practice in question, the subject and relation that matter, what is known about them, and any remaining question for action or inquiry.

### MDPE.8:0 - Use This When

Use this method when a request to create, improve, teach, perform, preserve, spread or modernize music, dance, a style, a school
or a scene leaves unclear which part of the work matters. The same problem arises when explaining a past performance or practice.

A team can improve a recording while musicians still cannot play the passage, teach a dancer a figure
that a pair cannot perform together, or publish a course without establishing whether its learners can use the method in
practice. A style name can remain familiar after the practice that made it recognizable has disappeared.

When a consequential claim has an unclear subject, use C.36.P. [MDPE.Application:5.2](#mdpeapplication52---recover-the-subject-of-a-music-or-movement-claim) applies it to claims about music, movement, styles, schools and events. Use the clarified claim to answer the question at hand.

A bounded development focus states the question, describes the relevant work and identifies what
must be understood or changed. For a decision, include any alternatives that still matter and any
uncertainty that affects the choice. Describe the following where they bear on the question.

- the intended use and, for a decision, what is to be chosen and who has the authority to choose
- the Music-or-Dance work under consideration
- the subject of the claim or proposed change, with its state at the time in question
- competing subjects, methods, explanations or changes that would lead to different conclusions
- any uncertainty that changes the answer, and what evidence could distinguish the live possibilities
- for a proposed change or test, who could carry it out, what they would do and which method they would use
- the finding, choice or remaining condition that answers the present question.

Finish when the subject is clear enough to answer the question, choose the next bounded work, or identify
the specific information needed for either. An earlier observation can already supply that answer.
Use a direct method when it already identifies the subject and supplies the result. This
may be a method for composition, choreography, improvisation, rehearsal, teaching,
production, event support, preservation, ethnography, history or systems engineering.

### MDPE.8:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

Terms such as “the dance” or “the music” can refer to several different things.

- a **performance occurrence** and the material or recording left by it;
- a **performing capability** and the Work in which that capability is exercised;
- a **Method** for composing, moving, partnering, teaching, judging, or organizing and a description of that Method;
- a performing whole, including the performer, body or effector, instrument, partner,
software or venue equipment and their relations in sensing, timing and correction,
- a practice or style that participants produce, recognize, select,
teach, transmit and retain across performances and populations,
- a medium or source of support, such as a venue, school, festival
series, archive, platform, instrument-making capability or software service.

In a single dance a person or pair can regulate movement, coordinate with a partner, shape a phrase and participate in a social practice at the same time. The work can enact several methods, including a style-specific method. A musician or robot can control an effector, produce attacks and sustained sound, shape a phrase and coordinate with an ensemble in the same performance. Identify which actions form parts of that work and which conditions enable it. Rehearsing before the performance and building an instrument before playing it are temporal relations.

Ask what the evidence establishes about its subject. A performance can show what the participants did, a video can preserve a record,
and a course description can state what the course proposes to teach. For transmission, examine what the recipient received and enacted. For continuation, examine use
over time. To establish capability, examine the performer’s work in the claimed conditions. A robot’s autonomous playing can establish
its contribution to a performance. A claim about who chose the development of the practice needs evidence about that choice.

### MDPE.8:2 - Solution

Use the **bounded Music-or-Dance development focus** to connect the question with the subject, performance or practice that can answer it.


Revisit a distinction when new evidence changes the question or the answer that depends on it.

#### MDPE.8:2.1 - Begin with the question or decision

State the question in the terms of the work. For a decision, identify the choice and who will use the result. For example, ask one of the following.

- Which Zouk teaching and partnering change should we trial next?
- Can this robot–instrument configuration perform the selected material under live tempo changes?
- What limited the pair’s use of this figure in the recorded social improvisation?
- Should this festival change its judging and presentation arrangement?
- What must be rebuilt before this nearly lost repertoire can be performed again?

If the subject remains unclear, say which ambiguity prevents an answer. A record that already settles what happened can complete a question about that performance.

#### MDPE.8:2.2 - Identify the subject of the claim or change

Choose the narrowest subject that still covers the question. Common subjects include the following.

- musical or movement material;
- one performance occurrence or its production and presentation arrangement;
- a performing Agent's capability;
- a performer–instrument, partnered, ensemble, robotic, or hybrid performing whole;
- a Music-or-Dance Method or Method family;
- a teaching, recognition, selection, transmission, or continuation relation;
- a supporting event, school, venue, archive or platform; or
- the architecture by which a practice or style is produced and reproduced.

When two subjects can change independently, ask separate questions or explain their relation. A new
recording arrangement and a new performing method may have different consequences for the music.

Distinguish what existed at the time in question, what is proposed, what a qualified source establishes and what remains
unknown or unavailable. A score can establish the intended phrase, and a performance record can establish what was played.

#### MDPE.8:2.3 - Recover the Work and Method that matter

Identify the work and method relevant to the question. For a proposal, describe the work that would use the method. For a past event, establish what its participants did. Look for distinctions such as the following.

- who performs the Work, which other participants support it, and which material or descriptions are used;
- a reusable Method from its MethodDescription and from dated Work;
- performance Work from engineering or inquiry Work that changes or studies the practice;
- simultaneous contribution at several holonic scales from a temporal or logical unfolding inside one Method;
- capability-development Work from later Work in which capability is exercised; and
- enabling or build-the-builder Work from the performance it later enables.

Use systems engineering for an engineered performer, instrument, interface, venue, platform, school
or archive when the question concerns its design or operation. Use FPF Core’s general method-development
guidance for a method, family of methods, description, collection, support for enactment or trial.
Keep the musical or dance work and the result required from that specialist contribution explicit.

#### MDPE.8:2.4 - Identify the cultural relation at issue

For a question about a style, school, scene, tradition or practice, identify the relevant process. It might concern
generation, transmission, reconstruction, recognition, selection, retention, loss or the effect of an earlier
event on later production. Identify the population, place, period, carriers and evidence the claim depends on.

A style name can document how a practice was labelled, an archive can preserve its materials, and a platform count can show measured activity. A continuation claim needs evidence of the relevant practice over time. Use C.36 to identify the cultural relation and its grounds, and C.36.P when the wording still hides the subject. MDPE.21 addresses how to design the production and reproduction of a style, MDPE.19 its continuation under specified conditions, and MDPE.20 competing future trajectories.

#### MDPE.8:2.5 - Keep live alternatives and uncertainty visible

Retain competing subjects or explanations when they would change the answer or the next work. A difficulty with a turn could concern individual capability or partner
coordination. A change in an artifact could leave the performing method unchanged. Identify what could discriminate the live accounts, using available evidence
where sufficient. If the evidence leaves a question open, state what remains possible. Treat local recurrence and wider recognition at their respective scopes.

#### MDPE.8:2.6 - Select a contribution that can answer the question

Use the available result or method suited to the question. For example, the following methods can supply different contributions.

- MDPE.9 or a composition, choreography, improvisation or rehearsal-prototyping method can
