construct or compare performance possibilities, including an already adequate candidate,
- MDPE.10 or a capability-development method can specify a needed capability, prepare a performer for it or assess evidence of transfer to representative work,
- MDPE.3 or an ensemble, partnering, staging, instrument-interface or systems engineering method
can establish a suitable performing configuration or what an actual configuration allowed,
- MDPE.12 or an observation and comparison method can assess the evidence for a specified question,
- MDPE.17 or a teaching and transmission method can design a handover or assess what the recipient enacted and what the supplied material, instruction or demonstration contributed, or
- a historical, ethnographic, causal, preservation, production, event or
organizational method can supply its own result when it covers the question.

If a needed contribution is unavailable, identify it. It may be a method description, performer, input, evidence, authority, access or relation. State
which conclusion or action depends on it and give any answer already supported. Indicate a way to obtain more when the task requires it.

### MDPE.8:3 - First Useful Result

For example, a short account can use the following form.

> The question is **[what needs explaining, designing or deciding]** about **[the work, practice or other subject]**.
> For a past event or existing condition, **[the evidence]** supports **[this finding]**. For a design, state **[the proposal and its premises]**.
> Where alternatives remain open, state **[what the evidence distinguishes]** and **[any attainable observation that could change the answer]**.
> For a decision, **[the authorized decision-maker]** can use **[the applicable finding or method]** to consider **[the available choices]**.
> The result is **[a supported conclusion, a selection or the specific condition still needed]**.

Use the account for the question it answers. For a claim that a proposed change altered the work, establish what occurred and how the change contributed.

### MDPE.8:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.8:4.1 - A social-dance style project

Suppose a local Zouk school wants dancers to respond to unfamiliar partners over a wider range
of music. In class the dancers reproduce a taught sequence with familiar partners. The school
has no observation yet of transfer to social dancing. It considers two possible difficulties.

- The transfer task may demand individual movements the dancers cannot yet
execute. Suitable embodied exercises could help if that is the difficulty.
- The difficulty may lie in reading and responding to a partner’s cues or retrieving a
response under changed conditions. Rotating partners or varying music might address it.

A recording or observation of social dancing could establish what the dancers can already do.
In this case the teachers lack that evidence and choose a trial with unfamiliar partners and
varied music. They examine the partner-readable response, balance, recovery and the timing that
distinguishes the style. Where a dancer has trouble across partners, the teachers can investigate
the individual movement as well. The immediate result is a question about partnered transfer
within the school. Wider change in Zouk practice would need evidence beyond the trial.

In a constructed continuation, the teacher compares familiar and unfamiliar partners
using the same recording. The learner maintains balance in both conditions and
continues the taught sequence when the unfamiliar partner pauses. The immediate
question is whether the learner recognized that cue and what the response shows. The
observed balance and familiar-sequence performance remain available as evidence.

The teachers use MDPE.10 to examine recognition of the cue and ability to
enact a suitable response. If the learner needs more practice, the teachers can help them
develop that part. If the partners used incompatible cue conventions,
MDPE.3 helps assess their joint configuration. The observed response leaves
those explanations open. The school can report what happened in the trial
or continue its broader work on responsive partnering across music.

#### MDPE.8:4.2 - Shimon

The Georgia Tech account describes Shimon continuing seeded material and playing the result.
It supports a bounded claim about composition and performance by this robot in its configuration.
To establish who chose a later change to the composition method, instrument interface or
public practice, use evidence of that decision. When the human project team makes the choice
and Shimon plays the material, attribute those contributions to the respective participants.

#### MDPE.8:4.3 - A dance party

At a dance party, bodily regulation, movement, partnered coordination, phrase shaping and
event support can occur together. Evidence of a dancer’s particular turn can answer a
question about that turn. A project to improve it may instead need to examine coordination,
the figure method itself, floor organization, teaching or individual capability. Claims about the wider production
and recognition of a style need evidence from the relevant participants and occasions.

#### MDPE.8:4.4 - *The Call*

Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s project *The Call* includes a songbook, choir work, recordings, datasets, models, an
installation and rules for participation. A question about choir–model material, one about the recording or model
system, and one about the proposed participant practice each need a suitable method and evidence for the claim. The documented artifacts and exhibition
can answer what the project produced. Establishing a durable style requires evidence of later uptake and retention.

### MDPE.8:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question and use | A broad topic hides the working problem. | Name the finding, design or choice needed. For a decision, identify the choice and its authorized holder or the unresolved authority. |
| Subject | “The music” or “the dance” hides several subjects. | Identify the material, capability, method, performance, system, relation or cultural process the question concerns. |
| Proposal and occurrence | A brief, course, score or model is cited as proof of performance. | State what the proposal specifies. Use evidence of the event or its outcome for a claim about what occurred. |
| Performer and other contributors | The credited participant differs from the one that acted. | Name who did what and which instrument, software, record or venue contributed. Give the technical system or assignment when attribution depends on it. |
| Relation among scales | The order of a list is taken for a performance sequence. | Establish which actions occur together, which constitute the whole, which precede or enable another, and where capability is developed. |
| Alternatives and uncertainty | The first explanation obscures another that matters. | Compare any live accounts and give the supported answer. If no account can yet be formulated, identify the missing information. If several remain, identify what could distinguish them. |
| Result | Describing the material leaves the question unanswered. | Give the supported finding, design or available next action. Where the answer depends on missing evidence, identify the specific gap. |


### MDPE.8:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source line | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF E.10.ARCH, C.36.P, A.3.1, A.3.2, A.15.1, C.32.MWA and C.36 | Guidance for placing domain precision-restoration advice, recovering the subject of cultural wording, distinguishing methods, descriptions and work, comparing differently organized practice structures, and investigating cultural change. | Apply them to the music or dance work, participants and evidence relevant to the question. |
| [Renata Peçanha interview, Zoukology](https://zoukology.com/renata-history/) | Peçanha’s account links music, partner experiments, movement, teaching, choreography, criticism and continuity in her own practice. | Claims about sole origin, effectiveness or recognition across the field require independent evidence of the wider claim. |
| [Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, *The Call*, Serpentine](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | The project record identifies the choir work, songbook, recordings, dataset, model, installation and proposed participation. | The exhibition and its artifacts can be documented directly. A claim about a general method needs evidence beyond this project. For later retention, establish the relevant practice in the population and period claimed. |
| [Georgia Tech Shimon account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2017/06/13/robot-uses-deep-learning-and-big-data-write-and-play-its-own-music) | Evidence of the robot’s contribution to bounded composition and performance. | Attribute later project choices to the agent that made them. Use evidence from the relevant population for a claim about cultural continuation. |
| [Pavel Sobiray, Street Tango Concept](https://tangonuevo.ru/stc7eng) | The author’s proposed Street Tango Concept, exercises, teaching and participant reports document a bounded practice. | Use independent evidence for claims of superiority, sole origin or recognition across the field. For long-term retention, establish continued use during the period claimed. |

Reconsider the conclusions that depend on a changed source, assumption or receiving use.

### MDPE.8:7 - Relations

- MDPE.1 can use a suitable account of the subject, current conditions and any alternatives to frame a project. An existing brief can already supply that account.

- `MDPE.21` and `MDPE.24` become relevant when the question concerns style-production architecture or the
  identity of the whole that organizes a practice, including a question about its formation or continuity.
- MDPE.9, MDPE.10, MDPE.3, MDPE.11, MDPE.12 and MDPE.17 supply different methods for designing, developing capability, performing,
observing or transmitting music and dance. Use the contribution that the particular question needs.
- MDPE.14 can use the account of the subject, participating systems and
remaining alternatives when assessing or resolving a conflict in practice.
- MDPE.16 uses the subject, intended use and any material uncertainty to determine
which performance or development options are available or worth retaining.
- MDPE.18 can use the clarified subject to identify which sources, lineages, reconstructions
or gaps matter. The historical account relies on evidence about that history.
- Systems engineering can address a selected engineered system. FPF Core’s
method-development guidance can address a method. Bring the result back to the music
or dance work, its participants, its evidence and the question it must answer.


### MDPE.8:End

## MDPE.1 - Frame a Music-or-Dance Work, Practice, Style, or Medium Project

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance project-framing pattern

> **Public result:** one scale-bound Music-or-Dance project brief

### MDPE.1:0 - Use This When

Use this method to prepare or assess a project brief when “create”, “preserve” or “develop” could refer to different results. Before
committing people, equipment, a venue, money or publication effort, establish which result the project requires. Four common ambitions are to

- produce one artifact or performance occurrence;
- establish or change a repeatable performance practice;
- deliberately develop a style line across several variants and generations; or
- build or change a medium or support system through which participants
produce, learn, present, recognize or retain music or dance.

A concert can satisfy a commission for that event. To establish a repeatable practice, examine who can perform it again and under what conditions. A course can specify instruction, a platform can provide access, and a manifesto can state a proposed method. Claims about learned capability, development of a style or use of the method need evidence of those respective results.

The brief identifies the subject and scale, intended work and use, what must be preserved and
what may vary. Name the affected recognition, authority or participation conditions where the
project relies on them. For a proposal, identify how it could be realized and what would count
as meeting the brief. Preserve any conflict between commitments and explain what choice
it changes. A service that has already delivered a suitable brief can supply this result.
Use a direct commissioning, choreography, production, co-creation, event or systems
engineering method, or another direct method, when it already supplies the project basis that the work needs.

### MDPE.1:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

“Make a piece”, “launch a dance style”, “build an AI music practice”, “run a festival” and
“preserve the tradition” can name quite different commitments. Ask the participants what
result each expects, or use their existing agreement when it already settles the scope.

Four project subjects recur:

| Project subject | What the project changes | Evidence that begins to matter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Artifact or performance occurrence | Musical or movement material, or a bounded performance with its production. | For a promised artifact, inspect what was made. For a promised performance, establish what occurred. Check access or use when the commission includes them. |
| Performance practice | A repeatable method, performing capability, configuration or conditions for teaching and receiving it. | Determine who can perform representative work under the stated conditions, with the required continuity and variation. |
| Style-development line | How participants produce, recognize, select, transmit and retain variants, and how those results affect later production. | Assess whether the proposed arrangement supports these relations. For a claim about an actual change or subsequent uptake, use evidence of the relevant relations and population. |
| Medium or support system | An instrument, software, venue, platform, school, archive, event series, provider or another source of support. | Assess what it would enable in the proposed use. For a claim about actual provision, use or performance, examine the evidence for that claim and its assurance conditions. |

Several subjects can belong to the same project. Give each the result and success
conditions it needs, and link their briefs where one undertaking supplies another.

### MDPE.1:2 - Solution

Frame or assess the brief around the subject, result and use the project brief must cover. For a new commitment, identify what would justify it.

#### MDPE.1:2.1 - Select the subject and scale

Start with the question from MDPE.8 or a clear project question from another source. Identify the
primary subject of this brief. When it depends on other subjects, explain how their results contribute.

A festival project may change the system that produces one event while investigating whether its curation
and teaching support development of a style. Results from that event concern the specified
occasion. A claim about the whole series or the style needs evidence at the corresponding scale.

For an engineered system, use an existing suitable engineering result or obtain the one
the project still needs. The table locates the corresponding systems engineering methods.

| Engineering result the project needs | Direct Systems Engineering pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Which actual or intended System is the project System-of-Interest, and when that focus must reopen | `SYSE.1 — Choose and Reopen the Project System-of-Interest` |
| Which linked use and System concepts make the intended value and boundary testable | `SYSE.2 — Develop Linked Use and System Concepts` |
| Which functional organization, bearers and interfaces are supported, and what viable alternatives remain? | `SYSE.5 — Develop an Engineered System's Functional Organization and Bearer Alternatives` |
| Which architecture is selected and what evidence reopens it | `SYSE.6 — Decide and Reopen the Engineering Architecture` |
| Which recursive realization arrangement can create, integrate, qualify, operate, and change the System | `SYSE.3 — Plan the Next System-Realization Action (Recursive Realization Network)` |
| What assurance does the evidence support, and is any further challenge or condition for reconsideration needed? | `SYSE.4 — Decide Whether and How to Challenge an Engineering Claim` |

State what the engineered system is meant to enable in musical or
dance work, including any needed style distinction, performance
relation or cultural consequence. Use FPF Core’s general method-development
guidance when the project concerns a method or family of methods.

#### MDPE.1:2.2 - State the intended Work and first use

Describe who would use the changed subject, what they would do, for whom and by which method. This might be composing, choreographing,
practising, teaching, partnering, improvising, rehearsing, performing, listening, judging, curating, producing, presenting or archiving.
For an existing project, establish what its agreement requires and what participants have already done as needed for the question.

Name the performers, decision-makers and other contributors in ordinary terms. A musician or a software system
can perform an assigned part. An instrument, score, recording, venue or publication can support it. Where an
attribution depends on particular technical systems, roles, assignments or capabilities, identify them.

#### MDPE.1:2.3 - Separate proposal from realization

State what already exists and what the project proposes. A score can be the commissioned artifact and
prescribe a future performance. A lesson programme can specify teaching, and an architectural description
can specify a system. To claim the teaching, performance or operation took place, establish what happened.

For a project expected to realize a change, describe the work needed and the earliest suitable evidence that could show that
the result serves its intended performers and recipients. Use relevant existing observations
where their conditions match. A proposal can answer a design brief before that work takes place.

#### MDPE.1:2.4 - Choose preservation and variation

Identify what the project must preserve and what it may vary. Rhythm, timing, sound, movement
quality, partner response, form, improvisational freedom, instrument relations, participation,
social function, authorship, lineage or another characteristic may matter differently to different projects.

Holding one version fixed can prevent the variation a living practice requires. Broad variation
can also erase the distinction the project seeks to retain. Use MDPE.12 to examine an
observable distinction or MDPE.23 when a participant needs a capability for recognizing it.

Where preservation, variation, safety, access, visibility, cost, authorship, participation or continuity
involve consequential trade-offs or require incompatible commitments, identify the conflict, the people or systems affected, and the
choice it changes. Use the evidence or authority needed for the decision. State a disputed objective as
disputed. A supported assessment of the incompatibility can answer a question about the existing brief.

#### MDPE.1:2.5 - Name participants, affected Systems, and decision rights

Identify who contributes and who bears the effects where the brief depends on them, such as performers, learners,
teachers, curators, organizers, funders, publishers and judges. Establish authority for the particular decision.
A venue’s power to set its safety conditions and a dancer’s choice to take part have different holders.

If a change depends on permission, consent, funding, access, contest, refusal, exit, revision or stewardship,
identify the applicable agreement and whether it covers the proposed use. Use a sufficient existing permission
directly. Where authority or participation remains unsettled, state which part of the proposed work depends on it.

#### MDPE.1:2.6 - Set the recognition and reopen boundary

When recognition matters to the brief, specify who is expected to distinguish or use the result, under which conditions
and what could show whether they do so or the brief needs to change. A label, press notice, official listing or favourable response can document
that particular occurrence. A claim about recognition by other participants needs evidence from the intended use.

The brief is sufficient when the person using it can identify what is promised, what would satisfy it and any specific
limit. An authorized decision-maker can then make or decline the commitment. Reconsider the affected part if representative
work, participant response, feasibility, authority, safety, recognition, cost or another relied-on condition changes.

### MDPE.1:3 - First Useful Result

For example, a project brief can give the following information where the project needs it.

> - **Project question or commitment:** [what the brief must settle].
> - **Primary subject and scale:** [artifact or occurrence / performance practice / style-development line /
>   medium or support System].
> - **Intended Work and use:** [who does what, using which domain Method, and for whom].
> - **Linked subjects:** [only those whose result is used, with the relation stated].
> - **Existing and proposed:** [what is already available and what the project could bring about].
> - **Preserve / vary:** [domain distinctions and allowed variation].
> - **Conflict or unresolved choice:** [any material trade-off or incompatible commitments, who or what is affected and what information or authority could resolve the choice].
> - **Recognition:** [who needs to distinguish or use the result and under which conditions].
> - **Participants and decision rights:** [deciding Agent, affected Agents or Systems, and relied-on authority or
>   permission].
> - **Realization and assessment:** [the work that would produce the result and the earliest suitable evidence that can establish
>   whether it serves the intended use].
> - **Limit or reconsideration:** [what the brief settles and any condition that would change the assessment].

Use the brief for the question it answers and to guide any commissioned work. For a claim about an outcome, examine the evidence for that outcome.

### MDPE.1:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.1:4.1 - A filled brief for a local Zouk trial

In this constructed example, a local school is deciding whether to commit six weeks of teacher time and one
social event to a changed partnered practice. Its brief is:

> - **Project decision:** fund and run one bounded class-and-social trial, or keep the present course unchanged.
> - **Primary subject and scale:** one repeatable partnered-performance practice at this
>   local school. The proposed trial concerns that practice with the named participants.
> - **Intended Work and use:** teachers use embodied and partnered exercises; dancers then improvise with
>   unfamiliar partners to varied music at the local social event.
> - **Linked subjects:** the teaching method and the event arrangement
>   supply different conditions for the partnered practice trial.
> - **Existing and proposed:** current learners reproduce taught sequences with familiar partners; the proposal
>   introduces rotating-partner cue–response tasks, varied music, and supervised social-floor trials.
> - **Preserve / vary:** preserve partner-readable response, safety, balance, and the intended timing distinction;
>   vary figures, partners, music, and phrase choices.
> - **Conflict or unresolved live choice:** a filmed showcase rewards fixed camera-legible choreography, while
>   the stated project needs unfamiliar-partner social transfer. That fixed-choreography showcase would not test
>   transfer to unfamiliar partners in social improvisation. The school selects social transfer for this
>   commitment and leaves a showcase as a separate later project.
> - **Recognition:** participating partners need to distinguish and act on the cue
>   during social dancing. The trial examines their response under those conditions.
> - **Participants and rights:** the two teachers decide on the local teaching trial. Dancers
>   give or withhold consent and may leave an exercise. The venue sets its safety conditions.
> - **Planned trial:** teachers would run the changed classes and observe unfamiliar pairs
>   across two music conditions for readable response, balance loss, recovery and refusals.
> - **Stop or reconsider:** stop work under unsafe conditions or without the required consent. Reconsider
>   the teaching choice if transfer fails across unfamiliar partners or the timing distinction disappears.

Without the conflict in view, the team would have funded a fixed showcase and treated its results as
evidence of social transfer. The agreed brief instead selects the unfamiliar-partner trial. What
happens in that trial and what the wider Zouk population later takes up require their own evidence.

Suppose the first class trial yields the observation in MDPE.8:4.1. The learner maintains
balance but continues a taught sequence when an unfamiliar partner pauses. The teachers revise
the planned exercise within the agreed class time. They simplify the figure choices and focus
on noticing the cue and choosing a continuation. The revised plan varies one partner or music
condition at a time when that comparison can distinguish the source of the difficulty.

The local practice and unfamiliar-partner use remain the subject and
aim. Consent, venue rules and six weeks of teacher time remain
conditions of the brief. Within them, the teachers select the
revised task and its planned comparison. If the required instruction or extra
time is unavailable, they can return the narrower proposal for a
funding or scope decision and retain what the first trial established.

#### MDPE.1:4.2 - *The Call*

*The Call* combines a songbook, singing exercises, choirs, recordings, datasets, AI models,
exhibition equipment and proposed rules for participation. A brief can distinguish musical material
and performance, a choir–model medium and a participant practice. They can belong to one project
while needing different modes of realization or assessment. The recordings and installation are among the project’s outputs. They
can be examined for the claims they bear on. Use evidence of later participation for claims about retained practice.

#### MDPE.1:4.3 - Street Tango

The Street Tango source publishes concepts, exercises and a lesson programme, and reports
teaching and participant experience. These support an account of the creator’s proposal
and bounded existing practice. A brief can state what the creator can decide and realize
locally. Wider recognition, superiority, sole origin and longer-term retention require
grounds for the participants, population and period of each claim.

#### MDPE.1:4.4 - A commissioned work

For one commissioned musical work, the existing commissioning method may already settle the parties,
artistic objectives, development events, deliverables, costs and rights. Use its result directly. Apply
MDPE.1 if an unresolved question about the work, a repeatable practice or a new medium affects the project.

### MDPE.1:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary subject | A project funds a different subject or scale from the one it needs. | Identify which artifact or occurrence, practice, style-development line, medium or support system the brief must address. |
| Linked subjects retain their identities | One subject’s result is used to approve a different subject. | State each result and the relation by which another part of the project uses it. |
| Proposal and realization | The brief is cited as evidence that its proposal has been implemented. | State what it specifies and use the appropriate evidence for any claimed delivery or use. |
| Preservation and variation are explicit | The project either freezes a practice or erases its distinction. | State what must survive and what may change for the receiving use. |
| Material conflict | Incompatible commitments appear as one agreed objective. | Identify the incompatibility or trade-off and its effects. If resolution is required, use the available evidence and authority or identify what is missing. |
| Recognition | A promotional mention is treated as recognition by the intended audience. | Identify what the relevant participants need to distinguish, the conditions and the observations that bear on the claim. |
| Ability and authority | A provider’s technical or financial contribution is taken as permission for another participant’s work. | Establish the right, agreement, participation or consent required for the particular decision and the arrangements for refusal or revision. |


### MDPE.1:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Practice or source line | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [American Composers Forum, *Anatomy of a Commission* and Sample Deal Memo](https://composersforum.org/anatomy-of-a-commission) | Direct commissioning practice for a selected new concert work, including deliverables, costs and rights. | Adapt the agreement to the commission. A project about a repeatable practice or a medium needs its own frame. |
| [Common Ground Manual 2024](https://fabric.dance/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Common-Ground-Manual-2024.pdf) | A method for participatory dance co-creation by people, with shared direction, participant voice, named contributions, access, discussion and revision. | Use those arrangements where the participants and project have the corresponding relationship. For another project, apply the participation conditions its work requires. |
| [Renata Peçanha interview, Zoukology](https://zoukology.com/renata-history/) | A practitioner account of deliberate practice change and continuity. | Use independent evidence for wider origin, prevalence, recognition or effectiveness claims. |
| [Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, *The Call*, Serpentine](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | A project connecting a medium and participant practice, including actual artifacts and proposed uses. | General claims about AI art and claims of later retention need evidence relevant to their scope and time. |
| [Pavel Sobiray, Street Tango Concept](https://tangonuevo.ru/stc7eng) | A practice design and reports of teaching and participant experience in its author’s setting. | Wider recognition, superiority or long-term retention requires evidence for the population and period claimed. |

The four subjects above distinguish commitments that need different evidence. Use a direct method
if it settles the project question at lower cost. Use an omitted subject for this project if it changes the commitment. Reconsider the four-part distinction when
evidence of repeated use establishes an independent recurring subject that the distinction misses.

### MDPE.1:7 - Relations

- MDPE.8 can help clarify the subject. Begin directly with a sufficient existing project question when one is available.
- `MDPE.21` supplies a style-production and reproduction architecture when that is the selected subject.
- MDPE.24 can identify the organization that carried a practice at a given time. A brief can also propose a new organization and specify the evidence
  that would establish its formation.
- `MDPE.9`, `MDPE.10`, `MDPE.3`, `MDPE.5`, `MDPE.12`, and `MDPE.23` supply different realization and test results.
- For an engineered medium or support System, select the needed Systems Engineering contribution in
  [§2.1](#mdpe121---select-the-subject-and-scale).
- Use FPF Core’s method-development guidance for recovery, construction, composition, support,
trial or revision of a method. Bring the relevant result back to the artistic and embodied
practice, recognition, style development or cultural question the project needs to address.

### MDPE.1:End

## MDPE.21 - Design How a Music-or-Dance Style Is Produced and Reproduced

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance style-development architecture pattern

> **Public result:** a justified local arrangement for producing and reproducing the intended style distinctions, or a finding about an arrangement under review. Specify a representative test when a consequential question remains and the test is worthwhile.

### MDPE.21:0 - Use This When

Use this method when a project needs to establish how a musical or dance distinction could recur under the
intended conditions. A distinction can appear in a manifesto, choreography, recording, tool, class or
showcase while training, instruments, partner habits, curation or circulation still favour the preceding
practice. The question can also concern how an existing arrangement already sustains the desired recurrence.

A repeatable style depends on relations among the people, methods, tools and arrangements
involved. A dancer may be able to execute a movement that partners cannot read. A composer’s new
rhythmic language may exceed available notation or rehearsal methods. A class can transmit
a phrase while an event, camera, judge or platform selects another quality. A recording
may circulate while its recipients still lack what they need to reconstruct the
method and perform it. Examine the relation on which the intended recurrence depends.

The first useful result can explain how the local arrangement supported recurrence or where it fell short. For a proposed change, identify
the relation to retain or change and the grounds for that choice. An existing arrangement may suffice. Consider a
representative test when a consequential condition remains unestablished and the observation is worth obtaining.

When teaching, competition and social participation benefit separately but conflict in shared use, see
[MDPE.25 - Renew a Shared Music or Dance Practice](#mdpe25---renew-a-shared-music-or-dance-practice) for changes to provision,
learning, recognition and resource allocation. [MDPE.Application:5.2](#mdpeapplication52---recover-the-subject-of-a-music-or-movement-claim)
identifies the subject of an ambiguous music or movement claim, and [MDPE.Application:5.3](#mdpeapplication53---connect-style-method-structure-and-acquisition)
distinguishes style structure, recovery of its description and what a performer has learned.

Use the relevant analysis, composition, choreography, performance, production or historical method
to describe a style, classify a genre, write its history or create one work when that is the
whole task. Enter here when the way an arrangement supports recurrence is itself in question.

### MDPE.21:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

A project can start from a trait, a creator, an artifact or an institution. Each starting point can leave an important relation open.

- **Trait.** Rhythm, timbre, movement vocabulary, posture, texture, form or costume can
specify the intended distinction. Establish how later performers can reproduce or vary it.
- **Creator.** A performer or another creator can originate material, alone or with others. A manifesto can state a proposal and a
tool can contribute to its realization. Use evidence of later participants’ work to establish what they took up. For a decision, establish who can make it.
- **Artifact.** A track, video, score, choreography, dataset or tutorial can make material
available. Transmission and retention depend on what other participants received, enacted and kept.
- **Institution.** A class, festival, platform, archive or competition can support the practice.
Identify what its participants do or what its proposed arrangement would enable.

Follow the contribution into later work. Which relations allow performers, teachers, listeners,
dancers, partners, producers, curators or technical systems to produce or recognize the distinction
under changed conditions? Existing representative performance may already show the answer.

Here a style is a reproducible cultural distinction or family of
distinctions. Identify the methods, performances, capabilities, systems,
memories and relations on which that reproduction depends in the project.

### MDPE.21:2 - Solution

Design or assess the local arrangement that makes the intended distinctions possible in later production, performance,
recognition, selection, transmission or recovery. Several of these processes can occur together in a living practice.

#### MDPE.21:2.1 - Begin with a representative recurrence

Identify a result that should recur beyond an initial example, or a recurrence the inquiry asks you to explain. Examples include the following.

- dancers can use a changed partnering and timing practice with unfamiliar partners at a social event;
- musicians can learn, rehearse, vary, and perform a rhythmic or timbral language beyond the founding ensemble;
- teachers can develop capability without reducing the style to copied figures or one recorded phrase;
- listeners, partners, judges, curators, or sensing Systems can discriminate a relied-on difference under the
  conditions where their response changes later Work.

Identify what persisted in the recurrence being examined, or what should persist and what variation is valuable in the proposed practice. If the target is unclear, use an existing brief
or MDPE.1 to clarify it. A commission for one work can be completed by its direct production method.

#### MDPE.21:2.2 - Recover the current reproduction architecture

Trace an observed performance to the conditions that made it possible and to the conditions for reuse. For a design,
use a representative proposed performance and state the premises. Examine the relations relevant to the question.

| Architecture concern | Practical question |
| --- | --- |
| Variant production | How do composing, choreographing, improvising, arranging, rehearsing or using a tool produce alternatives that differ for the intended practice? |
| Performing capability | Which bodily, perceptual, instrumental, ensemble, partnering, or technical capabilities must function during representative Work? |
| Performing configuration | Which Agents, instruments, software, spaces, cues, permissions, and signal, contact, access, control, timing, or coordination relations must obtain together? |
| Recognition | Who or what must distinguish the feature, under what conditions, and what observation bears on that capability? |
| Selection and amplification | Which teaching, repertoire, programming, judging, peer-copying, audience, market, or platform relations make some variants more likely to recur? |
| Transmission and reconstruction | How can another performer recover the method from a lesson, imitation, notation, recording, model, example or joint practice and enact or adapt it in representative work? |
| Memory and recurrence | Which embodied capability, repertoire, archive, curriculum, instrument setting, venue practice, or recurring event makes later recovery possible? |
| Supporting environment | Which schools, ensembles, venues, platforms, instruments, software, providers, archives, or event series enable or constrain the other relations? |

In one dance, bodily coordination, a response to a partner, execution of a figure, use of a
style and participation in an event can coincide. Some of these actions also constitute a
contribution to a continuing practice. In music, fingering, phrasing, ensemble coordination,
presentation and contribution to a repertoire can likewise operate at different scales in
one performance. Establish the relevant part–whole relation where the claim depends on it.

Use a suitable systems engineering result when a question concerns an instrument, venue, school, platform, archive
or other engineered system. When changing or assessing a composition,
training, teaching, rehearsal, recognition or transmission method, use FPF
Core’s method-development guidance. In either case, identify the music or
dance performance and cultural relations the supplied result needs to support.

#### MDPE.21:2.3 - Find what currently reproduces the predecessor

Compare the recurrence in question with relevant observations or, for a design, with the conditions the arrangement would provide. Where the intended distinction is missing, look for a
relation that could account for what happened. The following cases illustrate different possibilities.

- candidate generation changes, but training and rehearsal still develop the predecessor's capability;
- performers can enact the distinction, but partners, listeners, teachers, or judges cannot recognize it;
- a workshop produces local success, but receiving Agents cannot reconstruct the practice elsewhere;
- a platform amplifies camera-ready hooks while the project needs partner response, long form, or live musical
  variation;
- an archive retains records while embodied capability, instruments, venues, or teaching Methods disappear;
- one school stabilizes a useful practice but its authority, access, or incentives suppress valuable variants.

Identify the relation at issue. State its observed consequences or what the design predicts under its stated conditions. A claim that the relation caused the outcome needs grounds for that attribution.

#### MDPE.21:2.4 - Compare consequential architecture candidates

When a comparison is needed, compare materially different arrangements that bear on the question, including the current one where relevant. Develop another candidate when its possible contribution could change the conclusion. If an option cannot meet a required condition, use that finding in the comparison. The following directions can help locate alternatives.

| Candidate emphasis | Change considered | What it may reveal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capability-first | Change drills, embodied correction, listening practice, rehearsal, or ensemble training. | Whether performers can enact the distinction in representative Work. |
| Recognition-first | Change examples, comparison tasks, partner cues, judging or curation, and how learner, partner, listener, judge, or curator observations are used in later teaching or selection. | Whether a relied-on Agent can discriminate the distinction and use that observation in the next Work. |
| Transmission-first | Change teaching, joint practice, notation, demonstrations, recordings, or reconstruction tasks. | Whether another Agent can reproduce and adapt the practice rather than copy one artifact. |
| Circulation-and-memory-first | Change event recurrence, repertoire, archives, publishing form, access, or retrieval. | Whether later Work can recover the practice under changed people, places, or media. |
| Medium-first | Change instrument, software, camera arrangement, platform, venue, or production System. | Whether the support System enables the intended Work instead of selecting another result. |
| Coupled change | Change two or more tightly linked relations whose separate repair would fail. | Whether the joint change resolves a conflict that neither local repair can resolve alone. |

Describe the proposed arrangement or the existing one under review. Identify the people, systems and methods
involved, and the signal, contact, access, teaching, observation or selection relations it depends on. For a
change, identify the required authority or consent, expected effect and what evidence could count against it.

#### MDPE.21:2.5 - Select a bounded change and any needed test

For a choice, compare the arrangements on their expected contribution to recurrence, feasibility and full cost, including any relations that must change together.
A project can retain its existing arrangement or choose a local change in a class, tool, event, repertoire, recording practice, platform feature
or recognition task. Claims about wider recognition, selection, transmission or retention depend on evidence of what the relevant population did in the period at issue.

Use available evidence for the recurrence under the conditions claimed. When a consequential condition is still open, consider an obtainable representative test whose expected contribution warrants its cost. It might vary a performer, partner, ensemble, teacher, venue, instrument, repertoire item, audience, medium or interval. Identify the condition the evidence must cover, what response and unwanted effects to observe, and how the result would inform the question or decision.

The result can be a justified arrangement, a finding about an existing one, or a scoped limitation. Include a proposed test when it is needed and worth conducting. An authorized change or test can use MDPE.15 or the relevant direct method. For a claim about an actual intervention, recurrence or wider uptake, identify what happened at the appropriate time and scale.

### MDPE.21:3 - First Useful Result

A compact account can record the result or support a local decision.

> - **Recurrence:** [the recurrence being examined or the work that should remain possible beyond the first example].
> - **Continuity and variation:** [what remained recognizable or varied, or the continuity and variation the design requires].
> - **Reproduction of the practice:** [the methods, participants, systems and relations that support reproduction in the period being examined].
> - **Condition affecting recurrence:** [what supports or interferes with the intended difference, and on what evidence].
> - **Alternatives:** [any arrangements that need comparison, including the existing one where relevant].
> - **Arrangement:** [what the assessment established or what is proposed or selected. For a change, name the relations involved and any authority required].
> - **Effect on performance:** [what the evidence establishes or what the arrangement is expected to make possible under the stated conditions].
> - **Grounds and any proposed test:** [the available evidence and, if a consequential condition remains open, any worthwhile representative observation that could resolve it].
> - **Scope:** [the population, practice and time covered, and any question about causal effect or later uptake that remains].
> - **Completion or reconsideration:** [the supported answer and any changed condition that would affect it].

The account can establish which arrangement the project can use or what an existing arrangement
supported. Establish a past intervention and later cultural retention from the evidence for each.

### MDPE.21:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.21:4.1 - Selecting an architecture for local Zouk recurrence

In a constructed case, a local Zouk project wants unfamiliar partners to reproduce a timing and partner-response
distinction during social dancing. The present classes teach fixed sequences with familiar partners,
and the event rewards a polished showcase. The following proposals would change different relations.

| Candidate architecture | Contributions and participants | Proposed or observed relations relevant to recurrence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choreography and showcase | A choreographer would fix the phrases, teachers would teach them, familiar pairs would rehearse, and the event and camera would present the performance. | In this unselected proposal, teachers would use a phrase description or video, familiar partners would rehearse together, and selectors would use camera-facing observations to choose showcase material. |
| Partnered recurrence | The two teachers would use capability and cue-response tasks, dancers would rotate partners and music, and observers would follow supervised social dancing. | The selected trial requires teachers to use the tasks, rotating pairs to perform under altered conditions and observers to report what occurs. The project proposes that teachers use those reports for later revisions. |

The project selects the partnered-recurrence proposal for the six-week teaching trial and
supervised social event because its question concerns unfamiliar partners. Observers are
to note readable responses, balance, recovery, refusal and whether the timing survives.
Their results can support a bounded statement about local performance and show where cueing
or capability needs attention. To attribute a result to a specific part of the arrangement,
or to claim wider recognition or retention, use evidence for that further claim.


The selected trial still admits two ways to run one 120-minute session. In this constructed
case, twelve consenting participants, two teachers and one room are available. The room
safely accommodates two small groups using the same music. Each teacher has 20 paid
minutes of preparation and 120 minutes in class, for a total of 2 × (20 + 120) = 280
teacher-minutes. Both already have the cue-response exercises and observation method.

| Viable arrangement | Relations and whole-session allocation | Gain and accepted loss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short clinic followed by extended shared practice | One teacher would lead the cue task while the other observes, then both would support rotating-partner practice. The 120 minutes comprise 20 for setup and warm-up, 20 for cue work, 60 for shared practice, 10 for review and 10 for changeovers. | More receiving interaction with changed partners, less protected time for examining an individual difficulty in responding to a cue. |
| Two teaching stations followed by a receiving attempt | Groups would rotate between cue-response work and guided improvisation, each with one teacher, then join the receiving attempt. The 120 minutes comprise 20 for setup and warm-up, two station blocks of 35, 10 for the receiving attempt, 10 for review and 10 for changeovers. | More individual feedback and a controlled return to the whole interaction, with 10 minutes of final shared practice and more coordination. |

Both arrangements fit the stated room and teacher time and address unfamiliar-partner recurrence.
The school initially chooses the short clinic. Its priority is more receiving practice, and
the teachers expect the cue task to fit the 20-minute block. The school accepts less protected
feedback time and keeps the station arrangement available. It will reconsider the choice if
classroom recovery depends on teacher prompts absent from social use. Consent and the six-week
limit still apply. Assess effectiveness from suitable evidence of what the arrangement contributes to the intended performance.

Suppose learners recover the movement when the teacher prompts them but repeatedly continue the
memorized sequence after an unfamiliar partner’s cue. This shows what they did with the prompt
and what happened in the receiving interaction. The teachers choose the two stations for the next
session. One can investigate recognition and response execution while the other preserves partnered
use. That choice spends more time on feedback and gives up 50 minutes of final shared practice.
The target, available staff, common music and consent and safety conditions still apply.

An observation with the intended partner cue can establish whether learners give the needed response under that
condition. If existing evidence already supports that use, the longer shared-practice arrangement remains an
option. If cue conventions conflict or a teacher becomes unavailable, assess what can be done under the changed
condition. A prompted performance remains evidence for its own conditions. The constructed comparison informs
a local teaching choice. It cannot isolate a population effect of one among several simultaneous changes.

#### MDPE.21:4.2 - Choreo-camps and short-video selection

Consider a constructed travelling-workshop network linking teachers, cities, learners, cameras, archives,
reputation and later bookings. Its selection arrangements could favour front-facing phrases,
synchronization, short hooks and camera-legible detail even where teachers describe a broader practice.

The project might change the camera and publication arrangements, change the way teachers use observations of learners, or change
both along with the conditions for later practice outside the group. Use suitable evidence about receiving dancers’ ability to
learn, vary and perform the intended qualities in another class or event, and about what the publication arrangement selects.
If those conditions remain open, assess whether a representative trial is worth its cost. View counts can describe circulation.

#### MDPE.21:4.3 - *The Call* as a medium-and-practice case

The Call connects a songbook, singing exercises, choirs, recordings, datasets, AI models, exhibition
equipment and proposed participation. The produced works can be studied where they are accessible. A claim about
recurrence concerns the relations that let other participants perform or adapt the practice.

A proposal could emphasize choir capability, model and dataset interaction, teaching for a receiving group, or exhibition circulation
and memory. To assess recurrence, examine whether another suitably configured group can learn, adapt and perform the intended musical
relations. Use an adequate existing observation or a warranted representative test. Recordings, publicity and a successful installation
bear on the work produced and its presentation. For later recognition or retention, examine the relevant participants over time.

#### MDPE.21:4.4 - One commissioned work

For a commission limited to one composition, choreography, recording or performance, use
the direct domain and project methods. Use style-development architecture when the intended
result includes reproduction across variants, performers, conditions or generations.

### MDPE.21:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intended recurrence | A new label or list of traits leaves the intended use unclear. | Identify what later performers or recipients should be able to perform, recognize, transmit or recover. |
| Current reproduction | A proposed diagram is treated as a history of the practice. | Use evidence from a representative occurrence for its work, capability, systems and enabling relations. State a design comparison under its premises. |
| Concurrent concerns | Generation, training, performance, recognition and memory are put into an unsupported sequence. | Identify what occurs together, what forms part of a larger action, and which temporal dependencies the chosen method requires. |
| Alternatives | A candidate is chosen without considering an available arrangement that would change the comparison. | Include relevant alternatives and retention where feasible. Develop another candidate when its possible contribution could change the answer. |
| Authority and action | A proposal attributes a local decision to an entire culture, market or platform. | For a proposed change, identify who could decide, the work, system or method affected, and the signal, access, contact, participation, observation or selection relation on which it depends. |
| Evidence for recurrence | An initial demonstration or publication is presented as recurrence under a later condition. | Use evidence that covers the relevant later performance, recognition or recovery. If a consequential condition remains open, state the limit and consider what an obtainable, worthwhile comparison could establish. |
| Local and wider claims | A local authorization or performance is taken as a population’s selection. | State which local work was proposed or performed. For wider transmission, recognition, selection or retention, establish the relevant activity in that population. |


### MDPE.21:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source or practice line | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [FPF `C.36 — Cultural Evolution and Cultural-Evolution Engineering`](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#c36---cultural-evolution-and-cultural-evolution-engineering) | General distinctions between a local intervention and distributed generation, transmission, recognition, selection, retention and loss. | Use music and dance sources for the domain methods, cases and representative evidence. |
| Music-and-Dance eco-evo-devo synthesis (unpublished source note) | Hypotheses and cases concerning development, ecology, recognition, selection, memory, conflict and the formation of new practice wholes. | Use evidence of the relevant practice for claims about prevalence or whether an arrangement works. |
| [Vanchurin et al., *Toward a theory of evolution as multilevel learning*](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2120037119) | A model of learning-like dynamics across scales and effects from higher to lower scales. | Applying the model to cultural or engineering work is a hypothesis whose suitability must be established for the proposed use. |
| [Mauch et al., *The evolution of popular music: USA 1960–2010*](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.150081) | A method for classifying styles from audio features at scale, applied to harmonic and timbral change in 17,094 songs from the US Billboard Hot 100 between 1960 and 2010. | Establish how a particular practice is produced, taught, performed, recognized or retained from evidence about that practice. |
| [Urban Dance Showcase information](https://www.urbandance.eu/show/infos/) | The provider describes a connection between camp participation and a showcase event. | Its undated description supports that account. Current prices and dates, the reach of a travelling network, video-related effects and provider effectiveness need their own evidence. Section 4.2 is a constructed case. |
| [Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, *The Call*, Serpentine](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | The project documents choir, model, dataset, recording, exhibition and participation arrangements. | A general AI-music method or durable cultural uptake requires grounds for that wider claim. |

Use the concerns that affect the question. Reconsider an arrangement when changed conditions defeat a premise or a domain method offers a better way to obtain or assess the intended recurrence.

### MDPE.21:7 - Relations

- `MDPE.8` identifies the subject and the question about its practice or change; `MDPE.1` frames the project scale.
- `MDPE.9`, `MDPE.10`, and `MDPE.3` supply candidate, capability, and performing-configuration results when
  their results bear on the arrangement being examined or designed.
- `MDPE.11`, `MDPE.5`, `MDPE.12`, `MDPE.23`, and `MDPE.13` keep enactment, occurrence, observation, recognition
  capability, and recognition-and-selection arrangements separate.
- `MDPE.6`, `MDPE.17`, `MDPE.18`, and `MDPE.19` address receiving use, transmission, usable memory, and continued
  reproduction.
- MDPE.22 addresses an enabling environment or a change in it, MDPE.14 a conflict between practical aims, MDPE.16 the availability of alternatives, MDPE.20 a forecast or comparison of trajectories, and MDPE.24 which whole carries the practice or whether a different whole formed. Use each result for the question it answers.
- Use applicable systems engineering results for an engineered system and FPF Core’s method-development guidance for a method.

### MDPE.21:End

## MDPE.24 - Decide Whether a Music-or-Dance Practice Has Formed a New Whole

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance whole-reidentification pattern

> **Public result:** a finding about which whole carries the claim, including what can be established about its formation or continuity. A project can also obtain a recommendation or an authorized decision about retaining or changing its boundary.

### MDPE.24:0 - Use This When

Use this method when you need to identify the whole that organizes a school, scene, camp network, event circuit,
platform practice, canon, genre or style, or determine whether a different whole formed. You might be asking which
organization operated at a given time or what a project should engineer, fund, maintain, measure or govern and where its responsibility lies.

A teacher can attract new pupils, an archive can preserve a repertoire and a recommendation
algorithm can change which phrases people see. Each can influence an existing practice.
A network may also acquire a continuing organization of its own. For example, shared
selection and teaching across cities might preserve repertoire through teacher
turnover and change what local dancers train. Establish the organization and effects
the claim relies on before choosing the practice or the network as its subject.

For the claim and period in question, the evidence can establish that

- the existing whole still carries the claim, with any relevant change in a participant or relation identified,
- an identifiable whole carries the claim, with its formation or transition from a prior arrangement dated when the evidence supports that further finding, or
- a required condition fails or remains undetermined. Report what this rules out or what information would distinguish the remaining possibilities.

For teaching difficulty, a skill grade, a change of analytical scale or a step in a Method, use the corresponding learning,
capability, architecture, part–whole or unfolding method. Ask about a new whole only if its actual organization matters.

### MDPE.24:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

A named practice can have followers, its own vocabulary, classes, media coverage and a recognizable
appearance while still drawing its teachers and selection rules from an older scene. A producer
can run successive festival editions. A platform can amplify a dance phrase. A canon can guide
performers as a body of knowledge they use. Each case has an identifiable participant, source or
relation whose influence can be examined before attributing it to a distinct acting organization.

A mistaken boundary can have either consequence.

1. **Premature enlargement.** The project invents governance, measures, maintenance, ownership, or causal powers
   for a “new level” that is only a label, a local system-role kind, a classification under that kind, an analytical grouping, or an influential participant.
2. **Missed reidentification.** The project continues optimizing isolated classes, artifacts, or events although a
   persistent network now has its own architecture, constraints, risks, memory, and recurring Work.

Ask which whole carried or would carry the capability, responsibility or other property the claim concerns.

### MDPE.24:2 - Solution

Ask which whole the claim concerns and whether a prior whole has been identified for comparison. With an established prior whole, examine two explanations.

- **Existing whole.** Changes in participants, capabilities, Methods, measurements, media, selection or architecture can account for the observed difference
  while the previously identified whole retains its identity.
- **Different whole.** The claim depends on a boundary, architecture, capability, continuity, effect or responsibility that requires
  an independently identifiable whole.

Use `B.2` to test whether the prior whole suffices. If a different whole is required, establish its construction and kind under `A.1` and explain why the prior whole cannot carry this claim.
For a first recognition, apply A.1 and the kind criterion to the relations already in place. To establish first formation, also recover the events that brought those relations into being. To establish a transition, recover the prior identity and the change. Report how far the available facts take the particular claim.

#### MDPE.24:2.1 - State the claim and any project consequence

Name the claim that would change, and any project decision that depends on it. For example, the difference can affect

- whether to engineer one festival edition or an enduring festival-series System;
- whether to improve one school or work on a teaching-and-performance network spanning schools;
- whether to tune one publication channel or address a platform-mediated dance practice with its own memory and
  trend dynamics;
- whether to preserve individual records or maintain a living repertoire-and-performance whole;
- whether responsibility and assurance stay with local providers or must also address a separately identified
  coordinating System.

If the same whole suffices for the work, measure, authority and boundary under consideration, the project can continue on that basis. A separate historical question may still require identifying which organization existed.


#### MDPE.24:2.2 - Identify the candidate and any prior whole

Identify the candidate. For comparison with a prior whole, establish that whole’s identity through change, its parts and relevant participants.
If a transition matters and those grounds are disputed, compare the proposed identity rules and their consequences. A genre, scene, school or
platform name can help locate it. Establish what the name denotes and what holds that entity together.

For a choreo-camp, compare the wider commercial-dance scene with a proposed cross-city network.
Recurring provision, teaching, migration and publication might link providers, teachers and learners
as constituents, customers or other participants. Establish which relations form the network. For
a festival, an existing producer might organize one edition. A continuing series organization
may have different operations, commitments and an identity that persists between editions.

Changing the scale of a description can reveal a pattern in many lower-level states.
To identify a whole, establish the actual constituents, the relations through which
they compose it, the other construction conditions in `A.1` and the criterion for
its proposed kind. A macrovariable or a different view can guide that investigation.

#### MDPE.24:2.3 - Look for Music-and-Dance whole-making relations

Select observations that bear on the claim. For a comparison with a prior whole, look for facts that distinguish the two explanations. Use
adequate existing evidence, including a qualified finding about the construction or its
kind. To identify a whole in §2.5, establish the full A.1 construction and apply the separate criterion for
the kind. The table below suggests observations for particular field claims. A scheduling
organization can exist without selecting musical variants. A claim that it preserves
a repertoire through teacher turnover does require evidence of that continuity.

| Probe | Music-or-Dance observation that could matter |
| --- | --- |
| Boundary | Participation, repertoire, performance, teaching, publication, or access relations distinguish the candidate from neighboring practices. |
| Constitutive relations | Establish which coordination, supervision, commitment, exchange, teaching, performance or mediation relations actually organize the constituents into this candidate. Identify external participants and suppliers where the distinction matters. |
| States at this scale | The candidate can be in materially different states such as expanding, fragmenting, canonizing, losing capability, changing repertoire, or changing circulation. |
| Memory | A repertoire, teaching lineage, curriculum, archive, instrument setup or handover can support recovery of material or the practice after turnover. For a claim about actual recovery, identify who used it, in what work, and what was recovered. |
| Transitions | Identify the candidate’s states and what changed between them. Use individual performances or publications as evidence where they bear on that change. |
| Recognition and selection | Variants, teachers, performers, works, or Methods are amplified, suppressed, retained, or dropped through relations that obtain at the candidate boundary. |
| Downward effect | The candidate changes what performers train, what creators make, what teachers teach, what partners expect, or what events and media present. |
| Persistence and identity | The candidate remains identifiable across turnover of individual Agents, artifacts, events, venues, or trends under a stated reidentification rule. |
| Temporal scale | Compare the duration of the candidate’s states or memory with the lower-level work relevant to the claim. Establish the times on which a conclusion about persistence depends. |
| Larger-assembly compatibility | Identify a rule by which a larger scene, discipline, organization or cultural ecology could integrate the candidate. Establish whether its boundary, interfaces and identity can satisfy that rule. |

If an assignment is offered as evidence of continuity, use `A.2.1` to identify its kind, the relation it
establishes, the participants and its extent. Examine whether the work performed, a maintained result or
another contribution supported continuity or made later recovery possible. To report actual use or recovery, establish
what happened. An assignment or a retained configuration may already settle what was assigned or retained.

A popular name may cover several unconnected practices. An archive may retain a phrase after local
performance has ceased. Organizations may continue exchanging performers while keeping separate
operations. A platform may influence selection while the artists who use it sustain the practice.
Each finding identifies a different relation and directs attention to a different possible subject.

#### MDPE.24:2.4 - Try the existing-whole explanation

When a prior whole is identified, ask whether a change within it explains the finding under its identity rule. For example,

- a performer or teacher developed a new capability;
- a Method or repertoire changed while the practice remained the same whole;
- an event series added a provider, venue, or publication System;
- a camera, judge, recommender, or market relation changed visibility or selection;
- a new archive or curriculum improved memory;
- measurement or recognition became more discriminating;
- an architecture view omitted an already existing relation.

When one of these explanations supports the claim, retain the existing whole. If a change is
needed and commissioned, address the relevant system, Method, capability, memory or other
relation. The novelty or importance of a change alone says little about the identity of the whole.

#### MDPE.24:2.5 - Establish which whole carries the claim

For a first identification, or when the existing whole cannot carry the claim, establish all six construction conditions of `A.1`
and the separate criterion for the candidate’s kind. Use the evidence for that candidate to
explain why the particular boundary, architecture, capability, continuity or effect belongs to it.

Identify the whole that bears the claim, its boundary, constituents and relevant interfaces, and how it persists through change.
State what this establishes about the work or capability being examined. If the task includes a project
change, identify the architecture, work, affected participants, observations and responsibilities
to reconsider. Each attribution of agency, authority, goals or performed work needs its own basis.

When the evidence leaves a required A.1 condition, the kind or the project claim undecided, identify exactly
what is unknown. State which observation could resolve it if further inquiry is needed and feasible.
To assess continuity after founding teachers leave a camp network, trace the continuity-bearing relations before
and after turnover. For a cross-city production effect, compare the publications, teaching
relations and work in those cities. For a festival’s promised recurrence, examine the evidence for maintaining production
between editions. Use the observations needed for the particular claim.

### MDPE.24:3 - First Useful Result

When someone will rely on a finding, give the following details that apply to their question.

> - **Question and use.** Which claim is at issue? If the result affects a decision, identify the engineering, funding, maintenance, measurement or responsibility it bears on.
> - **Prior whole, when relevant.** Identify the established prior whole, its period and its identity rule. For a transition question, state any missing or disputed identity grounds.
> - **Candidate.** Identify the proposed subject and the admitted kind whose criterion it must meet.
> - **Change or claim under examination.** Identify what was observed or proposed and any features the evidence leaves undetermined.
> - **Comparison, when a prior whole is established.** Explain how its relations and identity rule account for the change, why the claim needs another whole, or which deciding fact remains unknown.
> - **Construction and evidence.** To identify a whole, establish its constituents, their constructive relations and assembly, its identity rule, a composition-dependent characteristic and compatibility with a governed larger assembly. Apply the separate criterion for its kind. Include evidence about memory, selection, continuity or effects where the claim needs it.
> - **Finding.** State which whole carries the claim for the period. For formation, transition or continuity, identify the dated events and relations that support the finding. Specify any failed condition or what the evidence leaves open.
> - **Project consequence, if any.** State what the finding means for the project, including grounds for retaining its boundary or a proposed, authorized or completed change, as applicable.
> - **Further evidence, if needed.** Say what the comparison still requires and whether that evidence can be obtained.
> - **Reopen condition:** [new construction, loss of persistence, changed identity rule, or contrary evidence].



### MDPE.24:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.24:4.1 - One choreo-camp versus a persistent network

Teachers and learners meet at one camp. Its classes are recorded and the videos published. Those
events can belong to the work of an existing dance scene. Visibility, international
attendance and recurring branding can increase without a new continuing network being formed.

Recurring teaching, travel, booking, publication, status and learner migration can organize a continuing
network. Look for the relations that hold it together, retain repertoire across camps, affect the selection
of teachers or phrases, or change training and choreography in the cities concerned. Which are established?
An event provider may suffice for a claim about one camp. A claim about cross-city persistence may require
evidence of the network’s construction and continuity. For a claim about access or effects, examine those relations. If the available material does not establish the relevant continuity
or a claimed effect, state the outstanding question. A project choosing whom to support can use that comparison.

#### MDPE.24:4.2 - A short-video platform and a dance practice

A recommender, camera convention or viral phrase can affect visibility or selection.
When that explains the result, identify the mediating system and relation. Address
them directly if the task includes changing how the platform or practice works.

Suppose the project claims that a participant practice persists beyond individual trends and changes what people
train. Production, imitation, publication, recognition, retained material and recurring selection then suggest
observations that could distinguish that claim from the effects of one recommender or short-lived trend. Determine
which relations actually constitute the selected candidate, which only connect it to others, and whether the
claimed continuity and training effect obtain. A different project claim can require different observations.

Then apply :2.4–:2.5: compare the existing-whole explanation and establish the candidate's complete construction
and admitted-kind conditions separately. The software platform, a wider participant practice and a particular
style remain different referents; the project selects and grounds the one that would carry its current claim.
Failure to observe trend memory matters to the continuity claim above, but does not disqualify every possible
candidate System or Method.

#### MDPE.24:4.3 - Annual social-dance festival editions

One festival edition is bounded event Work. Recurrence can depend on a continuing organization, but the name of
the series does not identify that organization or establish its construction.

Consider this **constructed case**. Harbour Production already operates
the North festival. It is an identified operational System: its booking desk and local production crew are
integrated under one operating manager. Its continuation rule permits replacing staff and equipment through
handover while retaining the North production organization and its live commitments. An edition starts with
that edition's preparation and ends with its settlement; changing editions does not end Harbour Production.

The new funding question is whether to support reliable production and rescheduling across North and South
editions, including the months between them. The following arrangement is already operating in the case.

| Required distinction | Concrete case facts |
| --- | --- |
| Exact candidate and kind | Harbour Series Operations, an operational `U.System`, distinct from Harbour Production, the series name and its individual event Work. |
| Constituents | Harbour Production, the separately operating South Production unit and a joint scheduling unit. Each is an identified operational System with its own continuing team, equipment and operating boundary. Visiting teachers, venues and ticket buyers remain external participants or suppliers. |
| Actual construction | From the joint arrangement's start, the three units function as integrated components of Series Operations under the adopted production rule: the scheduling unit commits the shared teacher-time pool and joint calendar; North and South production accept those allocations, realize the local events and return cancellations and remaining capacity to that same unit. A local unit cannot independently spend time already allocated elsewhere. These obtaining component relations and connected operations constitute the assembly under `A.14`, `B.1` and `C.13`; agreements describe the rule but are not themselves the components. |
| Identity through change | The continuing Series Operations organization retains one live commitment-and-allocation process joining a scheduling unit and at least two local production units. Staff or a unit may be replaced through transfer of live commitments and operating control; a scheduled suspension with that continuity preserved does not end the whole. Dissolving the joint allocation process and returning to independent local production ends this organization, even if the brand survives. |
| Composition-grounded characteristic | The integrated organization can check both cities' remaining capacity and make one executable reallocation of the shared teacher-time pool. Neither local producer can do that alone; the scheduling unit cannot realize an edition alone. In this constructed case a withdrawn North session has been reallocated to an available South session through the common process and carried out there. |
| Acting eligibility | The connected scheduling and production operations change bookings, resource use and realized sessions while the organization continues under its identity rule. This supplies the operational organization required for `U.System`. |

A larger assembly also needs a particular construction rule. In this case, the regional arts-season organization
already uses a rule for integrating continuing production units beneath its season office. Each unit must expose
one scheduling contact, available capacity and confirmed commitments; accept a bounded season resource allocation
through the common calendar; return changes before that allocation is spent elsewhere; and keep its own internal
