The equal-pulse grid makes spacing and alternation calculable. Timing nuances and musical criteria may require other representations or observations. These two hand rules specify particular physical methods. An electronic instrument can reproduce their sounds through different actions, and another performer may need a different realization.

### MDPE.30:7 - Conformance Checklist

- The seed's onset positions, cycle length and last-to-first gap are recoverable.
- The phase is related to a fixed receiving origin and the entries or silences that matter.
- The action rule states whether attacks or all pulses advance it and continues across the boundary.
- The comparison shows which required sounds the action and instrument mapping supplies over the stated span and where it falls short, if anywhere. A claim that the sounds were produced identifies the evidence from that performance.
- For a changed span, show whether the construction preserves the required relation and fits the receiving accompaniment.

Inspecting the score can settle its structural requirements. A capability claim needs evidence of the performer under the conditions of the receiving music, with assistance that will be available and permitted there. Reuse adequate observations, or pursue a further trial if it can resolve the question on acceptable terms. Reliability over time and learning require evidence appropriate to those claims.

### MDPE.30:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Invited mistake | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| Treat cyclic rotations as interchangeable against a fixed accompaniment | Compare each placement’s entries and silences against the same receiving origin. |
| Restart hand alternation at the bar line without changing the stated rule | Continue the rule through the boundary and determine the complete hand-labelled period. |
| Rehearse an allocation that gives the wrong entry sound by construction | Change the rule or arrangement. Use practice for an attainable performing goal. |
| Extend a part by a convenient arithmetic operation that loses its musical relation | Choose the preserved relation first, derive the changed part and check the join with the accompaniment. |

### MDPE.30:9 - Consequences

The arranger obtains a part whose spacing, timbre and actions can be explained and changed separately where the music permits. A new phase or rule may suffice without a new seed. The required effort includes following the combined period and investigating the performing demands that matter to the intended use.

### MDPE.30:10 - Architectural Rationale

A seed acquires a musical use through its phase against the accompaniment and the actions and sounds chosen for it. This explains how the same onset polygon can support different parts and why a change at one entry can require a different action rule.

### MDPE.30:11 - SoTA-Echoing

| Source and use | Adopted or adapted contribution | Boundary and alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toussaint, *The Geometry of Musical Rhythm*, second edition, 2020, chapter 21, especially Figure 21.2 | Use the explicit three-onset, eight-pulse construction and the distinction between a spacing family and its performed phase. | Other seeds may be supplied by the chapter's general algorithm or another qualified construction. The shown calculation is not that whole algorithm. |
| Toussaint, chapter 31, “Alternating-Hands Method”, pp. 218–220 | Alternate the hands on audible attacks across the cycle boundary and assign the strokes to sounds. | A known part or simpler allocation may already meet the musical requirement. Compare their performing costs when cost bears on the choice. |
| Toussaint, chapter 32, pp. 225–230, especially Figures 32.1–32.2 | Adapt pulse-wise alternation and the smooth-toggle splice into an arrangement with explicit receiving conditions. | The family construction preserves specified relations; it establishes neither universal musical quality nor a performer's capability. |
| RHY.7, RHY.8 and RHY.11 | Use their structural comparison, transformation and shared-performance methods when the work needs those broader results. | Their general operations do not by themselves select this specialized seed and action construction. |

The receiving constraints, candidate arrangements and revisions here illustrate applications of Toussaint’s constructions. Use the source’s historical and cultural cases for their documented settings. Reconsider the present arrangement when another method, instrument or observation changes a result or cost relevant to the music.

### MDPE.30:12 - Relations

- MDPE.9 can compare the constructed parts or other available material when a comparison is needed.
- MDPE.3 can use the part in an arrangement with its accompaniment and other performing means. Evidence of its actual realization can answer a further performance question.
- MDPE.10 addresses a missing performing capability when the intended rule permits the required result and capability development is requested.
- Use MDPE.11 to distinguish the choices the score fixes from those the performer can make during performance.
- RHY.7, RHY.8 and RHY.11 provide the broader comparisons, transformations and coordination named above.
- Application 5.3 connects the recoverable structure of a method, its description and acquisition when this construction is taught.

### MDPE.30:End

## MDPE.10 - Develop and Test Music-or-Dance Performing Capability

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance performing-capability pattern

> **Public result:** a finding about what a performer did or can do under specified conditions, a proposed development activity or transfer test suited to the performer, or a result from carrying it out with the limits of that finding

### MDPE.10:0 - Use This When

Use this method to determine what a particular performer did or can do in specified Music or
Dance work, or to develop a capability that work requires. A course, training run, equipment change
or isolated exercise may be well documented while the relevant performance remains untested.

Identify the performer whose capability is in question. A person, pair, ensemble,
robot, AI system or equipped performer may require different methods of development
and evidence. For example, calibrating a prosthesis, practising with it and
assessing the resulting combined performance answer different questions.

A useful result may establish what the performer did then, could do then or can do now,
under the conditions the evidence covers. It can also identify an observed difficulty or
where capability remains unknown. A rehearsal or development decision may use that finding.

FPF `E.23.CDI` explains capability development and `A.2.2` identifies the holder,
work, operating range and evidence for a capability claim. In Music and Dance,
examine the bodily, rhythmic, perceptual, partner, ensemble, instrumental,
expressive or technical relation that matters in representative performance.

Use a suitable existing result, or a direct teaching, rehearsal, adaptation, control, training or engineering method
that can supply the needed contribution for this performer and work. For missing creative
alternatives use MDPE.9, and for the arrangement of already capable performers use
MDPE.3. Curriculum design and population-wide cultural transmission have other subjects.

### MDPE.10:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

Capability-development projects often start from an available intervention instead of the Work that must become
possible. A class is purchased, exercises are assigned, a model is fine-tuned, a prosthesis is built, or rehearsal
hours are increased before anyone states who must become capable of what.

Common errors include the following.

- **activity replaces transfer:** completing an exercise, course, build, training run, or rehearsal is treated as
  ability to perform under representative conditions;
- **the wrong holder gets the capability:** a person's adaptation is attributed to a device, a component result to
  a robot, one member's ability to a pair or ensemble, or a generated output to an entire human–AI arrangement;
- **one successful context becomes universal:** a result is generalized beyond the repertoire, partner,
  instrument, software, cue, venue, assistance, or time window that made it possible;
- **development becomes unbounded:** “master rhythm”, “learn the style”, or “build artistry” replaces a current
  Work family, limiting contribution, test, and stopping point.

A musician can control posture and phrasing, listen, interact with the instrument and
coordinate with the ensemble during one passage. A dancer can articulate timing,
transfer weight, respond to a partner and navigate the floor during one figure. These
are simultaneous contributions to the performance. A teacher and learners may work on them in
sequence. The representative task tests the relations that need to function together.

Attribute capability to the identified performer or performing system. Distinguish
what the performer was assigned, what they could do and what they actually performed.
A teacher, tool or other provider may contribute to the development. Where an
ensuing project decision is required, identify who has authority to make it.

### MDPE.10:2 - Solution

Identify whose performance or capability is at issue, which work it concerns and the conditions on which the finding depends. If the work calls for development, use that finding to choose what to develop and how to assess it.

#### MDPE.10:2.1 - Name the performer and receiving Work

Identify the following as they apply.

- the performer or configured whole whose performance or capability is in question,
- the musical or dance work, its conditions and the intended use of the finding,
- any decision that depends on the result and the consequence that matters to it,
- who holds the relevant authority if a decision needs to be made, and
- any provider, support or other participant whose contribution the claim concerns.

A performing assignment identifies who was expected to act. Use performance evidence to determine what occurred and capability
evidence for the range claimed. For an equipped person, distinguish the individual, device and combined configuration.
Attribute capability to a pair or ensemble when it is an identified whole and the claim concerns that whole’s coordination.

#### MDPE.10:2.2 - Set the target from representative Work

Work from the actual performance question. Identify the material, configuration, required
result, protected conditions and musical or technical criterion. Relate them to representative
work. Specify a period of qualification or a currentness condition if the claim needs one.

“Know Balboa” leaves the target unclear. Can this pair maintain continuous movement while placing a
partner-readable weight arrival across the specified phrase and tempos? If the phrase also requires free-leg
accents, assess the regular pulse and the placement of those accents together. For a marimba robot the
question might concern its dynamic and timing range over a specified repertoire and gesture configuration.

When a style name or copied example leaves the target unclear, identify the distinction to retain, the operations that produce it and what the performer can do with the intended support. If the claim concerns understanding, use evidence of what the learner can explain or apply. [MDPE.Application:5.3](#mdpeapplication53---connect-style-method-structure-and-acquisition) develops this use of E.23.CDI:4.2.1. The comparison can establish what the performer understood or could do. If the target is unmet, use that finding to identify any needed change in description, method, learning or provision.

MDPE.9 can supply the demands of candidate material and MDPE.3 the performing configuration. A claim about capability also needs evidence of the named holder in the relevant work.

#### MDPE.10:2.3 - Find the limiting contribution and protected trade-offs

Identify the contributions on which the receiving work depends. If performance falls short of the target, identify the limitation the evidence supports.
For a past performance, a finding about what happened may be sufficient even when its cause is unknown. The relevant condition or contribution may concern one of the following.

- perception, attention, anticipation, pulse, rhythm, timing, or recovery;
- bodily or effector control, posture, effort, weight, contact, articulation, breath, or endurance;
- instrument, voice, software, sensor, actuator, model, or interface control;
- reading, memory, repertoire access, improvisation, or material transformation;
- partner, ensemble, group, conductor, audience, or interactive-System coordination;
- phrasing, dynamics, timbre, movement quality, expressive range, or controlled variation;
- safety, latency, reliability, error recovery, or support dependence.

Trace a difficulty far enough to answer the question or, when development is
requested, to choose an intervention and representative check. Preserve
interactions. A change that improves speed, range, accuracy or visibility
can reduce expressiveness, autonomy, safe recovery, readable partnering or independent performance.

#### MDPE.10:2.4 - Choose a development Method that fits the holder

| Capability holder | Examples of direct development Methods | Boundary to preserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| person | focused practice, coaching, imagery, listening, movement, feedback, repertoire work, tool-supported practice | attendance and exercise success are not transfer; protect health, autonomy, and performance conditions |
| pair or ensemble | rehearsal, cue design, shared timing, partner feedback, coordination games, arrangement change | member capability and whole capability remain different |
| robot | control learning, trajectory or gesture adaptation, actuation change, calibration, mechatronic integration, rehearsal | a component benchmark or software result is not whole-robot performing capability |
| AI System | data, model, prompt, interface, fine-tuning, evaluation, recovery, and deployment Methods | output quality remains configuration-, distribution-, and use-bounded |
| equipped performer | human practice, device design, sensing and control calibration, co-adaptation, interface and safety Work | person, device, and combined-configuration capabilities remain separate |
| hybrid or collective | allocation, coordination, interface, communication, rehearsal, adaptation, and support Methods | the group label does not identify a capability holder by itself |

For human learning, choose an attentional or teaching intervention for this learner, material and desired outcome. Hohagen and Immerz (2024) report mixed findings for internal and external focus in music. Silang, Zhou and Gao (2026) describe an uneven basis for comparing teacher-led and learner-led dance pedagogy. Demonstration, correction, exploration, reflection, peer feedback, choice or a return of attention to an automatized detail can serve different difficulties. Judge the selected contribution on the musical or dance task.

For partnered movement, [MDPE.26](#mdpe26---construct-and-change-a-partnered-movement-organization) can help identify an existing organization and, where practice is needed, design it around a specific difficulty with joint support, articulation, cue use, attention or transition. Use an attainable joint attempt or an adequate observation of one. Return a practised change to the passage it should enable.

Participation can involve ending an encounter or receiving a refusal. [MDPE.27](#mdpe27---end-voluntary-partnered-performance) helps locate a missed ending, unavailable stopping movement or unreleased contact. [MDPE.28](#mdpe28---receive-a-declined-invitation-and-find-an-available-next-action) distinguishes bargaining after a refusal from difficulty carrying out the inviter’s chosen next action. An existing observation can establish how the encounter ended. To claim how a participant felt, use evidence of that experience. Choose practice or support when a further capability is needed.

#### MDPE.10:2.5 - Design practice for later contexts, not only acquisition

If flexible or delayed use matters, establish the cues available before action, the feedback afterwards, the
recent context sequence and the conditions of the intended work. A person may group situations differently from
the teacher. Repetition in one setting can support acquisition there while leaving performance elsewhere open.

COIN models human sensorimotor adaptation. Inferred context affects which motor memories
are created or updated and how their contributions are expressed. After a change of
cue, a previously available response might fail to appear even if the memory persists.

When the mechanism matters, use an existing or attainable comparison that could distinguish this hypothesis from a rival. Depending on the question, a practitioner might

- examine a return to a previously successful context before choosing whether to reteach,
- alter one cue while keeping the task fixed,
- compare blocked and interleaved practice when flexible switching matters,
- vary cue reliability or the order and frequency of changes between contexts,
- assess an unfamiliar but relevant context or delayed use, or
- compare recovery, blending, interference or generalization while monitoring the conditions that must be protected.

Consider alternatives that fit the observations. The target may exceed the performer’s demonstrated range,
the relevant coordination may still depend on a surrounding style, or fatigue, tempo, partner or equipment
may have changed. Use a suitable existing or attainable comparison if distinguishing the explanations
matters. Prefer an explanation where the evidence distinguishes it from its rivals. If several fit equally well, report what the observations establish and leave the cause open.

Context affects several kinds of memory and decision, which can motivate a discriminating test
of a shared mechanism. In work on robots and AI, domain randomization, curriculum design, retrieval
conditioned on context and tests on held-out situations provide direct techniques. A machine’s
response to a changed input does not establish the context-inference computation proposed for
human motor learning. That stronger claim needs evidence about how the response was produced.

#### MDPE.10:2.6 - Perform development Work and test transfer

If the commission is to design practice or a transfer test, specify the performer’s task and any help the design requires. When carrying it out is also in scope, perform the selected work with the appropriate person, pair, ensemble or machine configuration. In a retrospective assessment, identify
what was done from the existing evidence. Distinguish the method and description, the performer and capability holder, any provider’s contribution and the observed result.

Evidence that the proposed practice was carried out establishes what work took place. For a capability change, compare the holder,
configuration, measures, operating range and relevant time periods and establish which before-and-after results are comparable. A claim that a particular exercise,
provider or device caused the change needs grounds that distinguish that contribution from other changes.

Use existing observations if they cover the target work, holder, permitted assistance and protected conditions. They may establish a representative success, an observed limit or a narrower capability. If an important question remains, weigh an attainable transfer test against its full burden. Vary the material, tempo, partner, venue, equipment, cue, fatigue, interruption or reassessment delay when that difference matters to the claim. If the necessary evidence is unavailable, state what was observed and what remains undetermined.

The scope of evidence adequate for a reversible artistic experiment
may be too narrow for a safety-relevant public performance.

### MDPE.10:3 - First Useful Result

Give the requested performance or capability finding with its evidence. For a development design, state the intended change, proposed work and how the result could be assessed. Include the following details when relevant.

> - **Capability holder:** [performer or configured performing whole].
> - **Music-or-Dance Work family:** [the receiving Work].
> - **Baseline and operating range.** What could the holder do, at what time and under which conditions?
> - **Target and protected conditions.** What must this performance achieve, with which assistance and constraints?
> - **Limitation, if established.** Which contribution constrained the result, and what evidence supports that finding?
> - **Development, if in scope.** Identify the proposed or performed work, the method and, for a proposal, who would do the work and provide any needed help. For completed work, identify who performed it and who contributed.
> - **Practice contexts:** [cues, feedback, transition history, and variation when these affect transfer].
> - **Evidence from representative performance, when required.** Identify the task, configuration, conditions and observations available. For a proposed test, say what would count as evidence.
> - **Supported finding.** What did the observations establish about the performance or capability at the time and under the conditions in question?
> - **Limits.** Which relevant conditions and claims lie beyond the available evidence?
> - **Use in a decision, when applicable.** What action can the finding inform, and who is authorized to decide it?
> - **Grounds for reconsideration.** Which change of holder, material, configuration, condition, criterion or evidence would affect reliance on the finding for this use? Include a relevant time limit where one applies.

If the required transfer evidence is unavailable, state what evidence is missing and which capability claim remains open. Identify the effect on a decision only if a decision depends on that claim.

### MDPE.10:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.10:4.1 - Balboa pair: readable weight timing

The [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) distinguishes
continuous contact and movement from a pressure change, change of direction or weight arrival that articulates
the time. Here the target is the named pair’s ability to retain the continuous movement and make the
weight arrival readable to the partner, with posture, connection and readiness to redirect preserved.

Practice can contrast full, partial and zero transfer, move the articulated event and interleave a few phrases.
Use adequate evidence of this pair dancing under representative conditions to assess its joint capability. The source
supplies the design of the practice. Evidence about a particular pair comes from that pair’s performance.

In this constructed case Lina and Owen form the identified pair through their
continuing initiation and response under an agreed contact and timing convention.
They are considering their eight-pulse weight-timing phrase for the next
supported studio rehearsal. The intended conditions retain their footwear,
floor, contact and two selected recordings at 120 and 132 beats per minute.

In the initial trials at those same settings, the pair completes the phrase when the teacher speaks each weight-arrival cue. Without
that extra count, Owen reads Lina's free-leg brush as the transfer and responds before the standing-leg weight
arrival in four of six phrases. Both can repeat the simple full transfer in isolation; the selected limitation
is making its timing readable inside the continuing phrase. The target is a jointly readable arrival without
the teacher's extra count, while keeping continuous movement, comfortable contact, balance and the ability to
stop or redirect. Loudly accenting every step might make arrival obvious but would sacrifice the chosen movement
quality, so it is not an adequate repair.

The pair and teacher carry out two short practice periods. They first alternate full and partial transfers while
Owen reports when weight arrival becomes usable, then insert the selected full transfer into the phrase without
changing its legato carrier. The teacher gives feedback after a phrase instead of counting through it. They interleave
the target phrase and an already familiar walking phrase, returning to the simpler transfer when readability is lost. In the first uncounted
attempt the brush still misleads Owen; they reduce that free-leg accent and repeat the actual partnered task.

On the next day, the pair performs two three-minute takes, one with each selected recording, without the teacher's
spoken count. Across the twelve selected phrase entries, Owen's reported arrival and the observed response agree;
continuous movement and comfortable contact remain, and the pair stops and redirects at the agreed musical break.
These observations support using this pair and phrase in the next studio rehearsal under
the stated conditions. Claims about long-run success, an entire public evening, a new
partner, other recordings or a wider tempo range need evidence for those additional demands.

The teacher stops this exercise and returns the phrase to rehearsal. Music and
partner contact remain available while the extra spoken count is removed. Keep the
observed result for the original pair and settings. For a changed phrase, partner
or contact convention, or a later failure to reproduce the phrase, reconsider what the earlier evidence supports for the new use. The improvement
after practice informs the rehearsal choice. Attributing it to this exercise
needs evidence that distinguishes the exercise from other intervening factors.

#### MDPE.10:4.2 - Multidance, clean switching, and intentional transfer

Two different difficulties occur in multidance. A performer may blend two taught movement organizations while
intending to switch between them, or switch cleanly but fail to carry one chosen coordination into the other.
Specify the movement instructions and musical material separately before choosing either target.

In this constructed exercise, phrase A is a travel-and-pivot phrase taught in the local tango class; phrase B is
a close-contact walking phrase with completed weight arrivals and a pause before redirection, taught in the
local kizomba class. These instructions identify the task fragments; the class labels do not define all
performance under either name. The pair has already performed each fragment with the same selected practice
recording R at its fixed tempo. That established compatibility permits keeping R, partner Q, room and contact
conditions fixed while changing the movement task.

Dancer P can use a small torso-initiated direction change C in A, and Q can read it. P can also perform B, but
when asked to introduce C after B's pause, either omits it or imports A's travel-and-pivot sequence. The target is
C within B's stated weight-arrival and pause conditions. It is not a new classification of the recording or a
requirement to make all of B resemble A.

An `A–B–A` probe uses A with C, then B with the attempted C, then returns to A without new teaching. The same
recording, tempo and partner remain. The observations can answer what happened and may inform later work.

- if C returns promptly in A, that weighs against a general loss of C and can support examining cue recognition,
  interleaving or deliberate transfer if intervention is requested,
- difficulty both in the initial A and on returning to A weakens the simple context-switch explanation and leaves open a need for
  further practice of C or a change of conditions,
- C in B accompanied by A’s unwanted travel-and-pivot sequence shows that on that attempt the performer did not
  separate the requested coordination from the surrounding movement, and
- a difference related to partner, tempo or fatigue calls for specifying the holder and the relevant conditions before generalizing.

A later comparison may keep the movement instruction fixed and change only to another recording
already usable for that task. If the movement instruction and recording both changed, report that
joint difference. To attribute it to one change, examine additional evidence that distinguishes the
two. Reconsider compatibility when either change affects a requirement of the partnering method.

The practitioner report supplies the recognizable problem and a contextual-inference hypothesis. These specified
probes are constructed applications, not evidence about a named dancer, all methods taught under those labels or
the prevalence of the difficulty.


#### MDPE.10:4.3 - Shimon: robot capability, human development decision

The Shimon sources describe different configurations for composition continuation, marimba playing, actuation
and musical gesture. The actuator study compared striking speed and dynamic range. Attribute each performance capability to the robot configuration, material, measures and conditions
tested. Generation, sensing, control, actuation, rehearsal and performance made distinct contributions.

In the cited projects the human team changes the software, mechatronics or trial
conditions, interprets the results and chooses the subsequent development work. A
finding about what the robot played does not settle who held that decision authority.

#### MDPE.10:4.4 - Jason Barnes and a robotic prosthesis

Identify Barnes, each prosthesis and the performing configuration it formed with him. Distinguish
his musical and bodily control, the device’s sensing, grip and actuation, their combined drumming
or piano performance, the team’s engineering and Barnes’s practice and co-adaptation.

Repeated performances can support a claim about the documented setup under comparable conditions. A faster or
autonomous strike addresses a different question from expressive control, endurance, performance on piano or
uptake by other musicians. Check the relevant configuration and outcome before carrying a finding across them.

#### MDPE.10:4.5 - JIZAI ARMS and generated movement

A wearable-limb project can supply prototypes, reachable poses and observations of interaction.
For a dance-capability claim, identify the equipped performer, representative work and evidence. If new bodily practice is needed, choose a method appropriate to that performer and its physical conditions.
Partner coordination, timing, force control, recovery and reproduction each require grounds
suited to the claim. A role-play may already answer a question about the documented interaction.

A model may generate movement material that viewers judge danceable. MDPE.9 can use that material directly. For
bodily feasibility, examine the required trajectories, available means and limits of the intended performer.
To establish that a dancer, robot or configured whole actually performed it, use evidence of that performance.

#### MDPE.10:4.6 - Learn to vary accents over a continuing pulse

The execution in [MDPE.11:4.5.2](#mdpe11452---one-coordinating-method-two-physical-realizations) gives two human practice tasks. A drummer varies accents with one hand while the other maintains a regular brush pulse. A Balboa dancer varies free-leg accents while maintaining support and weight arrival, including a change of supporting leg. The two contributions can interfere during the same passage. In each exercise, assess the accent and continuing support together using observations appropriate to the activity.

In this constructed teaching example, first establish which comfortable supporting action and articulation the learners can already perform. When a missing prerequisite requires teaching or support, obtain the necessary contribution before combining the actions. Choose tempo, accent, material and contact for the later performance.

| Purpose of the shared exercise | Brush realization | Partnered Balboa realization |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Make the required relation recoverable | Hear or demonstrate a continuing sweep with one offbeat accent; relate the sweep to an external beat. | Demonstrate continued pressure–release with an unweighted free-foot accent; identify the later full weight arrival separately. |
| Perform the actual overlap | Continue the familiar sweep while the other hand prepares, articulates and releases. | Continue the standing leg's support while the free foot prepares and articulates; include its return before the scheduled transfer. |
| Identify a limitation, when present | Listen separately for the pulse and the required accent. Observe whether one hand mirrors an unintended movement of the other. | Observe support, timing and the free-foot event. Use the partner’s response or account, with the other available observations, to judge when the cue became usable. |
| Change one controllable action and rejoin | Shorten an excessive accent stroke or begin its preparation earlier while the sweep continues. | Reduce a free-foot excursion that pulls the body into loading, or prepare its return earlier; keep the accent recognizable and the transfer on time. |
| Expand the needed choice | Move the accent to another subdivision, then play a new short accent sequence without restarting the sweep. | Change the free-foot accent places within the feasible support interval; then include the taught support exchange and later accents by the newly free leg. |

In one example, request the midpoint accent, then a later subdivision while keeping the supporting period. A midpoint accent on the second request misses the requested place. A correct later accent followed by a longer pulse misses the timing condition. If teaching is commissioned, demonstrate a revised preparation and try the joint passage. Give advance notice suited to the preparation time. A finding about the existing attempt can stand on its own.

Select further practice from the intended work. The relevant variation may concern a sequence, intensity, tempo, phrase, allocation or partner. Start under conditions suitable for detecting a change, then vary the demand that matters. [RHY.12:4.2.1](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/EMBODIED-RHYTHMICS-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#rhy12421---derive-practice-from-the-pulse-and-accent-construction) develops the shared pulse-and-accent exercise and its feedback.

When performance without a teacher’s count is required, withhold that extra cue in the transfer check. Feedback can follow the phrase. Keep the music, partner contact or accompaniment that belongs to the intended performance and will be available there. A new accent sequence can test choice, a tempo or reference change can test synchronization, and a later performance can support a retention claim. Use relevant existing or new observations of the accent, pulse and protected conditions together.

The result can support using a phrase in the studied range, identify an unavailable accent phase or support exchange, or show which technique needs attention. When a new decision about using the phrase is needed, it belongs to whoever holds that authority. An existing applicable decision can already authorize its use. For another activity, identify its continuing action, articulation, means and feedback. Structural similarity can justify a proposed teaching construction. Evidence from representative performance is needed to establish actual transfer.

### MDPE.10:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Performer and work are named | A course, tool or vague mastery goal determines the target by default. | State whose performance or capability is at issue, which work it concerns and which conditions bear on the answer. |
| Capability has the right holder | An individual, pair, robot, device or equipped performer is credited with another’s capability. | Use evidence of the holder and configuration that the claim concerns. |
| Target and protected conditions precede intervention | Available exercises become the objective. | Derive the required capability demand from representative Work. |
| Contribution is specific but not isolated falsely | A local gain damages performance elsewhere. | Keep simultaneous interactions and protected trade-offs visible. |
| Development Method fits the holder | Human training language is copied into robot, AI, equipped, or collective cases. | Use the direct holder-specific Method and evidence. |
| Practice prepares later contexts | Repetition in one context masquerades as transfer. | Vary relevant contexts, cues, transition history, and delayed use where the claim requires it. |
| Context inference remains a hypothesis | Apparent forgetting is automatically assigned to one mechanism. | Compare rival explanations. A return-to-context observation can be informative when it distinguishes them. |
| Capability in the receiving work has representative grounds | Activity or isolated exercise success leaves the required performance open. | Use relevant existing evidence. When a further worthwhile test can resolve a material gap, seek it or report the remaining limit. |
| Causal attribution | An improvement is credited automatically to an exercise, provider, model or device. | Distinguish the intervention, observed change and the evidence that identifies the cause of that change. |
| The finding has a stated range and time | One success is generalized to materially different conditions. | State what the evidence covers and identify any change or time limit that calls for reassessment of its use. |

### MDPE.10:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

When capability development is the task, connect the learning or technical intervention with representative performance and transfer. In an assessment, state what the evidence establishes about the named performance or capability, with its time and conditions.

| Source or maintained result | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF `E.23.CDI` and `A.2.2` | General holder–Work–limitation–intervention–transfer Method and holder-dependent capability identity. | They do not supply Music-or-Dance material, body, rhythm, instrument, partner, ensemble, context, or performance filling. |
| Timing examples in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) and the local Balboa cases | Layered timing, contact, weight, partner feedback, and variation for Dance capability design. | Method-design input only; no named-holder capability or mandatory lesson order. |
| Heald, Lengyel, and Wolpert, [COIN sensorimotor model](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04129-3) | Separation of motor-memory creation or updating from context-dependent expression; graded mixtures under inferred context. | Tested in human sensorimotor adaptation; other performance and learning uses remain hypotheses requiring discriminating probes. |
| Heald, Lengyel, and Wolpert, [Contextual inference in learning and memory](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2022.10.004) | Context dependence across conditioning, episodic memory, economic decision-making, and motor learning motivates cross-domain tests. | It does not establish one COIN computation for every memory, reasoning task, or learner. |
| Ogasa et al., [decision uncertainty as a context for motor memory](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-01911-x) | Internal decision conditions can contribute to context-dependent expression. | One motor-adaptation factor does not reveal a learner's unrestricted context categories. |
| Kumar et al., [contextual cues and transition statistics](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.116281) | Cue availability, recency, transition history, blocked and interleaved schedules, and competing motor-memory expression. | Six visuomotor experiments do not establish one optimal schedule for every learner, Music or Dance task, or non-motor domain. |
| Reybrouck and Schiavio, [Music performance as knowledge acquisition](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1331806); Hohagen and Immerz, [focus of attention review](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1290596); Moura et al., [solo assessment criteria](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1467434) | Coupled bodily, auditory, visual, instrumental, attentional, technical, interpretive, expressive, rhythmic, and instrument-specific pressures. | These sources do not supply one universal cue, rubric, or capability-development Method. |
| Fitch and Barnstaple, [Dance as mindful movement](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12868-024-00894-9); Silang, Zhou, and Gao, [Dance pedagogy review](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1840900) | Automatized subskills, deliberate attention, demonstration, correction, exploration, reflection, dialog, feedback, and choice as candidate components. | The sources do not establish one definition of Dance, lesson order, or universally superior pedagogy. |
| Georgia Tech [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon), [2017 account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2017/06/13/robot-uses-deep-learning-and-big-data-write-and-play-its-own-music), [actuator study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14850), and [gesture study](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1461615) | Robot-holder capability, generation/control/actuation separation, bounded performance evidence, and separate human development decisions. | Results remain configuration-, material-, measure-, and condition-bounded. |
| Georgia Tech [Barnes prosthesis account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2014/03/06/robotic-prosthesis-turns-drummer-three-armed-cyborg), [finger-control account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2017/12/11/force-strong-amputee-controls-individual-prosthetic-fingers), and [Drumming Arm study](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561943) | Person, device, combined-configuration, engineering, co-adaptation, and performance distinctions. | One performer and device lineage does not supply a universal prosthesis or teaching Method. |
| Yamamura et al., [JIZAI ARMS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581169) | Equipped-body configuration, co-design, embodied observations, and open questions. | Physical possibility and prototype interaction do not establish Dance capability or transfer. |

Reconsider the relevant development choice when another field method can supply the needed result at lower cost, a changed performer or configuration requires a different kind of evidence, or new observations challenge an explanation of transfer. The finding for earlier conditions can remain valid.

### MDPE.10:7 - Relations

- `MDPE.9` can establish the demands of a candidate, and `MDPE.3` can supply the
  performing configuration and coordination. Use evidence about the identified holder
  to determine whether it could meet those demands under the stated conditions.
- `MDPE.5` can use a current capability finding for the same holder, material,
  configuration and conditions. A claim about the later event needs evidence of that event.
- MDPE.14 can use capability limits or protected conditions where they change a choice about a practice conflict, a trial or the distribution of burdens.
- For human-general varied practice, applicability recognition, transfer, retention or tool dependence, use the applicable direct teaching or capability-development Method. Use a published Human Capability Development result when it answers the current question under its stated conditions.
- Use `C.36`, `MDPE.17`, `MDPE.19` or `MDPE.20` when the question concerns cultural
  transmission, continuation or a trajectory extending beyond one holder’s capability.
- Systems Engineering can supply findings about equipment, interfaces and a performing configuration.
  Core’s method-development guidance can support constructing, testing or revising a method.
  Use the contribution required to explain, assess or develop this performer’s capability.

### MDPE.10:End

## MDPE.3 - Configure and Coordinate a Music-or-Dance Performing Whole

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance performing-configuration pattern

> **Public result:** an account of an existing or past performing configuration, a proposed arrangement, or a finding about its coordination, readiness or an unresolved condition

### MDPE.3:0 - Use This When

Use this method to identify how a particular music or dance performance was organized, design a configuration for
a proposed performance, or assess whether its participants and means can coordinate. A successful joint performance,
a design on paper or a mismatch among individually capable performers can each supply the starting point.

A partner cue can be unreadable, a response delayed, a connector incompatible or authority to change a system
missing. Each contribution can work on its own while the combination falls short. A score or stage plan can
establish the intended arrangement. To explain what happened, use evidence of the setup and its operation.

Identify the performing whole, its essential relations and the conditions that must hold together for the particular
work. The result can be an account of the setup that was used, a design with its conditions, or a finding about how
it coordinated. Where a needed part, permission, capability or safe test condition is missing, identify what this
prevents. Consider a further check when an attainable result could settle a consequential question at a worthwhile cost.

Use ensemble, partnering, staging, instrument-setup, control, rehearsal, venue or Systems
Engineering methods for the results they supply. MDPE.3 connects those results around the
simultaneous work of the performers, including timing, material, partner relations and recovery.
Use a complete existing account or a direct field method when it already answers the question.

### MDPE.3:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

A music or dance project can improve its parts separately and discover an incompatibility only when they are brought together. A dancer knows a figure but cannot lead
it through the intended contact. A musician can play a part but cannot hear the cue in the venue. A model produces
material faster than the performer-facing control can expose it. A robot reaches the notes but its actuation
noise, latency, gesture, or recovery changes the musical relation. A prosthesis increases striking speed while
moving control away from the musician. A stage plot lists equipment without saying who senses which state or how
a failure is corrected.

Some descriptions and claims can obscure whether the performing arrangement works.

- a diagram line is called an interface without naming the connector, signal, protocol description, or actual
  interaction;
- a score or count is treated as coordination rather than a description used by performers;
- a performer label is treated as an obtaining assignment and sufficient capability evidence;
- a component test is treated as evidence that the whole can perform;
- a proposed configuration is written as though its Systems and relations already obtain.

Select the smallest performing whole whose construction and coordination support the claim. Establish constituents from the
relations that actually compose the whole, or specify the required composition for a design. Identify venues, services, archives,
audiences, platforms and other participants separately where they supply an external condition or receive the performance.

Several relations can operate at once. During partnered dance, bodily control, weight transfer,
partner communication, figure execution, musical timing, floor navigation and social participation
can matter at different scales in one passage. Rehearsal can address them in sequence. Use
their simultaneous organization to understand the joint performance. Use constructive relations to establish which participants belong to the performing whole.

### MDPE.3:2 - Solution

For the named performance or family of work, establish the configuration and its coordination to the extent the question requires. Use
available system or music-and-dance results where they answer the question. When further work is needed, use Systems Engineering for boundaries, architecture, realization or assurance and a field method for the relevant
interaction. A plan specifies a possible arrangement. A historical account identifies the arrangement and work supported by the evidence.

#### MDPE.3:2.1 - Identify the material, performance and use

Identify the material, performance, receiving use and conditions. If an assumption matters to a proposed configuration, say what
depends on it. For a past performance, establish the relevant conditions from the evidence available for that occurrence.

Identify the concrete use, such as a social-dance phrase, concert set, improvisation constraint, installation interaction, recording occurrence or rehearsal family.

MDPE.9 can supply candidate material and MDPE.10 a capability finding. To identify the performing whole and its coordination, establish how the material and capabilities are joined in the particular configuration.

#### MDPE.3:2.2 - Choose the performing boundary

For the work in question, select the minimum performing configuration sufficient for the claim. For an existing whole, establish its actual construction, coordination and identity. For a design, specify the required relations and any conditions for realizing them. Identify the following as applicable.

- the proposed, available or past performing whole relevant to the work,
- its constituents and the part relations required in a design or actually obtaining for an existing whole,
- external participants and their interactions or enabling relations,
- the material and conditions the work uses, including scores, prompts, choreography, props,
  space, energy and network access. Establish any claimed part relation separately, and
- the relevant interval, conditions and configuration.

For an existing whole, include a component or material portion as a constituent when its kind and its actual part relation support that claim. A constituent need not itself be a System. Exchanging signals, sharing a diagram or using the same resource may instead establish an external relation.

A pair can be the relevant whole for joint cueing, an equipped performer for a
particular instrument or prosthesis, or an ensemble for joint timing and delivery. For
generated material, establish what the model supplied. If a performance is proposed, identify the intended performer. If it took place, use evidence of who or what performed it.

Use the general holon and Systems Engineering criteria when determining whether these relations constitute the proposed whole or an acting system. A group name alone can locate the question.

#### MDPE.3:2.3 - Choose views for the performance question

Choose the views that reveal a relation needed to describe, design or assess the configuration.

| Concern | What to make visible |
| --- | --- |
| Functional contribution | Who or what produces sound or movement, senses timing, supports weight, generates material, cues another performer, presents the result, or recovers from failure. |
| Construction and physical connection | Bodies, instruments, devices, effectors, props, connectors, rooms, floors, wearables, and the physical relations specified for a proposed setup or established for an existing one. |
| Timing and rhythm | Continuing carriers, discrete events, anticipated or perceived centres, timing tolerances, cue relations, and recovery after drift. |
| Sensing, control, and feedback | What state each performer or controller can sense, which action it can change, what feedback returns, and who corrects failure. |
| Placement, access, and safety | Spatial reach, visibility, audibility, movement paths, audience and performer access, collision, load, fatigue, and exit. |
| Participation and decision rights | Who performs, leads, follows, conducts, controls, authorizes, refuses, interrupts, or changes the Method. |
| Material and description use | How scores, choreography, recordings, prompts, generated material, rule cards, and cue sheets enter Work without becoming performers. |

Where several views concern the same performing arrangement, identify the corresponding participants and relations needed for the question. One view may organize functions, another physical links or mutual cues. A configuration drawing can settle what it specifies. Use evidence of the actual setup for the claim that the parts and interactions were in place.

#### MDPE.3:2.4 - Name load-bearing relations and interfaces

For a relation essential to this work, identify the participants, direction or reciprocity, relevant conditions
and consequence. Examples include partner contact and weight exchange, a cue between musicians, an audio
signal, a control display, an actuator command, a sensing relation, audibility at a particular position
or access to an emergency stop. Use the observation or design constraint that bears on the actual claim.

When “interface” leaves the needed relation unclear, identify the connector or boundary,
functional port, protocol or API description, signal or interaction that is meant. Common
use of the word does not establish that a diagrammed connection already carries a signal.

A score can establish prescribed timing, a rule card the contact it prescribes and a protocol the required
messages. To report actual use, determine from appropriate evidence what the performers or
devices did in the occurrence and which relations obtained. An existing record can establish it.

#### MDPE.3:2.5 - Ground timing in processes and events

Identify the timing process and event relevant to the question. A notation or timestamp can establish a
specified landmark. A claim about joint performance or a perceived cue may require different evidence.

In Balboa, continuing floor contact and movement can carry time. A pressure change, direction
change or weight arrival can articulate it. Foot contact, acoustic onset, intended beat
and the event a partner can use may occur at different times. In music, a physical attack,
sound onset, perceived beat centre, gesture and software timestamp may likewise differ.

Select the observation for the timing relation at issue. A waveform with a known time reference can locate an acoustic onset at the recorded point. To establish when a partner could use a weight cue, look for evidence of that cue under the conditions of the interaction.

#### MDPE.3:2.6 - Establish coordination and examine an unresolved relation

If the work includes realizing a performing arrangement, choose the direct setup, fitting,
calibration, rehearsal, cue design, control, safety or access work it requires. To assess a design
or a past performance, use the appropriate existing specification, observation or operating record.

If an important joint relation remains in question, use any adequate existing finding or compare the likely results and full costs of feasible checks. A
partnered phrase can test a cue, a rehearsal excerpt can expose latency and recovery, a venue check can establish
audibility or sightlines, and a robot test can reveal noise or control delay. When an important
uncertainty cannot be resolved on acceptable terms, state what the design or earlier evidence establishes and where the answer stops.

Where recovery matters, state who or what can detect the deviation, the corrective action and the
condition for stopping safely. To report an actual correction or stop, establish that it occurred.

### MDPE.3:3 - First Useful Result

Give the configuration and its relied-on conditions. Include the entries below when they help answer the receiving question.

> - **Music-or-Dance Work:** [selected material, occurrence or Work family, and receiving use].
> - **Performing whole.** Identify the observed or proposed configuration and the construction and coordination on which the claim depends.
> - **Constituents.** Identify the entities and their actual kinds. Specify the part relations that obtained in an existing setup or are required for the proposed one.
> - **External enablers and interactions:** [participants, conditions and direct relations outside the whole].
> - **Material and descriptions.** Identify the score, prompt, recording or rule used or proposed for use, as applicable.
> - **Selected views:** [only the functional, physical, timing, control, placement, participation, or material views needed].
> - **Load-bearing relations:** [participants, conditions, timing, control, and correction].
> - **Capabilities and assignments.** Identify those relied on at the time and under the conditions in question.
> - **Coordination evidence, where needed.** What existing observations establish the relevant joint work? If a further test is proposed, identify its purpose and the conditions for carrying it out.
> - **Unresolved dependency, if any.** What required component, relation, capability, authority, evidence or safe condition is missing, and which conclusion does this affect?
> - **Fallback or stop.** Describe the required or observed correction, recovery, refusal or safe stop where it matters.
> - **Reassessment, where needed.** What change of material, performer, relation, venue, configuration or evidence would affect reliance on this result?



### MDPE.3:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.3:4.1 - Balboa pair, carrier, and readable event

For a partnered phrase, identify the pair and the joint contact, bodily support and continuing movement central to its
timing. A pressure or direction change or weight arrival may articulate the time. Use evidence of the partner’s access and
response to identify when the weight event was usable. Foot contact or a count can settle the time of a different event.

A suitable record of a partnered phrase can show whether the continuous movement persisted, the partner used the cue and the pair recovered
after redirection. If this remains an important open question, consider a short trial with the relevant tempo, pair and contact conditions.

Where the phrase also needs variable free-foot accents, identify the continuing support, foot articulation and the intended change of supporting leg. Compare pulse regularity, accent placement and readable weight arrival. [MDPE.11:4.5.2](#mdpe11452---one-coordinating-method-two-physical-realizations) explains how those contributions work together. For a claim about the actual pair, use evidence of their joint execution.

#### MDPE.3:4.2 - Shimon, marimba, control, gesture, and people

For the documented robot-only marimba event, Shimon is the performer. Generation software, control,
actuation, marimba, seed, room and human engineering work contribute differently. Identify their
actual relations to the particular setup. The project’s human team chose later development work.
That responsibility does not make the team a constituent performer of each robot performance.

The actuator studies concern speed, dynamics, noise and strike control. The head and
arm gesture studies investigate interaction, attention and synchronization with
human musicians, including how they interpreted the robot’s cues. Attribute each result to its tested configuration and conditions.

#### MDPE.3:4.3 - Jason Barnes as an equipped performer

For the named drumming work, Barnes with a configured prosthesis can be the performing
whole. Identify Barnes, device, sensing, controller for the autonomous stick, drum kit and audio input, along
with their actual part or external interaction relations. An account of shared
control may need the particular sensing and audio response, actuation, stick-to-drum contact, correction, stop and redirection.

Evidence about the equipped performance supplies a result that Barnes’s prior musicianship and a device
description alone leave open. The later finger-control and piano work used another configuration.
Reconsider each claim whose holder, connection, control, material or receiving conditions changed.

#### MDPE.3:4.4 - Separate performing arrangements in *The Call*

The project links a songbook, exercises, choirs, a recording protocol, datasets, choral models, a spatial-audio
installation and an experiment with a data trust. These belong to different working arrangements.

For a choir recording, identify the singers, material, protocol, space and recording work. For
the installation, identify the model execution, spatial sound, visitor controls, signals, responses
and venue. Project membership can connect the two accounts. To identify a constituent in either
performing arrangement, establish the part relation through which it helped constitute that arrangement.

#### MDPE.3:4.5 - JIZAI ARMS before a Dance claim

JIZAI ARMS supplied prototypes of a wearable body system and observations of embodied role-play.
Those results can answer questions about design and interaction. Whether the apparatus formed a
performing whole for a particular dance depends on that work and the evidence for its configuration.

For a dance application, specify the work and identify the required wearer, wearable base, arms, sensing, control, space,
timing, safety, correction and recovery. Include a partner or ensemble when the work calls for them. A design can specify the intended configuration.
To claim that it performed, examine the actual setup and its performance or state what that evidence leaves unknown.

#### MDPE.3:4.6 - Direct-Method stop

A solo musician already has the instrument, room, material, monitor, permissions and fallback
needed for the proposed performance. An earlier setup check or a suitable field service establishes
the configuration and coordination relevant to the decision. The musician can use it directly.

#### MDPE.3:4.7 - Antiphonal ensemble: cue, late response and acoustic recovery

In the constructed MDPE-PERFORM case, a singer, clarinettist, cellist and
electronics performer are preparing an antiphonal passage at 96 beats per minute.
Each can perform the assigned part. Sometimes the generated answer arrives after
the intended response begins. The group needs to arrange the next studio
rehearsal of this passage. Readiness for a full concert is a separate question.

For this joint timing question, the four performers, their configured instruments and the
electronic rig form the ensemble through their agreed call, cues, monitoring and response.
The room and mains supply provide external conditions. The later audience and the playback system through which it hears the work are
relevant to presentation. The score and sound files supply material. A different room or
score can change the required interactions without becoming a constituent of the ensemble.

The score gives the singer a four-beat call and the ensemble the following four-beat answer. The protected
musical result is a clearly heard exchange with the singer's breathing space intact. Merely delaying the entire
answer until generation finishes destroys that relation. The group compares preparing all electronic answers
in advance with retaining live generation and providing a timely acoustic answer when needed. It chooses the
second arrangement for this passage because live variation remains useful and the acoustic answer is already
performable. The first remains a simpler alternative if live variation ceases to warrant the complexity.

The group realizes these relations through rehearsal and the electronics performer's available queue, gate and
mute controls:

| Participant and relation | Agreed cue, action or correction |
| --- | --- |
| Singer to electronics performer | The agreed breath/hand cue at the start of the call initiates generation; the performer watches that cue and monitors the response buffer. |
| Electronics performer to clarinettist and cellist | Before the final beat of the call, the performer gives the agreed visible ready sign only if the response is queued. Everyone can see that sign from the selected positions. |
| Downbeat response | A response signalled ready by the cutoff is released on the answer downbeat. Without the ready sign by the cutoff, the clarinettist starts the prepared acoustic answer and the cellist supports it. |
| Late-generation recovery | If the cutoff is missed, the electronics performer keeps the generated answer muted for the whole exchange, even if it becomes ready meanwhile. Discard or retain it for another use, then rearm generation for the next call. |
| Lost common cue | If the performers cannot agree which exchange is current or cannot hear one another, they stop at the agreed break and reset together; guessing does not count as successful recovery. |

The stipulated trial contains four ordinary exchanges and two deliberately late generations. With the given
placement and monitor mix the performers hear the call. The ready sign is visible when given. All four ordinary
answers enter on the intended downbeat. In both late cases the acoustic answer enters there, the late
electronic sound stays muted, the singer retains the scored breathing space and the next call starts together.

The ensemble retains the cue, cutoff, mute, acoustic answer and placement for the next
rehearsal of this passage. The six observed exchanges also answer the historical
question of how recovery worked under that setup. For a concert, audibility for the
audience, the longer set and a new venue remain untested by these six exchanges. Use an existing assessment or obtain the needed evidence through MDPE.5. If
changed placement hides the sign, reassess its visibility and the affected joint entry, retaining the usable score and acoustic answer. If the clarinettist lacks the
required technique despite an adequate cue, use MDPE.10 for the capability question.

### MDPE.3:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Performing work and boundary | A broad project label is treated as one performing System. | Name the occurrence or work family and identify the whole that supplied the relevant joint performance, or specify the organization required in a design. |
| Constituents and external enablers stay distinct | Every venue, service, audience, or platform becomes a part. | For an existing setup, identify the established part relations. For a design, specify the required composition. Identify external interactions in either case. |
| Views fit their questions | Function, construction, timing, control and placement are forced into the same hierarchy. | Use a view for each relevant relation and establish correspondences where the claim depends on them. |
| Configuration and description | A score, stage plot or approval is treated as proof of an operating arrangement. | State what the description specifies. For an actual realization, identify the participating resources, obtaining relations and their evidence. |
| Interface wording is recovered | A line or noun hides the load-bearing relation. | Identify the connector, port, protocol description, signal, representation, or direct interaction meant. |
| Timing is grounded | A count, timestamp or onset is used to stand for another timing relation. | Identify the relevant continuing process, articulation, cue or perception and the evidence for its timing. |
| Joint coordination | Component success is extended to a whole without support. | Use evidence of the joint operation to report it. For a plan, state how the required relation would work. Seek a further test where it can resolve a consequential uncertainty. |
| Correction and safe stop are explicit | Readiness assumes a perfect run. | Identify the sensing, feedback, recovery, refusal or stopping conditions required for the particular work. Distinguish a planned fallback from a correction or stop that occurred. |
| Performing and deciding | A robot, platform, controller or conductor is given decision authority solely because it produces a signal. | Identify who performed the work and who held authority for the relevant choice. For an actual decision, determine what was chosen. |

### MDPE.3:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source or maintained result | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF `A.1`, `A.22`, `A.6.F`, `A.6.M`, `A.6.RSIR`, `A.2`, `A.2.1`, `A.2.2`, `A.15.1`, and `F.6` | Holon and System recognition, selected structures, function, module and interface-claim recovery, assignment, capability, Work, and attribution. | They do not supply Music-or-Dance material, performer, carrier, articulation, partner, ensemble, or performance use. |
| [Develop an Engineered System's Functional Organization and Bearer Alternatives (SYSE.5)](Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/SYSTEMS-ENGINEERING-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#syse5---develop-an-engineered-systems-functional-organization-and-bearer-alternatives) | General engineered-System functional organization, bearer, allocation, interface, feasibility, and conflict alternatives. | A possible architecture is distinct from the configuration that exists; MDPE specifies the performance relations. |

| Georgia Tech [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon), [2017 account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2017/06/13/robot-uses-deep-learning-and-big-data-write-and-play-its-own-music), [actuator study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14850), and [gesture study](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1461615) | Robotic generation, performance, actuation, gesture, timing, interaction, and performer/developer separation. | The sources do not establish one timeless configuration, robot-held development authority, or cultural retention. |
| Georgia Tech [Barnes prosthesis account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2014/03/06/robotic-prosthesis-turns-drummer-three-armed-cyborg), [finger-control account](https://news.gatech.edu/news/2017/12/11/force-strong-amputee-controls-individual-prosthetic-fingers), and [Drumming Arm study](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561943) | Equipped performer, shared control, device-to-instrument interaction, representative performance, and changing configurations. | One performer/device lineage does not define every equipped performance. |

| Serpentine, [*The Call*](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | Named choirs, recording protocol, datasets, models, installation, and participation arrangements. | The source describes distinct performing arrangements; it supplies no universal Music Method. |
| Whitehead et al., [interpersonal coordination in Dance improvisation](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1465595) | Movement relation, directed influence, participant report, and other observations for human dyads. | One synchrony score does not configure a pair or prescribe a partnering Method. |
| Abalde et al., [joint music making](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2024.105816) | Prior knowledge, social relations, goals, strategies, cueing, anticipation, correction, and mutual adaptation as ensemble concerns. | The research framework is not one ensemble configuration or Systems Engineering Method. |

Use an applicable existing result or a direct field method if it answers the coordination question at acceptable cost.

### MDPE.3:7 - Relations

- `MDPE.9` can supply material for designing or assessing the configuration, including material the existing arrangement already supports. Generating a candidate does not establish
  the whole.
- `MDPE.10` can supply capability evidence for one holder or configuration. Check what any joint capability finding establishes for the question. Current use and constituent relations each need
  evidence of the relevant operation or construction.
- `MDPE.3` uses applicable system and architecture results from `SYSE.5` and other Systems Engineering
  patterns; the music, movement, partner, ensemble, timing, and performance specialization remains here.
- `MDPE.11` and `MDPE.5` can use the configuration in later Work. Availability of the whole produces neither an
  interpretation nor a performance occurrence.
- MDPE.14 can use a conflict among part relations, overlapping work, scale, constraints or representations and support a recommendation or a decision by whoever holds the relevant authority. Delivery of the chosen change requires its own work.
- `A.1` governs constructive holon and System recognition; `A.22` selected structures; `C.30` architecture; `C.29` representation use; and
  the direct Method, Work, capability, assignment, evidence, and measurement patterns govern their own claims.


### MDPE.3:End

# Part III - Performance, Observation, Recognition, and Selection

## MDPE.26 - Construct and Change a Partnered Movement Organization

> **Type:** Method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### MDPE.26:1 - Problem frame

Use this method to understand, design or change how two people organize a partnered passage. The question may concern a movement quality, a response to music or a transition the pair needs to make together. A teacher can use the result to identify a learning need. For a live attempt, choose a comfortable, attainable passage and agree how either participant can pause. A workable passage or an account of a past performance can answer the question.

A **movement organization** is how a performer supports the body, prepares and combines movements, and makes the action available to a partner. Two performances with the same foot positions can differ in the timing of transfer, continuity of torso travel and response available to the partner. The historical term *style engine* refers here to a prepared bodily capability that can produce a range of performances. Use MDPE.Application:5.3 when the question concerns a stylistic distinction or the method that produces the example.

For a bounded passage, connect the movement relation to be explained or achieved with the bodily means, attention and transition it requires. The examples below develop this construction from the sources in §11.

**First useful move.** Identify the passage and the relation the two people need to sustain. For a design, establish the starting conditions or state which you assume. For a past performance, use evidence of that pair. A demonstration can show how a passage might work. When perception or intention matters, use the participant’s account if available or obtain it when needed. If a required contribution is missing, locate the point where it becomes unavailable.

Use a passage that already meets the purpose. For a missing composition use MDPE.9, for equipment or ensemble configuration MDPE.3, and for learning a known movement method MDPE.10. Use the construction below for the bodily and interactive connection. Physical trials require a comfortable, attainable attempt. Clinical assessment, injury rehabilitation and disengagement from a weight-bearing lift require the appropriate specialist method.

### MDPE.26:2 - Problem

Foot positions alone can leave the needed support, preparation, body travel and information for the partner unspecified. Knowing both passages separately can leave their transition unavailable.

Connect the wanted effect to bodily means both participants can use together. A shorter step may improve support and miss a required accent. Watching the feet can steady a movement and obscure the partner’s next cue. Judge a local change against the whole passage.

### MDPE.26:3 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Familiar material and new organization | Reusing a figure saves work. Check whether it supplies the support and preparation this passage requires. |
| Individual means and joint continuation | A solo action can work while its cue, exit or entry remains unusable to the partner. |
| Attention to detail and responsiveness | Focus can expose a limiting movement, while continued monitoring can make music or partner changes unavailable. |
| Adaptation and the required effect | Removing an optional flourish can help; removing a required relation changes the task. |
| Small inquiry and whole use | An isolated attempt can locate a possible repair. A representative connected performance can show whether the change serves the intended passage. |

### MDPE.26:4 - Solution

Work backward from the required movement and forward from the starting conditions of both participants. Identify how an existing organization connects them, or construct a means to do so. An observed failure can itself answer the question. If its cause or repair matters, compare plausible explanations or assess a change in the shared passage. Reuse an adequate construction or observation when it answers the question.

#### MDPE.26:4.1 - Start from the continuation the participants want

Identify the relation the passage requires. For example, two dancers must continue a small shared trajectory, detect when a transfer permits the next direction and make their travel more compact for a quieter phrase. Mark what must remain, including a required offbeat. The pair may omit a flourish when it is optional.

Locate the musical event or relation in the material for this passage, such as a pulse, phrase boundary, entrance of a voice or change in accent or texture. Establish what movement should respond to it. If the relation needs clarification, use the recording, score or other evidence for the event and for the movement intended to answer it. Work with the given music or, when the purpose permits, select or prepare material that makes the relation available. MDPE.30 develops rhythmic construction.

For a proposed performance, use the pair’s established joint capabilities or specify the capabilities and conditions the design assumes. Before a live attempt, the participants need an agreed attainable range of movement and a recognizable request to continue, change or pause. They may use sight, touch or speech. Account for the available space. Neighbouring dancers may require a smaller extent or a different direction than an empty studio permits. To describe a past passage, use evidence of its conditions and of any agreement the claim requires.

#### MDPE.26:4.2 - Examine the shared passage and its constraints

Examine a suitable observation of the passage or arrange a comfortable attempt when the remaining question warrants one. Identify where both partners continued or where the required relation became unavailable. For a claim about what someone felt, detected or intended, use evidence of that participant’s experience. Visible foot placement can establish a different part of the account. When the cause matters and remains uncertain, use a comparison that can distinguish the explanations if it is attainable and worth its cost. Otherwise state the limit of the evidence.

| Observation | A comparison that could distinguish the difficulty | What the result can change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The intended action is unavailable even with an understood cue and time to prepare | Locate the difficulty in entering support, preparing the moving part or completing the transfer. Compare a shorter path or a longer preparation that retains the wanted effect. | The comparison can establish which part is unavailable. If the action is required in a harder phrase, develop or replace the means it lacks. |
| Both participants can perform the movement, but the partner starts the next action at a different event from the one required | Keep the passage and vary the disputed signal. Distinguish preparation from completed transfer or use an agreed available channel. Establish what the partner detected. | Use the comparison to locate the difficulty in producing, accessing or interpreting the signal. Change the relevant part when a repair is wanted. |
| Two passages work separately and the join fails | Compare the end of the first with what the second needs at entry. Identify the missing condition. A previous instance may show what supplies it. Try a proposed connecting action if evidence of its use is needed. | Change the exit, entry or connection as the result warrants. |
