| Details consume the attention needed for a partner or musical change | Use a smaller viable passage with one relevant change to notice and answer. | Develop the combined task or keep support permitted in the intended performance. |

These observations suggest explanations. With an unfamiliar partner, a different convention, fatigue, insufficient support or a capability gap can produce the same difficulty. When the cause matters, use observations that distinguish these explanations if they are available. A repair decision may justify a further comparison. State any remaining uncertainty about the cause.

#### MDPE.26:4.3 - Construct usable bodily means at the scale of the gap

Work backward from the required movement. What support and moving part must be available? Where must the body be going, and what must the partner be able to detect in time to act? Work forward from the participant’s starting state. An available technique can supply the connection. If it falls short, design a small change and use a fitting observation or attempt to assess the result.

For a compact travelling step, establish which foot bears weight and which can move. Prepare a reachable placement for the moving foot, carry the body into the transfer and release the former support as the new support becomes usable. If reaching ahead leaves the body behind and makes the transfer abrupt, compare a shorter step with the original. Assess the resulting body travel and whether the partner can read the transfer.

For a continuous torso path interrupted at each footfall, distribute travel through the interval between transfers. Keep transfer timing fixed in the comparison. Reduce the excursion if the performer cannot maintain the path on their own support. The partner can report whether continuation becomes easier. Use only the agreed assistance permitted in the passage. Where the task calls for self-support, arrange the movement so that the partner need not pull the performer through it. If the passage requires an arrest or sharp articulation, construct it with support and an available continuation.

For an articulation within continuing support, separate the part maintaining support from the part making the articulation, and recover the latter's preparation and return. MDPE.11:4.5.2 supplies a developed Balboa realization and the corresponding drum-brush contrast; RHY.11:4.4.1 explains how pulse and accents can disturb one another. Use those operations intact when this is the limiting relation.

Change one consequential relation, then restore the passage. For example, prepare earlier, reduce an excursion, take another available path or assign the articulation to a free body part. Reject a change that removes required timing or movement quality. If the action remains unavailable, identify the missing contribution. When further performance is wanted, obtain suitable instruction, assistance or another means and reassess the passage. “Prepare the free foot and return it before the transfer while support continues” gives instruction a specific target.

The floor and footwear belong to these conditions. If a previously usable step now catches or slides unexpectedly, stop that attempt and reassess the surface, footwear or movement with appropriate assistance.

#### MDPE.26:4.4 - Make attention available for the next consequential change

Identify what the participant needs to notice, such as the partner’s readiness for a transfer or the entrance of a musical voice. In an attempt, the performer attends to that cue while retaining viable support. To assess responsive performance, establish whether the participant detected it, chose an available response and continued. Existing evidence of that combined task may suffice.

When working on the performance, if attention to a foot detail makes the partner's response disappear from notice, return temporarily to the simpler shared passage. Work on the foot detail in a portion where the interaction remains manageable, and then restore the partner or musical decision. If the cue is inaccessible, change its presentation or the interaction arrangement before prescribing more concentration. If it is perceived but its meaning is unfamiliar, clarify and practise the choice.

A performer can return attention to a familiar detail to change movement quality. Keep permitted assistance when it serves the task. Reduce it when the performance requires action without that help. Characterize the ability to sustain and respond in terms of what was observed and under which conditions.

#### MDPE.26:4.5 - Build the transition from the next entry back to the present movement

Identify the entry conditions of the next organization, including support, free body parts, direction, ongoing movement, an accessible cue and musical time. Compare these with the actual or specified exit from the preceding passage. Check the connection for both participants. The same foot label may have different functions for the two partners.

When the exit supplies what the entry needs, prepare and signal the change in time for the partner. Otherwise construct a connecting action that provides the missing support, facing, free part or preparation time. Place it in the musical phrase. For an actual performance claim, examine evidence of the pair using that connection.

Examine the whole interval across the change. Could the partner detect the preparation in time? Did the partner use it? Did both arrive with usable support and retain the musical relation? Was continuation available? If the question concerns what followed, did they continue? For a claim about their choice, what evidence supports it? Assess felt clarity, movement and musical timing from the evidence for each.

During performance, use a prepared continuation or recovery suited to the partner’s response. If the partner is unready, continue a viable movement or pause. An optional change can wait. If the exact change at that boundary is required, report the missed transition and what the fallback preserved. Earlier preparation, different means or a revised arrangement may support a later attempt.

When applying a transition with another partner, establish whether the earlier evidence covers this partner’s response. Use an existing shared movement or establish a legible change together when needed. If the music changes, reconsider the timing or expressive relation it affects. A report about the original pair remains tied to its own conditions.

#### MDPE.26:4.6 - Choose practice for a movement capability the pair needs

When practice is needed, use the identified relation to select it under MDPE.10. For a learner who cannot distinguish preparation from transfer, provide accessible contrasts and feedback on what they detected. For one who recognizes the transfer and cannot make the action, work on the support or coordination. If separate passages work and the join fails, practise the connection and the choice of entry.

Start from a supported joint attempt when feasible. Isolate a portion when it makes the limiting action obtainable. For example, prepare the free foot during a supported hold, bring it back before transferring, then include the operation in the shared phrase. Check whether it still works with the time and attention the full phrase permits.

Within an attainable range, vary the choice. A partner can offer either of two familiar continuations while the supporting movement continues. Observe detection, choice and response. Give feedback on the contribution that needs it and withdraw an extra cue when the intended task requires that independence. MDPE.10:4.6 develops practice for pulse–accent interference and MDPE.10:4.2 gives A–B–A comparisons for movement organizations that become confused across contexts.

For a claim covering a different partner or musical passage, use evidence under the relevant variation. For retention, use evidence of a later return. Existing observations may suffice. When trying new conditions, choose an order that helps the pair identify the difficulty. A correct explanation gives evidence of understanding. Actual performance with the named help, transfer and retention each need evidence of that work.

### MDPE.26:5 - Archetypal Grounding

**Connection through a small travelling passage.** Maya and Lin want comfortable continuous travel over four musical pulses and a readable change of direction at the next phrase. Both can already step and pause together. Maya copies the foot positions from a demonstration, but reaches far ahead, leaves the torso behind and then pulls through the contact to catch up. Lin reports detecting that pull as the instruction to turn before Maya has completed the transfer.

The pair keeps the four transfer times and reduces step extent. Maya prepares a reachable placement and carries the torso through each interval as weight changes. The extra catch-up pull disappears. They compare one transfer, then restore all four and the direction change. In the constructed result, Lin distinguishes transfer from the following change and both continue. The figure names and coarse foot sequence have stayed the same while the organization of the passage has changed.

The first success requires Maya to watch the feet throughout. When a quieter phrase starts, Maya misses it and keeps travelling at the former extent. This leaves the musical requirement unmet. The pair repeats the smaller passage with a choice to continue at the same extent or make the phrase more compact when the music changes. Lin responds in each attempt. With feedback, Maya later makes that choice while keeping the transfer legible.

Another partner reports finding the change abrupt. Maya and that partner use a small shared passage to adjust the preparation. The earlier result still describes Lin’s response. If either participant reports a feeling of unity, report it as that participant’s experience. The cause of the transfer needs evidence of the mechanism.

**Fusion through a prepared change of bodily roles.** Maya and Lin can travel with continuous torso motion and a full weight transfer on each pulse. Separately, they can stop on their own support, maintain a small regular body pulse over the supporting leg, articulate two events with the free foot and resume travelling. Their chosen response to a new phrase keeps that pulse while the accompaniment becomes sustained, marks two short events on counts 5½ and 6½, and resumes travel with a full transfer on 7. This response requires both accents and the continuing pulse; it permits holding support on 4 and makes a free-foot touch on 4 optional.

The initial join fails. After the transfer on 3, Maya is supported on the left foot and Lin on the right. Their usual full transfer on 4 would load Maya's right and Lin's left foot—the feet with which they learned the next articulations. They change that particular transfer. First they shorten the step onto the supports used on 3 and finish the forward travel before 4. On 4, each touches the free foot to the floor without putting weight onto it, then returns it beside the supporting leg before the first accent. Maya remains supported on the left and Lin on the right. Their already available supported body pulse continues through the hold. After the second accent, they prepare a reachable placement for the full transfer on 7. A version requiring a full transfer on 4 would need a different construction.

They also obtain a timely cue. During preparation, both agree that Maya's small palm-up gesture means “keep this support on the next pulse”; Lin's nod confirms receipt. Both have a free hand and an available sight line. They first try this with one transfer and the following hold. Maya presents the gesture on 3, after reaching support; Lin must perceive it and confirm before the expected transfer on 4. They compare a cue arriving after Lin has begun that transfer with one arriving while Lin can still choose the hold. They ask what Lin detected and observe which action followed. In the stipulated timely attempt, both retain the intended support. If confirmation is absent, Maya uses their prepared continuation instead of assuming that the planned hold has become available.

They now restore the complete phrase at an attainable tempo: approach, cue and confirmation, unweighted touch and return, held pulse with the two accents, then transfer on 7 and continued travel. RHY.11:4.4.1 and MDPE.11:4.5.2 supply the selective timing work inside the hold. The transition supplies those operations' support, free foot and cue, and connects their result to travel. In this constructed successful attempt, both accents occur, support remains usable and both participants resume together.

In a faster version, the choreography also moves the first required accent from 5½ to 4¼. The optional touch on 4 now leaves too little time for either free foot to return to its prepared position before that accent. They remove that touch: after the transfer on 3, each brings the free foot directly to the accent's prepared position before 4. The held support and regular body pulse continue; the agreed cue still has to be perceived before 4. In the changed trial, both can make the earlier accent, retain the second accent and transfer on 7. If the receiving choreography also required the touch on 4, removing it would fail that task; they would need another obtainable preparation or articulation. To establish that the revised join works in performance, use a suitable observation of the whole phrase.

Both examples connect a movement relation to a bodily means, an accessible partner cue and the next passage’s entry. Where practice was needed, the pair returned the learned action to the shared phrase. To assess whether the passage belongs to a recognized style, use the comparison in MDPE.Application:5.3. MDPE.25 examines adoption, reward or rejection of a variant by a community.

### MDPE.26:6 - Bias-Annotation

This method concerns bounded partnered movement by human performers. For physical practice, both must be willing and able to attempt the passage comfortably. Either can pause. Bodily support and teaching require the relevant agreement. Judge the combination required by this passage, distinguishing observed motion, reported experience and evidence of cause. A smaller movement or retained help can be sufficient when it preserves the required response and the task permits that help. Apply the examples to the bodies, conventions and style in question.

Use the observation to identify the movement it shows. Use evidence of the partner’s experience to report a sensation. For a changed partner or context, compare what the person could detect and do under the new conditions.

### MDPE.26:7 - Conformance Checklist

For a proposed construction, trace the required movement through bodily means, cue, entry, exit, attention and support. For a claim about an actual passage, use evidence of its joint execution under the relevant conditions. Draw on a participant’s account when the question concerns what they perceived, felt or intended.

- Which result must the passage retain, and which flourish may change or disappear?
- Can each participant supply their own required support and prepare the next action in time?
- What makes the intended cue detectable and distinguishable from preparation or incidental motion?
- Does the transition supply the second passage's entry for both people?
- Does a local correction remain useful when the preceding and following actions return?
- Which musical or partner conditions does the available evidence cover? What remains open if the claim extends further?

If an explanation of a difficulty is still provisional, identify which comparison could distinguish it when the cause or a repair matters. State what the observations already establish about the pair’s performance.

### MDPE.26:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Misreading | Consequence and repair |
| --- | --- |
| Treating two known figures as a complete transition | Compare the actual or planned exit and entry. Identify an available connection or construct the condition the join lacks. |
| Relying on a partner’s pull for movement the performer must support | Obtain support the performer can use or modify the movement. Keep only the assistance the participants agree to and the passage permits. |
| Prescribing concentration for every missed cue | Check the availability and meaning of the cue and whether the combined task is feasible with the available attention and help. |
| Dropping a required event to simplify the passage | Retain the required effects. Reject a construction that removes a necessary accent or response. |

### MDPE.26:9 - Consequences

The result may identify how an existing passage worked, specify a viable movement organization or name a missing contribution. When learning is wanted, a specific difficulty can direct practice towards support, signal interpretation, transition or combined responsiveness.

Further practice can require time, a teacher, an accessible place and a willing partner. A smaller adequate passage can complete the task. For a claim about new partners, music or bodily conditions, reassess the relations the change affects. Earlier observations retain their scope.

### MDPE.26:10 - Architectural Rationale

The construction starts with the receiving passage because the same bodily change can help one performance and spoil another. It uses both participants' conditions because a solo demonstration shows what that performer did alone. Working backward from the next entry exposes conditions that separate practice of whole figures can omit.

Use an available technique, partner adjustment or permitted support when it supplies the whole passage. If capability is missing, a smaller attempt can make a contribution available and its return to the whole tests whether it works there.

### MDPE.26:11 - SoTA-Echoing

Levenchuk’s [account of kizomba connection](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1315064.html) links torso and leg action, readable weight, attention, musical voices and partner response. The practical proposals depend on the school and situation and include interaction without touch. The [style-engine example](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1373388.html), [movement holarchy](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1371120.html) and [multidance discussion](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1370125.html) describe prepared bodily means and their use with changing material. How to construct an arbitrary style or acquire it rapidly remains open. The partnered constructions above develop one bounded part of that question.

The posts also propose explanations involving particular muscles, myofascial chains, tensegrity and NLP. The practical movement comparisons can be used independently of those proposals. To attribute a result to a particular tissue or neural process, obtain evidence that distinguishes the proposed mechanism.

[Fitch and Barnstaple (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12868-024-00894-9) propose roles for automatization and deliberate renewed attention in movement. Their theoretical account offers testable predictions. [Wiese, Ambegaonkar and Martin's review (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1123/jsr.2023-0047) found mixed effects of attentional focus on dancers’ performance across four studies. [Zeng, Zhang and Wang (2026)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1916455) examine heterogeneous study-level effects in the wider attentional-focus literature. Use these findings to frame the task and examine the individual’s response in context. A study-level estimate does not establish that individual response.

[Charbonneau, Andrade Chavez and Mombaur (2024), §§V–VIII](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05301v1) compared haptic, visual and spoken signals in a robot-led box-step interaction. Participants rated how well they knew which step to take and how comfortable they felt. The two ratings did not always favour the same signal. The setting involved limited reciprocal interaction and no music. Human partnered fusion under music would require evidence under those conditions.

For a finding about a particular pair, use evidence of the part in question. An account of a transition through to the next passage needs evidence across the change and its continuation. For a conclusion about joint performance, a solo demonstration or an explanation can identify the construction, while evidence of joint execution establishes what occurred. If the intended music, partner response, bodily means or performing conditions change, reconsider the affected finding. Consider further inquiry when its result would settle an outstanding question at a worthwhile cost.

### MDPE.26:12 - Relations

- MDPE.9 supplies material alternatives; MDPE.11 connects their interpretation to actual musical and movement Work.
- MDPE.3 supplies the performing configuration. Return unavailable channels, equipment or whole-configuration conditions there.
- SOM.5 supplies adaptation of bodily coordination to changing support and load; its result must still serve the partnered passage.
- MDPE.10 can supply an existing capability finding or help develop and test a needed capability. RHY.11 and MDPE.11:4.5.2 supply the pulse–accent work within the constructed transition.
- MDPE.Application:5.3 connects stylistic distinctions, Method structure and acquisition. MDPE.25 concerns renewal across a community's participation, teaching and recognition.
- MDPE.27 uses an available stopping movement and can return a missing entry or support condition to this construction.

### MDPE.26:End

## MDPE.11 - Interpret or Shape Music-or-Dance Material While Performing

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance performance-enactment pattern

> **Public result:** an interpretation realized, or material generated or revised, during performance, or a supported account of what that performance realized

### MDPE.11:0 - Use This When

Use this method to interpret or shape material during a performance, or to establish what was performed on a particular occasion.
A score, choreography, generative rule, prompt, rehearsal result or configuration can show what was available or prescribed.

A musician can interpret a score, a dancer can adapt learned coordination to a partner, an improviser can generate material within a form, a live coder can change running code and a robot can perform a generated phrase. Identify what was available beforehand, what the performer could change during the work and what interpretation or material resulted.
Give the prepared material and constraints, the performer and method, and the interpretation, new material or change
realized in the performance, or the limit of what the available evidence shows. Identify the evidence that supports the finding or that a later use will
need. Distinguish the material, its description, the work, resulting artifacts and the occurrence.

Use a direct method of interpretation, improvisation, live coding, partnering, conducting,
instrumental or vocal performance, robotic control or co-performance when it supplies the needed
result. Use `MDPE.9` to compare alternatives, `MDPE.10` to assess or develop performing capability, `MDPE.3` for
configuration, `MDPE.5` to produce and present the occurrence and `MDPE.12` to observe or compare
it. Use this method when the connection between the material and what was realized still needs work.

### MDPE.11:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

Prepared material can leave choices to the performer. A classical musician can vary
the realization of a score. A social dancer can adapt learned coordination to the
music, partner, floor and surrounding dancers. Jazz improvisation, movement improvisation
and live coding can produce new material while the performance is in progress.

Distinguish the contributions that matter to this performance.

- A score, choreography, prompt, code listing, cue or rule may describe material, a method, constraints
  or a combination of them.
- A performer uses or generates musical or movement material. Identify its bearer when that affects access or use.
- Identify which conditions of contact, timing, safety, instrumentation, latency or participation held
  during the work. A rule card can establish a prescribed condition.
- Identify who performed the work, when it took place and which method that performer enacted.
- Identify the interpretation or newly generated material within the work.
- A recording, code state, changed score, sensor trace or note can preserve evidence of particular actions and results.
- Identify the bounded performance occurrence and any presentation to listeners, viewers, partners or other
  participants when that is the question.

A rehearsal may succeed before the premiere. An improvisation can introduce a change absent from the score. A recording
can preserve aspects of the performance while leaving the performer’s choice unclear. Keep evidence for the question
in hand. Recording every choice can interrupt the work and burden later readers without helping them answer it.

### MDPE.11:2 - Solution

For a bounded performance, establish what was prepared, what the performer did and what resulted.
Generation can occur during performance. A performer can make the same choice again or return to an earlier option.

#### MDPE.11:2.1 - State the receiving question and performer

State the receiving question. It may ask what happened during a former performance, what to do in a current
phrase, or what should inform rehearsal, creative revision, capability development, production, comparison
or teaching. Identify the performer or performing whole, the bounded work and its field method.

When a subsequent choice is involved, identify who holds or held authority
to make it. Shimon can play a marimba phrase while the human project
team chooses the subsequent engineering or development work.

#### MDPE.11:2.2 - Recover what exists before Work

For the performance in question, recover the relevant starting conditions.

| Before-Work position | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Material | Which rhythm, melody, texture, phrase, figure, coordination, code-produced structure, or other content was available for that performance, and which version did the performer use? For a proposed performance, which version is needed and what material is already available? |
| Bearer or memory | What gave the performer access to the material, or what would give access in the proposed setting? Consider embodied memory, instrument configuration, score, choreography, recording, code, demonstration, or cue. |
| Description | Which indications guide action, and do they describe material, a Method, constraints, or several of these? |
| Proposed constraints | Which relations are intended to hold among which participants and under which conditions? |
| Conditions in place | Which body, instrument, partner, timing, space, latency, safety, access or participation conditions affected that work or are available for the proposed performance? |

A candidate from `MDPE.9` can supply material, a description or a constraint specification. Establish whether the material was available and which constraints actually held if those are part of the performance claim.


#### MDPE.11:2.3 - Distinguish preservation, variation, and generation

Recover what the performance allowed or required beforehand. In a new arrangement, specify the distinctions needed for its use.

- **preserve:** a rhythmic relation, melodic contour, partner cue, interaction rule, lyrical meaning,
  recognizability condition, or another relation must survive;
- **vary:** the performer may change timing nuance, ornamentation, path, dynamics, phrase order, code parameters,
  articulation, or partner response;
- **generate or revise during Work:** new movement, melodic continuation, running-code transformation, spatial
  response, or a new constraint may arise only as the situation develops.

These distinctions depend on the performance agreement and use. A competition may
fix an articulation that an ensemble or social partner allows the performer to vary.

#### MDPE.11:2.4 - Identify the performer’s method and choices during performance

Perform the passage using the relevant domain method, or establish which methods contributed to the performance being studied. A dancer can use balance and timing,
partner interaction and an Urban Kiz method simultaneously. When these relations matter, establish the temporal order from the performance. To identify one method as a part of another, establish which contribution the encompassing method calls for.

When sound, movement, a partner’s or audience’s response, running code, equipment or safety changes what can be done
next, use FPF situation-responsive work steering. Choose among the available actions from the facts, intended result,
authority and conditions for stopping. A score, recommendation, signal or response can inform the choice. To explain
a past choice, establish what was available to the performer at that point and what evidence supports the account.



#### MDPE.11:2.5 - Identify what interpretation or material was realized or changed

At a significant point in the passage or after it, examine the questions that bear on the receiving use.

1. Which prepared material was used or interpreted?
2. What material or operative constraints, if any, were generated, selected, transformed or revised during the performance?
3. Which distinctions had to be preserved? Which held, which changed and which does the evidence leave open?
4. Which observation or resulting artifact supports the claim about that performance, and what remains unknown?

For example, the pair kept the pulse and a weight transfer the partner could read, changed path as the floor grew crowded
and added a turn response. Video can show the path. Perceived pressure needs evidence of the partner’s experience.

#### MDPE.11:2.6 - Preserve only traces with a use

| Receiving use | Possible direct trace | Important limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rehearsal or performer reflection | short audio/video segment, code state, cue note, performer annotation | recording or self-report can omit partner, body, or audience relations |
| creation revision | changed score, choreography note, diff, stem, take, marked phrase | the revision does not establish later enactment |
| technical diagnosis | sensor trace, latency log, actuation record, synchronized capture | measured features may not represent artistic or partner meaning |
| teaching or transmission | annotated example and conditions under which the distinction was recoverable | one example does not establish transfer or retention |
| later observation | identity of the occurrence, accessible evidence and the conditions under which it was observed | Use this material to answer the historical question. For an additional observation or comparison, use `MDPE.12` |

Establish access, currency, publication or provenance when the later use depends on it. Use the
relevant publication, memory or lineage method when the status of an artifact still matters to the use and remains unclear.

### MDPE.11:3 - First Useful Result

State the finding with the detail its use requires.

> - **Receiving question.** What do you need to establish about the performance, or which choice should it inform?
> - **Performer and Work:** [dancer, musician, pair, ensemble, robot, hybrid; bounded Work and Method].
> - **Before Work:** [material, bearer or memory, descriptions, proposed constraints, obtaining conditions].
> - **Preservation, variation and generation.** Which distinctions applied to this passage?
> - **During the performance.** What did the performer do under the conditions of the performance? Describe any consequential choice, change of material or constraint, continuation or stop.
> - **Performed result:** [the interpretation realized or material generated or revised during the Work].
> - **Direct traces:** [artifacts or observations and the claim each can support].
> - **Unknown or unsupported:** [any material question the evidence leaves open].
> - **Later use, if relevant.** What can this result support, and which changed condition would affect that use?

Report what the pertinent evidence establishes about the interpretation or generated material under the conditions of that performance.

### MDPE.11:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.11:4.1 - NDT premiere preparation and performance

The NDT production team developed the choreography, costumes, props, lighting, sound and staging,
considered touring constraints and arranged filming and archiving before the premiere. The account of this preparation identifies
the material, descriptions, configuration and constraints available for the premiere.

To establish what the premiere realized, identify the dancers and other performers, their methods, the prepared movement and production material they used, and which relations held during the work. Use `MDPE.5` for the occurrence and its presentation and `MDPE.12` for subsequent observation or judgement. Report a limit where the record does not establish the particular realization.

#### MDPE.11:4.2 - Live coding

In live coding, distinguish the code visible on screen, activation of a queued change and the resulting sound. Their times
can answer a historical question or help determine whether the material, interpretation or technical timing needs revision.

In a constructed case, live coder Ivo and vocalist Nara perform an
eight-pulse cycle. The low percussion attacks at 0, 2, 4 and 6, with 0
marking the start. The score permits removing or restoring an interior
attack while retaining the cycle duration, pulse spacing and first attack.
In their system a queued change becomes active at the next cycle boundary.

Nara lengthens an answer into pulse 6, where the low attack now obscures its ending. Ivo hears that collision
and chooses the permitted removal of attack 6, leaving attacks 0, 2 and 4. During cycle 22, at pulse 5, he edits
the pattern and queues it for the next boundary. The screen already shows the sparser pattern, but the attack
at pulse 6 of cycle 22 still sounds. At the start of cycle 23 the queued pattern takes effect; its final two
pulses leave space for the vocal ending. Nara can hear that space and continues her held ending while both
performers retain the cycle's first-pulse reference. Her timing and vocal interpretation remain her contribution.

The synchronized code and activation trace and the audio excerpt locate the edit, boundary and emitted sound.
Attack 6 still sounds in cycle 22 and is absent in cycle 23. The first-pulse attack remains. Nara reports that
the sound in her own monitor leaves room for the held ending. Her report gives evidence of her experience,
while the recording addresses the captured sound. What others heard depends on their listening conditions.

The pair retains the sparser variant and rehearses queuing it before the intended
boundary. The extra attack after the edit in cycle 22 agrees with the activation
rule. If attack 6 persisted at a scheduled occurrence after the recorded activation boundary, that would raise a technical
timing question. If the intended pattern sounds on time in the relevant channel and the vocal relation still fails,
reconsider the material or its interpretation. A saved pattern, synchronized excerpt
and performer’s note can settle what happened or support the rehearsal choice.




#### MDPE.11:4.3 - Social dance

A dancer enters a song with learned coordinations and a domain Method. Partner response, floor density, phrasing,
and balance can change the next contribution. The dancer may preserve pulse and readable connection while changing
path, figure, timing nuance, or articulation.

Describe what was preserved, any change and how the partner’s response figured in the performance when the evidence establishes it. Use the observation or report that
supports the particular finding. A teacher may use it later to choose practice; their judgement has its own grounds.

To establish how the pair achieved a quality or transition, or to construct one that familiar figures leave unavailable, [MDPE.26](#mdpe26---construct-and-change-a-partnered-movement-organization) develops the bodily means and relates them to the music and partner’s response. It can identify the means already used, prepare the next entry, or address a specific remaining difficulty. When a capability gap is established and developing it is wanted, select suitable practice.

#### MDPE.11:4.4 - Shimon generation and performance

People provided a four-measure seed. Shimon generated the continuation and performed the piece
on marimba. To determine whether generation occurred before or during the performance, use
evidence of the timing. A continuation generated first supplies prepared material for
subsequent playing. Attribute a change to the playing itself when the evidence connects it to the work of performing.

#### MDPE.11:4.5 - Balboa, brushes, and event timing

Drum brushes can maintain a sweep on the drumhead while increased pressure creates an audible accent. In a partnered Balboa phrase, continued floor contact and body movement can carry a distinct weight transfer. Compare the continuing movement and the event made perceptible within it. Foot contact, weight arrival and the partner’s perceived timing can differ. The [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) gives the source and its scope.

##### MDPE.11:4.5.1 - Choosing an optional articulation during a phrase

In this **constructed performance case**, a pair has prepared a repeating small-step phrase followed by a change of direction. Its agreed material fixes the transfer timing and direction change but leaves a free-leg tap optional. Both participants can already perform the simpler phrase. During one repetition, the initiating performer adds the tap before that foot accepts weight. The partner starts the direction change at the tap and then hesitates because the transfer is not ready. The performer feels the unexpectedly early response through their connection. That response warrants adjusting the phrase; it does not reveal, by itself, everything the partner perceived.

On the next repetition, while the performance continues, the performer omits the optional tap. The foot continues its sliding preparation, the body completes the transfer at the agreed point, and movement carries on into the direction change. The performer changes articulation within the prepared material; neither the transfer timing nor the next direction is newly composed. In the stipulated result, the partner continues without the earlier hesitation. After the phrase, the partner reports having taken the earlier tap-related contact change as weight arrival, whereas the second repetition made the arrival clear. The source analogy helped identify a variable to change: remove the competing accent while preserving the continuing movement and usable transfer.

The pair has changed the articulation within the performed phrase and continues with the simpler version on the next repetition. If an audible ornament is wanted later, MDPE.9 can compare candidates. The observed response and the partner’s report support this local choice. Audio can locate an audible tap, video can show contact and motion, and a force trace can locate a change in contact force. Use evidence of the partner’s experience to locate the event they perceived, and physical measurements to locate a force maximum.


##### MDPE.11:4.5.2 - One coordinating Method, two physical realizations

Now consider a passage that requires the accents. Its task is to retain a regular supporting pulse while placing those accents at selected positions, including positions between beats. Both can be accurate separately and interfere in combination: an accent pulls the pulse out of time, or the habitual pulse movement postpones the accent to an easier place. [RHY.11:4.4.1](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/EMBODIED-RHYTHMICS-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#rhy11441---keep-a-common-time-while-allowing-different-actions) develops the common Method: recover the joint timing, prepare the accent within the continuing action, choose compatible means, correct any missed contribution and retain the required range of choices.

For **drum brushes**, use an already learned comfortable sweep as the supporting action. One practical realization keeps one hand on a repeatable circular path while the other places audible strokes or pressure accents. Relate the circle to the beat, then prepare each accent so its audible event reaches the selected subdivision while the sweeping hand continues through it. If lifting the articulating hand also lifts the sustaining hand, keep the latter's contact and shorten the former's stroke. If the stroke waits for the circle's turning point, change when its preparation starts instead of postponing the musical target. Listen for the sustained texture, the regular reference and the accent's placement; a sweep can remain audible while its period changes.

This realization adapts the progression in [*A Fresh Approach to the Drumset*, Lesson 29, printed p. 73](https://ae.vicfirth.com/wp-content/uploads/Fresh-Approach-to-Drumset-SAMPLER.pdf): repeatable legato movement, a beat-related pressure pulse, and varied articulation by the other hand. The new performance question is whether the chosen offbeat can move while the support remains regular. [Ed Soph's two-legato-hand alternative](https://www.moderndrummer.com/article/foundational-brush-technique/) realizes the same contribution distinction differently: pressure can articulate without lifting a hand. Select the means compatible with the required sound and the performer's available technique.

For a **partnered Balboa fragment**, continuous support and weight organization carry time while a free foot can articulate without accepting weight. In a constructed fragment, the pair has a supported hold through beats 1 and 2 and a planned full weight arrival at 3. A small unweighted toe contact is wanted halfway between 1 and 2; another may be wanted halfway between 2 and 3. The standing leg continues its taught pressure–release, and the free foot makes the chosen contact without moving the body's support onto it. The foot then returns along a manageable path in time to prepare the scheduled weight arrival. Early floor contact is possible without early loading.

At the full transfer, the previously free leg becomes the support. The pulse must continue through that exchange; later free-leg articulation belongs to the newly available leg. The action therefore preserves a temporal function through changing body-part roles. It cannot be implemented by freezing one leg as permanent timekeeper. If a large tap pulls the torso into premature loading, shorten or redirect that free-foot action while preserving its required accent. If the smaller action becomes inaudible when sound is required, select another available articulation or return the technique question. The partner's response checks usable weight arrival and continuation; sound locates an audible accent, and observation of loading checks a different event.

Both constructions prepare and articulate a chosen event within continuing support and assess each against the intended time. Brushes require contact, stroke and sound control. The Balboa passage requires usable support, a timely exchange of bodily roles and a continuation the partner can read. This shared relation can guide design. Whether drum practice improved leg control would require evidence connecting that practice to a change in the dancer’s performance. The examples here are constructions. Measurements and the partner’s account can establish different features of a performed phrase, as in §4.5.1.

##### MDPE.11:4.5.3 - Keep freedom when the passage changes

Change the accent from the midpoint of an interval to a later subdivision, then use a new short sequence of accent places. Keep the selected pulse and required accent character. A performer who can only repeat the first joint pattern still has a useful pattern, but not the range this new passage needs. If the musical reference changes tempo, locate the continuing pulse and accents against the new intervals. Move any old absolute event time that no longer meets its required musical position.

When the choices cannot yet be performed and the task calls for developing them, [MDPE.10:4.6](#mdpe1046---learn-to-vary-accents-over-a-continuing-pulse) develops the needed capability from this construction. During an occurrence, use an already available variant within the agreed material. Omitting an optional tap, as in :4.5.1, can solve that occurrence's problem; a phrase that requires the tap still needs a means of performing it.

#### MDPE.11:4.6 - Direct-Method stop

An ensemble’s existing interpretation and rehearsal method identifies the score edition,
choices, performers, work, recording, limits and use of the result. Use it directly if
it answers the question. Return to `MDPE.11` where in-performance generation or the
relation among material, its description and the conditions of performance remains unclear.

### MDPE.11:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure it prevents | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material, description and performance | A score edit is credited as a change in performed interpretation. | Identify what changed in the score and use evidence of performance for the interpretation realized. Distinguish the material, bearer, performer, work and occurrence as the claim requires. |
| Prescribed and actual conditions | Specified contact is treated as an observed relation between partners. | Read the agreement or score for the prescription. Use suitable evidence of the named participants’ interaction to establish which relation actually held. |
| Preservation and variation | “Improvised freely” leaves a consequential constraint unclear. | State what was fixed, what the performer could vary and which facts, permissions or stop conditions mattered to the choice. |
| Direct domain Method remains primary | A generic pattern replaces music, dance, live-coding, partnering, or control practice. | Use `MDPE.11` only for material–Work integration. |
| Simultaneous methods | Concurrent contributions are taken to show a teaching sequence or that one method includes another. | Identify the concurrent contributions and establish any temporal order from the work. To show inclusion, identify the contribution that the narrower method supplies within the encompassing one. |
| Performance and a later development choice | Authority to choose a change is inferred from who performed. | Identify who performed. If a development choice matters, identify who held the authority and, for a past decision, what they decided. |
| The evidence fits the claim | A recorded image is interpreted as a direct measurement of pressure, felt control or audience experience. | State what the observation supports. If further evidence is needed, use a suitable existing source, seek a worthwhile observation or report the remaining limit. |
| Cost of keeping traces | Documenting each choice interrupts the performance. | Preserve the information the receiving question or subsequent use requires. |

### MDPE.11:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source or maintained result | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF `A.15.7` Situation-Responsive Work Steering | Choose the next action from current facts while preserving the field method, chooser, performer, authority, stop and feedback. | Use the relevant music or dance practice to identify material and the performance method. Evidence of the particular occurrence and what it realized comes from that performance. |
| FPF `A.15.1` Work, `A.2.1` assignment, and `F.6` attribution | `A.15.1` governs dated Work, the performing Agent as a sufficiently agentic System, enacted Method, containing System, and direct result relations; `A.2.1` governs a declared assignment species and obtaining occurrence; `F.6` governs performed-Work attribution through that assignment. | These results do not determine material, interpretation, occurrence, or presentation, and an assignment does not establish Work. |
| [Live Coding: A User’s Manual](https://livecodingbook.toplap.org/book/) and [Algorave guidelines](https://github.com/Algorave/guidelines/blob/master/README_en.md) | Running-code changes and improvisatory composition during performance; visible technical Systems and public conditions. | The sources describe heterogeneous practice, not one universal Method or one local application. |
| [Kloosterman and van Kempen, NDT production case](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccs.2026.100710) and `MDPE.5:4.2`, *Tell Your Mom You Love Your Skin* | The production team developed and rehearsed the work. NDT’s own film crew recorded the premiere. Outside critics reviewed the performance, and the case describes its archival use. | The case documents one production. Claims about its moment-by-moment interpretation need evidence of those particular actions. |
| [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon) | Robot generation and marimba playing, with human-led engineering and development. | Establish the timing of generation for the occurrence being attributed. Cultural authority is a further claim with its own grounds. |
| Drum-brush explanation in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants), drawing on Ed Soph, and the constructed Balboa case in :4.5 | Continuing movement with a perceptible event, a permitted change of articulation, the partner’s response and the performer’s next choice. | The analogy guides construction. The pair and observed actions are stipulated in the case. A claim about learning, exercise order or other pairs requires evidence at that scope. |

Use a direct field Method when it supplies the same result with less burden. Keep the material–Work distinctions that change the current action or evidence.

### MDPE.11:7 - Relations

- `MDPE.9` can supply material, a description, or a constraint specification for the performer's Work.
- Use `MDPE.10` to assess or develop performing capability. Use `MDPE.3` to identify or prepare the required configuration.
- `MDPE.5` helps the practitioner identify or present the performance occurrence. Use `MDPE.12` when the question calls for an observation or comparison.
- `MDPE.18` governs usable cultural memory and lineage when direct traces enter later continuation Work.
- Direct Music and Dance Methods govern subject Work. Current FPF governs general steering, Work, Method,
  description, evidence, and publication distinctions.
- This specialization uses applicable Systems Engineering and Method Engineering results when Systems or Methods
  are changed.

### MDPE.11:End

## MDPE.27 - End Voluntary Partnered Performance

> **Type:** Method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### MDPE.27:1 - Problem frame

Use this method when either participant wants a voluntary partnered encounter to end or when someone needs to establish how it ended. A track can continue after the dancers stop, a partner can offer another figure or contact can outlast the movement. When someone wants to stop, cease offering figures, preserve bodily support, release unwanted contact and make the wanted next action available where possible. The dance may already have stopped while a route out remains blocked.

In the ordinary case, each person supports their own weight and the pair has a familiar small movement or halt. In a lift, dependent lean or other action where one person supports the other, use a practised means of returning both to support. If the pair lacks that technique, obtain it before rehearsing a support-dependent ending.

MDPE.29 helps compose an ending from a physical relation or scientific image. MDPE.11 addresses how performers interpret or shape it during the dance. Use MDPE.26 if the pair needs a movement or transition for the stop, and MDPE.5 for floor and exit conditions. A pair can complete a final shape while one person is still being held, or end participation successfully midway through a track.

For a live ending, make the decision understandable while the partner can still change the next movement. Use the stopping action available to the pair. For a past encounter, start with the cue and response the evidence can establish.

An already completed ending can answer the practical or historical question. When developing that capability is part of the task, choose practice for the part that needs it. A choreographed finish concerns the form of the performance. The ordinary ending here assumes cooperative disengagement and the support conditions above.

### MDPE.27:2 - Problem

A person can decide to stop while the partner continues to offer another figure, a usable halt is missing, or contact continues. An announced finish or the end of the music can thus leave a participant physically engaged or under pressure to continue.

Connect the decision to what participants can do in their present movement while preserving support and choice. A missed cue, an unavailable stopping movement and an obstructed exit call for different contributions. When the question is historical, determine which of these conditions mattered in that encounter and how far the evidence goes.

### MDPE.27:3 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Planned form and present choice | A musical endpoint can guide both dancers while they want to continue. A participant’s decision to stop withdraws agreement to further figures at once. The partner needs a usable cue to act on a decision they have not yet perceived. |
| Prompt release and bodily support | End unwanted continuation promptly. If one dancer is supporting the other, use the practised disengagement needed to return both to support. |
| Courtesy and autonomy | Acknowledgement can clarify the ending. Further contact or an escort must be wanted by both. Either can stop or decline without giving a reason. |
| Personal action and provision | A dancer can practise a signal or stop. Space to leave depends on the actual floor and traffic. |

### MDPE.27:4 - Solution

For an ending, connect the decision to stop, a movement that preserves support, release and an available onward action. For an account of an ending, identify the events and conditions relevant to the question, including any delay between release and the next action. Stopping movement, releasing contact and taking the next action can overlap.

#### MDPE.27:4.1 - Construct the ending from the present situation

Begin with the decision that affects the next movement. A chosen musical endpoint guides preparation while both people want to continue. Either person can decide to stop now. Use a signal the partner can perceive and understand in time to change the continuation.

For the ordinary case, connect these actions:

1. **Make the finish legible.** Stop offering new figures. While the partner can still change the next action, say “Let’s finish at the end of this phrase” or, for an immediate ending, “I need to stop now.” A previously agreed signal can convey the decision when the partner receives and recognizes it in time. Slowing alone could look like preparation for another figure. Acknowledge a partner’s request to stop and act on it immediately.
2. **Use the stopping action available now.** Reduce travel or use the pair’s familiar small transfer or halt while avoiding surrounding dancers. Keep just the movement needed to settle and disengage. In a support-dependent action, use the practised return to support. Waiting for a favourite figure or the end of the song would extend the encounter after the decision to stop.
3. **End contact and the expectation of continuation.** Release contact that is no longer wanted as soon as it is unnecessary for bodily support. A brief acknowledgement or thanks can clarify completion. Either person may then decline another handhold, an escort or further conversation.
4. **Choose an available onward action.** The person may stay where it is safe or take a clear route to a chosen place. If they want to leave and traffic blocks the route, wait clear of moving dancers where possible and leave when passage opens. The dance can already have ended while both people remain nearby.

The music, movement, contact and participation can end at different times. A usable cue lets the partner stop offering movement. Release contact when bodily support permits it, even if a person is still walking on their own support. A clear path permits departure. These actions can overlap. Act on a present decision at once, allowing the movement needed for physical disengagement.

If someone prevents release or departure when a participant wants to stop and the pair cannot disengage cooperatively, seek available assistance.

#### MDPE.27:4.2 - Practise a needed part of the ending

When practice is wanted, start with a short passage whose movement the pair can already perform. Include the ending and the onward action whose availability or execution they need to practise. Each person can choose to end, including during practice. Use a suitable observation of the whole encounter to select any correction. Where the question is what already happened, an adequate observation may complete the work.

| Observation | Contribution that may be needed | Return when practising |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One person stopped while the other offered another figure. | Check what cue the partner received and how they understood it. If the signal was unclear, demonstrate an audible or otherwise usable ending signal. | In a short passage, let a participant choose the ending with the support the task permits. Leave their own cue distinguishable from the teacher’s. |
| Both noticed the ending, but the stopping movement pulled one person off support. | Return to the available stopping action and its entry through MDPE.26. Reduce travel or change the preceding action if that makes the halt usable. | Restore the preceding passage and check both participants' support through the stop. |
| Movement ended, but a handhold drew the partner back or kept them waiting. | Practice ending the contact and making departure available. Distinguish a courteous optional offer from a continued demand. | Include release and each person's onward action in the next complete attempt. |
| Both were ready to leave, but the arrangement blocked the exit. | Use a suitable available route. If another provision is needed, use MDPE.5 to arrange it with whoever can change the floor or exit. | Establish whether the route is usable in representative traffic, using adequate existing evidence or a suitable trial. |

Give feedback on the specific action that needs practice, then let learners use it in the whole passage. If the intended use changes the music, request time, partner or exit, use an adequate existing observation or try that condition when needed. Use a participant’s account to report what they perceived. Compare it with their action when the connection between perception and action matters. To establish that a dancer’s own cue was usable, distinguish it from a teacher’s gesture that the partner may have followed.

### MDPE.27:5 - Archetypal Grounding

Lena and Omar can perform a short side-to-side passage and stop with their weight on their own feet. At a social evening Lena wants to finish after the present phrase. She reduces her movement, but Omar reads that reduction as a pause before a new turn. He offers the turn and she follows reluctantly. The difficulty is the information connecting her decision to his next action.

In an agreed practice attempt Lena says, “Let’s finish at the end of this phrase,” while Omar can still change the continuation. He acknowledges her, stops offering the turn and uses their familiar small stop. They settle, release hands and each looks for a clear way off the floor. The DJ has mixed directly into another track, and their encounter has ended. Further dancing together would require their continued willingness.

In the changed attempt, Omar asks to stop halfway through the phrase. Lena drops the planned endpoint. They use the available stop, settle and release. Another pair briefly occupies the way to the edge, so they wait clear of its movement and then depart. The request ended the planned continuation, and traffic delayed their departure after release.

These observations can complete an account of the two endings. If Lena hears a future request but cannot enter the stop from a travelling action, the transition is a target for practice when she wants to develop it. An account may identify a persistently blocked exit. If a usable exit is required, look for suitable existing provision or involve whoever can change it.

### MDPE.27:6 - Bias-Annotation

Either participant can end this voluntary encounter. A usable signal, bodily support and conditions on the floor affect how the pair can disengage and where either person can go next. Identify separately when the music, movement, contact and participation ended. Use a modest available stop at the time it is wanted. During practice either person can stop the attempt, and what the pair demonstrated applies under the conditions actually tried.

A community's customary thanks or hand-connected exit can be useful without governing every participant. Preserve a person's ability to end that contact or choose a different onward action.

### MDPE.27:7 - Conformance Checklist

For an account of the ending, examine evidence of the finishing decision, cue, offers of further figures, bodily support, contact and available onward action as far as the question requires. A witnessed or filmed release can settle when contact ended. If the question is what the partner understood, seek evidence of their response or experience. Where traffic delayed departure, establish whether participation had already ended.

To assess the learner’s own cue or stop, distinguish what the learner supplied from a teacher’s help. Interpret a changed partner, time or exit under its actual conditions. Use evidence of the relevant performance to claim that an ending occurred.

### MDPE.27:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Misreading | Consequence and repair |
| --- | --- |
| Finish the phrase before honouring a stop. | Honour the present choice immediately and use the stopping action available. |
| Release every contact instantly, whatever its role. | A lift or dependent lean needs its practiced disengagement. Obtain the technique before attempting the action if the pair lacks it. |
| A good final shape proves the encounter ended. | Check whether the demand ceased, unwanted contact ended and each person had an onward choice. |
| Rehearse the participant when the exit is missing. | Identify a usable route or have the responsible organizer address the obstacle. |

### MDPE.27:9 - Consequences

The dancers can prepare or perform a complete voluntary ending. A teacher can focus practice on a particular cue or movement, an organizer can address an obstructed exit, and an observer can establish what happened in a previous ending. Evidence of the person’s performance can establish ability under those conditions. To claim that they acquired it, establish the change from their earlier capability.

A prompt stop may change an intended artistic phrase. A supported disengagement or a crowded path may take time. Deliberate restraint calls for assistance, and a support-dependent stop calls for a technique appropriate to that action.

### MDPE.27:10 - Architectural Rationale

The decision governs further voluntary participation. The way each person is supported constrains which disengagements are feasible. They can acknowledge a stop at once while using the particular movement required.

When a cue was missed, examine how it was given and received. When the pair had no suitable halt, examine their movement and the entry into it. When traffic blocked the path, examine the provision. An account can establish any of these causes. If a change is wanted, direct it to the relevant participant, teacher or organizer.

### MDPE.27:11 - SoTA-Echoing

[WSDC's Social Etiquette](https://worldsdc.com/social-etiquette/), updated in 2019, discusses a considerate floor exit, thanks and stopping when uncomfortable or at risk. The custom of leaving the floor hand in hand can serve participants who both want that contact. The [Victoria Latin Dance Association's code](https://vlda.ca/about/code-of-conduct/) permits ending participation for any reason and calls for clear communication. [Section 2.1 of NAWCSA’s code](https://www.northalabamawcs.org/code-of-conduct) requires participants to honour a request to stop immediately.

Use MDPE.26 for the stopping movement and its transition, MDPE.5 for the floor or exit, and MDPE.10 when a participant wants to learn a missing part. These connections let a teacher help the participants practise through release and a freely chosen next action. Lena and Omar illustrate the construction. Its effectiveness as instruction would require evidence from learners.

A description can support preparation or recognition. To establish what a particular pair did, examine evidence of the cue, joint action, support, contact or departure relevant to the question. For a claim about what a partner felt, use evidence of that person’s experience. A discriminating response or their account can show what they understood. To claim capability under changed conditions, use suitable observations of the pair under those conditions. Recheck only the contribution affected by a different support relation, communication channel or floor arrangement.

### MDPE.27:12 - Relations

- Use MDPE.26 to establish or construct the stopping movement or transition. Either participant already has the right to end the encounter.
- Use MDPE.5 to establish which floor or exit provision was available, or to obtain a usable route when one is needed.
- Use MDPE.10 for a question about performing capability or to plan wanted practice for a specific cue or movement.
- MDPE.11 governs interpretation and live shaping; MDPE.29 supplies composed movement from a physical relation or scientific image when that is the source of the wanted ending.
- MDPE.28 concerns an invitation declined before the proposed encounter, with a different next-action problem.

### MDPE.27:End

## MDPE.28 - Receive a Declined Invitation and Find an Available Next Action

> **Type:** Method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### MDPE.28:1 - Problem frame

Use this method when an invitation to voluntary partnered performance is declined. The inviter may need to stop asking or find a wanted continuation. An inviter, observer or other practitioner may also be asked what happened in an earlier exchange. Someone can acknowledge the answer courteously and still lack a way to take the break or other action they want.

End further pressure about this invitation. Where the inviter also wants a next action, identify one that is available, help them take it if they wish, or establish the particular obstacle. They can remain disappointed throughout. A question about a change in the intensity or duration of that feeling needs its own evidence and, if help is wanted, suitable means.

This method concerns ordinary voluntary participation and practice. The invitation can end, and each person can choose whether to accept further contact or help. If participation is obstructed or someone prevents disengagement, use an available way to get clear or obtain suitable assistance when needed.

In the encounter, acknowledge the refusal and stop making that invitation. If you want a next action, identify it and what it requires. For a past exchange, use the relevant answer and subsequent conduct to establish what happened.

Take an already available continuation if you want it. A courteous ending, listening where you are or leaving can complete the task while the feeling persists. MDPE.27 applies when partnered performance has already started. If the person wants help with distress, obtain help suited to that aim. A question about their past experience may be answered from an appropriate account.

### MDPE.28:2 - Problem

An etiquette rule can call for accepting a refusal. In an actual encounter the inviter may need to stop bargaining or find the conditions for a wanted next action. A person can repeat the polite reply and still wait beside the partner for another answer.

Check where the obstacle lies. Someone who already accepted the refusal may still need a place to rest or willing support to get there. Outward compliance establishes the observed conduct. A claim about disappointment requires evidence about the person’s experience.

### MDPE.28:3 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Independent choice and desired company | An inviter may want to dance, and the invited person remains free to decline. |
| Answer and interpretation | The refusal concerns this invitation. Other people’s intentions, the invited person’s reasons and the inviter’s own worth are separate questions. |
| Action and feeling | A wanted action can become usable while disappointment continues. |
| Support and choice | A willing helper can make an action available. The inviter can decline the offer, stay, leave or choose a different action. |
| Rehearsal and event conditions | A voluntary role-play can show how someone responds in rehearsal. A claim about use at a real event with emotional significance needs evidence under the relevant conditions. |

### MDPE.28:4 - Solution

End the invitation. If a continuation is wanted, identify what the person can do under the actual conditions. Take an already available action, obtain a missing contribution if wanted or state the limit. For an account of a past exchange, use evidence of the answer, subsequent conduct and support relevant to the question. Choose practice when the person wants to develop a learnable part of the task.

#### MDPE.28:4.1 - Let the actual answer end the invitation

For a clear refusal, acknowledge the answer briefly and stop making that invitation. “Okay” or “Thank you for letting me know” can be enough. Leave the person space to choose their next action. Asking for reasons as a condition of accepting the refusal, bargaining for a shorter dance or waiting for the answer to change keeps the demand in place.

An unclear answer leaves agreement to dance unestablished. Give the person room to decline or leave. A volunteered “maybe later” leaves a future possibility. A later invitation is a new choice. Starting a later partnered encounter requires agreement at that time. The inviter can choose another activity.

Follow the rules of the event. For example, NAWCSA:2.1 rules out asking the same person again during that song and directs the inviter to stop asking them that evening after several refusals. A later opportunity allowed by the local rule remains a choice for both people.

#### MDPE.28:4.2 - Obtain a next action from what is actually available

After disengaging, identify what the answer establishes. “Ren declined this invitation” states the event. “Nobody here wants to perform with me” adds a claim about other people. A reason Ren offered can be reported as Ren’s explanation. Otherwise leave the reason open where the evidence does.

Choose what you want and can currently do. You might listen, take a break, talk with someone who wants company, make another appropriate invitation or leave. Identify any place, means or permission the particular action needs. “Sit in the available chair and listen to the next piece” gives an action a person can take. A different invitation still gives its recipient an independent choice.

If the seat is accessible and you are free to use it, the break may already be available. Take it if you want to. A reliable observation or account of your taking the break can establish what you did, and you can decide again afterwards. If a wanted action remains beyond reach, identify what is missing. Disappointment may continue during a perfectly usable break.

#### MDPE.28:4.3 - Find out what help is wanted, available or needed

For a practical difficulty, find the condition that would enable the person’s wanted action. For a past exchange, use the relevant evidence about what the person could do, what they did and what help they used.

| Present difficulty | Possible action | Supported conclusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The inviter keeps asking after a clear refusal. | If the inviter wants practice, contrast an acknowledgement and disengagement with bargaining. Let them try the complete exchange. | Describe whether the invitation ended without pressure in the observed conditions. |
| The inviter wants another activity and has yet to choose one. | Compare available activities and let the person choose one they want. They can take it or change their mind. | The choice identifies a continuation. Its conditions establish availability, and evidence of performance establishes whether the person took it. |
| A wanted break or departure has no accessible place or route. | If a change is wanted, arrange it within your authority or request it from the provider who can supply it. The person may instead choose a suitable available alternative. | Verify the result that matters, such as an accessible seat, a clear route or the person’s actual movement. |
| The person knows the action and has access, but cannot begin it alone. | Ask whether they want support for that action. A willing companion might offer to walk to a seat, or an agreed reminder might mark the first step. | A completed supported action can establish what happened with that help. An unassisted action, a claim that the support made the difference, and a reduction in distress each need evidence about that result. |
| The wanted action remains unavailable with the help tried, or the person wants to reduce distress. | A person can end an exercise at any time. Ask which result they still want and whether they want help with it. | Report the actual limit of the participation method. For a claim about emotional change, use suitable evidence over the relevant period. |

A companion may be occupied or a reminder unhelpful. An inviter can decline support, stay to listen, choose something else or leave. Respect the first person’s refusal throughout. Any further help comes from someone willing to provide it.

If recurring events raise a question about access or exclusion, examine the arrangement through MDPE.25 and MDPE.5. Use evidence about that arrangement and its participants. Preserve each person’s freedom to refuse when changing event provision.

#### MDPE.28:4.4 - Choose practice and assess what happened

Use voluntary role-play when the learner wants to practise the invitation, response and subsequent choice. Both participants understand the purpose and can stop. Begin with the whole exchange so that a courteous sentence can be examined alongside any bargaining, obstruction or unavailable continuation.

Use a suitable successful attempt when it already answers the learning question. When a particular connection fails, demonstrate or discuss it, let the learner retry and return to the whole exchange. Vary the answer, time, partner or help when the question requires that change and existing evidence leaves it open. Give learners their own choice and keep any teacher cue visible. MDPE.10 and HCD.6/HCD.9 supply representative practice, assistance, feedback and return. The participation conditions here supply the domain criteria.

An observer can report the answer, whether pressure continued, the available space and the action taken. The inviter can report how they interpreted the exchange, what they wanted and how they felt. Suitable experience at an actual event can establish use under its uncertainty and emotional conditions. A role-play in which nobody felt disappointed can still show the outward interaction.

When the task is learning, agree on the aim with the learner. To establish that an action is available, examine the conditions that make it possible. To report actual use, examine the action and any support used. To assess a change in distress, use evidence about that experience over the relevant period. If the person wants help reducing it, choose an approach suited to that aim. A smile or a courteous reply alone leaves that change open.

### MDPE.28:5 - Archetypal Grounding

Alex invites Ren, who says “No, thank you.” Alex replies, “Why? Just one piece.” That response keeps the invitation open. In an agreed role-play, a teacher demonstrates a brief acknowledgement, stepping away from the exchange and leaving Ren free to choose what to do. Alex tries again and ends the invitation.

Alex then says, “That proves the evening is a failure.” The teacher and Alex distinguish Ren’s answer from that wider interpretation. Alex chooses to sit at the edge and listen to one piece. The seat is available, Alex takes the break and still feels disappointed. This establishes a continuation Alex actually used and preserves Alex’s account of the feeling.

In another attempt Alex knows the wanted action but stays near Ren rehearsing what to say. Alex wants help leaving the exchange, and a willing friend offers to walk together to the seat. They take the break. Alex could instead decline the offer and choose to stay and listen. If Alex still wants the break and cannot take it, identify what remains unavailable and ask whether Alex wants a different contribution.

Now suppose the usual friend is absent and the seating area is closed. Alex might ask an available volunteer about a place to pause, choose another wanted activity or arrange to leave. If none of the wanted options is usable, state that limit. The changed arrangement leaves intact the earlier observation that Alex acknowledged the refusal.

In a further exchange Ren volunteers “maybe later.” Alex keeps that possibility open and moves on. At a later appropriate opportunity, both a fresh invitation and a fresh answer remain voluntary. An attempt under those conditions can show what Alex did with the information.

### MDPE.28:6 - Bias-Annotation

This method concerns ordinary voluntary participation. Respect the refusal and the inviter’s choice about further help. Participant action, companion assistance and event provision are distinct contributions. A witnessed refusal, a reported motive, a performed action and an experienced feeling have different grounds. A supported break or departure can suffice. A voluntary role-play can show what the participants did. How far that observation supports a claim about capability depends on how well the task and available help represented the intended use.

State the relevant local convention about sociability, outward behaviour or repeated invitations. People may still experience the exchange differently.

### MDPE.28:7 - Conformance Checklist

For a claim that pressure ended, examine what the inviter did after the answer. For a question about continuation, establish the result it asks for. This may be the available options, the person’s choice or the action they took. Include any help or obstacle that bears on that result.

For a claim about past performance, use evidence of what the person did and under what conditions. For a claim about capability, assess how well those conditions represent the intended use. To establish that the person learned something, compare their contribution with an appropriate earlier basis. An earlier observation can suffice when it covers those conditions.
