For a claim about distress, use evidence about that experience. A smile or outward compliance may be observed while its emotional meaning remains open. Report any continuing obstacle to the action the person wanted.

### MDPE.28:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Misreading | Consequence and repair |
| --- | --- |
| A possible reason for refusal is reported as the actual reason. | Report the answer and any reason the person gave. Where evidence of the reason is missing, leave it open. |
| A courteous reply proves the whole task is complete. | Inspect whether pressure ceased and, if the person wants another action, whether it is available. |
| The next action must be another invitation. | Let the person choose listening, rest, willing company, departure or another appropriate activity. |
| The refusing participant is expected to help the inviter recover. | End the demand. If help is wanted, seek a separately willing source of it. |
| Repeated staged refusals are credited with necessarily reducing distress. | Identify what was practised and observed. Use grounds suited to an emotional outcome before claiming it changed. |

### MDPE.28:9 - Consequences

The inviter can end the demand and identify a continuation, including listening where they are, leaving or asking for help. An observer can account for what actually happened. When training is wanted, a teacher can address the action the learner needs to develop.

Support may be unavailable. Report any particular unmet need and any voluntary action that was available or completed. A respectful ending can be a finished result while the inviter still feels disappointed.

### MDPE.28:10 - Architectural Rationale

Ending the demand releases the other person from further pressure over this invitation. It may leave the inviter with another question about a next action. Keeping the answer given separate from an interpretation helps the inviter choose on the basis of what the exchange actually established.

Examine whether the chosen action has any place, route or willing help it needs. A suitable observation can show actual use and reveal a missing contribution. Choose learning for a skill the person wants to develop. An action with permitted support can meet the aim.

### MDPE.28:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The community guidance in MDPE.27:11 concerns participation. WSDC describes accepting a refusal and offers possible reasons. NAWCSA limits repeated invitations and addresses outward behaviour, including pouting. VLDA preserves voluntary participation. Use Ren’s actual answer for Ren’s stated choice and evidence about Alex’s own experience for Alex’s feelings.

A polite reply followed by an end to the demand can settle the invitation while leaving the inviter without a usable next step. Identify what the person wants, whether the action is available and the contribution it needs. An offered arrangement can be considered with the person. Its use and its effect can then be established on their own evidence.

[Engelskirchen, Asbrand and Tuschen-Caffier (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-09565-z) studied online ostracism in 73 participants aged 14–21. Both groups had previously received instruction in noticing and allowing unpleasant thoughts and feelings, termed *acceptance* in the study. After exclusion, one group was prompted to use that approach for three minutes. The comparison group reflected on profiles without a specific emotion-regulation instruction. The corrected group-by-time analysis left an affective advantage of the prompted application unestablished. A claim about adult dance invitations or other uses of acceptance would need evidence for those conditions.

Retain the respectful response, the conditions for a wanted action and the evidence of any emotional result each within its scope. When local rules, support or evidence about a proposed means of help change, reconsider the action or claim that depended on them.

### MDPE.28:12 - Relations

- MDPE.27 supplies ending an encounter already in progress.
- MDPE.5 helps identify existing event provision or arrange missing access to a place, route or help.
- Use MDPE.10, HCD.6 and HCD.9 when the person wants representative practice, feedback and another attempt under the participation conditions here.
- MDPE.25 examines recurring participation arrangements when evidence concerns exclusion or reciprocity beyond one declined invitation.
- MDPE.12 helps establish what could be observed, what a participant reported and what additional evidence a stronger claim would require.

### MDPE.28:End

## MDPE.5 - Integrate Production and Presentation for Performed Music-or-Dance Work

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance production-and-presentation integration pattern
> **Public result:** Depending on the task, develop a feasible arrangement for one bounded music or dance performance, establish what happened and what was available, or deliver the performance with the production it requires. Identify any relevant containing event, artifacts and limits.

### MDPE.5:0 - Use This When

Use this method when the way production and presentation fit together matters to a music or dance
performance. The question might concern a proposed event, a performance you are preparing to give or a
past occasion. Identify what the performers, partners or audience need from the occasion. Examine how
the venue, sound, recording, access, safety, publication and operating arrangements affect the musical
or participatory relations they rely on. A suitable earlier result can already establish the answer.

A costume can fit its wearer and still block a turn. A camera can capture the
stage yet omit the change to the code that produced a sound. At a dance the sound
system can operate as specified while dancers lose the cue for a weight change.
A venue can admit spectators while giving them no space to join in. In each case
the production question concerns what the combined arrangement lets someone do.

Start with one intended or past performance, its performers and recipients. Name the relation that matters, such as
hearing a response in time, and what existing results establish about it. Depending on the commission, deliver the performance, propose a feasible arrangement, or report a supported finding
or a specific limit when it answers the request. Name the remaining integration question when there is one.

Use performance, social-dance, event, stage, venue, sound, lighting, recording, streaming, accessibility,
safety, publication and operations practice for their own results. Here their results meet in a concrete
question. Can this camera angle show the collaboration, or did the dancers hear the cue with this sound
and floor arrangement? Where one established way already gives the required answer, use it directly.

Other questions have direct methods.

- Use MDPE.9 to develop or compare candidate forms. For interpretation, improvisation and material created in performance, use MDPE.11.
- Use MDPE.10 to assess or develop performer capability and MDPE.3 to establish how performers and their means work together.
- If one production method already gives the arrangement, performance or access finding the
question calls for, use its result. Retain any relevant conditions, artifacts and limits.
- Use an applicable specialist result for a venue, safety, platform, organizational or operational question. Obtain further help if the needed result is missing.
- For observation and comparison use MDPE.12. Use MDPE.23 to assess recognition,
MDPE.13 for a recurring recognition and selection arrangement, or MDPE.19 for cultural continuation. Use this method for the production arrangement itself.

### MDPE.5:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

The subject is one bounded music or dance performance. An actual performance is U.Work by the performers who enact the relevant music or dance method. A soloist, pair, ensemble or an autonomous robot can perform. In planning, specify the intended performance and the conditions on which it depends.

A score or choreography specifies material. Rehearsal can show what someone did under rehearsal conditions. A configured instrument or a
capable performer can support a future performance. To report that the performance took place, use evidence of the occasion. A recording,
stream or publication can provide such evidence and have its own use. A series, style or continuing cultural practice has a different extent.

Production, venue operation, recording, moderation, curation and publication can require separately identified
Work. Their distinct Methods do not by themselves establish distinct occurrences: one Work may enact several
Methods, or a separately identified occurrence may constitute, overlap or support another. Recover the actual
performers, extent, contribution and results when the distinction changes production or attribution.

A concert, party, milonga, competition, festival, class, exhibition or online session can coordinate several performances.
Identify the particular performance within the event when the distinction matters. At a social dance both partners
perform and receive one another’s actions. A question about their communication can arise without an audience.

Distinguish three questions when reading a production report.

- **Readiness.** A rehearsal demonstrates work under rehearsal conditions. To establish that the intended performance took place, use evidence of its execution on that occasion.
- **Recording.** A file, photograph, sensor trace or stream can document aspects of the performance. Identify the event it represents and what it records.
- **Access and response.** Admission and view counts can establish access or a counted use. An
inference about recognition, artistic value, selection or retention needs grounds for that particular judgement or activity.

A venue, camera angle, competition format or platform measure can change movement,
sound, interaction or access. Describe the effect and any trade-off and, if a choice is needed, identify
who has authority to make it. Judge a party, jam, battle or improvised duet by what
its participants need. A stage-front view suited to theatre can miss their exchange.

### MDPE.5:2 - Solution

Connect the production arrangement with one identifiable music or dance performance and the use in question. Work from its requirements when planning. In performance, coordinate the contributions on which the music or dance depends. Use evidence of the occasion when reporting what happened.

#### MDPE.5:2.1 - Identify the performance and the use in question

Identify the following details as the question requires.

- The intended or past music or dance performance and any larger event needed to identify it.
- The performers and the music or dance method used or specified for them.
- The partners, participants, audience, recording users or other recipients relevant to the use.
- What the recipient needs to be able to do, such as join the dance, hear a rhythmic relation, see a
process or use a recording. For a past use, ask what the arrangement made possible and what happened.
- The musical, movement, interaction, authorship or participation qualities that matter to that use.
- Where relevant, who may make artistic or safety decisions, what permissions apply and who may refuse or stop.

Choose an extent that fits the question. A festival organizer may coordinate a
programme of several performances. A pair can investigate one dance at a party.
A recording team may trace one take into a later release. Identify the relevant
performance even when the production decision covers the containing event.

#### MDPE.5:2.2 - Find the specialist results relevant to the use

Determine which specialist results apply to the performance’s time, material, performers,
conditions and use. For example, consider the following when they bear on the question.

- Material or an interpretation proposed for a performance, or evidence of what the performers enacted on a particular occasion, through MDPE.11.
- Evidence of the capability needed or shown, from MDPE.10, and an account of the performing arrangement, from MDPE.3.
- A venue, floor, medium, sound, light, costume, prop, instrument, recording, stream, access, safety, permission,
  operating, or publication result from the practice that supplies it.

A plan can establish proposed placement or the conditions needed for access. Use evidence of provision or performance for a claim that the arrangement was in use or that the event occurred.

#### MDPE.5:2.3 - Examine how production choices affect the performance

Examine a production choice where it matters to the performer or recipient. The relevant question may
already be answerable from a drawing, operating limit or observation. Examples include the following.

- Can performers hear, see, feel, or predict the cues their Method needs?
- Does costume, prop, instrument, stage, floor, latency, or camera position change feasible movement or timing?
- Does the arrangement preserve partner response, improvisation, visible process, spatial relation, or performer
  control when one of these carries the intended meaning?
- Can intended participants enter, understand conditions, take part, refuse, and leave safely?
- Does recording or streaming preserve the relation needed by its later use, or only a visually or audibly
  convenient fragment?

Describe any conflict in terms of the music or dance it affects. When a choice is needed, compare feasible
alternatives and identify the relevant artistic authority, safety requirement, permission and participant rights.

For an ending or invitation to voluntary partnered performance, [MDPE.27](#mdpe27---end-voluntary-partnered-performance) helps identify how the dance ended and [MDPE.28](#mdpe28---receive-a-declined-invitation-and-find-an-available-next-action) how a declined invitation was received. A record of the exchange may show that the partners disengaged, yet the exit remained blocked. Examine the floor, a place to pause or available support when the practical question concerns event provision.

#### MDPE.5:2.4 - Assess how the combined arrangement serves the intended use

First examine the available layout, earlier rehearsals and observations for the stated conditions. They may establish compatibility, identify a conflict or leave a specific question open. For that question, compare what a rehearsal,
sound check, floor trial, costume run, camera or network test, or access walk-through could establish with the cost of obtaining it. Use a representative test when justified and feasible, with the required safety and permissions.

A floor trial may show whether dancers could change direction at the intended density. A sound check can reveal whether a performer hears a cue
at event volume. A camera test can show whether the frame includes the live code, and an existing recording can show whether the rhythmic event
required for a later lesson was captured. Claims about what an audience saw or a learner understood need evidence about those recipients.

Report what the available evidence establishes under its conditions, including the result of any probe. A production decision can use that finding alongside the artistic and practical requirements. The authorized decision maker may accept the arrangement, request a change or stop.

#### MDPE.5:2.5 - Carry out the performance or establish what happened

When delivering the performance, coordinate the performers’ music or dance work with the operation of the agreed production arrangement. Respond to conditions during
the work within the relevant scope of authority. A plan specifies intended actions. A missed cue, an unsafe floor or someone declining
to continue can change what should happen next. To study an earlier occasion, examine its records and other suitable evidence.

For an account of the occasion, identify what the evidence supports about the matters in question.

- the performed Music-or-Dance `U.Work` occurrence, performers, material or interpretation, and actual conditions;
- the containing event or production relation, if it matters;
- The conditions under which intended participants or audience members could encounter the performance, and any use that was observed.
- direct artifacts such as recordings, programme items, photographs, code states, or sensor traces;
- any later release or publication Work, and what it made available to whom;
- Departures from the plan, connections that failed, the limits of the available evidence and any decision still needed.

To report attention, response, recognition, selection or cultural continuation, use evidence
about that result. Opening access can already answer a question about what was available.

If the intended performance was cancelled, identify the occasion and the evidence of cancellation. If a stream was inaccessible,
a recording unusable or the floor unsafe, state what this prevented and what is known about why. That finding can finish
the report. If someone is considering another performance, identify the conditions it would need and who can act on them.

### MDPE.5:3 - First Useful Result

> **Production and presentation result**
>
> - **Performance and use.** Identify the bounded intended or past performance, its period or occasion and what recipients needed from it.
> - **Performers and method.** State who is to perform or who performed and the relevant music or dance method.
> - **Relations to preserve or investigate.** Name the musical, movement, interaction, authorship or participation relation that matters for the use.
> - **Production basis.** Identify the specialist results that apply under these conditions and what they establish about the combined arrangement.
> - **Any unresolved connection.** Identify any remaining uncertainty. If a trial was used, describe what it showed under its conditions. Record any consequent choice and who made it when relevant.
> - **Result requested.** For a design, give the proposed arrangement and its grounds. For a past occasion, report what took place, including a cancellation if established. For performed work, identify the performance, material and actual conditions.
> - **Access and use.** State what the arrangement made or can make available. Distinguish delivery from participation, listening or other actual use. Report each to the extent established.
> - **Event, artifacts and publication.** Relate any containing event, recording or later release to the performance where relevant.
> - **Limits.** Name any blocked use or unsupported conclusion. If a future attempt or decision is requested, give the conditions it needs.

### MDPE.5:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.5:4.1 - *The Call*: a human–AI choral medium

In *The Call*, Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst and their collaborators worked with fifteen UK community choirs. The
choirs sang shared musical material, and the project team recorded them using its protocol. The recordings contributed to a dataset for bespoke
models. The spatial audio installation used those models to make a human–AI choral experience available to visitors. An account of this
production traces how the singing, recording and model training contributed to the installation.

The choirs’ performances, their recordings, the dataset, the trained models and the exhibition are identifiable results. The project account can establish their roles in this case.
Comparative cost, recognition of a style, a production method’s wider applicability and cultural continuation each require evidence about those questions.

#### MDPE.5:4.2 - `TYMYLYS`: a modern-Dance production

The NDT production of *Tell Your Mom You Love Your Skin* combined a guest choreographer and design team, dancers,
costume and technical capabilities, suppliers, venue, final rehearsal, film, archive, and touring constraints.
Costume and hanging wooden elements had to meet aesthetic, movement, material, robustness, and transport needs.
Final rehearsal integrated light, sound, stage, and Dance before the premiere.

The choreographer Alan Lucien Øyen, the dancers, costumers, lighting and sound teams, stage crew and other contributors supplied different parts of the
production. The question here is how their combined work affected what the dancers could enact and what spectators could encounter. The
company’s film and archive document aspects of the production. Critics’ reviews and the artistic director’s judgement provide material
for MDPE.12 when the question concerns observation or evaluation. Touring, organization and operations retain their own requirements.

#### MDPE.5:4.3 - A social-dance integration trial

In this constructed example, a weekly West Coast Swing organizer must decide whether to open the next party at the planned floor density after moving to a smaller
room. In this case the usable floor is eight by ten metres. The intended Music-or-Dance Work is one representative three-minute pair dance inside the party. The
partners must be able to hear the timing, maintain partner-readable response and their slots, adapt movement to
nearby pairs, decline any figure, and leave safely.

The partners use their West Coast Swing method, the DJ supplies music and playback, the venue
supplies the room and electricity, and the organizer provides for conduct and emergencies. WSDC
guidance addresses slot orientation, adaptation, partner attention, refusal and safe stopping.
CDSS guidance covers floor, capacity, sound, access, equipment, staffing and contingency. In
this case those sources leave open whether the pairs can hear the timing and use their slots
safely together at the expected density. The organizer chooses a representative trial.

During a representative floor trial, ten volunteer pairs dance to the planned track at event volume. In the first
configuration, pairs at the far side report losing the pulse, two slots repeatedly cross the traffic line, and
several dancers shorten movement enough to break the intended elastic response. The organizer refuses the
planned configuration and realizes a specific alternative. A two-metre-wide passage along the ten-metre side
leaves a six-by-ten-metre dance area. Six pairs use two rows of three slots oriented along its long dimension;
the other four pairs wait off the floor. The speakers are re-aimed toward the far side while the planned track
and event volume remain. In the second three-minute trial, the representative pair completes the track with
readable timing and elastic partner response, and observers report no slot crossings between pairs or into the passage.
The successful three-minute result applies to the combined sound arrangement, placement and six-pair density. To isolate the
effect of changing speaker direction or pair density, a comparison that distinguishes their contributions would be needed.

The pair performed the dance under the second arrangement. The first trial coordinated ten pairs, the
second six. The sound-check record,
floor sketch and video can document different features of the event.
The result covers the conditions observed. Claims about artistic value, recognition
across the scene, long-term safety or cultural continuation call for evidence about those outcomes.

For the next party the organizer retains the tested six-pair limit, passage, slot orientation,
speaker direction and volume. Fewer people dance at once, so waiting pairs need access
between tracks. Reconsider the choice if the room, music, sound, attendance arrangement or
incident reports change the grounds for expecting the timing and safe slot use to hold.

#### MDPE.5:4.4 - Algorave guidance without performed local Music Work

The Algorave guidelines can help an organizer prepare a programme and production brief. They address a dance-event
setting, sound, visibility of the algorithmic process, varied technologies, programme diversity, affordability,
conduct, access and community contact. A local event needs performers and collaborators, the means and authority
to use the venue, feasible costs and any necessary rehearsal. To describe a past event, use evidence from
that occasion. A request for a programme can finish when the local design and its conditions are established.

#### MDPE.5:4.5 - Recording and publication

A singer performs one studio take. The take is a performed Music `U.Work` occurrence; the audio file is a direct
artifact. Editing and mastering produce later artifacts. The chosen Music release/distribution Method makes one
master available for listening under stated access conditions. Keep that release activity, recording availability
and any later listening separate from the original take.

If an accompanying programme note says who performed the take or how the
master was edited, E.24.PUB helps describe publication of that claim-bearing
edition, its intended audience and its use. For a master released for
listening, use the music distribution result to establish availability.
Evidence of listening or recognition concerns what recipients actually did.

#### MDPE.5:4.6 - Shimon and its development team

When Shimon autonomously continues a composition and plays its marimba under the supported
conditions, the robot performs that bounded music work. People configure it, organize and
operate the concert and choose later changes to the practice. Producing, curating or selecting
later performances depends on the contributions and authority of whoever does that work.

#### MDPE.5:4.7 - Direct-Method stop

A small acoustic duo uses its established performance-and-venue method. The existing result identifies the
performers, material, room, permissions, safety, performance, recording, audience access and relevant limits. It
can answer a question about the concert or inform the next choice directly. Return to MDPE.5 when a change of medium,
participating group, specialist contribution or intended use leaves a question about the combined arrangement.

### MDPE.5:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What happened on the occasion? | A rehearsal, plan, event, file or programme is treated as the particular performance. | Identify the performers and interval. Use the records for what they establish about the performance, and identify any containing event and artifacts separately. |
| Intended use is visible | “Produce the show” hides what participants or audience members need. | State what they must be able to do and which artistic or participatory relations must survive. |
| Which production results already answer the question? | A general integration account repeats the choreography, sound, venue, safety, recording or operating practice. | Use the direct result. Examine connections when their combination matters to the music, movement or participation. |
| Who or what performed? | A performer, instrument and venue receive the same role in the account. | Identify the performer, pair, ensemble, robot or other agent and the method their work enacted. Describe equipment and support by what they provided. |
| Who can make a consequential change? | Venue approval is treated as the artistic decision. | Identify who can decide the artistic change, who is responsible for safety and what permission, technical limits and participant rights affect that decision. |
| How did participants contribute? | The account assumes a stage and passive audience for a social or participatory form. | Identify each contribution relevant to the question and what the evidence shows about its reception. For a paired dance, consider how the partners both performed and received each other’s actions. Name the containing event when it matters. |
| How does a recording relate to the performance? | The particular performance is identified solely as a file. | Distinguish the performance, recording, later publication and access. Use each as evidence for the claim it can support. |
| What did recipients do? | Counts of attendance or views are treated as recognition or value. | State the access or counted use they establish. If an interpretation of audience response is required, use the evidence about that response with MDPE.12. Use MDPE.13 when the question concerns recurring selection arrangements. |
| What did the failure establish? | A report of unavailability leaves the affected use unclear. | Identify the blocked use and report what is known about the missing condition. That can complete a report of a cancelled event. If a renewed attempt is contemplated, state what it would require. |
| Does the integration method add anything? | A direct production method already gives everything needed. | Use the existing result. |

### MDPE.5:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source or maintained result | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, *The Call*, Serpentine](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | Herndon, Dryhurst and their collaborators worked with fifteen UK community choirs. Recordings of their singing supplied training data for models used in the exhibition’s spatial audio installation. | The source documents this production. | [Kloosterman and van Kempen, NDT production case](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccs.2026.100710), *Tell Your Mom You Love Your Skin* | The authors describe how choreography, costumes, suspended set elements, light, sound, venue, rehearsals, film, archive and touring requirements affected one dance production. | The well-resourced NDT case shows how these contributors worked together. To rank its artistic result or generalize across other productions, use evidence relevant to the comparison. |
| [Algorave guidelines](https://github.com/Algorave/guidelines/blob/master/README_en.md) | Organizers can build a programme and brief for setting, sound, visibility of the algorithmic process, variety, affordability, access, conduct and contact with the community. | The completed local brief can answer a planning request. The performers, rehearsal, event, response and continuation each require the arrangements or evidence appropriate to the local case. |

Establishing who selected the programme, whether a style was recognized or whether a practice continued requires evidence about that particular claim. |
| Yamaha, [*Seven Ways to Ensure a Smooth Sound Check*](https://hub.yamaha.com/proaudio/livesound/seven-ways-to-ensure-a-smooth-sound-check/) (2022) | The engineer and performers can prepare an input list and stage plot, communicate during setup, save a console scene, check monitor and house mixes, listen in the room and use a show checklist. | A completed sound check can establish particular signal or listening conditions. A conclusion about an artistic relation or the performance and its use depends on what was actually checked or observed. |
| World Swing Dance Council, [*Social Etiquette for Swing Dancers*](https://worldsdc.com/social-etiquette/), and Country Dance and Song Society, [*Community Culture and Safety Toolkit*](https://cdss.org/wp-content/uploads/resources/ccs-toolkit/CCS-Toolkit-Full.pdf), especially Part 5 (2024) | WSDC addresses partner attention, floor conduct and safe use of a shared floor. CDSS gives organizers ways to examine access, acoustics, sound, capacity, staffing, equipment safety, responsibilities and contingencies. | The guidance helps prepare an event. Assess a particular pair’s timing, their performance, its artistic value or safety across the community from evidence with the corresponding coverage. |
| Los Angeles Department on Disability, [*Accessible Public Meetings and Events Toolkit*](https://resources.disability.lacity.gov/guidance/events) | Plan accommodations for performers and audiences, captions, transcripts, audio description, accessible media and technical checks. Correct recorded or streamed material where necessary. | An accommodation can establish access to a particular feature. To assess whether the musical, movement or participation relation survived, examine the arrangement or the material. For actual recognition or value, use evidence about its recipients. |
| FPF A.15.1, A.15.7, A.22 and E.24.PUB | Identify actual work, steer it in response to conditions within the relevant authority, describe the relevant structure through constituents, relations, constraints and use, or account for publication of a claim-bearing edition. | Use the music or dance requirements to assess a production choice. Each general method contributes where the task needs its operation. |
| Systems Engineering, Operations Management and production practice | These practices can supply configurations, services, operating results, specialist evidence and performed work. | Use their results directly or examine the combination where the artistic or participatory use depends on it. |

The following examples connect specialist results with questions about one performance. Apply the available result directly
when it answers the question. Where several results must work together, examine their relation under the applicable conditions.

| Direct practice | Available result | Question about the combination | How to answer it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Live music sound checks and Algorave event programming | An input list, stage plot, checked signals and monitors, plus a programme and brief | Can recipients encounter the intended sound or see how a code change shapes it under the assembled conditions? | Use MDPE.5:2.3–2.5 to inspect the arrangement and existing observations. If an important condition remains uncertain and a trial is justified, test that condition. Use evidence of the occasion for a report of performance or reception. |
| WSDC social-floor guidance and CDSS event preparation | Slot orientation, adaptation, partner attention, freedom to refuse and stop, and provision for floor, access, sound, capacity, staffing, equipment and contingencies | At the intended density, can the partners hear the timing, read and respond to one another’s movement, and use their slot safely? | Under MDPE.5:2.4, use an applicable floor, sound or pair-work result. When their interaction still leaves an important question open, consider a representative check. Report the extent of any observation. |
| Accessible live, recorded and online provision | Accommodations, media forms, technical checks, captions, transcripts or audio description | Which relation does this recipient need and has the chosen medium preserved it? | In MDPE.5:2.1 identify the use. In MDPE.5:2.5 distinguish access to the relevant material from evidence of a recipient’s actual use or recognition. |
| NDT guest-choreographer production | A premiere and results from costume, set, light, sound, stage, touring, film and archive work | How did these choices affect what the dancers could do and the audience could encounter? | Use MDPE.5:2.2–2.4 to compare the relevant specialist results with the requirements of the dance and the available evidence from the production. |



Reconsider the integration method when a direct practice supplies the required result at lower cost, or when a representative performance challenges a condition on which the approach depends.

### MDPE.5:7 - Relations

- Use an established project focus and intended use. When the brief needs developing or reviewing, MDPE.1 can supply that work.
- MDPE.9 can supply candidate forms, MDPE.10 can assess or develop capability, and MDPE.3 can identify or design the performing arrangement.
- MDPE.11 can supply a proposed interpretation or material for a performance, a way to realize material while performing, or an account of what was realized on a past occasion.
- Use MDPE.12 when a question calls for observation or comparison of the performance, its artifacts
or the conditions under which it was encountered. Existing observations can supply that comparison.
- Use MDPE.13 for a question about a recurring arrangement for recognition and selection. Evidence of one presentation concerns that occasion unless other grounds establish recurrence.
- This specialization uses applicable Systems Engineering and Method Engineering results when an engineered
  System or Method is changed.

### MDPE.5:End

## MDPE.12 - Observe and Compare Music-or-Dance Performance and Cultural Results

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance observation-and-comparison pattern
> **Public result:** An observation or comparison that answers a question about a performance, a score or other artifact, a participant’s experience or a cultural result. State what the evidence establishes and use it in a decision when one is called for.

### MDPE.12:0 - Use This When

Use this method when a rehearsal, performance, recording, class, event, publication or change in practice
raises a question about its result. Applause, a sensor trace, a teacher’s approval, felt fluency, attendance,
a competition score, a platform count or a review can each answer a particular question. Identify what
it indicates before using it to judge the performance, someone’s experience or a cultural change.

Begin with the question the observation should answer.

> Identify the subject, the conditions and who or what could observe it. Use a comparison
> when the question requires one. State what the evidence establishes and any material limit.

For example, a teacher choosing a Balboa exercise can compare three instructions. Ask the
receiving partner which directions were clear or ambiguous and relate the account to the movement and
sound. A claim about wider recognition needs evidence of recognition in the relevant population.

A first result identifies the subject and question, the indication, its observer or instrument,
the method, the conditions and the representation. Give the finding, any comparison it uses
and any material uncertainty. If the result informs a decision, identify the choice it bears on.

Direct listening, movement analysis, participant observation, motion capture, sensing, judging, ethnography, corpus comparison, archival
inquiry and audience studies can supply observations or adequate conclusions. Use their results directly where sufficient. Use this
method when you need to distinguish or connect different kinds of evidence, observers or results for a practical or historical question.

Choose another method when it can answer the question directly.

- Use MDPE.5 to plan or deliver a performance and its production, or to investigate what was presented. An existing artifact or proposed version can be examined before a performance.
- Use `MDPE.11` to establish what material someone performed or changed during the work.
- Use a direct observation method when its existing result or ordinary application supplies the evidence, comparison and limits you need.
- Use `C.11` to choose among existing options when their evidential grounds are sufficient.
- Use MDPE.23 to assess or develop recognition capability, and MDPE.13 to
examine or redesign a recurring recognition and selection arrangement.
- Use the applicable FPF method when a general question about evidence, a characteristic or cultural evolution
  can be answered without a music- or dance-specific analysis.

### MDPE.12:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

A microphone can record sound, a camera can show movement and a force sensor can record
contact force. Each registers a different aspect of the performance. A dancer can report effort
or surprise. A partner can say when a cue became readable. A teacher, judge, listener,
curator or historian can interpret the indications their work covers. State who interpreted
them and how. An automated system can make an inference when it has the method and
means to do so. A plain sensor reading may already settle a question about force.

A technically precise performance may feel hard to its performer, be unreadable to a partner and
excite a listener. It can be rejected in one scene, promoted on a platform and disappear from the
repertoire. Identify the performer, population, relation and period for the result under discussion.

The following inferences need evidence beyond the indication named.

- onset detection becomes “good rhythm”;
- performer confidence becomes transferred capability;
- applause or attendance becomes recognition;
- competition rank becomes artistic value;
- the prominence of a practice in the press, citations, standards or university programmes is taken to establish its prevalence;
- platform visibility becomes cultural retention.

Institutional sources may give prominence to ballet, formal concerts, government standards or
widely publicised engineering methods. Adult dancers and commercial teams may practise
something else. To examine discourse or availability, those publications can be appropriate
evidence. To estimate actual use, look for observations relevant to the population and period.

A large controlled study can be costly or impracticable. Use the evidence already
available for the claim it can support. For a reversible choice, a practitioner’s
judgement or an expert estimate may suffice if its basis, uncertainty and reason to
reconsider are clear. An archive can also establish a particular past fact directly.

### MDPE.12:2 - Solution

State what you need to find out, then use observations that cover the relevant conditions. A recording can show an event and a participant can
describe their experience during or after it. Evidence of cultural continuation may accumulate over a longer period or already exist in an archive.

#### MDPE.12:2.1 - Start from the question and the claim

Identify the information that sets the scope of this inquiry.

- What the task asks about creation, performance, capability, production, reception, teaching,
practice development, continuation or a forecast. Name any decision that the answer is to inform.
- Who needs the result, when that affects its use. Identify authority or permission when the question concerns it or obtaining or using evidence requires it.
- The subject and the claim for which evidence is needed.
- The observation or comparison that could distinguish material alternatives, if more than one remains.
- The period the claim covers and the effort justified by the question.
- Whether the existing evidence is sufficient and what attainable further observation, if any, would justify its cost.

If the available evidence already answers the question, return that conclusion. If no attainable observation can
settle what remains, state the limit. Revisit a decision only when one is at issue and the limit matters to it.

#### MDPE.12:2.2 - Separate the subject, indication, and judgement

The **subject** is what the question concerns. It may be a past performance, a recording or score, the relation between
two movements, a rhythmic structure, performer capability, partner interaction, a recognition response or changes
in a practice over time. In a comparison of score versions, the notated structures can themselves be the subject.

An **indication** is a detected onset, force trace, coded movement, report, count or document used as evidence. Explain what it shows about
the subject under the available conditions. The same recording can be the subject of a comparison or evidence about the event it captured.

A **judgement** interprets the observations for the question or use. Identify the practitioner
or other capable evaluator responsible for an inference when attribution or competence matters.

Examples of observation families include:

| Observation family | What appropriate evidence can support | A further conclusion requiring its own basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical indication | Timing, pitch, kinematics, contact, latency or code state under stated conditions | The performer’s experience, partner interpretation, artistic value, recognition or uptake |
| Performer’s account or conduct | What the performer reported about effort, control, fluency, comfort, surprise or expression, or what their actions showed in the task | Transfer to other contexts, the cause of the experience or an audience’s response |
| Partner or participant response | What the participant perceived or did, the consent they expressed or withdrew, the timing they could read, and their experience of connection, difficulty or safety in that encounter | Population-wide recognition, stylistic legitimacy or safety outside the observed conditions |
| Practitioner judgement | A musician, dancer, teacher, judge, curator, historian or other qualified evaluator’s interpretation for a specified use | Authority over other participants or prevalence in a population |
| recognition observation | discrimination or identification by a named population in a stated task | selection, adoption, value, causal effect, or retention |
| cultural observation | transmission, copying, teaching, event use, amplification, persistence, transformation, or loss in a named practice and period | project authority, universal prevalence, or intervention effect |



#### MDPE.12:2.3 - Choose capable observers, instruments, and direct Methods

For each claim, ask:

- Who or what can access the relevant phenomenon?
- Which capability is needed to discriminate it?
- Which direct Method preserves the timing, embodiment, interaction, medium, population, or historical relation on
  which the claim depends?
- Did the observer perform, teach, judge, organize, participate, operate the platform
or develop the practice? How does their position bear on the interpretation?
- Which existing report, trace, coding scheme, instrument, corpus or interview answers the
question? If further evidence is needed, which observation or comparison could supply it?



#### MDPE.12:2.4 - Choose a representation that preserves the needed structure

Representations support different operations and hide different relations:

| Representation | Useful for | Frequent blind spot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| audio or acoustic features | timing, pitch, timbre, onset, balance, alignment | movement, effort, partner relation, experienced meaning |
| video or movement coding | path, geometry, visible articulation, coordination | pressure, proprioception, attention, some contact and effort |
| motion or force sensing | kinematics, contact, force, timing, repeatability | artistic interpretation without an argued bridge |
| notation, choreography description, or code | declared structure and version comparison | what performers enacted and participants encountered |
| interview, report, rating, or commentary | experienced meaning, control, judgement, recognition, reasons | recall, framing, demand, competence, and population limits |
| corpus, event record, platform count, or archive | availability, distribution, recurrence, and lineage clues | actual use, recognition, selection, value, and undocumented practice |

Notation, onset lists, interval vectors and geometric diagrams represent selected features of a rhythm.
For intervals between attacks, an onset sequence can suffice. To study brush continuity, weight arrival
or a pressure cue a partner can perceive, choose a representation that preserves that relation.
When the question concerns the notation itself, inspect the relevant marks and their timing rules.

For score study and rhythmic-form memory, [Score study and memory with timed vocal groups](#mdpe12431---score-study-and-memory-with-timed-vocal-groups) gives an entry to Makarome's method. It connects cells in a score to a timed spoken stanza, the larger phrase's organization and its use in rehearsal.

State the performer configuration, task, venue or medium, comparator, population, period, and access condition
whenever changing one could change the observation.

#### MDPE.12:2.5 - Obtain observations before interpreting them

Keep enough information to establish the following points where they bear on the claim.

- what was observed;
- by whom or by which instrument;
- through which Method and representation;
- under which conditions and time span;
- what direct indication or report was returned; and
- what source, artifact or qualified account supports the result, and what can be checked under the available access conditions.

Distinguish interpretation from observation. If a teacher judges a movement more readable, identify what supports the
judgement. It might be the receiving partner’s account, an observable continuation or a comparison under stated conditions.
Identify the evaluator’s relevant competence and make the evidence available to the extent the use requires and access permits.

#### MDPE.12:2.6 - Compare without inventing one universal score

Combine values directly only when the comparison relation is meaningful. Timing error can be compared across
trials under one definition. Partner readability, performer effort, safety, novelty, access, and cultural value
usually require several criteria, a trade-off, or a veto rather than one average.

Keep differences that change the conclusion or what someone can do with it. Examples include:

- audible onset, weight arrival, perceived beat location, and partner-readable pressure can disagree;
- a movement can be feasible for one body or prosthesis and unavailable to another;
- experts and new social dancers can recognize different distinctions;
- platform visibility and practitioner reproduction can move in opposite directions; and
- rhythm can persist while melody, movement, medium, teaching, or social meaning changes.

#### MDPE.12:2.7 - State the result's epistemic status

State what supports each claim and how it was obtained. These descriptions can apply together: a bounded study, for example, can combine direct observations with practitioner judgements.

- **Direct observation.** A person or instrument registered the indication under the stated conditions.
- **practitioner judgement** — an identified capable practitioner interpreted observations for one use;
- **bounded study result** — a study supports the claim for its population, task, Method, and period;
- **Expert estimate.** A suitably informed evaluator estimated a result on a stated basis. Report its uncertainty and the conditions under which it could be revised.
- **Open hypothesis.** An explanation remains possible. State what evidence could support or challenge it when that matters to the inquiry.
- **Unsupported claim.** Indicate what evidence or connection the claim requires and why the available material leaves it open.

An open hypothesis can guide a cheap, reversible probe. For costly, irreversible, potentially harmful or
population-wide action, compare what attainable further evidence could change with its cost and delay
(`C.11.DUA`). Consider a smaller step, narrower use or stop when uncertainty makes the proposed action
unacceptable. Applicable authority and binding conditions still govern the action.

#### MDPE.12:2.8 - Return the observation or comparison for its intended use

Give the subject and question, the relevant observations, their sources and conditions. Explain any comparison
or judgement the answer uses and state its limits. Use this account directly when it answers the request.
If it informs a further choice, identify what it contributes and the authority or consent needed
to act. Reconsider a finding if a change in its grounds affects the conclusion someone uses.

### MDPE.12:3 - First Useful Result

> **Observation or comparison result**
>
> - **Question and use.** What does the recipient need to know? If a decision depends on the answer, say which one and what evidence could matter.
> - **Subject and claim.** Identify the occurrence, artifact, structure, capability, response or cultural process in question.
> - **Observer or instrument:** [listener, performer, partner, teacher, judge, researcher, sensor, software].
> - **Direct Method and representation:** [what makes the phenomenon accessible and what it omits].
> - **Conditions, population, and time span:** [only distinctions that change the claim].
> - **Observations:** [indications and reports with provenance].
> - **Judgement or comparison, when needed:** [what the observations support; what the values can be compared on and which criteria remain distinct].
> - **Epistemic status:** [direct observation, practitioner judgement, bounded study, expert estimate, open
>   hypothesis, or unsupported claim, as applicable to each claim].
> - **Limit and further use.** State what the evidence establishes and what it leaves open. Name a further use, decision or reason to revisit the result when relevant.

### MDPE.12:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.12:4.1 - A Balboa-and-brushes comparison

In this constructed comparison a teacher must decide whether to keep articulation B as the next
brush-and-weight-transfer exercise without enlarging the step. The exercise concerns one pair’s performances
over repeated trials. A population claim or explanation of the cause would need additional grounds.

For this comparison the same recorded brush pattern supplies the audible timing reference in every trial. The three instructions call for the same small-step phrase and continuous movement. They ask the dancer to align a movement event with the recorded accent: **A — first floor contact, B — arrival of weight on the supporting foot, or C — change of travel direction**. To establish an achieved alignment, the observations must locate the corresponding movement event as well as the accent.

The observations below concern one pair at one tempo, using the same eight-bar phrase. The instructions were
given in random order.

- an audio trace gives the audible brush onset for each trial;
- side video gives visible foot placement and step size;
- the receiving partner reports an ambiguous direction in three of six A trials, none of six B trials, and two of
  six C trials; and
- the performing dancer reports similar effort for A and B but greater effort for C.

The teacher provisionally keeps instruction B for this pair and phrase. Its trials had the fewest reports of ambiguous direction,
the dancer reported effort similar to A and the video showed no larger step.
Randomizing the trial order addresses one possible order effect. The comparison does not establish whether
the performers achieved each specified alignment or what caused the difference in reports.

For the next class the teacher plans to test B with four unfamiliar partners under two music
conditions. Reconsider
the choice if the contrast fails with other partners or the audio–weight relation changes at
another tempo. Long-term learning and recognition of a style require evidence for those claims.

For variable-accent coordination in MDPE.11:4.5.2, identify the selected support events and requested accents, then locate the actual supports and accents against the same reference. Include the support following each accent. A recorded pulse can supply that reference. To establish regularity of the learner’s support, examine the events they produced. Sound can locate a free-foot accent, while visible loading and a receiving partner’s response can inform an assessment of weight arrival and continuation. Compare a changed accent sequence when the claim concerns variation beyond the practised figure. An existing receiving performance may provide the needed evidence for MDPE.10:4.6.

#### MDPE.12:4.2 - Direct Dance-observation Methods

Dance researchers can compare kinematics and directed influence, use coded observations and validate a
classifier, ask experienced improvisers to segment and rate a performance, or combine field observations with
participants’ accounts. Choose the method for the question. An observed movement relation, an audience’s
recognition, selection in a particular scene and transmission over time require evidence with different coverage.

For a question about contact force, a suitable force trace can give a bounded answer. For a participant’s meaning or a
contested interpretation, examine what they said or did and the conditions in which that expression occurred.

#### MDPE.12:4.3 - Comparative Music and rhythm-aware representation

Comparative-Music sources use listening, notation, acoustic features, coded corpora, macro-features and
rhythm-aware sequence comparison. McBride and Fitch's 2026 preprint uses a metrical grid for selected same-meter
Irish dance-tune parts before examining substitution, positional conservation and covariance. Finding related
pitch sequences and aligning their musically corresponding positions are different operations.

Consider a **constructed one-bar comparison** for a lesson about variation. Both monophonic versions use 4/4,
the same bar origin and octave, with one eighth note as the grid unit. The question is whether the second-beat
note moved or the first-beat note was subdivided.

| Version | Notated durations | Attack position, pitch and duration in eighth-note units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | D4 quarter, D4 quarter, E4 quarter, D4 quarter | (0, D4, 2), (2, D4, 2), (4, E4, 2), (6, D4, 2) |
| B | D4 eighth, D4 eighth, D4 quarter, E4 quarter, D4 quarter | (0, D4, 1), (1, D4, 1), (2, D4, 2), (4, E4, 2), (6, D4, 2) |

A pitch-only sequence is `D D E D` against `D D D E D`. A plausible leftmost alignment matches A's second D
to B's second D and treats B's third D as the insertion. It matches the pitches but pairs positions 2 and 1,
losing the metrical correspondence needed by the lesson. Another gap placement has the same pitch-match count;
changing a gap penalty cannot recover durations that the representation omitted.

For this comparison, retain attack positions and durations on the common grid. A's D at position 2 then
corresponds to B's third D at position 2; the two initial eighth notes in B fill the first quarter-note duration
in A. Keep the reattack at position 1 distinct from a sustained D at that position. A grid containing only the
sounding pitch at each instant would also lose that distinction.

The score versions retain the later attacks at the same positions. B subdivides the first-beat D by adding an attack at
position 1. That correspondence answers the notational question and can be used in the lesson. Historical descent,
performed timing, artistic value, audience recognition and a player’s experience each require evidence about that subject.

For these two versions of the bar, manual comparison using the common grid gives the answer. McBride and
Fitch’s rhythm-aware alignment can be useful for a larger compatible corpus. The source treatment
excludes grace-note detail, polyphony and changes of metre. This bar grid also omits expressive
timing. Choose a representation that preserves any such feature the question requires.



##### MDPE.12:4.3.1 - Score study and memory with timed vocal groups

To study how a longer passage hangs together rhythmically, a score reader, conductor or instrumental teacher can use Makarome’s [score-study exercise](https://ejournal.upsi.edu.my/index.php/MJM/article/download/814/550/1322#page=10), printed pp. 46–48. Take the score, familiar syllabic groups and a steady reference pulse. Assign a group to each rhythmic cell and preserve its complete duration, including rests. Recite the groups as a stanza against the pulse. Use their recurrence and expansion to explain the score and prepare rehearsal.

In the overture to *The Marriage of Figaro*, each underlined group in Makarome’s example fills one minim. *Takadimi* covers four eighth-note attacks. *Ta* covers a quarter-note attack and a quarter rest. The one-syllable and four-syllable groups therefore take the same total time. Figure 11 on printed p. 48 connects the groups with the score. Preserve the sound and rest in each span when reciting or demonstrating the correspondence.

The stanza lets the reader trace a one-bar opening, a two-bar development and a three-bar continuation. The phrase resolves at the start of bar seven. Use the groups to explain or recall that expansion. Consult the score for pitch, articulation and the sounding or silent portions, and return to it when preparing the instrumental passage or comparing a revised version.

If the score changes a cell’s duration or replaces sound with a rest, read its new timing and adjust the stanza where needed. A longer cell can shift the next entry with all the spoken labels unchanged. Use the published exercise directly for the score-study question. An appropriate observation can show what this learner recognized or performed. Use MDPE.23 when recognition itself needs assessment.

#### MDPE.12:4.4 - Institutional visibility versus actual practice

Suppose official standards, university courses, and professional press repeatedly name one engineering Method,
while project teams are observed using other Methods and reporting compliance in the official vocabulary. Or
suppose academic Dance literature is dominated by ballet while adult social-dance events are much more common in
everyday practice. The two source sets describe different cultural processes.

Use records suited to the population and period. Sparse documentation of an informal practice can leave its prevalence unknown. When a
large prevalence study is infeasible and an estimate will serve the purpose, identify the expert’s sources, population and uncertainty.

#### MDPE.12:4.5 - `TYMYLYS`: occurrence, reviews, and process judgement

NDT produced and premiered *TYMYLYS*. Accounts of the production, audience conditions, critics’ reviews and the artistic director’s judgement
concern different questions. Compare them for the question asked. An account of what reviewers reported can finish there. To decide
whether to retain a guest-team production approach, use the relevant findings. To establish cultural retention, examine later practice.

#### MDPE.12:4.6 - Shimon and Jason Barnes

Reports on Shimon and on Jason Barnes with a prosthesis can establish particular results about generation, actuation, control,
dexterity or coordination under the observed conditions. Identify whether Shimon, Barnes, the prosthesis or a development team
supplied each contribution. For a claim of transfer, compare a relevant prior performance with the one under altered conditions.

Media coverage establishes that those outlets published accounts of the performances. Recognition by a population, emergence
of a style or assignment of continuing cultural authority each requires evidence of that result.

#### MDPE.12:4.7 - Missing recognition evidence

Suppose a proposal claims a population will recognize a distinction. Guidance supplies example material, yet
the proposal identifies no relevant group, comparison task, transfer conditions or observations. Report that
limit. Use relevant earlier evidence if available and state the conditions under which it supports the forecast. MDPE.23 can help assess or develop
recognition, and MDPE.13 can examine or change a recurring selection arrangement when that is what the project needs.

#### MDPE.12:4.8 - Direct-Method stop

A musician’s listening and acoustic comparison method already identifies the recordings, listeners, competence,
conditions, representation, comparison, uncertainty and implications for the mix. Use that result. A further
comparison through MDPE.12 can help when the remaining question requires connecting distinct indications, observers, results or time periods.

### MDPE.12:5 - Checks and Common Repairs

| Check | Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What question does the evidence answer? | Material is collected because it is obtainable. | Identify what is already known and what a further observation could change. Stop when the answer or its evidential limit is sufficient. |
| What is the subject? | A reader infers a performance from its notation alone. | Name the phenomenon and the source that bears on it. For a comparison of two scores, identify the actual versions and the notated relation in question. |
| How does the indication support the judgement? | A raw sensor value is called artistic quality. | Name the indication and conditions, the inference and its evaluator. If a decision uses the result, explain how it bears on the choice. |
| Who observed and who performed? | A dancer’s report, an instrument trace and a software classification are assigned the same role. | Identify the contribution of each relevant performer, partner, listener, teacher, judge, sensor or processing system. |
| Direct Methods remain primary | The pattern becomes a universal evaluation Method. | Use Music, Dance, sensing, field, historical, and recognition Methods for their results. |
| Does the representation preserve the needed structure? | Onset positions are used to infer a continuous gesture or weight arrival. | Identify the feature or relation the operation requires and choose a representation that preserves it. For a timing comparison, specify the event being timed. |
| Do the values support the proposed comparison? | An average hides differences in criteria or scale. | Compare like measurements and preserve relevant trade-offs, limits, vetoes and distributions. |
| Does the evidence cover actual use? | Press coverage, a curriculum, attendance or views are taken as prevalence. | Identify the recorded publication, access or performance and its population and period. Give the basis and uncertainty for any broader inference. |
| Is further evidence worth obtaining for this use? | An estimate is presented as an established fact, or an expensive decision automatically triggers more research. | State what the evidence supports and respect any binding conditions. Obtain further evidence when its attainable contribution warrants its cost and delay. For an action, use a bounded judgement where adequate, narrow the action or stop (`C.11.DUA`). |
| Who may act on the comparison? | An evidential conclusion is treated as authority to act. | Give the findings when they answer the question. Where a decision follows, establish the relevant authority, consent and ethical conditions for the action. |

### MDPE.12:6 - Sources and Epistemic Boundaries

| Source or maintained result | Contribution used here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF A.10, C.17, C.29 and C.36 | Ground evidence, specify a characteristic claim, choose a representation or distinguish cultural-evolution processes, as the question requires. | Identify the music or dance subject, observers and observation method from the domain and the use. Reuse an established result where it suffices. |
| Tony Teck Kay Makarome, [*South Indian Konnakkol in Western Musicianship Teaching*](https://ejournal.upsi.edu.my/index.php/MJM/article/view/814), 2016, pp. 46–48 | Section 4.3.1 uses the author’s score cells, timed syllabic groups and stanza to study a passage and prepare rehearsal. | The article demonstrates the method and describes teaching experience. A particular learner’s recall or instrumental performance requires evidence of that task under the relevant support. |
| [Comparative musicology](https://doi.org/10.1093/9780191872303.003.0002), [Global Jukebox](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0275469), and [rhythm-aware melodic alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12673), discussed in the Architectural Reference | Listening, notation, acoustic, coded, macro-feature, and rhythm-aware comparisons. | Corpus and alignment results do not decide artistic value, investment, recognition, or current performance fit. |
| [Whitehead et al., spontaneous Dance interactivity](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1465595), discussed in the Architectural Reference | Whitehead and colleagues compared hand-movement measures, observers’ coding and the improvising partners’ segmentation and ratings of their own interaction. | The study concerns the seated hand-improvisation task it examined. Audience recognition, selection and historical transmission require evidence of those processes. |
| Timing examples in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) and the local Balboa cases | Distinctions among contact, onset, weight arrival, perceived rhythmic position, partner-readable pressure, and useful representations. | A design and observation basis, not evidence of universal improvement or transfer. |
| [Kloosterman and van Kempen, NDT production case](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccs.2026.100710), [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon), and the [Drumming Arm study](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561943); see §§4.5–4.6 | Creator reports, participant responses, critic judgements, process judgements, performance evidence, and later decisions remain separate. | No single case establishes whole-field prevalence, superiority, retention, or causal intervention effect. |

Where measurement or relevant literature is unavailable, an appropriately grounded expert estimate can support a limited use. Identify
the basis, uncertainty and any condition that would change it. When even an estimate lacks adequate grounds, state what remains unknown.

### MDPE.12:7 - Relations

- Use MDPE.5 when the task requires planning or delivering a performance and its production, or establishing what was presented under what conditions. An existing record or artifact can answer the relevant observational question.
- Use `MDPE.11` to establish what material the performers enacted, created or changed during the work when the observation depends on it.
- Use MDPE.10 to assess capability when evidence from representative performance bears on the claim. An existing observation may suffice. One fluent rehearsal shows what the performer did on that task with the assistance used.
- MDPE.23 can assess or develop recognition capability. MDPE.13 can
examine or redesign recurring arrangements for recognition and selection.
- MDPE.19 and MDPE.20 can use compatible observations to describe continuation, assess a possible
trajectory or inform a decision. Carry the relevant period and uncertainty into that use.
- This specialization uses applicable FPF evidence, characteristic, representation, and cultural-evolution
  results.

### MDPE.12:End

## MDPE.23 - Develop and Test Music-or-Dance Recognition Capability

> **Status:** Stable

> **Pattern type:** Music-and-Dance recognition-capability pattern
> **Public result:** A finding about a recognizer’s response or capability under stated conditions, a plan for developing or testing it, or evidence of what changed through practice. State the limits of the finding. Identify any change in the distinction, support or task that the intended use requires.

### MDPE.23:0 - Use This When

Use this method when you need to know whether a person, group or machine can recognize a musical, movement, rhythmic, interaction or stylistic difference
under specified conditions. The question may concern what happened in a past task, performance with an allowed aid, transfer to a changed situation or a
capacity the project needs to develop. Familiar music, a partner or a label can either be part of the task or disclose the answer, depending on its rules.

A partner may detect a change of contact before they can name the weight shift. A musician might
identify a familiar rhythm after its name is supplied and still miss it in unfamiliar material. A
judge may follow a costume or school reputation, and a classifier may succeed on recordings of its
training performers but fail on new ones. Specify what recognition should depend on in this task.

Identify what the question requires from the following.

- The holder or sampled group whose capability or performance is at issue.
- The musical or dance difference and how it was or could be made perceptible.
- The response that counts as recognizing the difference.
- The cues and assistance the task permits, and any cue that could supply its answer without the intended discrimination.
- The direct perceptual, bodily, music, dance or machine-learning method if development is requested.
- The conditions and evidence needed for this observation, transfer or retention claim, including an applicable result already available.

Use the relevant ear-training, rhythm, movement-perception, partner-sensing, somatic, style-comparison, perceptual-learning, judging,
curation or machine-recognition method for its own result. This method connects the target distinction with what the
holder could recognize in the task, how a change of conditions affects that result, or what development is warranted.
A question about learnability needs evidence about learning. A particular recognized signal can be reported directly.

Use a more direct approach in the following cases.

- For a question about what an already capable observer found, use an adequate observation or MDPE.12 to establish or compare the available evidence.
- When the holder recognizes the cue and the remaining question concerns performing the response, use the relevant performance method or MDPE.10 for a capability question.
- Use MDPE.13 to examine, choose or redesign a recurring recognition and selection arrangement.
- If a direct method or existing result answers the recognition question under its conditions, use it.
- For classification of material alone, use the relevant subject method. A question about what someone or some system recognized in a past classification can justify a separate inquiry here.

### MDPE.23:1 - The Recurring Difficulty

A physical difference can be present even when a recognizer cannot detect it. Discriminating two examples,
naming a category, locating the relevant event and recognizing when a response is called for are different tasks.
The same recognizer may succeed at one and miss another, or respond differently after a change in conditions.

Identify whose capability is at issue and which tasks it must cover. The holder might be a musician, dancer,
partner, teacher, listener, curator, judge, another performer, a technical recognizer or a group acting together.
If several holders are sampled, their responses give a distribution for that sample. Inferences about a wider population depend on how the sample was selected.
For a claim about one coordinated group or system, examine the response it produced as a whole under the relevant conditions.

Useful recognition tasks include:

- discriminate whether two occurrences differ in a stated respect;
- identify which distinction or category obtains;
- locate a difference in time, space, body, sound, or interaction;
- predict the next relevant change;
- notice that a learned coordination, concept, or Method applies in the current situation; and
- act on the recognized difference with the support the task permits and without being supplied the very answer it is meant to test.

These tasks can rely on different capabilities. A dancer can hear that two rhythms differ yet be unable to locate
the event that changes partner timing. A teacher can name a style but fail to distinguish its enacted movement from
a costume cue.

Three failures are especially costly:

1. **Cue dependence.** The training and test might share a teacher, label, costume, recording, partner or fixed order. If
   the response follows that cue while the target distinction varies, the outcome may overstate recognition of the target.
2. **Context-dependent expression.** A response observed earlier may disappear after the music, partner, venue, body state, task or recent transition
   changes, and reappear under the earlier conditions. Consider the change in access, support or demand as well as possible memory explanations.
3. **An inaccessible or ill-defined distinction.** Intended recognizers may have no access to
   the signal, the categories may overlap for the intended use or the representation may omit
   what matters. Examine the signal, task and possible proxy before asking for more repetition.

Recognizing a variant, selecting it and having authority to decide are distinct. A listener can recognize
and reject it. A platform may amplify material for reasons unrelated to what listeners recognize. A judge’s
ability to tell variants apart establishes a capability within the task. For a question about an actual
selection arrangement, bring the relevant findings to MDPE.13. Establish who decided under which rules when the inquiry concerns a decision that took place.

### MDPE.23:2 - Solution

Identify the recognizer, the target difference and the evidence already available under the task’s conditions. Give the supported result or its
limit. If development is needed, use or select an appropriate method for the target and any established difficulty. If further evidence is needed, compare the contribution
and burden of the available tests. Perception, bodily regulation, memory, interaction and action can operate together during a single task.

#### MDPE.23:2.1 - Name the holder, task, and receiving use

Identify the following as the claim requires.

- The holder of the capability, or the sampled units and population for a distribution of responses.
- The music or dance activity and the past or intended use in which the distinction matters.
- The subjects to compare and the relevant difference between them.
- The response required, such as discrimination, identification, localization, prediction, recognition of applicability or action.
- The consequences of a false positive, false negative, late response or uncertainty, where they affect the criterion.
- Any decision that will use the assessment. If the task is to determine what the holder recognized on an earlier occasion, state that question.

For a festival teaching decision, specify which two movement and partner-interaction variants of Urban Kiz learners
should distinguish and which music, clothing or teacher cues may vary. A past event can instead raise the narrower
question of whether these participants could tell the two enacted movements apart under the observed conditions.

#### MDPE.23:2.2 - Ground the distinction and expose cue leakage

Identify the target characteristic and the indications available for recognizing it. Use existing
evidence, a direct observation method or MDPE.12 as needed. Distinguish the following roles.

- the world-side rhythmic, acoustic, movement, contact, spatial, or interaction difference;
- its representation in notation, syllables, audio features, video, geometry, labels, or examples;
- cues available and permitted in the task being investigated, including any receiving use; and
- cues that can predict the required answer without the intended discrimination, wherever they occur.

When capable observers disagree under a suitable task, examine access to the signal, the category boundary and the representation
before proposing practice. The findings can support narrower categories, two separate distinctions, an altered signal or representation,
or dropping the proposed distinction. An inquiry into the earlier responses can also finish by describing their disagreement.

#### MDPE.23:2.3 - Establish a baseline with plausible rivals

Use a sufficient observation to answer the recognition question. If a material uncertainty remains, compare the attainable value and burden of a baseline test. Same/different cases or matched alternatives can show whether answers follow a label when the target difference varies. Record the results, timing, uncertainty and errors the claim needs. An established access failure can finish a diagnosis. If restoration or teaching was requested, use an adequate existing diagnosis to plan or obtain the required contribution.

Consider alternative explanations where distinguishing them would affect the answer or a requested action. For example, the following can account for different failures.

- the holder cannot perceive the signal;
- the signal is available but the category or boundary is unclear;
- the distinction is recognized but the required action cannot be performed;
