The descriptions identify the originating phrase, the translation, the exchange they share, and the contact and cue conditions for each. This documents derivation within the case. A wider claim of historical lineage would require further evidence.

If the programme becomes one short demonstration of the common exchange, C can suffice under the conditions already tested. The same applies if the additional partner rehearsal would displace a required ensemble run and the shorter version still serves the aim. Another trial of the established shared exchange would not alter the current trade-off. If a partner later reports difficulty with a particular contact transition, reconsider its fit and whether the planned rehearsal would address it.

The choice to maintain both phrases applies to this block. Before changing descriptions or arranging a later rehearsal, use the authority, permissions and assignments that cover the work and obtain any that are missing.

The movement-translation approach comes from [Stopgap, *Inclusive Choreography — Translation*](https://www.stopgapdance.com/inclusive-choreography/) (text consulted 4 October 2026). Ada, Bo, the phrases, alternatives and receiving-use choice are part of the constructed case.


#### MDPE.6:4.3 - Stop when the direct Method already returns the whole answer

A prosthesis can be designed for Jason Barnes. His playing and his own assessment in a trial can establish particular facts about control, rebound, strokes and synchronization under the tested conditions. DanceAbility offers work on inclusive improvisation for mixed-ability groups. JIZAI ARMS co-design can produce and test an exploratory equipped-body prototype. Use a suitable existing result for the question it already covers.

Use MDPE.6 when a further question concerns how a musical or movement result worked in changed conditions, whether it suits a proposed use, or which treatment to choose. A direct design or trial may already settle the source condition, the receiving question or both.

### MDPE.6:5 - Recognition and Assurance

Use the questions that bear on the requested suitability assessment, recommendation, decision or historical account. For a past use, establish what the evidence supports for that period.

- Which source result was available, or what did the proposal specify? Where it matters, identify the work and method that produced it.
- What receiving condition and intended use changed?
- Who made the decision, recommends a treatment or has authority to adopt one?
- Which options are or were available for the choice, if one is at issue?
- Which Music-or-Dance relation is a veto, and which differences are trade-offs?
- What is preserved, changed, added, lost, or still unknown for each serious option?
- If further inquiry is an option, what could it establish and would that result justify its cost? If it is unavailable, how does that limit the answer?
- What was recommended, chosen, rejected or left open?
- Which permissions and commitments apply or applied to the use in question? Which claims about capability, implementation, transmission, lineage or cultural effect need separate grounds?
- If the decision is still in use, what change in its grounds would warrant reconsideration?

Assess the answer against the source result and evidence it uses. A filmed performance can show the exchange in that event. A prototype, course description or official endorsement can establish other particular facts. For a claim about use under new conditions, prevalence, effectiveness, style identity or continuation, examine evidence that covers the claimed result. If an expert estimate serves the task, state its grounds and uncertainty.

### MDPE.6:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “It has the same name, so use it unchanged.” | Compare the decision-bearing Music or Dance relations under the receiving conditions. |
| “It looks different, so it is a new style.” | Establish the relevant difference in use or derivation. A claim about style identity or population recognition needs evidence about the practice concerned. |
| “Adapt it somehow.” | Identify what might need revision and the relation it should preserve or restore. If an option is missing, develop one through the relevant practice, `MDPE.9` or `C.18`. |
| “The prototype works, so the repertoire transfers.” | Separate the engineered System and capability evidence from the musical or movement result being considered. |
| “A successful trial proves transmission.” | State what the receiving performer did and what assistance, if any, they used. For a transmission claim, establish the contribution of the source as well as the relevant receiving enactment, using MDPE.17 where needed. |
| “The decision authorizes the change.” | Use authority, permission, consent or commitments already in force within their scope. Obtain what is missing when action requires it. If implementation is commissioned, plan the work separately. |
| “More evidence is needed,” without specifying the gap. | Identify what a further observation could establish and what it would cost. If sufficient evidence exists, give the supported conclusion. Where it does not, state the consequences of the remaining uncertainty. |

### MDPE.6:7 - Consequences

| Benefit | Cost or caution |
| --- | --- |
| Shared labels no longer decide receiving use. | The team must identify the actual bearer, relation, and changed condition. |
| Useful source and receiving alternatives can both survive through branching. | Branches add maintenance, description, teaching, and comparison cost. |
| Established domain practice can supply an adaptation, design or lesson directly. | Use MDPE.6 where a question remains about applying the result under changed conditions. |
| A well-chosen observation can prevent a costly mistake. | Obtaining it takes time and can displace work. Reuse an adequate existing result. |
| A local use can be assessed or chosen on its own grounds. | Claims about historical lineage, population recognition or continuation need evidence about that history or practice. |

### MDPE.6:8 - Rationale and Source Use

The direct music, dance, teaching, control, instrument-design and systems-engineering methods can produce the particular result. Here the practitioner compares what the changed use preserves, makes possible or loses, and the effort of repairing a mismatch or maintaining alternatives. Use that comparison to judge suitability, recommend or choose a treatment, or establish what happened in an earlier use or choice from the available evidence.

| Source or maintained result | Use here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C.11 Decision Theory | Define the decision, identify who can make it, compare available options and decide whether another observation is worthwhile. | Identify the concrete music or dance treatments and their practical comparison criteria from this case. |
| C.17 and C.11.CRC | Establish a relevant characteristic or compare contributions of available treatments in the receiving configuration. | Judge suitability against the receiving requirements. Identify who can decide or authorize implementation when a choice or action is requested. |
| McCloskey et al., [automatic arrangement for monophonic instruments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12084) | Finds a feasible pitch and part assignment within the specified ranges when one exists, preserving rhythmic values and bar lines. | Sound balance, the players’ capability and actual concert use require evidence from the relevant ensemble and setting. |
| [Inclusive Choreography](https://www.stopgapdance.com/inclusive-choreography/) | Translate movement across physicalities by attending to effort, spine, focus, direction, rhythm and detail. | Observations or accounts of the translating work can establish how the new phrase derives from the source movement. Claims about a partner’s response, authorization or cultural continuation need their corresponding grounds. |
| [Drumming Arm study](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561943) and [JIZAI ARMS co-design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581169) | Use the drumming study for its tested performer–prosthesis coordination and the co-design study for its equipped-body prototypes. | To assess a different musical or movement use, compare its requirements with the tested configuration and performance. |

Reconsider a live choice if changes in the source, receiving conditions, intended use, viable alternatives, binding requirements, evidence or authority would alter its grounds. A change today can affect future use while leaving an established past decision intact.

### MDPE.6:9 - Relations

| Relation | Use in this pattern |
| --- | --- |
| `C.11`, `C.11.CRC` | Govern the local choice and finite contribution comparison. |
| `C.17`, `A.10` | Ground the characteristic and evidence claims used by the choice. |
| `A.22.CGUS` | Describes a maintained branching unfolding when one is needed. |
| `MDPE.9` | Use MDPE.9 to generate candidate material when needed. Here compare feasible treatments of an identified result for the receiving use. |
| MDPE.10 and MDPE.3 | Assess performer capability and identify or design the configuration that supplies a particular performance. |
| MDPE.12 | Use a relevant observation or comparison of an earlier performance or a changed condition. Obtain a new observation when its added contribution justifies the cost. |
| `A.15.7`, `C.11`, and the applicable direct Music-or-Dance Method | Govern a next action during current Work, an already formed bounded choice, and the later selected change respectively. |
| MDPE.17, MDPE.18 and MDPE.19 | Address transmission, usable cultural memory and evidence of lineage, and continuation or loss, respectively. |
| `C.36`, `C.36.P` | Keep population-level cultural claims separate from one receiving-use choice. |
| `C.24` and applicable planning Methods | Use a suitable existing plan when implementing a choice, or plan the work when it is commissioned. |

### MDPE.6:End

## MDPE.17 - Design and Test Transmission of a Music-or-Dance Method

> **Status:** Stable

> **Type:** DPF pattern body
>
> **Primary working result:** a design for transmitting a Method, or a finding about a particular part of transmission, such as access, the receiver’s performance, transfer, retention or the source’s contribution. Identify the received variant when the evidence supports it. A project choosing its next step can use these findings to keep, change, narrow or stop the arrangement.

### MDPE.17:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern to design how another practitioner will take up a Music-or-Dance Method, or to investigate an attempt to pass on a method through a lesson, demonstration, score, choreography, recording, prompt, model or software, including whether the intended receiver could use what was offered. A copied artifact can be examined even when its use remains unknown.

The need arises in situations such as these.

- dancers reproduce one shown phrase while the teacher supplies every cue, but cannot use the Method with another partner, tempo, phrase, or music;
- musicians read one score or repeat one example, but the intended rehearsal, interpretation, improvisation, or ensemble Method does not appear in later Work;
- an event guide reaches an organizer, while the local event is run through another practice;
- a team copies code, model weights, movement traces or a control policy to a robot or AI service and wants to know what the configured receiver can do;
- the receiver creates a useful changed variant, but the project calls every difference a transmission failure; or
- one successful occurrence is reported as capability, population adoption, or long-term continuation.

The practical question depends on the receiving use.

> What would let the receiver perform this work under the intended conditions? In an earlier attempt, what did the receiver do, which relations carried over, and what can be attributed to the source?

Use the steps that bear on the question.

1. identify the intended use and the work that would represent it,
2. distinguish the source, its carrier, any provider and the receiver,
3. for a question about how the work was done, identify the method the evidence supports; for a design, choose or specify the teaching, rehearsal, reconstruction, learning or control work needed,
4. use observations made under the relevant conditions or design a feasible trial when its expected answer would justify the burden,
5. report what is known about source use, performance, transfer, retention and source contribution, and
6. if a next step is wanted, compare the feasible choices, including keeping an adequate arrangement, changing it, narrowing its use or stopping.

Providing materials, using them and observing a performance can be parts of one event or take place at different times. A performer studying a score alone may have no separate instructor.

Use an adequate result of music, dance, teaching, rehearsal, reconstruction, robotics, machine learning, event programming or community practice directly. Use this method for a remaining question about how to arrange transmission or what a source, performance or comparison establishes about it.

Use `MDPE.6` when the question is whether to reuse a result. For a documentary instruction whose meaning or status is unclear, consult `A.3.1.DR`. For a possible method suggested by performance evidence, use `A.3.1.MR`. A question about cultural memory or lineage belongs to `MDPE.18`, and continuation in a population to `MDPE.19`. For development of a human learner’s capability, use the relevant human capability method.

#### MDPE.17:0.1 - Working Distinctions

| Name | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| **source content** | A score, description, recording, prompt, code or model may supply material for the receiving work. A live demonstration is work performed by the demonstrator. Its recording can be studied later. Establish what was available, what the receiver actually used and what it supplied. |
| **provider Agent** | A teacher, coach, director, developer, model-training team, organizer or other agent that provides instruction, material or assistance. Someone studying a recording can proceed without a separate instructor. |
| **receiving Agent** | The person, pair, ensemble, organization, robot, AI service or combined performing agent expected to do the work. Identify it separately from the file, model checkpoint or other carrier it receives. |
| **receiving enactment** | The receiver performed representative work using a way of working established as a Method under the stated conditions. A description can specify the intended method. A hypothesis about what the receiver did needs supporting evidence. |
| **transfer** | A receiver who has demonstrated a method performs it under a relevant changed condition or on a held-out task. Reproducing a phrase under the original cues establishes how the receiver performed with those cues. |
| **source contribution** | A causal finding about the part played by particular material, instruction or assistance. Earlier use followed by a similar performance is compatible with several explanations, including prior skill. |
| **receiving method** | The reusable way identified in the receiver’s work. Compare the relations it preserves, changes, adds or omits with those needed for the intended use. Another phrase, tempo or partner can fall within the same method. A proposed variant requires a difference in the reusable way. |



### MDPE.17:1 - Problem

A score can give a performer the relations to play, and a teacher can demonstrate how to play them. A delivery record can show where the score was sent. To establish access, check that the intended performer could retrieve and read it. A teacher’s demonstration shows the teacher’s performance. To establish which method the learner used, examine evidence of the learner’s work. For robots or software agents, distinguish a delivered model or program from the work of the configured performer.

A dancer can preserve effort, timing, focus or partner dialogue through a different visible movement. A musician can preserve rhythmic or ensemble relations with another instrument, notation, interface or improvisational vocabulary. A robot can meet the same performance demand through different sensing and control. Judge the receiving method by the relations that matter to the use.

An observation of a successful performance can establish what the receiver did under the partner, material, tool, room and support conditions it covers. For a broader claim, consider which of those conditions mattered. Teacher cues might have supplied the timing, a familiar phrase might have supported recall, or the performer might already have had the skill. For a retention claim, check performance after the relevant delay. For transfer, examine performance under the changed conditions, whether it succeeded or failed.

For a claim that the receiver took up a method from a source, identify the method in representative work and establish the source relation the claim requires. A record may document both the source’s contribution and the receiving performance, or only the delivery, access, source use or performance that it actually covers. A plan specifies what the receiver will need and how to recognize the intended result.

### MDPE.17:2 - Forces

| Tension | What must remain visible |
| --- | --- |
| access ↔ enactment | Source content can be available without the receiving Agent being able to use the Method. |
| fidelity ↔ useful transformation | A dancer may preserve the visible shape or preserve the timing and interaction through a different shape. The intended use determines which matters. |
| support ↔ independent use | Teacher, partner, prompt, score, controller, or tool support can belong to the intended configuration; keep permitted support when judging the performance that use requires. A separately justified comparison with less support can test independence or the aid’s contribution. |
| blocked practice under one condition ↔ transfer | A performer who succeeds with familiar cues may struggle with a new partner, tempo, material, venue or task. |
| capability ↔ source contribution | A receiver may have the skill before using a source. Use of a source can also be established when the receiver cannot yet perform the task. |
| local result ↔ cultural continuation | One receiving Agent can perform Work that enacts a Method while the population never recognizes, copies, or retains it. |
| human learning ↔ other Agents | Human motor-learning evidence can guide hypotheses; robots and AI Agents require their own direct learning and control Methods. |

### MDPE.17:3 - Solution

Start with the work the receiver needs to do and the claim or decision in question. For an existing attempt, use suitable evidence to establish the receiver, support, action or resulting variant that the question concerns. Report a failed attempt or an unresolved outcome where the evidence warrants it. For a proposed arrangement, choose the materials, help and conditions that would make the relevant relations available. A claim about actual performance or the effect of that arrangement needs evidence of the relevant work and, for an effect, grounds for attributing it to the arrangement.

#### MDPE.17:3.1 - Begin with the receiving use

Identify what the recipient needs to establish or decide. A question can end with what a pair did in one earlier lesson, or with the limit on what the evidence shows. Other uses include a decision to

- admit a movement or musical Method into one performer's repertoire;
- let a teacher offer a class under stated conditions;
- rely on a pair or ensemble in a performance;
- program a local event under a community Method;
- use a robot, AI Agent, or equipped performer in one performance configuration; or
- choose the next repair to a teaching or reconstruction arrangement.

Identify work representative of the use. Use existing evidence of that work for a retrospective claim, or specify it for a design. A workshop exercise may represent the next lesson. To rely on it for social dancing, identify the relevant partners, music and conditions. A short robot trial can establish a control range, and a repeated phrase can show immediate reproduction. Concert use or improvisation calls for work representative of that further demand.

#### MDPE.17:3.2 - Name source, provider, receiver, and carrier separately

Describe the arrangement through the participants and their actions.

- What material was available, proposed or used? What establishes how it was used?
- Who provided or would provide instruction, material or assistance, and how, if a provider is needed?
- Who performed the work, or who is to perform it?
- Which method was intended, and which method does the observed work support?
- What constitutes the performing whole, how do its parts work together, and which conditions or services support it from outside?
- What relevant observations are already available from records, witnesses or instruments? What further evidence, if any, is needed?

One participant may have several roles, and one occurrence may realize several methods. Establish separate occurrences or constituent work from what happened. A performer may study a recording alone. A founder can teach. An organizing team may take up an event-programming method while the musicians learn a performance method. A team may configure a robot for music that the robot later performs.



#### MDPE.17:3.3 - Choose what should persist and what may change

Name the **transmission-relevant relations** for this receiving use. Examples include:

- Music: pulse, articulation, phrasing, rebound, ensemble cueing, relation to musical structure, improvisational response, or live transformation;
- Dance: weight transfer, effort, focus, timing, contact, invitation, partner readability, spatial relation, or response to music;
- human–technical performance: sensing, control, actuation, model use, correction, stop authority, or division of initiative; and
- teaching or event practice: exercise, correction, turn-taking, participation, conduct, access, programme, or feedback relations.

State which differences are acceptable, which changes are wanted and which would make the chosen way unsuitable for this use. Give the timing, movement or interaction relation when a shared style name alone leaves that distinction open.

#### MDPE.17:3.4 - Design support and context variation for the claim

For a proposed arrangement, choose the method needed for teaching, rehearsal, reconstruction, learning, evaluation or control. For earlier work, establish which method was used when that matters. Use existing observations when they cover the question and conditions. Design a trial when its answer could justify the effort. If the necessary observation is unavailable, identify the conclusion that remains open.

| Claim | Evidence to seek in existing work or obtain in a trial |
| --- | --- |
| **immediate receiving enactment** | What the receiver did, by which established method, under the support and configuration in question. |
| **less-supported enactment** | Work with the particular teacher, model, prompt or partner cue reduced or absent to the extent required by the intended use. |
| **transfer** | Compare established performance with work under the relevant changed partner, tempo, music, material, instrument, room, cue, source example, input distribution or task. |
| **retention** | Performance of the previously demonstrated method after the stated delay, with the available support and relevant intervening practice accounted for. |
| **source contribution** | A source-specific comparison, such as withdrawal, an alternative source or a changed demonstration, qualified for a causal claim through `C.28`. |
| **correction and adaptation** | What information about the error was available and how the receiver responded, including an unchanged action where observed. A suitable case may already have occurred. |

Vary a condition when it can distinguish cue dependence or support a claim about transfer. A constant-practice condition can answer a narrower question. Record material differences in the task, exposure, fatigue, order and support when they could explain the result.

When a person no longer performs a skill demonstrated before, consider context-sensitive recall alongside lost support, changed demands, fatigue and intervening learning. A safe comparison with the earlier condition can distinguish some of these explanations. Use existing comparable observations or arrange a return when its contribution to the question justifies its cost. An established device failure can finish a diagnosis. If there is no earlier demonstration, state the limit on a claim of loss. Arrange repair or learning only when that is the task.

Suppose loss of a teacher cue coincided with a move to another room. Comparing performance with one of those conditions held constant may help decide between practising with less cueing and practising in several rooms. A recovered response establishes what the person could do on that occasion. A claim about selection of a motor memory also needs to distinguish fatigue, intervening practice and other explanations. COIN suggests a hypothesis from sensorimotor tasks. For a claim about use elsewhere, examine representative performance there.

#### MDPE.17:3.5 - Establish what the receiver did

Use the evidence for the part of transmission that the question concerns. The following findings have different grounds.

1. **source available** — the intended receiver can access the source content in a usable form; identify mere receipt of the carrier separately when that is all the evidence shows;
2. **source used** — provider or receiving Work actually relies on named content;
3. **receiving enactment** — the receiver performs representative work by a way of working established as a Method under the stated conditions;
4. **transfer** — enactment occurs under the changed condition required by the use;
5. **retention** — the receiver can perform the previously demonstrated method after a stated delay, under the reported practice and support conditions;
6. **source contribution** — a suitable comparison supports the causal claim about named content or provider Work; and
7. **population continuation** — the practice persists in the relevant population, a question addressed by `MDPE.19` and `C.36`.

For example, a recording may establish that a pair performed variant V under conditions K. Say whether there is evidence that they used source S. If use is established but the available evidence leaves its causal contribution open, say so. Report that no test was made only when the evidence establishes that history. If the source was merely present, the finding about the pair’s performance can still stand.

Describe an unsuccessful attempt if the evidence establishes it. When a possible method matters but remains unidentified, use the observations for Method recovery.

#### MDPE.17:3.6 - Identify the receiving method and its possible use

When a receiving performance is at issue, describe the relations it preserved, changed, added or omitted and any that remain unknown. For a design, identify the relations the intended receiving work should preserve or may change. When change is at issue, identify what changed or what the proposal would change in the method, its description, the material, the configuration or a performer’s capability. A new phrase can be taught by the same method, and a new model can be used by the same performer in the same way. Identify a candidate variant when the repeatable way of coordinating or deciding changes. If the same rule admits both performances, describe how the performances differed. Identify a change in the setting or material only when one occurred and matters here.

If a further choice is required, keep an arrangement already adequate for the use. Compare the likely contribution of a change with its cost and delay. A different carrier, demonstration, exercise, cue, partner, feedback method, tool setting or source comparison may address the particular limitation. Narrow or stop the proposed use when its requirements cannot be met.

Report the design or the supported finding and its limits. Include the following details as applicable.

```text
receiving Agent, use, and representative Work:
source content, its availability and any established or proposed use:
provider Agent and Work, when present:
receiving Method and performing whole:
support and context variation:
observed work or proposed trial, relevant change or delay, and limits:
receiving Method or candidate variant — preserved, changed, added, absent or unknown relations:
source contribution — supported | not supported | undecided | not needed:
next step, if requested — retain arrangement, proposed or chosen change, narrower use, or stop:
grounds for reconsidering a decision, when relevant:
```

Distinguish what is proposed from what the available evidence establishes about access, source use, performance or a decision.

An observation or changed receiving variant can affect a previous `MDPE.14` conflict
decision if it crosses a stated limit or changes the conflict, candidate, comparison,
remaining tension, burden on another participant or representative test. If
the observation leaves the grounds of the decision intact, the existing decision remains usable.

### MDPE.17:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.17:4.1 - A partner-Dance transmission trial

In this constructed example, a Tarraxo teacher must decide whether dancers `P` and `Q` can use a taught
partner-coordination Method in the next supervised social practice without continuous teacher cues. The receiving
use requires weight transfer, timing, partner-readable invitation and response, musical adaptation, and recovery
after an interrupted connection. Variation in the visible phrase is acceptable if those relations hold.

For this constructed class the teacher uses a local written instruction, two exercises
and a demonstration. In the first exercise the dancer completes the weight transfer
and gives a readable invitation. In the second the dancer varies a two-bar phrase
while preserving the invitation and its fit to the chosen music. These teaching
materials belong to the constructed class. The Tarraxo Agency page describes a setting for
teaching. During the first two lessons, the teacher gives continuous timing cues
and corrections. Dancers `P` and `Q` repeat the phrase together with the original
music. That performance establishes what the pair could do with the teacher’s help.

The receiving trial removes continuous cueing and uses three ninety-second dances: (1) the original `P`–`Q`
pair with an unheard track in the taught tempo range; (2) `P` with experienced changed partner `R`; and (3)
`Q` with another experienced changed partner `S`, with an unexpected pause and restart during the `Q`–`S`
dance. The teacher observes but does not cue.

The observed pairs preserve weight arrival, timing, and readable invitation and response across the changed music and
partner trials until the interruption in the `Q`–`S` dance. After that pause, `Q` restarts the memorized phrase
instead of first re-establishing partner information; `S` stops the attempt. Seven days later, the original `P`–`Q`
pair again performs Work that enacts the Method without reteaching under the changed-music condition.

These observations support the taught timing, weight transfer and partner dialogue with changed music or
experienced partners until the pause in the `Q`–`S` dance. The receiving variant permits a different visible
phrase. Seven-day retention is supported for `P` and `Q` together under the changed-music condition. `Q` did not
recover the interrupted connection with `S` on that trial. The trials leave use with novice partners, a
wider tempo range and unsupervised parties open. The class used the named sources and instruction. These
observations do not distinguish their causal effect from the dancers’ previous ability or other practice.

The teacher chooses an exercise in stopping, sensing the partner again and rebuilding the invitation
before restarting. The teacher plans another trial of the interrupted connection for `Q` with two
changed partners to find out whether the new exercise helps recovery. Reconsider reliance
on the earlier result if the trial shows another failure or success relevant to that use, the
setting demands a wider partner or music range, or later evidence changes a transfer or retention
limit. The positive observations from the earlier dances still apply within their conditions.

#### MDPE.17:4.2 - Music: distinguish receiving performer Work from event-organizer Work

A live-coding performer studies *Live Coding: A User's Manual*, examples, and tools. An organizing team separately uses the Algorave guidelines for programme, access, conduct, technological diversity, visible process, and community contact.

At one event, the relevant work can therefore involve different receivers.

- the performer changes code or an algorithmic process during a bounded Music performance under the selected live-coding Method; and
- the organizing team programs and runs the event under the selected event-programming Method.

Use the performer’s set for a claim about live coding and the organizers’ work for a claim about event programming. For a transfer claim, use suitable evidence of the relevant changed performance or organizing work. If more evidence is needed and attainable, vary material, tool or venue for the performer, or programme or access conditions for the organizers, preserving the community requirements. Establish use of the manual or guidelines separately from their causal contribution.

#### MDPE.17:4.3 - Robot or AI Agent: copied values are inputs, not transmission results

A team copies code, weights, movement data or a control policy to another robot or AI system. A verified copy can establish which values reached the destination. Installation or activation requires evidence from the configured system when either matters. Identify the configured performer and its work to establish what it can do with those inputs.

When the configured system acts as the receiver, examine evidence of its representative work. If an open question warrants a feasible test, adapt one suited to the direct learning method, such as removing a demonstrator, using a held-out task or changing the demonstration. Bhoopchand and colleagues used such comparisons in GoalCycle3D to distinguish following, recall within an episode, generalization and use of information specific to a demonstrator. A music or dance application needs a task and measure suited to its own work.

When a technical system contributes under another agent’s control, examine how it is connected and how they interact. Establish whether it is part of the performing whole or supplies it from outside. A constituent can also perform work of its own.

#### MDPE.17:4.4 - Stop when source material does not yet yield a reusable Method

For *The Call*, the project team brought together a songbook, exercises, recordings, datasets, choral AI models, an installation and governance experiments. Its project page identifies materials and their roles. For a later choir–model project, identify or use the method its participants need for the work in question.

Name the new project’s use. Apply `A.3.1` when an available account gives a candidate method ready to identify. Use `A.3.1.DR` for a question about the meaning or status of an instruction. Use `A.3.1.MR` when observations or reports of performances may support a reusable method. Choose the operation according to what the document contributes. A cultural-memory or lineage question may need `MDPE.18`. If the project needs an unavailable method, adopt an adequate alternative or develop one through the relevant music, dance or Method Engineering practice.

Use this chapter to design how a choir, organizer, model-development team or combined performer could take up an identified method, or to assess an attempt that has already taken place. The design can identify representative tasks and suitable evidence. A finding about actual reception depends on what can be established about that receiver’s work, including a failed attempt.

#### MDPE.17:4.5 - Music: choose turns at a shared instrument

Loria and colleagues’ [marimba study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-43485-w) compared individual practice with alternation between playing and watching a partner. The full dyads had fifty playing and fifty observation trials per learner, the half dyads twenty-five of each, and the individual group fifty playing trials. The musicians were new to marimba. On the changed phrase both dyad groups made smaller right-mallet landing errors than the individual group. There was no overall group advantage across mallets. The groups differed in exposure and spacing. Next-day tests included five minutes of preparation with score and metronome available. Those conditions delimit the result a teacher can borrow.

Consider a separate constructed lesson. Lea and Ren need a short alternating-mallet phrase for their next supervised ensemble rehearsal. Their teacher has one marimba and one forty-minute lesson. The selected direct teaching Method supplies the phrase, grip and stroke instruction, correction and suitable tempo. The remaining question is how to use the shared instrument. After common preparation the lesson can accommodate fifty short practice trials, changeovers, feedback and a final receiving attempt.

In individual blocks, each learner plays twenty-five trials with teacher feedback while the other can study something else. In alternating five-trial blocks, each plays twenty-five trials and watches the other twenty-five. Both arrangements use fifty instrument trials and the same teacher booking. Alternation requires both learners’ attention throughout practice, adds observation and changes the spacing of their playing. The teacher weighs what watching might teach against the loss of time for unrelated study and the change in spacing.

Both learners can attend the whole lesson. They have difficulty noticing an off-centre stroke before repeating it. The teacher therefore chooses alternation. The observer follows the score, watches the intended landing area and discusses an error at the block break. The teacher provides technical correction. The ensemble permits the score and metronome, so both remain available. In the final attempt each learner plays alone without teacher corrections.

Suppose both learners play the original phrase with its intended notes, sticking and landing areas. At the next lesson, after the same brief preparation, Lea plays the variant with the last bar reordered. Ren repeatedly misplaces one left-mallet transition. The teacher keeps alternating practice for Lea’s next phrase and gives Ren an individual correction block before relying on that transition. Ren’s original performance remains usable under the stated score, metronome and preparation conditions. Since the learners did not try the individual-block alternative, these observations leave its relative benefit and the learning mechanism open.

If a learner cannot stay to observe, individual blocks can make the available time usable. They may also be preferable when observation displaces necessary physical correction. Use the direct teaching method’s answer when it already settles this choice and the limits on later performance.

### MDPE.17:5 - Recognition and Assurance

Select the questions that bear on the design, observation or decision requested.

- Which use and representative task are in question?
- Who would perform or performed the task, with which participants, tools and external support?
- What material was available, and what establishes any actual use?
- What assistance was supplied or is proposed, who supplies it, and which part did or would the receiver perform?
- Which direct Methods govern teaching, rehearsal, reconstruction, learning, control, and observation?
- Which musical, movement, interaction, control, or participation relations should persist?
- Which conditions and support did the finding cover, or would the proposed task need? If a change matters to the claim, what changed?
- What supports a finding about access, source use, enactment, transfer, retention or cause?
- Which method did the receiver use, what difference supports a variant claim, and which features are still proposed or uncertain?
- For a further decision, what supports retaining, changing, narrowing or stopping the arrangement? What would warrant reconsidering that choice?

Match the conclusion to its grounds. Attendance or a delivery receipt can show presence or receipt. To establish usable access, check whether the intended receiver could reach the relevant instruction or material. A repeated example or a recorded concert can establish a bounded performance, while transfer and retention require evidence under the relevant conditions. Human motor studies, robotic learning experiments, practitioner accounts and project pages can supply hypotheses or ways of checking them within their own tasks and populations.

### MDPE.17:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “The lesson was delivered, so the Method was transmitted.” | Establish from available evidence what the teacher provided and what the receiver did. If transmission from that lesson is the claim, examine what supports its contribution to the receiving performance. |
| “The learner copied the example, so transfer succeeded.” | Examine work under the changed partner, material, cue, tempo, instrument, task or context required by the use. If further evidence is warranted, use a feasible test or identify the limit on the transfer claim. |
| “The receiver needed support, so transmission failed.” | Establish which support the intended use permits and which support the receiver used. Keep the help permitted in the intended use. If a comparison with less help is needed to assess independence or the contribution of the help, qualify that comparison separately. |
| “The receiving version differs, so it is wrong.” | Compare the performances under the applicable rule. If the original way permits both, describe the difference in performance and any relevant change in setting or material. Identify a variant when the repeatable way differs, with what is known about its origin and use. |
| “The result appeared after teaching, so teaching caused it.” | Report what is known about source use and receiving performance. A source-specific comparison can establish more when cause is the question. |
| “The model or file was copied, so the practice was learned.” | Identify what was copied and its role in the configuration. For a claim about the receiver, examine evidence of its work with that configuration. |
| “One receiver succeeded, so the culture retained the practice.” | Report the result for the receiving person, ensemble or other identified agent within its scope. For a question about a population’s continuation, apply `MDPE.19` to evidence about that population. |

### MDPE.17:7 - Consequences

| Benefit | Cost or caution |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence can distinguish what was delivered from what the receiver did. | A representative trial can cost considerably more than consulting a delivery record. |
| A performer’s adaptation can retain the relations that make the method useful. | State what the performer changed, whether it was allowed by the same way of working, and under which conditions it worked. |
| Context-bound performance is distinguished from transfer and retention. | More than one condition or time point may be needed. |
| An account can identify source use while leaving its effect open. | A source-specific causal comparison may cost more than the question warrants. |
| Human, robotic, AI, ensemble, and hybrid cases share one result boundary. | Their direct learning, control, safety, and capability-development Methods can differ sharply. |

### MDPE.17:8 - Rationale and Source Use

FPF `C.36` distinguishes generation, transmission, recognition, selection, retention, loss and intervention in a culture. Here the practitioner designs or examines a particular receiving arrangement. Identify how its participants, materials, equipment, support and tasks shape the opportunity to perform. Use evidence of the receiver’s work, including any relevant prior ability, to establish what the receiver could do.

| Source or maintained result | Use here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `C.36`, `C.36.P`, `A.15.1`, `A.3.1`, `A.3.2`, `A.10`, `C.28` | Distinguish cultural relations, work performed, methods and descriptions, evidence and causal claims. | The practitioner supplies the musical or movement task and the basis for identifying it in a receiving performance. |
| Crone et al., [synchronous versus non-synchronous imitation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2021.102776) | Novices either danced in synchrony with an expert or watched and then imitated. After twenty practice trials, both groups performed the same sequence without the expert. | The assisted and unassisted performances answer different questions about the same sequence. Extending that result to another choreography or teaching method needs its own grounds. |
| Loria et al., [dyad practice in Music motor learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-43485-w) | Compare performance during practice, after a delay and on a changed task. | Interpret the right-mallet transfer result with the differences in observation, total exposure and spacing. |
| Bhoopchand et al., [few-shot imitation as cultural transmission](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42875-2) | The researchers varied demonstrator support, demonstrations and held-out tasks to examine what artificial agents could recover and use. | Adapt the comparison to the music or dance task, performer and relevant criterion. |
| Ranganathan et al., [variability versus specificity in motor-skill retention](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2025.103431) | In a two-handed virtual shuffleboard task, practice on one target and practice on several targets showed no reliable difference in retention of the target task after 24 hours. | Interpret that comparison within its task and delay. A new task or transfer claim needs corresponding evidence. |
| Heald, Lengyel, and Wolpert, [COIN](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04129-3) and [cross-domain review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2022.10.004) | Supports return-to-context and context-variation probes for human sensorimotor memory. | Wider learning and cultural-transmission use remains a testable hypothesis. |
| [Tarraxo Agency](https://www.tarraxo-agency.com/) | Identifies a practitioner, promotion and event setting in which Tarraxo is taught and presented. | Its public description does not supply the written instruction or two exercises in :4.1; those teaching inputs and observations are constructed. |
| [TOCA Method](https://tocamethod.com/) | Dawou Tarraxo publicly describes an approach to learning and teaching kizomba, tarraxo and urbankiz. | To reconstruct the books’ full method or establish what a particular learner took up, examine the relevant books or the learner’s work. The constructed class in :4.1 uses its own instruction. |
| Blackwell et al., [*Live Coding: A User's Manual*](https://livecodingbook.toplap.org/book/) and Algorave [guidelines](https://github.com/Algorave/guidelines/blob/24b2ad588f7f0110e8b7d5e3c57736e6056c4270/README_en.md) | The book describes varied live-coding practices. The guidelines set out an approach to programming an event. | Actual performances, prevalence, continued use and the effect of these sources each require evidence at the relevant scale. |
| Serpentine, [*The Call*](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-the-call/) | Identifies materials, participants and their contributions in the choir and AI installation. | Use it for what this project did. To identify a reusable method or a later choir’s performance, examine evidence for the particular work in question. |

In Jacoby and colleagues' [*Commonality and variation in mental representations of music revealed by a cross-cultural comparison of rhythm priors in 15 countries* (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01800-9), a participant taps along with a repeating three-interval click pattern; a valid average reproduction supplies the next stimulus to that same participant. Across iterations the distributions reveal biases towards discrete rhythm categories, with differences among the studied groups. This is a within-person reproduction task, not an observed teacher-to-student chain. It motivates checking how received material changes, but it neither identifies why a particular learner changed nor supplies a universal teaching Method or a cultural-transmission outcome.

Reconsider a finding when a change in the receiver, task, method, configuration, source, instruction, context, help or evidence affects what it establishes. A new question about cause or future use can require different evidence.

### MDPE.17:9 - Relations

| Relation | Use in this pattern |
| --- | --- |
| `MDPE.6` | Use an applicable assessment of how a result serves changed conditions, an account of its earlier use, or a recommendation or choice about reuse as the question requires. Look to the receiver’s work for actual enactment. |
| `A.3.1` | Apply the Method identity test to a candidate way ready for that assessment. |
| `A.3.1.DR` | Recovers documentary contributions when their source meaning or status needs recovery. |
| `A.3.1.MR` | Recovers provisional candidate ways from observations or evidence about performances. |
| `MDPE.18` | Supplies a needed cultural-memory or lineage account. |
| `MDPE.10`, `MDPE.3` | Assess a performer’s capability or identify the configured performing whole when that distinction changes the receiving question. Use `MDPE.10` to plan development when a change in capability is wanted. |
| `MDPE.11`, `MDPE.5`, `MDPE.12` | Examine the method used in the work through MDPE.11, the performance and its production through MDPE.5, and the relevant observation or comparison through MDPE.12. |
| Method Engineering or an applicable direct Music-or-Dance Method | May supply a changed Method, MethodDescription, material, or configuration intended for another receiving Agent and guide the Work that makes the change. |
| `MDPE.19` and `MDPE.20` | Use receiving evidence for a further question about population continuation or likely trajectories within the relevant horizon. |
| `MDPE.14` | Revisit an existing conflict decision when the observation changes the conflict, candidate, comparison, remaining tension, burden or representative test that grounded that decision. |
| `A.15.7` and `C.11` | May use bounded transmission evidence when it changes the next action during current Work or one already formed bounded choice. |
| `C.28` | Qualify a causal claim about a source or provider when that contribution is in question. |
| applicable direct domain Methods | Use suitable results and methods of teaching, rehearsal, reconstruction, learning, control, event programming or evaluation for the particular work. |



### MDPE.17:End

## MDPE.18 - Build Usable Music-or-Dance Cultural Memory and Lineage Evidence

> **Status:** Stable

> **Type:** DPF pattern body
>
> **Primary working result:** an account of what the sources establish about a music or dance practice, its history or its lineage. Link each finding to its grounds. Identify materially different explanations, missing embodied knowledge or limits on present use where they matter. A historical question can end with the supported attribution, occurrence, relation or limit. A practitioner can also use that account for a current decision.

### MDPE.18:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern to establish what earlier musicians, dancers, teachers, organizers or communities did, what their tools did, which methods were used, or what a later practice took up from them. A creation, reconstruction, attribution, teaching, transmission, restoration or retirement decision may turn on that history. Use a sufficient existing account directly.

Difficulties include the following.

- a video, score, notation, playlist, event page, or software repository is treated as the reusable Method;
- an archived artifact is treated as proof that a living practice continues;
- a founder or institution's story is repeated as the complete lineage;
- a shared or changed label stands in for continuity or discontinuity of material, Method, performance, or population;
- visible movement or sounding result survives while partner pressure, bodily effort, instrumental technique, correction, or teaching practice disappears;
- the volume of academic, press, official, or platform material is mistaken for prevalence in actual Music or Dance Work; or
- an inquiry expands without improving the historical answer or the choice it was meant to inform.

Ask what the available material can establish.

> What do these sources support about this subject, place and period? What is the basis and reach of each finding? Which rival explanations or missing relations matter for the intended use?

To answer the inquiry,

1. name the question, subject, relevant population, place, period and intended use,
2. identify the work, methods, participants, artifacts and events that the records concern,
3. connect each finding to its source and limits,
4. compare plausible histories where the available evidence permits different explanations that matter,
5. identify any embodied, performative, technical or present-use evidence still needed, and
6. return the historical finding or its bearing on the choice in question.

A discrepancy can prompt a search for a specific further source or demonstration.

Use suitable results of oral history, historical or ethnographic inquiry, ethnomusicology, dance documentation, archival work, process mining, phylogenetic or network analysis, or preservation. Obtain specialist work when the question requires a contribution those results do not yet supply. Use this chapter to connect the sources with the particular music or dance question.

Use `C.18` to decide which variants to retain for exploration or which are non-dominated under a defined comparison. Use archival and preservation methods for the custody and care of historical sources. For a question about what a receiver performed use `MDPE.17`, for reuse under changed conditions `MDPE.6`, and for a practice’s continued reproducibility `MDPE.19`. Historical evidence can contribute to each.

#### MDPE.18:0.1 - Working Distinctions

| Name | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| **source object** | A recording, video, score, notation, interview, programme, review, photograph, event log, dataset, software artifact, instrument, costume, or other identified object used to support a claim. Keep its actual kind. |
| **work record** | A source about a particular occurrence. Establish what it records about the work and what the evidence supports about the method or performer’s capability. |
| **cultural-memory evidence** | Evidence about which materials, descriptions, capabilities, methods or relations from earlier practice can be recovered or used for the question. A surviving artifact may supply part or all of this evidence. |
| **lineage claim** | A claim about derivation, borrowing, mixture, convergence, branching, naming, teaching, influence, revival or succession among identified variants, methods, artifacts, occurrences, participants or populations. State what evidence supports the proposed relation. |
| **living continuation** | A population repeatedly enacts and reproduces a practice over a specified period and under specified conditions. Use `MDPE.19` for this question. An archive can preserve evidence of such work if it documents who actually carried it on. |
| **basis of a finding** | The source passage, item or observation that supports the finding, and the limits on relying on it. Several sources can support or challenge the same finding. |

Identify the subject of the memory or lineage claim: for example, a person or organization, material, Method, MethodDescription, Work, capability, performance, event, artifact, population or cultural relation.

A score or onset list can preserve selected rhythmic relations. A geometric representation, video or motion trace can preserve others. Identify what each representation specifies or records. A dated score can itself be the subject of a question about revisions to its notation.

### MDPE.18:1 - Problem

Music and Dance leave selective traces. A recording can preserve sound while losing fingering, actuation, ensemble cues, room interaction, or the Method that generated it. Video can preserve visible movement while hiding pressure, weight transfer, lead-and-response, muscular effort, attention, sensation, or corrections. Scores, choreography descriptions, prompts, code, instruments, costumes, datasets, and event programmes preserve other selections.

Different carriers therefore support different claims. A performer may retain capability without being able to describe the Method. An archive may preserve records after known holders lose representative capability. A school may preserve a name while changing its Methods. A revival may use old records while creating a new Method variant. A new body or instrument can preserve one function while branching another relation.

Different traits need not share one history. Musical material can come from one line, bodily or instrumental technique from another, event conventions from a third, and the name from a later instituting group. Borrowing, mixture or convergence may require relations that one genealogy would hide; geography, ecology and source bias can affect their interpretation. Use a tree when the relevant traits and supported relations warrant it. Neither a tree nor a network is the default conclusion before those subjects and sources are selected.

A bounded attribution can answer a historical question. A festival may also use it for a programme note, a teacher may choose a reconstruction trial, and a restorer may identify a capability worth testing.

### MDPE.18:2 - Forces

| Tension | What must remain visible |
| --- | --- |
| usefulness ↔ completeness | An identified date or relation can answer a question long before the history is complete. A decision may also have a deadline. |
| visible record ↔ embodied practice | Durable media may be accessible after performers, partners or witnesses have gone. A visible gesture can survive while the pressure felt by a partner or the correction that changed it goes unrecorded. Private, informal and marginalized work can also leave few public records. |
| attribution ↔ distributed change | Identify who created or taught the material and who later recognized, selected, transmitted or continued it. The same participants may do several of these things. |
| one lineage ↔ several trait histories | One tree is easy to tell; material, technique, event form, terminology, and teaching can have different relations. |
| official visibility ↔ actual practice | Standards, universities, theatres, platforms and archives produce records. The relative prevalence of less documented commercial, social and peer practices requires evidence about the populations involved. |
| source criticism ↔ source-community rights | Access and comparison can improve an account. Consent, attribution, privacy, return of materials and future-use terms determine how sources may be examined and shared. |
| precision ↔ readable use | Claims need clear kinds and limits, expressed in language that a reader new to the case can understand. |

### MDPE.18:3 - Solution

Identify the particular historical question or practical use. Connect each relied-on finding to an identifiable source and the portion that supports it. Where access is restricted, respect the source agreement and state the basis and limits of any permitted report or authorized inspection. Compare competing explanations when the choice between them matters. Identify what the sources establish, including an unresolved limit when it is the answer.

#### MDPE.18:3.1 - Bound the historical question or decision

Identify the following where relevant.

- who needs the historical account or will use it in another task,
- the question about attribution, reconstruction, teaching, changed-condition use, restoration, retirement or further development,
- the musical or movement subject,
- the population, place, period and intended use, and
- the precision and strength of evidence the intended use requires.

For example, a festival team needs to decide how to credit the sources for a Tarraxo workshop and which partnering distinctions to try. A source-attributed note and a justified choice of exercises can serve this purpose even though the worldwide genealogy remains open.

For a broad question such as the history of tango, identify the people, relations, practices and period the account needs to cover.

#### MDPE.18:3.2 - Identify source objects and world-side subjects

For every relied-on source, ask:

- Is the source a recording, testimony, method description, notation, event record, dataset, instrument, publication or another kind of object?
- Which participant, work, method, performance, artifact, event or population does it concern?
- Who created or recorded it, for what purpose, audience, language, and conditions?
- Which part of the source is used?
- What access, consent, attribution, editing, preservation, or future-use conditions apply?

If a way of doing is already recoverable, check its identity and applicability under `A.3.1` and use it where it fits. Use `A.3.1.DR` when a document’s meaning or the status of its guidance needs recovery. Use `A.3.1.MR` when observations or other evidence suggest a possible way of working, including evidence that has yet to establish a Work occurrence. One event can suggest a hypothesis. Identifying a reusable Method requires the corresponding grounds. Use `RMP.10` for a consequential reconstruction that exceeds ordinary recovery. Process mining can help where events, cases, activities, objects and their correlations are justified. A recurring log path may omit the embodied action and does not by itself establish a rule or a Method.

#### MDPE.18:3.3 - Connect the relied-on claims to their sources

Make the basis of each finding recoverable to the extent permitted by the source terms. Use a citation, a short account or a table such as this one.

| Source and retained part | Supported claim | Limit | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source object and relevant page, passage, recording time, frame or data sample | Finding and the period, place or population it covers | Missing information, competing explanation, uncertainty or access restriction relevant to the finding | Historical question the finding answers or decision it informs |

Distinguish an observed occurrence from an interpretation of it. Identify the position from which a practitioner, participant, institution, researcher, platform or later reconstructor reported it. Independent corroboration may strengthen an account. Following several copies back to one source establishes the common basis for the claim they repeat. Look elsewhere if independent corroboration matters.

Date the source relative to the claim. A recording made at a past performance can document that occasion. A teaching manual can establish what its author prescribed then. For a question about present practice, safety, preservation technology or effectiveness, use evidence appropriate to the current task. Official adoption or number of publications alone cannot establish performance or prevalence.

State whether the finding comes from observation, attribution to a source, corroboration or an expert estimate. Identify a material dispute or unknown where it remains. When a suitable population measure is unavailable or its cost is unjustified for the decision, a qualified estimate may still inform a reversible decision if its observations and uncertainty are explicit.

#### MDPE.18:3.4 - Compare lineage alternatives by the traits that matter

Identify the aspect of lineage the question concerns. Relevant histories can include

- musical or movement material;
- bodily or instrumental technique;
- Method or teaching line;
- event, venue, platform, or participation form;
- name, institutionalization, or publication line; or
- population transmission and continuation.

Compare the explanations the evidence still allows where the difference matters. Material may derive from one line, combine several, arise independently under similar constraints, branch deliberately or be reconstructed from surviving records. A tree can represent descent where each branch has one immediate predecessor. If material from one branch was also adopted on another, show that connection.

Return the supported attribution or relation and any uncertainty that affects its use. A single well-supported local finding may answer the question.

#### MDPE.18:3.5 - Establish what surviving sources reveal about the practice

Examine what the records can support about the relations relevant to the question, such as

- embodied or instrumental capability;
- pressure, weight, touch, effort, sensation, timing, articulation, or correction;
- partner, ensemble, audience, venue, or equipment relations;
- operative constraints and situation-responsive choices;
- teacher feedback and learning context;
- software, model, prompt, data, or control configuration; and
- present holders, access, transmission opportunities, recognition, selection, and reproduction.

Identify any gap that changes what the recipient can conclude. Existing performance evidence can already establish a past enactment or documented continuation. If further evidence matters, identify an available source, demonstration or other observation that could supply it. Use `MDPE.17` to examine a receiver’s performance and `MDPE.19` for reproduction in the specified population and period.

#### MDPE.18:3.6 - Return the supported historical account

Report the findings needed for the question. Select the prompts that apply.

```text
historical question or decision, recipient, subject, population, place and period:
source-to-claim links:
supported lineage relations by dimension:
explanations the evidence still allows, where the difference matters:
material gaps in evidence about movement, performance, technique or present use:
uses the evidence and agreements support:
claims still unsupported:
any further inquiry justified by the question, or the supported reason to stop:
changes in sources or evidence that would affect a finding:
```

A single attribution may be enough. A reconstruction inquiry may instead need a usable method description and the particular embodied relation the sources leave open. Pursue further inquiry or a demonstration when its attainable contribution warrants the cost. If the task is to teach, restore, transmit, retire or continue a practice, use the findings in the work you are authorized to do, or provide them to whoever is responsible for it.

### MDPE.18:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.18:4.1 - Dance: a Tarraxo workshop attributes claims without inventing a complete genealogy

A festival workshop team must choose an attribution note and movement and partnering distinctions to try. The three practitioner pages below are among the case sources consulted on 25 August 2026. They support a qualified note and a teaching proposal. A complete Tarraxo genealogy would require other evidence.

| Source and retained part | Supported claim | Limit | Decision use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tarraxo Agency home page | The organization describes its development and promotion of Tarraxo projects, artists, festivals, workshops and performances. | This is the organization’s account of its activities. For origin, prevalence, effectiveness or continuation, other evidence is needed. | Attribute the description of the organization and its events to the agency. |
| Gwany and Liliana practitioner profile | The profile credits Gwany with creating Tarraxo, dates the partnership and reports that they trained other teachers. | These are claims made in the profile. Sole origin would need independent historical grounds. | Cite the profile for those attributed claims. |
| TOCA Method page | This teaching account emphasizes touch, observation, control, awareness, connection, musicality, drills, isolation and placement. | It is a commercial practitioner description. Learners’ capabilities and the effectiveness of instruction require evidence of the relevant work. | Select specific distinctions to try in a workshop. |

These sources leave Angolan antecedents, predecessor relations, independent corroboration and current receiving capability open. The team can publish the attributed note and try the selected teaching approach. Use `MDPE.17` for a further question about how to arrange reception, what the learners actually did or how a source contributed.

#### MDPE.18:4.2 - Music: an Algorave brief uses a pinned community source

An organizer must decide what an introductory workshop and event should preserve from the documented Algorave line while allowing local variation.

| Source and retained part | Supported claim | Limit | Decision use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blackwell et al., *Live Coding: A User's Manual* (2022), sections “What is Live Coding?”, “Partial Histories”, and “Algorave” | Live coding is heterogeneous; Algorave is a coined rallying genre with changing local practices and communities. | Partial practitioner-scholar history; no one sound style, local enactment, global prevalence, or continuation result. | Describe the proposed event as a local interpretation of this varied practice. |
| Algorave guidelines, pinned commit `24b2ad5`, README lines 1–24 | The guidelines recommend that most acts generate music and visuals algorithmically and make the code or process visible. They allow other approaches and leave room for acts without live coding or a projected screen. | This is a community account of how to programme events. Actual use by organizers and actual performances need their own evidence. | Set workshop and programme constraints with appropriate local variation. |

The organizer can use these sources to write the event brief. For a question about a particular performer, code–sound control, a room, projection, an audience or an event already held, use relevant existing evidence. For an unresolved question about the particular event, identify what could establish the missing fact. A future trial can test a proposed setup.

#### MDPE.18:4.3 - A human–AI Music project page is not a style lineage

Serpentine’s page for *The Call* describes the artists’ songbook, singing exercises and recording protocol, the recordings made with fifteen UK community choirs, the resulting training data and choral AI models, and the use of the models in a spatial audio installation. It also describes the choristers’ participation in a Data Trust experiment concerning the powers of training-data contributors and model users. These details can support an account of the project.

To claim a reusable method, identify the work and relations a later project can reproduce. A claim about cultural memory in the model, a style lineage, receivers’ capabilities, recognition or continued practice calls for evidence of that specific result. A later project can cite the materials it uses, draw on `MDPE.6` for changed conditions and consult `MDPE.17` for the design or assessment of transmission.

#### MDPE.18:4.4 - Record survival is not living continuation

Consider this constructed reconstruction project. A workshop team has a dated 2021 class recording with accompanying notation, and a 2025 school page listing Mo as a current teacher. The proposed programme note says that Mo has continuously transmitted Erin's complete partnering Method since 2021. Before publishing it, the team compares the two source objects for that claim.

In the continuous class passage, Erin demonstrates a contact cue, Mo proposes a different one, and the pair tries Mo’s revision. This establishes a change in that lesson. The dated roster establishes that in 2025 the school listed Mo as a teacher. What Mo taught in between, the origin of the revised cue and whether students acquired the whole method remain open.

A twenty-minute review of the relevant passage and the dated roster changes the decision. The team credits the 2021 demonstration and revision separately, labels its workshop as a reconstruction from those materials, and drops the claim of continuous complete transmission. No rival genealogy or formal event log is needed. The source agreement permits this attribution and internal study but not republication of identifiable class footage; the programme note therefore cites the agreed source description without reproducing the video.

The recording shows a visible sequence and some cue timing. The felt pressure and a present holder’s ability to reproduce the complete relation remain open. Before choosing the exercise, the team asks a willing current practitioner to perform the partner relation and explain the pressure felt and used. A participant in the present demonstration can describe the pressure in that performance. To establish what was felt in 2021, seek evidence about that lesson, such as the original partner’s testimony. The team can already use its historical attribution. If the demonstration is unavailable, the workshop can examine the records within the agreement and describe the reconstruction within those limits. Use `MDPE.17` for receiving enactment or `MDPE.19` for a question about continuation or restoration.

Use a sufficient account from a historian or practitioner directly. This method helps when the relation between the historical finding, the evidence for embodied practice and the question still needs to be established.


### MDPE.18:5 - Recognition and Assurance

Check the claims on which the recipient will rely.

- Which historical question or use determines the scope?
- Which subjects, events and methods are at issue, and what evidence about them do the sources contain?
- For every relied-on claim, which source part supports it and what is the limit?
- Who produced each account, from what position, and what does each provide?
- Which trait and relation does the evidence establish? If a wider history matters, can a tree represent those relations, or do they require other connections?
- Which embodied, performative, technical or present-use relations can be recovered, and which relevant ones remain open?
- Which evidence concerns publication or visibility, and which evidence covers the distribution of actual practice?
- What is established, what is still uncertain, and what would the recipient gain from any further inquiry?

Check the source’s identity, the passage or item used, the conditions under which it was produced, permission to use it and its relevance to the claim’s period. Examine agreement and contradiction among sources where they bear on the finding. When a mutable page changes, check which claims or decisions depended on the changed material. A preserved dated version can continue to support what was reported then. Respect the limits of any authorized inspection.

### MDPE.18:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “The video preserves the dance.” | Identify the movement, sound or other relations the recording preserves and the particular claim it still cannot support, if any. |
| “The score contains the performance Method.” | Identify what the notation prescribes, any account of how to perform it, and, if the question concerns an actual performance, what the evidence shows about how the performer realized that notation. |
| “The founder's story is the lineage.” | Attribute the account to the founder. Compare other supported relations and traits when they matter to the historical question or subsequent use. |
| “The archive proves the practice is alive.” | Separate the survival of an archive from the work it documents. Use `MDPE.19` to assess actual reproduction when continuation is the question. |
| “The official or academic literature shows what people actually do.” | Examine what the cited work observed and the population it covers. Use practitioner, project or population evidence for any remaining question. Mark an estimate and its basis when a measure is unavailable. |
| “The frequent process-mining path is the Method.” | Check how events and their links were identified. Use `A.3.1.MR` for a remaining question about a possible method and identify any unrecorded bodily or tacit work that affects it. |
| “We need the complete history before acting.” | Return the source-supported answer the task needs and identify the particular inferences the available evidence cannot support. |

### MDPE.18:7 - Consequences

| Benefit | Cost or caution |
| --- | --- |
| Attribution, reconstruction, teaching, and restoration can proceed without invented certainty. | Keep the source and limits available for any continuing use that depends on them. |
| Different lineage dimensions remain visible. | The result may be a network or several partial relations rather than one simple story. |
| Records no longer stand in for embodied Methods or living practice. | Representative Work and specialist inquiry may still be needed. |
| Informal and practitioner accounts can contribute alongside institutional records. | An estimate of how widespread the practices were still needs observations and an explicit account of uncertainty. |
| New evidence reopens only dependent claims. | Tracing a disputed claim to its source takes time. Use an adequately sourced account when it already answers the question. |

### MDPE.18:8 - Rationale and Source Use

Use FPF for evidence, cultural evolution, the retention and comparison of candidate variants and treatment of a current pool, and recovery of a possible method. This chapter connects particular music and dance sources, including recordings, notation, bodily and partner accounts, instrument and software configurations, teaching and event histories, and disputed attributions, to the question they can answer.

| Direct Method source | Use here | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral History Association, [Best Practices](https://oralhistory.org/best-practices/) and [Ethics](https://oralhistory.org/oha-statement-on-ethics/) | Preserve narrator and interviewer positions, production and editing context, agreements, access, citation, and respectful contextualization. | New interviewing, participant review, preservation, and access Work stay with oral-history Methods. |
| Library of Congress, [Primary Sources](https://www.loc.gov/programs/teachers/getting-started-with-primary-sources) and Digital Inquiry Group, [Historical Thinking Chart](https://www.inquirygroup.org/history-lessons/historical-thinking-chart) | Separate observation and inference; recover creator, purpose, audience, time, place, context, corroboration, and contradiction. | General historical inquiry remains with its direct Method. |
