- the appropriate engineering, management, teaching, artistic, safety, legal or maintenance method supports each specialist finding,
- the claims about visibility and practice match what official, scholarly, press or platform sources establish,
- the appraisal accounts for lost alternatives and burdens shifted to others,
- the observation period covers the claimed outcome or retention interval, and
- a claim about a new scene, level, attractor or larger cultural whole has evidence of the particular organization, level or pattern of change being claimed.

### MDPE.22:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “Build a community around the new style.” | Identify the practice and the surrounding participation, teaching, event, recognition or memory relation needed to sustain it. Establish what already supplies that relation. |
| “The platform will solve distribution.” | Identify the publication, discovery, access, recommendation, payment, moderation or support service that the task requires. Use suitable evidence of actual uptake for a claim that someone received or used it. |
| “Add another class.” | Establish what the existing arrangement already supplies and whether the question leaves a gap in capability, uncued transfer, opportunity, organizing work, partner mix, recognition or continuity. |
| “The event happened, so the practice changed.” | Report the event within its scope. Use suitable evidence about later performance, transmission, recognition, selection or reproduction for a claim about subsequent practice. A claim about what caused a change needs a further basis. |
| “The infrastructure exists, so users can use it.” | Establish whether the relevant permission, time, configuration, capable provider and access were in place. For a claim of actual use, examine what the intended users did. Use a new test when the remaining question warrants it. |
| “Copy the successful festival, school, or platform.” | Identify which relations were present in the earlier case and which can be supplied in the receiving setting. Support any claim that a particular relation caused the earlier result before relying on that causal explanation. |
| “One environment change caused the cultural effect.” | Report the observed sequence. To attribute the difference to a particular change, use `C.28` to examine how well the evidence distinguishes its contribution. |
| “The whole ecology must be redesigned.” | Examine the support the intended practice actually needs. Compare keeping an adequate arrangement with changes whose likely contribution warrants their full burden. |
| “A local success created a new cultural level.” | Use `MDPE.24` to examine evidence that the required constituents and relations formed a distinct whole, or establish which existing whole the local work belonged to. Limit each claim to the evidence available. |

### MDPE.22:7 - Consequences

The method can support the following results.

- A project can distinguish the class, tool, event or archive it provided from the practice people actually carried out.
- Engineers and organizers can identify the musical or movement use their work needs to support and the evidence that would establish its success.
- A previously overlooked provider, venue, instrument or access dependency can enter a concrete decision.
- Infrastructure options can be compared by what they make possible and what participants have achieved under them.
- Practitioners can try a local change while the wider population makes its own choices.
- A documented failure can support stopping, trying another relation or giving the requested historical account.

Costs and limits:

- environment changes often require several independent Agents and authorities;
- observations relevant to the practice can arrive later than the technical or organizational change;
- observation can require performer, audience, teacher, organizer, or source-community participation;
- a bounded intervention can move burden, reduce diversity, or create new dependence; and
- the wider culture can ignore, transform, or reverse the project's result.

### MDPE.22:8 - Rationale and Source Use

Niche-construction and eco-evo-devo research suggest a question about artists’ environments. Artists and practitioners establish schools,
clubs, festivals, archives, tools and media. Which of these changes alters the conditions for later teaching, recognition, selection
or retention? The analogy motivates inquiry in music and dance. Establish the cultural relation from evidence about the practice.

Historically, studies of art worlds and music scenes identify cooperation, convention, distribution and support worth looking for. The studies
below also ask who maintains infrastructure under precarious conditions, who funds and runs a platform’s events, and how custodians, teachers
and performers shape what an archive can communicate and which uses its agreements permit. Use the relevant cases to investigate the particular arrangement.

| Source | Use in this pattern | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laland, Odling-Smee, and Feldman, “Niche construction, biological evolution, and cultural change,” 2000 | Supplies deliberate modification of conditions that can feed back on later practice and selection as a hypothesis-generating analogy. | Biological niche construction is not the ontology or universal Method of Music and Dance projects. |
| Howard S. Becker, *Art Worlds*, 1982 | Exposes cooperative Work, conventions, resources, distribution, support, and audiences behind artistic results. | Historical sociology does not select a current project architecture or establish one causal relation. |
| Andy Bennett and Richard A. Peterson, eds., *Music Scenes*, 2004 | Supplies local, translocal, and virtual scene cases and cautions against treating genre labels as the whole social organization. | Scene descriptions do not establish one current scene or authorize intervention. |
| Schmidt, Bork Petersen, Schnor, and Vedel, [“Dancing necessities: Infrastructures, interventions, and maintenance”](https://doi.org/10.7146/peri.v21i39.152261), 2024 | Adds venue economy, education, self-organized spaces and cooperatives, critique, self-archiving, maintenance, structural precarity and representation to a current Dance-infrastructure inquiry. | One Danish contemporary-Dance field inquiry does not establish the same relations or priorities for social Dance, another country, or Music. |
| Riom, [“Being a ‘Global Music Platform’: Platform Work in Light-Tech Capitalism”](https://doi.org/10.1177/20563051241274658), 2024 | Shows in one multi-sited Sofar Sounds ethnography that platform Work included digital incorporation, venture financing, event-format adaptation, and recruitment and generification of participants. | One company and field period do not define all Music platforms or establish the causal contribution of any operation. |
| Bench and Elswit, [“If the archive can’t consent: Reimagining motion data and AI ethics for dance’s embodied histories”](https://doi.org/10.1017/cfc.2025.10009), published 2026 | Adds embodied knowledge, community custodial relations, participatory design, consent, representational harm, pedagogical encounters, and limits of pose or motion data to current Dance-archive and AI Work. | An essay and bounded Dunham Technique collaboration do not supply a universal archive, consent, machine-learning, or reconstruction Method. |
| UNESCO, [Transmission](https://ich.unesco.org/en/transmission-00078) and [Safeguarding without freezing](https://ich.unesco.org/en/safeguarding-00012) | Keeps documentation, transmission, participation, recreation, and revitalization distinct. | Official recognition does not establish local enactment, prevalence, value, or continuation. |
| Blackwell et al., [*Live Coding: A User's Manual*](https://livecodingbook.toplap.org/book/) and Algorave [guidelines](https://github.com/Algorave/guidelines/blob/24b2ad588f7f0110e8b7d5e3c57736e6056c4270/README_en.md) | Supply source-local live-coding and event-programming distinctions for the worked case. | They do not establish prevalence, receiving enactment, continuation, or one preferred sound style. |

The three present-practice cases support different parts of an environment inquiry:

| Present-practice case | Relations examined or reported | Use in an environment inquiry | Scope and grounds for reconsideration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Danish contemporary-Dance infrastructure | The authors examine venues, economics, education, self-organized spaces, cooperatives, critique, self-archiving, precarious work and representation. | Examine financing, self-maintenance, representation, provider burden and alternatives in `MDPE.22:0.1`, `3.2`, `3.4` and `3.6`. | Use the findings at their field and expert scope. A claim about prevalence or cause in social dance or another setting needs suitable evidence there. |
| Sofar Sounds as Music-platform Work | Riom describes how Sofar’s digital systems and financing supported concerts and how its event format organized work across local sites by recruiting artists, hosts, volunteers and guests for common tasks. | Examine interface, ticketing, financing, recruitment, event provision and performers’ adaptation together where a change in discovery may also affect them. | This is one multi-sited ethnography. Check other operating arrangements before generalizing the relations or selecting a change elsewhere. |
| Dunham Technique, motion data and AI archive Work | The collaboration examines documents, film, motion data, oral history, teaching encounters, community custody, consent and the limits of representation. | Identify the sources, custodial rights and embodied knowledge needed to use a particular representation for teaching or historical interpretation. | A change in the receiving task, consent or community account may affect what can be inferred or used. Claims about later learners require evidence from their work. |

If a relied-on source changes, reconsider any dependent historical finding, proposal,
interpretation of a practice observation or grounds for a decision. Use a new publication, official rule
or widely reported case for the claims its content and authority actually support.

### MDPE.22:9 - Relations

| Related result | Use here |
| --- | --- |
| `E.10.ROLE`, `A.2.1`, and `F.6` | Use them to resolve ambiguous role wording, establish a formal assignment or attribute performed work where those distinctions matter. Ability, authority and actual performance each require grounds concerning the relevant participant. |
| `MDPE.21` | Use the style-development account to identify which supporting relation an existing or proposed practice arrangement needs, including support worth retaining. |
| `MDPE.12` and `MDPE.13` | Use suitable observations of performance, recognition or selection to establish what the environment did or did not support. |
| `MDPE.17` | Use `MDPE.17` to design a receiving arrangement or to establish provision, access, the receiver’s performance or a source’s contribution. A positive finding can establish adequate support. |
| `MDPE.18` and `MDPE.19` | Use historical, lineage or continuation evidence where the question concerns archive use, restoration or repeated practice. |
| `MDPE.14` | Examine a conflict among simultaneous work, structures, positions in a larger whole, slower constraints or uses of a representation. Use that account in a decision when a response is needed. |
| `MDPE.16` | Use `MDPE.16` to decide which alternatives to retain and what each could make possible if the proposed change would remove it. |
| `MDPE.20` and `MDPE.24` | Use local evidence, with its actual scope, in a forecast or in assessing a larger whole, its formation or its continuity. |
| `C.36` and `C.36.P` | Supply the general cultural relations and boundary discipline. |
| Systems Engineering, Organization Change Engineering, Operations Management, Organization Administration, Human Capability Development, and direct domain Methods | Use each for its supporting-System, organization, recurring Work, service, human learning, or specialist result; capable Agents perform the Work. |
| `C.28` and `C.11.DUA` | Use `C.28` to qualify a causal contribution. Use `C.11.DUA` to decide whether another investigation could improve the historical answer or practical choice enough to justify all its work, delay and cost. |

### MDPE.22:End

## MDPE.14 - Choose a Response to Conflicting Music-or-Dance Results

> **Status:** Stable

> **Type:** DPF pattern body
>
> **Primary working result:** an account of a conflict in a particular music or dance practice, a recommendation or a decision about how to respond.
> Identify the results at stake, the relation that makes them conflict, the protected conditions and any burden passed to others.
> Existing evidence can establish what happened, which responses fit or why the available responses fail.
> When a choice is needed, the holder of the authority to decide may select a change, keep an acceptable tension, use different variants for different purposes,
> choose a discriminating observation or reject the available options for the proposed use.
> Obtain further evidence when its attainable contribution warrants the full burden or an applicable requirement calls for it.
> To establish that the choice was implemented or that performance improved, examine evidence of that work and result.

### MDPE.14:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern when a change has improved or could improve one result while putting another at risk, or
when evidence about an earlier performance, judging arrangement or event reveals that conflict. Identify the relation connecting the two.
The relevant relation may concern a part and whole, an order of scales, overlapping work, a slower constraint
or use of a representation. If several criteria merely apply to one subject, use ordinary comparison.

Typical situations include:

- a larger social-Dance figure is easier for spectators to see but exceeds the space, partner information, or
  effort limits of a crowded floor;
- a musician improves one difficult gesture while control of phrase shape, ensemble coordination, sound, or attention to
  the whole performance deteriorates;
- a robot's visible social gesture becomes easier to read while timing, mechanical noise, or musical
  interaction crosses an accepted limit;
- a competition arrangement makes performances easier to compare while training, improvisation, participation,
  or cultural continuity is put at risk;
- a short-video carrier increases discovery while attribution, teaching use, partner response, or long-form
  composition remains unsupported; or
- a school makes entry easier by simplifying material but removes distinctions needed for later style
  development.

Ask which conflict the account must establish.

> Which results conflict here, through what relation, and with what consequences? If a response is wanted, which option protects the needed results
> and who would bear its cost?

Existing evidence can establish the conflict, a past choice or the grounds for a present recommendation or decision. Use it directly when it covers the question.

For a conflict across declared scopes, `C.30.ILC` can identify the remaining incompatibility
and `C.32.MLAO` can develop responses when needed. Use a sufficient result from
choreography, partnering, instrumental practice, rehearsal, production, judging, safety,
platform or engineering work directly. Continue here when the remaining account, comparison or
choice depends on the relations, criteria, limits or uses specific to music or dance.

Use the more direct route in these situations.

- For the order of steps in one method or occurrence, use the direct method or `A.22.CGUS`.
- For several criteria applied to one subject, use ordinary comparison unless a part–whole, scale, overlap, slower-constraint or
  representation relation changes the finding or choice.
- For a question about supporting provision, such as a venue, archive, platform or recurring access, use `MDPE.22`.
- To identify or configure the performing whole, use `MDPE.3`.
- To maintain distinct development alternatives, use `MDPE.16`.
- To implement a selected local change, use the appropriate direct method. For the question of what changed in practice or which local
  change to develop further, use `MDPE.15` as needed.

Revisit an earlier `MDPE.14` decision when a receiving observation or changed variant from `MDPE.17` changes
the conflict, candidate, comparison, remaining tension, burden on someone else or relevant performance test. An
observation that leaves its grounds intact can still answer a separate question about receiving performance.

#### MDPE.14:0.1 - Five Conflict Branches

Each branch identifies a different relation.

| Branch | Relation that must be stated | Typical Music-or-Dance use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **cross-holon** | A named part–whole relation connects a movement, phrase, performer, instrument, event part, Method part, or Work part to a named whole. | A phrase becomes more spectacular while partner coordination or the whole performance deteriorates. |
| **cross-scale** | A declared spatial, temporal, organizational, population, or other scale order connects the compared subjects. | A change helps one performance grain while a larger or slower scale result crosses a limit. |
| **simultaneous Work** | Work occurrences or parts overlap in a particular interval, or a proposed arrangement requires them at the same time. Overlap establishes neither parthood nor scale. | Phrase Work, partner sensing, floorcraft, audience-facing performance, and event participation compete for attention or space. |
| **slower constraint** | A teaching, repertoire, judging, platform, event, or institutional arrangement changes more slowly and constrains current Work through a named relation. | A judging system or recommender changes which variants performers prepare or present. |
| **representation use** | A representation makes particular features available to a recipient and may obscure others important to the intended use. | A camera view, score, sensor or metric may show one partner’s displacement while leaving the contact that guided it uncertain. |

A case can involve several branches. Establish the relation for each. A vertical drawing,
page position or simultaneous action does not establish an order of scales. Identify
the variable and its ordering, such as events within phrases within sets over progressively longer intervals.

Keep three additional distinctions visible:

- **Method unfolding** describes possible first–then or branching Work under a Method; it is not a simultaneous
  holonic architecture.
- **Coarse-graining** suppresses distinctions in a description for a use; it does not create a world-side holon
  or part–whole relation.
- **Observed difference and causal contribution.** An observed difference can justify
a reversible choice. To attribute that difference to a particular change, use
`C.28` and evidence that distinguishes its contribution from other explanations.

A dancer, musician, teacher, judge, robot, AI system or collective can be the
agent for a particular performance or choice. Identify bodies, instruments,
floors, software, venues and platforms by the relation that matters. Use
*System* for a physical or operational whole meeting those conditions. A recording
carrier or playback platform can participate in the arrangement, while
represented observations and claims are informational content. Use `C.2.1` when
the particular claim-bearing identity affects what the account can support.

### MDPE.14:1 - Problem

During one performance or practice situation, several results matter together. A dancer regulates effort and
balance while producing movement units, figures, phrases, partner interaction, a performance, and participation
in a social event. A musician regulates an effector while shaping notes, rhythm, phrase, ensemble interaction,
sound, and the whole performance. Teaching, repertoire, judging, event, and platform arrangements can constrain
what is prepared and performed.

These descriptions concern different kinds of subjects: Work parts, Systems in a performing whole, slower
arrangements, and representations. The recurring engineering difficulty is
that project participants optimize an easy local proxy and lose another result that remains important.

Examples of the failure include:

- larger movement is called better Dance while partner information, floorcraft, safety, or participation falls;
- timing accuracy is called better Music while expressive timing, sound, or ensemble response disappears;
- higher judging reliability is called better style while one criterion or one cultural arrangement dominates;
- platform attention is called cultural success while attribution, learning, enactment, or continuation remains
  unknown; and
- technical feasibility is called successful practice while the performers face excessive burdens, participants lack consent or access, or event
  operation fails.

The cost can be high: performers are injured, partners stop participating, instruments or robots are pushed
beyond reliable configurations, schools teach for the wrong use, competitions select brittle variants, and
later development follows evidence that no longer represents the intended practice.

### MDPE.14:2 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Local observability and whole-practice fit | A small feature is easier to measure and change; the wider Work and practice carry other results. |
| Virtuosity and sustainable capability | Technical challenge can expand expression while exceeding bodies, effectors, attention, rehearsal, or replacement capacity. |
| Coordination and local freedom | Partner or ensemble coordination needs shared information; improvisation and expression need room to vary. |
| Participation and precision | Wider entry can increase enactment while simplified distinctions can limit later mastery or style integrity. |
| Visibility and embodied use | Camera, stage, judge, or platform legibility can select features unlike those needed by partners, musicians, or participants. |
| Several structures and one practical question | A question about one performance can involve several views of it. Identify which relation changes the explanation, recommendation or choice. |
| Immediate observation and slower consequence | One occurrence or metric changes quickly; capability, repertoire, selection, and continuation can change later. |
| Improvement and moved burden | A candidate can reduce one conflict while moving cost, risk, attention, exclusion, maintenance, or evidence burden elsewhere. |

### MDPE.14:3 - Solution

Identify the particular music or dance situation, the results in conflict and the relationship that explains why the two matter together. Distinguish the observed conflict, a consequence that follows from the proposed conditions and a suspected consequence that remains untested. Use the FPF cross-scope methods where that relation is present. For a recommendation or decision, compare the relevant responses using the artistic, bodily and operating limits. A report about an earlier conflict or choice can end with its grounds and limitations. To implement an authorized choice, use the applicable direct method. For the resulting performance, use suitable observations, including available findings from `MDPE.12`.

A comparison may expose another affected participant or result. Add it if it changes the account or the choice.

#### MDPE.14:3.1 - Bound the situation and the question

Identify the details the question requires.

- the representative performance, work or proposed conditions,
- the performers and the organization of the performing whole,
- the result that changed or that someone proposes to improve,
- the other result and the condition it must or had to satisfy,
- the participants and systems affected,
- the place, interval, material, configuration and period of evidence, and
- for a recommendation or choice, who needs the result and how they will use it. Identify who may decide when a decision is needed. For a past choice, establish what was decided and identify the authority then in force if it bears on the question.

For a proposal, identify the assumed relations and what the design or available evidence already entails.
If evidence of actual performance is needed, specify what observation could support or defeat the claim.

A usable entry is:

> During dense-floor social partner-Dance Work, increasing the amplitude and speed of a turn–steps–counter-turn
> phrase is expected to improve distant-camera visibility while partner-readable weight transfer, floorcraft,
> rhythmic clarity, and bounded effort may cross their accepted limits.

#### MDPE.14:3.2 - Select and support the conflict branch

For every branch used, state the two subjects and the relation between them.

| Question | What establishes the relation |
| --- | --- |
| Which movement, method step or part of the work changed or would change? | Identify its larger whole and the part–whole relation that was assumed or established. |
| Which work overlapped or would have to overlap? | Identify the occurrences or proposed tasks, their common interval, participants, equipment and outcomes that must coexist. |
| Which scale order matters? | Name the variable and the ordering relation. When the case concerns only co-occurrence or parthood, use the corresponding branch. |
| Which slower arrangement constrains current Work? | Name the judging, teaching, platform, repertoire, event, or institutional relation and the current Work it constrains. |
| How does the representation affect the inquiry or choice? | Identify the subject represented, distinctions available or hidden and the use to which the representation was or will be put. |

Distinguish an observed difference, a design hypothesis, an association and a causal contribution. A structural
relation can explain why two results must be considered together while leaving open the cause of a reported change.

If none of these relations matters to the question, use ordinary comparison.

#### MDPE.14:3.3 - Use the residual frame when the conflict crosses declared scopes

Use `C.30.ILC` when the conflict is an architecture residual across named holon levels or declared scopes of the described whole or whole family, and a selected structure carries or relates those scopes. After that residual is recovered, use `C.32.MLAO` if residual-reducing architecture candidates are needed. In that branch:

- identify the remaining conflict and the affected holons or declared scopes,
- name the selected structures and architecture characteristics,
- when a requested recommendation or decision still needs alternatives, develop candidates that address the conflict,
- when responses are at issue, identify what each would preserve, lose or shift to others,
- state the time over which the arrangement could change and when the source grounds would need reconsideration, and
- use the applicable method for any remaining comparison, choice, intervention, observation or causal assessment.

If a conflict involves simultaneous work or use of a representation without a relation across declared scopes, use the participants, relations and limits established in §§3.1–3.2 directly. Propose a response when the task requires one.

In either branch, use the music and dance details that affect the finding or choice.

- movement, phrase, musical, partner, ensemble, performer–instrument, event, judging, platform, and
  representation relations;
- bodily, equipment, acoustic, floor, consent, attribution, permission, and access vetoes;
- candidate families such as changing local articulation, partner or ensemble interfaces, the performing whole,
  judging or publication arrangements, or separate variants for separate uses;
- criteria such as partner information, musical timing and sound, expressive control, floorcraft, injury risk,
  participation, recognition, attribution, teaching use, and retained variation; and
- evidence of the relevant performance or design, including representative trials or suitable earlier observations when these bear on the question.

Use the general FPF or direct domain result when it already answers the question within the relevant limits.

#### MDPE.14:3.4 - Identify or develop responses with different consequences

When a recommendation or decision calls for comparing responses, use the available responses, develop another if needed and identify which relations or burdens differ. Possible responses include

- change the local movement, articulation, fingering, actuation, phrase, or control relation;
- change the interface between partners, ensemble members, robot and instrument, performer and cue, or performer
  and venue;
- change the performing whole or the wider event arrangement rather than the local technique;
- change judging, publication, attribution, teaching, or platform relations;
- separate uses that need different variants instead of forcing one compromise;
- add capability, feedback, sensing, rehearsal, moderation, or evidence where the conflict is hidden;
- change the representation or metric so a protected result becomes visible; or
- preserve the current tension deliberately within stated limits.

Consider keeping the arrangement when the tension is useful or the feasible
changes would impose a greater burden. Choose a further comparison if it
could improve the answer enough to warrant design, participant time, delay,
cost and displaced practice. Retain applicable safety, permission and evidence
requirements independently of the expected benefit of optional testing.

For each response being compared, identify what would change or stay as it is, the expected result, what needs protection, any burden and the conditions required
to realize it. State what could change the judgement if relevant. Use a known limit directly when it settles feasibility.

#### MDPE.14:3.5 - Compare with domain criteria and vetoes

Compare responses with the music and dance criteria that matter here. Use `A.19.CPM` for a comparison of admitted profiles under a declared comparator and `C.11` when the task is to choose. Criteria can include

- performer effort, attention, injury risk, expressive control, and sustainable capability;
- partner or ensemble information, consent, coordination, and room for variation;
- timing, dynamics, sound, phrase, musical response, and interaction;
- audience, judge, teacher, partner, listener, or sensor recognition;
- participation, access, attribution, refusal, and exclusion;
- teaching, rehearsal, event, equipment, software, and maintenance burden;
- retained alternatives and repertoire diversity; and
- later transmission, continuation, and reversibility.

Show where results cannot be ranked, where evidence leaves a material uncertainty, whose judgements differ and which limits are binding. A weighted gain in
visibility cannot compensate for breached safety, consent, permission or equipment limits. Identify any work,
cost or burden shifted to a teacher, organizer, maintainer, partner or source community, including unpaid work.

#### MDPE.14:3.6 - Return one bounded response

An account can identify the conflict or establish a past response. For a recommendation, state which response the evidence supports and any decision that remains and who may make it. When a decision is commissioned, the authorized holder has five possible kinds of response.

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **selected change** | Select a change on sufficient grounds. Identify capability, permission, resources, protected conditions and how to reverse it where possible. Include a representative inquiry only when its attainable value or an applicable obligation warrants it. |
| **deliberately preserved tension** | Keep the arrangement when the tension is useful or the feasible changes impose a greater burden. State the operating limits and what would warrant reconsidering this choice. |
| **split use** | Choose different variants or arrangements for uses that have different requirements. |
| **next discriminating observation** | Choose an obtainable observation that could improve the grounds for the choice enough to warrant its burden, or that satisfies an applicable requirement. Name its subject, conditions, expected differences, full burden and stopping condition. |
| **reject current set** | Stop the proposed use when no current response, including retaining the arrangement or splitting uses, meets its required conditions and no worthwhile obtainable observation could establish that any response qualifies. Name the failed condition and preserve independently supported uses. |

For example, every available floor arrangement may breach a binding consent, permission or equipment limit. If no separate setting is available and no worthwhile obtainable observation could establish that an option meets the required conditions, reject this set for the proposed use. Name the missing provision if developing an alternative is part of the brief. When the evidence leaves an option’s status open, report that uncertainty separately from a finding that every option fails.

Identify the authority and permission for the chosen action. If implementation is commissioned, a capable provider carries it out through
the required music, dance, engineering, teaching, event, safety, judging, platform or production
method with its applicable assurance. Establish implementation and any improvement from evidence
of the action and its outcome respectively. A sufficient existing result can complete the task without a second experiment.

A short report can use the relevant entries below.

```text
situation and question, and the decision holder when relevant:
conflicting Music-or-Dance results:
branch or branches and supported relations:
basis — observation, design grounds or hypothesis, association, or causal contribution:
remaining cross-scope conflict, and any existing or needed candidate comparison:
music or dance relations, criteria, binding limits and options considered:
comparison and any recommendation or choice:
decision if requested — selected change | preserved tension | split use | next observation | reject current set:
direct Method for selected change, when applicable:
protected results, shifted burdens and possibilities or limits of reversal, where relevant:
what would warrant reconsidering the conclusion:
if further inquiry is selected: the question or obligation it serves, attainable observation and full burden:
```

#### MDPE.14:3.7 - Interpret observations of the response

Use suitable existing observations from `MDPE.12` or the relevant domain method to compare the local
and protected outcomes under representative conditions. Account for shifted burdens and any selection
rule that changed. Gather new observations for a warranted inquiry or an applicable obligation.


Revisit a decision when an observation changes its conflict, candidate, comparison,
remaining tension, transferred burden or relevant test. If the question concerns
the cause of a difference, use `C.28`. A local performance may answer a bounded
question while leaving wider artistic progress, cultural selection or retention open.

### MDPE.14:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.14:4.1 - Dense-floor social Dance uses cross-holon and simultaneous-Work branches

This constructed teaching application concerns an Urban Kiz pair. It is informed by current direct swing-floor
guidance, but it does not report an observed Urban Kiz population. The World Swing Dance Council guidance says
to adapt slot size, choreography, and footwork to available space and shifting dancers, attend to the partner,
and place partner well-being above display. The source supports the floorcraft and partner-use relations; it does
not supply this project's observations or a universal partner-Dance Method.

The pair considers enlarging and accelerating a turn–steps–counter-turn phrase. The phrase is a part of the
performance Work, while rhythmic interpretation, partner sensing, floorcraft, audience-facing display, and party
participation obtain together. This is a cross-holon and simultaneous-Work case; no scale claim is needed.

The pair compares three alternatives:

- reduce amplitude and travel while preserving phrase order;
- redistribute rotation and add earlier partner-readable weight-transfer cues; and
- keep the larger phrase for staged or low-density use and a compact variant for the social floor.

In the constructed trial the second variant preserved rhythmic order and the partner anticipated the turn more successfully, but the
variation still took too much space near the floor edge. The pair therefore chooses the compact variant for dense floors and the
larger one for the stage or a low-density setting. The participants accept lower visibility from a distant camera. Safety and a
partner’s right to decline remain binding. Reconsider the choice if floor density, partners, music or use changes its grounds.

For a later event with compatible floor, partner, music and use conditions, suppose existing representative
observations already support the compact variant and the split. The pair selects that variant from the current
basis. Another comparative trial would take time from the intended social practice without changing this choice,
so no new trial is added. Applicable event and partner conditions still have to hold. A new unresolved partner
cue or a changed floor condition can reopen the affected choice and make a targeted comparison worthwhile.

#### MDPE.14:4.2 - Robotic Music uses simultaneous Work and performing-whole relations

For the named Shimon trial, the robot had sufficient control of the music performance
to count as its performing agent. The human research team chose and changed the
configuration. Identify each contribution in the particular version and task.

A more visible head gesture may make the robot’s intended motion easier to read while timing, mechanical
noise or musical plausibility reaches an unacceptable level near a tempo transition. Examine the
robot–instrument configuration, gesture control, music performance and observers’ responses together.

The team could reduce head movement near difficult transitions, separate communicative motion from actuation
timing or accept a bounded timing deviation where legibility is part of the musical criterion. Compare those
options within the actual robot version, control architecture, safety limits and available evidence. A result
from a different configuration can inform that comparison if the relevant correspondence is established.

#### MDPE.14:4.3 - Judge agreement at the Paris breaking event and a proposed local comparison

Lerebourg and Guignard’s 2024 performance model for breaking relates technique, vocabulary,
originality, execution and musicality to the opponent, unfamiliar music, fatigue, injury,
audience and judging. It helps identify which relations and criteria to examine in
competition. The adequacy of a particular scoring arrangement requires grounds about its use.

Sato's 2025 analysis concerns sixteen men, thirty-two battles and nine judges at the Paris event.
Single-judge absolute-agreement ICCs range from 0.206 to 0.452; the corresponding nine-judge-average ICCs range
from 0.700 to 0.881. Agreement on originality was highest for both units, but a panel average and an individual judge are different
units. The paper's verbal labels are inconsistent with its stated thresholds, so preserve the numbers and units
instead of copying “good” and “poor” as unqualified verdicts. Five explicit categories did not produce uniformly
strong single-judge agreement in this event. No experiment compared adding categories or training judges;
agreement also does not establish external validity or cultural fit.

A French field inquiry covering 2019–2023 reports partial resistance to Olympic breaking among hip-hop
participants and organizations’ efforts to address cultural-preservation concerns. Its findings make
the competition’s format, institutions and relationship to practitioner communities relevant. They concern
that field and period. A broader causal claim about judging calls for evidence at the wider scope.

For a constructed local event, the team considers developing judges for each criterion and checking agreement within the existing format, separating ranked competition from unranked improvisation, or retaining the ranking while restricting what it may be used to say about improvisation and continuation. Before a lasting choice, the team selects a comparison of judge agreement by criterion and practitioner accounts of what the format makes harder to present. This is the planned comparison. It supplies no result about the effect of new criteria or training. Use `MDPE.13` if the remaining question concerns an existing recognition and selection arrangement or its design, and the applicable competition method to carry out an authorized change.

#### MDPE.14:4.4 - Short-video discovery, attribution, and teaching require different relations

This teaching application uses two distinct source contributions. Taylor's TikTok study separates the
recommendation feed, sound feature and captions and shows how each can enable or obscure attribution.

Blanchet and colleagues test a constructive preview–segment practice–fading–integration lesson arrangement.
In Study 1 the skeleton-based instructional bundle improved immediate short solo-dance similarity relative to
control; the movement-sheet bundle did not. Emojis were obscured in the experimental lessons. Study 2 found no
significant segmentation or emoji effects. The findings therefore do not isolate a benefit of emojis or establish
that a particular lesson structure is necessary or sufficient. Participant preferences inform design, while
immediate similarity, delayed retention and partner transfer remain different outcomes. Neither study tests the
proposed partner-Dance extension below.

In a constructed extension, a school wants both discovery and transferable
partner-dance learning. It therefore distinguishes the following contributions.

- a discovery carrier with source and dance-credit information;
- a teaching version with preview, practice by part, fading guidance and reintegration, and evidence of the learner’s own attempt if the question concerns their performance;
- the partners’ response to each other. A front-facing recording of both can show a visible movement or timing response if it captures the relevant cue and action. Contact, felt pressure and transfer to another partner need evidence suited to those relations; and
- platform visibility, attribution, learning, and social-practice observations.

The school proposes separate uses of the two videos and plans a trial of the complete phrase without
continuous teacher cues, followed by an appropriate partner-response condition. The researchers did not
run these partner trials in the short solo experiment. For the school’s choice, a crediting failure, cue
dependence, missing response or changed platform feature would warrant reconsideration. Use a suitable
method to teach the lesson. For a claim about acquired skill, use evidence of the learner’s performance under the required support and transfer conditions, and grounds for what changed.

#### MDPE.14:4.5 - Training before performance is not a lower simultaneous level

A dancer may first develop strength and later perform, or a musician may rehearse fingering before a
concert. The training and the later performance occur at different times. The performer’s capability at the time may
constrain the work during performance. Use Human Capability Development for the human learner’s
practice and a suitable assessment for what the performer can do. Use `MDPE.14` if the capability,
body, work, method or slower arrangement establishes one of the conflict relations in the present case.

#### MDPE.14:4.6 - Preserve a valued challenge while reopening social participation and the canon

This is the bounded conflict decision inside the [constructed Mara evening](#mdpe2551---a-complete-constructed-case-the-evening-that-became-a-qualification-course). The same four-hour main-floor programme must recover at least 150 minutes of open social participation while retaining an attainable challenge for experienced participants. Advanced dancers value mastery, shared standards and recognition; the school values their continuing participation. Newcomers value an evening in which they can actually dance. The team therefore compares the challenge and the time left for open dancing.

The schedule is a shared resource relation, while the contest's entry rule and criteria constrain which movement variants receive recognition. The team compares three arrangements for the same evening:

| Arrangement | Receiving result and accepted cost |
| --- | --- |
| Keep 90 minutes of class, 90 of contest and 60 of open floor | Preserves the familiar class and challenge. The main floor falls 90 minutes short of the agreed 150 open minutes. |
| Keep the 90-minute class and cancel the contest, leaving 150 minutes open | Meets the time promise with existing staff, at the cost of the challenge and its recognition. It remains feasible if the second teacher or side room is unavailable. |
| Use 30 minutes for an optional clinic, 60 for an improvisational challenge and 150 for open participation. Teach a 90-minute advanced class in the side studio. | Meets the main-floor promise and preserves two kinds of challenge. The schedule requires two paid teachers together. Total paid teaching contact rises from 90 to 120 minutes, counting the 30-minute clinic and the 90-minute advanced class. Contest entrants cannot attend the full simultaneous advanced class. Ren must explain and administer the changed challenge, and both programmes need preparation. |

The team chooses the third arrangement because the room, providers and paid preparation are available, and participants value preserving the challenge enough to accept the overlap. For this evening the improvisational challenge replaces the prepared-sequence contest. Past contest results retain their original scope. The new challenge uses both timely recovery after a partner’s pause and that partner’s report of comfortable continuation. A disagreement between those indications remains unresolved. Success supports that particular judgement. Overall mastery or permission to teach requires separate grounds.

In the constructed continuation most experienced participants stay with familiar partners after class. Staying with familiar partners can support demanding practice and may leave some newcomers without the contact the event hoped to provide. Mara preserves choice of partners and the advanced class, and arranges two optional five-minute welcoming opportunities with willing hosts. The ten minutes of the hosts’ time and the interruptions have real costs. Experienced dancers have no general teaching duty. If a class performance fails with a changed partner, examine that receiving task before deciding whether different instruction is needed.

An inherited entry rule also requires large visible variation. A small pause-and-response variant can meet the local recovery criterion and still fail that rule. Ren removes the large-change requirement for this use and brings observation close enough to inspect the response. A stage competition may still need a display criterion. The counterexample justifies changing this rule, while leaving earlier accomplishments and the separate merits of other new variants to their own grounds.

The decision depends on the named contributions. Loss of the side room reopens the timetable, not the already useful cue-teaching repair or the distinction between contest achievement and social capability. The complete case works through that changed condition. Reported Kizomba school/event histories and practitioner participation in shaping competitive formats motivate this comparison; they do not establish this constructed evening's efficacy or a general cultural trajectory.

### MDPE.14:5 - Recognition and Assurance

Check whether the account answers the questions that apply to its purpose.

1. Which Music-or-Dance results conflict in the bounded situation?
2. Which conflict branch applies, and what relation supports it?
3. If the conflict crosses declared scopes, what conflict remains under `C.30.ILC`, and does a comparison need architecture candidates from `C.32.MLAO`? Otherwise, which participants and structures account for the local conflict?
4. Which music or dance relations, criteria, protected limits and observations affect the account? If options are needed, which ones differ in a consequential way?
5. What does an available comparison establish? For a recommendation, choice, rejection or proposed inquiry, what supports that response? For an earlier choice, what decision does the evidence establish, and what, if anything, does it show about the reason?
6. If implementation is wanted, who has the capability and permission to carry it out by a suitable method? What could change a finding or a decision enough to warrant revisiting it?

Assure the result by checking that:

- cross-scale is used only with a stated scale order;
- part–whole, Work overlap, slower constraint, representation use, and Method unfolding remain different;
- actual and possible-future Work are not mixed;
- observed difference, association, design hypothesis, and causal contribution are not collapsed;
- local and protected results both have evidence or explicit uncertainty;
- safety, consent, authority, permission, access, attribution, and equipment limits are not traded away by a score;
- where several responses are compared, their differences in relation or failure mode matter to the question;
- moved burden and lost alternatives are visible;
- the decision holder and the performer or performing whole are identified separately when they have different responsibilities;
- results from direct comparison, choice, enactment, observation, and causal Methods remain separate; and
- a local decision is not reported as cultural selection, retention, progress, or a new whole.

### MDPE.14:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “These are the levels of Dance or Music.” | Name the subjects and relations; keep Method, Work, System, representation, capability, and cultural views distinct. |
| “They overlap, so one is part of or above the other.” | State overlap, parthood, and scale independently. |
| “First train, then perform, so training is the lower level.” | Keep capability-development Work and later performance separate; inspect obtained capability during performance only when it changes the conflict. |
| “The metric improved, so the practice improved.” | Identify the protected result and burdens on others. Use suitable existing observations and identify any outcome they leave open. Obtain further evidence when its attainable contribution warrants the burden or an applicable requirement calls for it. |
| “The camera shows the whole conflict.” | State the represented subject, preserved and hidden distinctions, and receiving use. |
| “The judging categories are explicit, so agreement and cultural fit will improve.” | Compare available evidence about judge agreement by criterion. For cultural fit, consider the relevant practitioners, format, improvisation and continuation. A proposed test is appropriate when a feasible comparison could resolve a material question at a justified cost or an applicable obligation requires it. |
| “The platform spread the clip, so it transmitted the Dance.” | Separate discovery, attribution, lesson structure, receiving enactment, transfer, and later continuation. |
| “We generated options, so the problem is solved.” | For a choice, compare the available options. Select a supported response, reject the set for the proposed use when every available option, including retention or split use, fails its requirements and no worthwhile obtainable observation could rescue one, or choose a worthwhile observation that the available evidence cannot supply. |
| “The best weighted score wins.” | Preserve vetoes, incomparability, uncertainty, and non-compensable harms. |
| “The trial worked, so the culture improved.” | Keep local observation separate from later recognition, selection, transmission, and retention. |

### MDPE.14:7 - Consequences

A practitioner can use the result in several ways.

- assess a local improvement against the wider performance relations it affects,
- identify the part–whole, scale, overlap, constraint or representation relation that changes an explanation or decision,
- choose separate variants where a compromise would damage both uses,
- account for distinctions lost by a representation or metric, and
- coordinate artistic, bodily, technical, event, platform and cultural requirements through the methods suited to
  their respective work.

Costs and limits:

- relation recovery can show that the case needs only ordinary comparison;
- representative trials may require performers, partners, venues, instruments, robots, audiences, judges, or
  teachers;
- later observations can overturn the current decision;
- some tensions should remain rather than be solved; and
- a bounded project cannot control distributed cultural evolution.

### MDPE.14:8 - Rationale and Source Use



#### MDPE.14:8.1 - What current FPF already supplies


Use `C.30.ILC` to identify a conflict that remains across levels or declared scopes. When new architecture candidates are
needed, `C.32.MLAO` relates them to the structures they preserve, lose or change, burdens they create and the time and
conditions for revisiting them. `C.32.MWA` distinguishes views organized by different relations. Use `A.19.CPM` for a formal
comparison of admitted profiles under a stated comparator, `C.11` for a bounded choice and `C.28` for a causal contribution.

For music and dance, identify which bodily and artistic limits bind, what the partners or ensemble
need, how the judging or platform arrangement works, and what evidence can establish the relevant use or feasibility. Those
details can explain a conflict or discriminate between retaining, changing or splitting the practice.



#### MDPE.14:8.2 - Domain sources and the decisions they change


| Source or maintained result | Action-changing use here | Limit and reason to revisit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [World Swing Dance Council, “Social Etiquette for Swing Dancers”](https://worldsdc.com/social-etiquette/) | Direct practitioner guidance supports adapting slot width, choreography, and footwork to available floor space and shifting dancers, attending to the partner, and putting partner well-being above display. This makes floorcraft, partner information, safety, and split use load-bearing in the social-Dance branch. | Updated content is attributed to 2019 and concerns swing. It does not establish Urban Kiz prevalence, one universal floorcraft Method, or the constructed trial observations. Reopen when current direct social-Dance guidance or a result from Work using such a Method changes the candidate set or vetoes. |
| Lucie Lerebourg and Brice Guignard, [“From theory to practice: modeling performance in breaking”](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2024.1489456), 2024 | Adds opponent-relative strategy, music not known in advance, audience and judging, fatigue and injury, and several performance criteria to the competition branch. It blocks reduction to one technical score. | This is a proposed performance model aligned with WDSF rules, not proof of adequate judging or cultural effects. Reopen when direct competition evidence changes the criteria or relation set. |
| Sato, [“Reliability of judging in Olympic breaking at the 2024 Paris games”](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1593158), 2025 | Distinguish single-judge from nine-judge-average agreement by criterion in the men's Paris event; :4.3 preserves the numerical scope. | Verbal thresholds are inconsistent. Agreement is not validity; category or training changes were not experimentally compared, and other populations remain outside this result. |
| Coralie Lessard and Ariane Demain Gan, [“Vers un ‘Breaking fédéral et olympique’...”](https://doi.org/10.1080/07053436.2024.2368674), 2024 | A 2019–2023 field inquiry reports partial non-adherence to Olympic breaking and preservation concerns. This adds practitioner, institutionalization, format, and cultural-continuity relations to the judging decision. | The French field case does not represent every breaking population or establish that one arrangement caused a cultural change. Reopen when a direct population or event result changes the response. |
| Taylor, [“Algorithms, affordances and the ambiguity of credit on TikTok”](https://doi.org/10.1080/10304312.2025.2518971), 2025 | Separates recommendation feed, sound, and caption affordances and shows how informal Dance-credit practices can succeed or fail. This makes attribution and platform relations separate from discovery. | One digital ethnography and challenge case do not establish the origin of every Dance, the causal effect of recommendation, or learning transfer. Reopen when a platform or creator result changes attribution choices. |
| Blanchet et al., [“Enhancing the Educational Potential of Online Movement Videos”](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3714062), 2025 | Supplies a preview–part practice–fading–integration construction; Study 1's skeleton bundle improves immediate similarity, while its sheet bundle does not. | Study 1 obscures emojis; Study 2's component effects are not significant. Bundle results and preferences establish neither isolated emoji benefit nor durable or partner-Dance transfer. |
| Timing examples in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) and the local Balboa cases | Distinguishes continuous contributions, articulation, timing centres and representation choices. For pulse-and-accent work, MDPE.11:4.5.2 develops a common coordination Method through different Music and Dance realizations. | The shared construction informs corresponding practice; it does not make the physical techniques, feedback or acquired skills identical. Each receiving use retains its own requirements and transfer evidence. |
| [Shimon project](https://gtcmt.gatech.edu/shimon), [mechatronic expressivity study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14850), and [social-gesture study](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1461615) | The sources identify version-specific actuation, gesture, timing, attention, noise and musical-plausibility questions for robotic performance. | Compare configurations and tasks before using findings together. The human researchers in these studies selected the design and experiments. An observed performance by the robot is a different contribution. |



Reconsider a source when its content or scope affects a relation, candidate, binding condition, observation or use. A paper, official rule or
platform metric can establish the particular fact its evidence covers. For a claim about a specific performance, use evidence that covers it.

### MDPE.14:9 - Relations

| Related result | Use here |
| --- | --- |
| `C.30.ILC` and `C.32.MLAO` | Supply residual triage for an architecture conflict across declared scopes and, after that triage, the residual-reducing candidate frame when needed. The local overlap and representation branches use them only if that cross-scope relation is established. |
| `C.32.MWA`, `A.22`, and `A.22.CGUS` | Keep non-isomorphic selected structures and first–then Method unfoldings distinct from simultaneous practice architecture. |
| `A.19.CPM` and `C.11` | Compare admitted profiles under a specified comparator when that form of comparison is required. Use `C.11` for a choice within the relevant authority. |
| `MDPE.8` | Supplies the bounded development focus when its named subject, live alternatives or uncertainty, affected Systems, or current decision changes the conflict. The focus does not decide the conflict. |
| `MDPE.3`, `MDPE.9`, and `MDPE.10` | Supply a configured performing whole, current candidates, capability limits, and protected conditions when these change the conflict. |
| `MDPE.12` and `MDPE.13` | Establish the relevant observations or compare how an arrangement permits actual recognition and selection. Use evidence of its operation for findings about particular outcomes. |
| `MDPE.15` | Follow an authorized local change into the work needed to implement it, or assess what happened when a previously selected change was made. |
| `MDPE.16` | Use `MDPE.16` to assess the value, feasibility and costs of retaining split-use variants and other alternatives. |
| `MDPE.17` | Use an observation of receiving performance or a changed method variant when it bears on the question. Reopen a decision only when it changes the same conflict, candidate, comparison, remaining tension, shifted burden or test. |
| `MDPE.22` | Use the evidence needed for the question about supporting provision, its use or the effects of a change. Use a finding about support when it bears on the separate practice conflict. |
| `MDPE.20` and `MDPE.24` | Use bounded findings from a practice conflict for a question about possible trajectories or the identification, formation or continuation of a larger whole. |
| Applicable music, dance, engineering, teaching, event, safety, judging, platform or production method | The capable, authorized provider carries out a selected change under the method’s conditions. Obtain additional observations only when the intended claim or an applicable obligation requires them. |
| `C.28` | Examine the evidence that a completed change contributed to a result, or assess a prediction about the effect of a proposed change when that causal claim matters. |
| Human Capability Development and other specialist DPFs | Use the appropriate result about a human performer’s capability or its development, or the specialist contribution required for the question. |

### MDPE.14:End

## MDPE.25 - Renew a Shared Music or Dance Practice

> **Type:** Method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### MDPE.25:1 - Problem frame

Use this method to understand or change how different parts of a shared music or movement practice affect one another. Organizers may find that improving a class, a contest or its provision impairs another activity they value. An archive can show how classes, awards and use of the shared floor fitted together in an earlier series.

Participants may reproduce increasingly difficult sequences in class yet struggle with unfamiliar partners at the social evening. A contest that attracts experienced performers can occupy the main social floor. A useful, appreciated phrase may fail an inherited entry rule whose purpose the organizers can no longer explain.

The result can be an explanation of what the arrangement made possible, or a feasible way to preserve participation, develop skill and try, recognize and retain variants. The organizers may keep activities separate, choose a narrower arrangement or stop when the conflict cannot be resolved within their means.

**First useful move.** Follow the connection in a representative past or proposed occasion. What did participants want to do, or what should they be able to do? Which conditions helped, impeded or would constrain them? If a change is sought, identify a connection the people responsible can alter.

Use a direct teaching, rehearsal, production or event method when it supplies the needed result. MDPE.20 addresses a forecast of the practice's development.

### MDPE.25:2 - Problem

Some informal practices develop schools, qualifications or competitions. To establish that development for a community, examine its history. To judge what a contest rewards, examine the actual task, criteria and use of the award.

Participants may want an enjoyable evening, teachers a learnable progression and sustainable work, skilled performers challenging partners and recognition, organizers a viable recurring event, and tradition bearers continued access to a meaningful repertoire. One person can share several interests. Examine which the arrangement can serve together.

How do these contributions affect the intended occasion and its continuation? A better-taught course can still occupy the only social floor. A more consistent panel can still reward an achievement that tells the organizer little about social partnering.

### MDPE.25:3 - Forces

An improvement for one activity can have the following consequences for another.

| Useful contribution | What can be impaired | Question that changes the response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A short entry into social participation | Preparation for difficult or unfamiliar situations | What must a newcomer do on this floor, and what can be learned later? |
| A demanding school progression | Time and money for participation; variation that the syllabus does not teach | Which exercises improve the receiving activity, and which serve another legitimate aim? |
| Competition, recognition and visible progress | Partner responsiveness, access across experience groups, willingness to experiment | What is actually rewarded, who can perceive it, and what later opportunities depend on the result? |
| Stable exemplars and stylistic continuity | Useful novelty and recognition of its contributors | Which distinctions must remain, for which use, and who can revise that claim? |
| Shared provision and a common event | Independent development of incompatible activities | What should be shared, what should have a separate setting, and what connecting opportunity is worth maintaining? |

A clearer explanation can leave a teacher with less income, an organizer with more work or a participant without a competitive outlet. If the group still needs a change, consider different provision, an agreed trade-off or rejection of the proposal.

### MDPE.25:4 - Solution

Identify the contributions that sustain the practice, what each supplied or could supply to the shared activity, and the evidence for any effects attributed to it. To design a response, identify the intended participation, the actual or suspected difficulty, the means available and who can change or supply what the proposal requires.

Start with the connection the question concerns. An earlier explanation, timetable, test or supported proposal may answer the question. For a design, use the intended occasion to identify what its parts need to supply. Check that their requirements can be met together, and use evidence of what actually happened for claims about provision, use or continued participation.

#### MDPE.25:4.1 - Start from the participation that should remain possible

Choose an occasion representative of the question. A newcomer at a social evening may want to arrive without a regular partner, find willing partners, enjoy dancing, recover from an unfamiliar response and come back. An ensemble may want to retain its recognizable sound while a new member introduces a variation. For a past occasion use what is known about the participants' aims and experience.

What preparation, access and support does each occasion require? A social evening can welcome newcomers while a demanding competition requires preparation. Preserve both opportunities when both are wanted and feasible.

Identify the time, space, money and capabilities each activity needs. Who controls the relevant timetable, teaching offer, entry rules, access and payment? For a proposed change, check the organizer’s or rule holder’s authority. Teaching expertise can establish a teaching capability, and a prize recognizes the achievement assessed at that event.

An existing arrangement that meets the requirements can be retained. A failed use or an opportunity worth its cost can warrant a change.

#### MDPE.25:4.2 - Trace the connections in a past or proposed occasion

Take an observed episode or state the premises of a constructed one. Trace relevant preparation, selection and support before it, then what followed or could follow under the proposed conditions. Determine which contributions and consequences the evidence connects to the episode and where an explanation remains open.

A learner completes a memorized sequence with the instructor, then interrupts an unfamiliar partner who pauses. Perhaps the instructor supplied an unnoticed cue, the lesson rewarded sequence completion, or the contest encouraged practice of a fixed routine. Compare these explanations with limited practice, an unclear signal, an unsuitable track or a partner choosing another activity. What in the record distinguishes them?

Look for connections that matter to the question. For a proposed repair, identify which can change. For example,

- a classroom result is used as evidence for a different receiving capability;
- a judge sees amplitude but cannot observe the partner response on which the social use depends;
- contest recognition controls teaching invitations, so changing the contest can also change someone's livelihood;
- a long teaching block occupies the only social floor;
- participants learn from a record that omits the condition under which a movement should be varied or stopped;
- a retained label groups music, movement and events, and the project mistakenly treats them as one unchanged subject.

Limit the causal claim to what the evidence supports. An association can justify asking how a school or contest contributed to a change in participation. A study of one city and period can suggest what to investigate in another setting.

Keep rival explanations that change the answer or the proposed repair. A change can be justified under more than one explanation even when the cause remains uncertain.

#### MDPE.25:4.3 - Construct an arrangement by working backward from its receiving use

Working backward from the occasion, identify what each activity needs and what existing work, participant or service can supply it. Develop a new contribution where it is needed to remedy a missing contribution, resolve incompatible requirements or realize a worthwhile opportunity.

If partners need to notice a pause and respond to it, an instructor can supplement or replace a continuous sequence drill with practice in noticing the cue, choosing a response and recovering when the expected continuation fails. Use the relevant musical and spatial conditions or explain what the simplified exercise prepares. To claim transfer, examine performance under the changed conditions. Arrange a qualified instructor when one is needed.

If the award selects an achievement different from the one needed, compare changes to the task, observation, consequences or relation between events. Possible responses include the following.

1. Retain a stage contest for its own audience, but stop using its result as a qualification for social partnering or teaching an unrelated capability.
2. Use an improvisational task with unfamiliar partners and music when the sought result is responsive partnering. Explain what observers can assess and what still needs the partner's account.
3. Add a separate opportunity for experiments, with its own stated conditions, so an unfamiliar variant need not first win under criteria designed for the established repertoire.
4. Keep distinct event or teaching branches where their desired results cannot be met in one setting, and deliberately preserve a useful connection between them.

The organizers can combine responses. Random pairing changes how partners are assigned. For enjoyment, examine participants’ accounts. Assess access or evaluation bias from evidence about the corresponding rules and their operation.

When continuity matters, identify the feature to preserve and the allowed variation. Musical phrasing, a partner relation, attribution, repertoire and the social occasion can call for different choices. [MDPE.Application:5.3](#mdpeapplication53---connect-style-method-structure-and-acquisition) relates those distinctions to the Method's organization and the performer's skill.

#### MDPE.25:4.4 - Compare whole arrangements, including who bears the change

Follow each serious proposal through the occasion. Include the current arrangement when retaining it is possible, and use the same requirements for each comparison.

Count each real use of space and instructor time, including simultaneous demands and the work of making the resources available. Count a shared contribution once when it serves both activities. A second room needs the floor, sound, staff and affordable access the activity requires. Moving advanced practice to another day can exclude people unable to attend twice. Welcoming newcomers can create a paid or unpaid demand on skilled participants.

Set aside proposals that would defeat a binding requirement. Compare the feasible alternatives on relevant differences in effort, access, achievement, continuity and development. Keep distinct criteria visible when combining them would hide a loss or a veto.

A technically suitable proposal can still lack a provider or a participant's agreement. If an agreement is needed, negotiate the work, compensation or allocation with whoever can decide. An existing agreement may suffice. If provision remains unavailable, consider a smaller feasible arrangement or separate activities. If provision is the question, identify what is missing and what that prevents.

#### MDPE.25:4.5 - Arrange acquisition and provision at the point where they are needed

A participant may need an explanation, an opportunity to learn, access to someone already capable, or a change to the task or environment. Identify the missing contribution and check the result appropriate to it.

A newcomer may need the pause-and-response relation explained, practice that makes the cue perceptible, or a willing partner. An experienced performer may already know the response but miss a quiet cue in a noisy room. Reducing noise can make that skill usable there.

When learning is wanted, establish what the performer can do, which help was available and used, and the conditions of the intended performance. Keep useful support that belongs in the receiving activity. Change or withdraw it when the task requires independence, the support will be unavailable, or another arrangement better meets the requirement. Use suitable evidence of performance under the conditions claimed. Arrange another attempt if the missing result warrants it.

Arranging a class and providing a place to use the skill solve different problems. A party can supply the occasion while an instructional or performing capability is still missing. C.36.RP distinguishes preserving an answer, making a Method obtainable and keeping a later occasion in which participants can use it.

#### MDPE.25:4.6 - Carry out the change and follow its consequences through receiving use

A request for a proposal can finish by stating what is feasible and any conditions still unresolved. For implementation, use the agreed resources to carry out the teaching, event, selection or support work. For a historical question, examine the provision, activity or result the surviving evidence establishes.

Use an observation suited to the claim, including an earlier result obtained under relevant conditions. A successful demonstration with the instructor's continuous cue establishes an assisted classroom performance. For an unassisted evening with unfamiliar partners, look for evidence of that performance. Several changes can affect participation, so assess other plausible explanations before attributing a decline to an intervention.

For a proposed change, compare the expected gain and other possible consequences. For a completed change, establish what happened. A separate advanced room may keep experienced participants at the event while reducing their time on the shared floor. A new award can change what performers practice to win. A shorter class can increase social time while omitting a necessary entry skill.

If further repair is wanted, return to the connection affected. An unavailable room changes the timetable; it need not alter how an audible cue worked in a different room. Keep the conclusions whose conditions still hold.

#### MDPE.25:4.7 - Renew the criteria as well as the selected repertoire

Keep a way for practitioners to bring forward an otherwise excluded variant. When one challenges a rule, identify the intended use it supports and the condition it violates. Compare these possibilities where they bear on the question.

- the variant fails a still-necessary condition;
- the condition described the predecessor too narrowly and should change;
- the variant serves a different valuable use and should remain a separate branch.

Try the receiving use when the available evidence leaves an important difference unresolved and a feasible trial could resolve it at a justified cost. A spectator, partner and teacher may observe different parts of the response. If their accounts must be combined, explain how the decision uses each observation and handles disagreement.

When revising a canon, retain the historical account of the repertoire, its contributors and the achievements the old criteria recognized. Identify the event or practice covered by the new rule. Wider adoption requires evidence at that scope.

Finish when the finding, proposal, decision or realized arrangement answers the question. Reconsider the affected part when a failed use, lost resource, changed group or previously excluded variant challenges a premise being used.

#### MDPE.25:4.8 - What must hold together

For a proposal, connect the account of the problem to a feasible arrangement. For each needed contribution, show how it can be supplied. Teaching may prepare a performer, permitted assistance may support the performance itself, and access may make an existing provider or resource available. Check competing demands on people, time and space. For an implemented change, examine what the receiving activity showed. A failed trial can identify a limit, justify stopping or prompt further development of the affected part.

When the request concerns an arrangement or proposal, identify which contributions can be obtained. If a necessary connection is missing, identify the limit and any useful narrower option. An account of past work identifies what was proposed, carried out, used or achieved, to the extent the evidence supports each claim.

Preserve the purpose, constraints and meaning of the results when varying schedules or providers. Reconsider an inadequate criterion. Moving from social participation to selecting a stage spectacle changes what the comparison should establish.

Show what each contribution must supply, whether it is obtainable and what follows for the occasion. A qualified provider can supply instruction or administrative work without disclosing every internal step. Finish with an adequate answer, the limit imposed by an unavailable contribution or an explicit change of purpose.

### MDPE.25:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### MDPE.25:5.1 - A complete constructed case: the evening that became a qualification course

This constructed example stipulates the people, resources and observations used to compare arrangements.

Mara organizes a four-hour Friday event. Sol teaches the introductory class, Jules is available to teach the advanced class, and Ren administers its small contest. The same main floor must accommodate a 90-minute class, 90 minutes of contest activity including changes between rounds, and 60 minutes of open social participation.
