#### MDPE.16:3.8 - Remove only for a supported reason

Before removing or merging a branch, identify the use it would leave, why that is warranted and whether the decision can be reversed. Consider who would lose source access, a minority practice, a comparison or a route to a later combination. Preserve useful source material in the archive and identify any condition that would warrant reconsidering removal.



#### MDPE.16:3.9 - Keep the result usable

```text
Availability question, use and date or horizon:
Branch and actual bearer or arrangement:
Intended or past use and distinguishing contribution:
Status at the relevant time:
Performing Agent or whole and required capability:
Dependencies, rights, access, permission, resources, and configuration:
Who is responsible and authorized for upkeep or reconstruction, if needed:
Any upkeep or reconstruction required, its method, status and any result obtained:
Existing arrangement and limits of availability:
Evidence under the relevant conditions, including its date and any actual deadline:
Observation, applicable constraint, causal hypothesis or supported causal finding under its stated conditions:
Selected worthwhile and feasible trial or observation, if any:
Source return or archive relation when needed:
When the supported use ends or a decision or availability finding needs reconsideration, if relevant:
```

Include the entries needed for the claim. Identify a trial or upkeep when selected, and a selection pressure when the question or conclusion relies on it. Give the limitation or reason for retaining a branch that matters to the interpretation or use of the finding.

A practitioner can use the finding directly, draw available candidates for a current `C.11 OptionSet`, apply a limit to an intervention or supply a usable branch to repertoire, archive, curation, teaching, production or engineering work. Use the actual conditions of that receiving work.

### MDPE.16:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.16:4.1 - Dance movement generation: different fidelity can preserve different value

Chédin and colleagues describe dancers and researchers curating movement material,
developing model and interface variants, improvising and revising the tool. Dancer-Y
alone took part in the final comparison of high-, medium- and low-fidelity outputs.
His uses for those outputs can suggest a comparison under `MDPE.9:4.1`. A new project
might keep both a recognizable output and a less faithful stimulus if their uses justify
the cost. Their suitability for another dancer requires evidence about that use.

To establish availability after the study, identify which model or movement material, rights, dancers, interface and configuration the intended use actually requires. An existing improvisation or reconstruction may supply enough evidence. A changed model, interface or movement task may justify another run. Stored outputs can be adequate for archival comparison even when using them with dancers would require reconstruction.

#### MDPE.16:4.2 - Balboa phrase family: carrier, articulation, and partner readability

Use the timing distinctions in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) when comparing continuous movement and the moment of articulation. A variant may relate a salient event to contact onset, a change of direction, weight arrival, pressure the partner can read or another specified event. Examine that timing within the continuous movement.

Visible footwork may interest a spectator while giving a partner a hard-to-read cue. Another variant may be clear at one tempo and hard to perform at another, or useful only as a teaching contrast. Identify performers, permitted material, tempo and partner conditions. An earlier paired performance can establish bounded availability. Practice can maintain a demanding skill; a changed partner or tempo or evidence of skill loss may justify a new check. The brushes analogy offers another way to compare timing. Membership in a common set still depends on a shared question.

#### MDPE.16:4.3 - Constructed Music case: restore a live-electronic branch before calling it available

A small ensemble wants to retain sparse acoustic and live-generated response arrangements for spring. The electronic branch appeared at one of the last four events. The trace leaves equipment access, venue rules, performer readiness, latency, curation, audience response and sampling as possible explanations.

The ensemble suspends the electronic branch because the old plugin fails on the replacement laptop and the venue has yet to approve the networked setup. The production lead authorizes configuration and rehearsal work within the equipment budget. An audio engineer restores the project from its stems in a supported environment, identifies the changed plugin's audible limits, obtains equipment permission and prepares the acoustic fallback. The musicians rehearse for twenty minutes with the intended laptop and monitoring, testing response timing and a simulated network failure.

The rehearsal record, latency trace, successful fallback, musicians' reports and venue permission support availability for that spring event and configuration. Audience preference and longer cultural retention remain separate questions. If the project requires a second machine and cannot restore the setup on it in time, that use is unavailable by the deadline. If the fault is recoverable and a later trial is useful, identify the repair it requires. Loss of rights or source access may leave only archive use. A subsequent refusal by a venue establishes an access constraint there. To attribute rejection by curators to latency, examine evidence that distinguishes that explanation.

With the same musicians, restored configuration, venue permission and spring window, the earlier rehearsal can still establish availability. Expired permission or a new plugin incompatibility can defeat that current use even if the record was made yesterday. The record continues to establish what was possible at the earlier time.

#### MDPE.16:4.4 - Robotic Music: social gesture and control branches

A Shimon project can compare gesture-amplitude, gesture-timing, sensing, control, and actuation arrangements. Mechanical evidence from one configuration, social-gesture evidence from another, and musical-plausibility observations from a changing-tempo trial remain configuration-bound.

Shimon can be the performer in a particular music trial. The human project team changes and maintains the alternatives in this case. Check the hardware, software, calibration, safety limits, operators and interface needed for the use. A previous representative run can suffice under unchanged conditions. A changed control path, recalibration or an applicable safety requirement may call for another run. A configuration record can aid reconstruction while an essential operating condition remains unverified.

#### MDPE.16:4.5 - Social-dance branches answer different questions

Identify the shared question before treating familiar names as alternatives. A milonga event, a recording
classified as milonga and a movement phrase can serve one project in different ways. Keeping the recording
does not by itself preserve the event or phrase. A local kizomba programme might offer sessions called
authentic kizomba, urban kiz and tarraxo. Examine the instructions, music and intended use for each. The
programme establishes what that organizer offered. A wider historical genealogy needs evidence of the relationships it asserts.

For a concrete movement-development comparison, suppose the teacher supplies two partnering instructions,
locally called tango and tango vals, and two recordings, locally classified as tango music and waltz music.
The candidate set contains four receiving uses:

| Candidate use | What must remain available |
| --- | --- |
| Tango partnering instructions with the tango recording | Those instructions, that recording and a performer/configuration able to realize their timing relation. |
| The same tango instructions with the waltz recording | The changed musical material and any required phrasing adaptation, with the intended partnering relations preserved. |
| Tango-vals instructions with the tango recording | The different partnering instructions and their usable timing relation to the first recording. |
| Tango-vals instructions with the waltz recording | Both selected inputs and the conditions that make their combination usable. |

These four combinations are proposals. Changing the recording, the partnering instructions
or both raises different questions about a pair's performance. Check compatibility
for the intended use. If an adaptation changes a defining feature of the method,
identify the new variant. Two combinations can be worth preserving when their distinct
uses justify the cost. A proposed combination can remain untested or unavailable.

For party programming, compare arrangements with their playlists, hosts or teachers, floor access, participant
capabilities, consent and timing. A track with the right name does not make the event available. For one adult dancer,
examine the coordination or partner-response variant, its practice conditions and evidence relevant to the intended use. Visibility in
ballet, a university, the press or a competition establishes where a variant was seen. Its usefulness for this
dancer needs evidence relevant to their aims, abilities and intended use. Keep programme and individual alternatives separate when their questions differ.



#### MDPE.16:4.6 - Constructed continuation: a small social variant becomes a usable combination

In the [shared-practice case](#mdpe2551---a-complete-constructed-case-the-evening-that-became-a-qualification-course), two participants can already use a compact pause-and-response phrase together on the social floor. Ren's prepared-performance contest excluded it under the large-visible-change rule. The participants also know a larger display phrase. Keeping both preserves a usable response and an achievement valued for display under different conditions.

When the local challenge changes to responsive partnering, the performers try to insert the compact pause and recovery into the larger phrase. Sol devotes twenty minutes of the staffed advanced lesson to the transition, displacing another figure. At first the visible sequence obscures the partner's pause. The pair shorten the approach, resume in time and report comfortable continuation. This establishes the combined phrase for this pair and task. Combining the component skills with a different partner remains a separate question.

The group retains the compact social response, prepared display and tested combination. Ren removes the large-change entry rule and observes from a position where the smaller response is visible. The earlier contest result remains evidence about display. The compact phrase contributed responsiveness, and the larger phrase a challenge its performers still valued.

The participants permit internal teaching use of their recordings. The teacher can explain the three uses, and Ren allocates four minutes of the existing briefing to the new judging task. These resources and the pair’s earlier performances can support the three uses while their conditions hold. If the three versions start to displace needed practice, compare that loss with the uses actually served. A programme needing only the compact response can archive the other descriptions. If a required performer leaves, determine whether another capable pair or arrangement is available. The changed entry rule alone cannot supply the missing ability. Continued use across a population would require evidence at that scale.

### MDPE.16:5 - Recognition and Assurance

Recognize a complete first result when a practitioner can answer:

1. What question, use and date or horizon are being investigated?
2. What actual bearer or arrangement constitutes each branch, and how does it differ materially?
3. Which branches were or are usable under the conditions, and which uses were or are blocked, and where is availability uncertain? If a further action is needed or an earlier one is being investigated, what supports maintenance, repair, archive retention, suspension or removal?
4. For each available branch, what performer, dependencies, rights, access, resources and configuration support the use? Which upkeep, if any, was needed?
5. What evidence supports this availability, and which actual change or deadline affects the conclusion?
6. If selection pressure matters, does the evidence establish a trace, a working constraint, a hypothesis or a causal finding?
7. If a decision is wanted, who can make it and what supports the choice? If work or a trial is proposed, what makes it required or worthwhile and feasible? What would warrant reconsideration?

For assurance, check the distinctions on which the finding relies.

- The branches each answer the same question differently. Components of one arrangement have their own uses.
- A file, snapshot, plan or former capability is used only for the availability conditions it helps establish.
- A claim of availability identifies the branch, time, use, capable performer and needed conditions, with suitable evidence. If upkeep was necessary, identify its authority and achieved result.
- Keep availability, archive and front membership, pool policy, selection and the current `OptionSet` distinct when a claim relies on them.
- Identify any musical, movement, partner, instrument, venue, source, access, capability or production difference that changes the finding or a proposed action, including a difference of style.
- For an attributed pressure, identify the observation, constraint or hypothesis and the evidence for its strength and scope. Include consequential uncertainty or a reason to reconsider a current choice when relevant.
- When keeping a weak branch for later use, identify the comparison, learning, combination, source access or other possibility it makes available.
- For removal, state the use the branch would leave, the losses and who would bear them. Include conditions for reconsideration where they matter.
- Use evidence of the wider population for cultural retention beyond the project.

### MDPE.16:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “Keep all variants.” | Compare the candidates for a specific use and establish what is available. A choice to maintain, restore or test a branch must justify the required resources and work. |
| “The maintenance record says it is preserved.” | Examine what the record establishes about the branch, performer, configuration and dependencies for this use. An existing record may show the needed work and its result. |
| “These files are our repertoire.” | For a performance repertoire, identify the material, performers, method, intended work and evidence of availability. For an archive question, the files may already answer it. |
| “Its use declined, so the platform removed it.” | State the observed change. Use an existing causal finding within its scope, or `C.28` if the causal question still needs work. A rule in force can establish an access constraint. The availability question may be settled while the cause remains open. |
| “The top-scoring candidates are the answer.” | Identify what was scored, the requirements and any incomparability. For a selection still to be made, use `C.11`. |
| “Not selected means eliminated.” | Establish separately what was selected and what remained usable for performance, source access, later combination or another task. |
| “Popular means culturally retained.” | For a claim of cultural retention, examine evidence of reception and reproduction. A popularity measure can establish the particular response it counts. |
| “All named styles belong to one space.” | Reidentify the development question and split the set when one alternative relation fails. |
| “The project kept it, so the culture retained it.” | Keep project availability separate from distributed recognition, selection, transmission, retention, and loss. |

### MDPE.16:7 - Consequences

Positive consequences:

- A project can retain source, minority, body-specific, less visible or exploratory branches whose use justifies their cost.
- practitioners know what each retained branch is for and which conditions sustain its availability;
- A precursor or teaching contrast can be kept for a particular use when the conditions for that use, including any necessary performer, access, permission, configuration and resources, hold.
- A comparison can identify lost expressive distinctions, an actual constraint or a supported effect that changes a development choice.
- The reasons to remove a branch can be inspected and reconsidered where circumstances change.
- Practitioners use the relevant music, dance, archive, teaching, production or engineering method for the work needed.

Costs and limits:

- maintaining identities, rights, capabilities, evidence, availability, and dispositions takes attention;
- some alternatives remain incomparable;
- representative trials can require performers, partners, instruments, robots, venues, audiences, or teachers;
- some branches should move to archive-only status or leave the current set; and
- a project cannot guarantee distributed cultural continuation.

### MDPE.16:8 - Rationale and Source Use



| Source or maintained result | Use here | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF `C.17`, `C.18`, `C.19`, `G.5`, `C.11`, `A.10`, `C.28`, `C.29` and `C.36` | Characterize and generate options, steward an archive or front, set pool policy, declare a selection and make a local choice. Establish evidence relations, causal claims, their representations and cultural relations as needed. | Identify the actual music or dance branches, availability, upkeep, performers and selection conditions from the practice. |
| `MDPE.9` and its sources | Identify or develop performance candidates, compare them and use a performer-involving trial when it is needed. Return supported alternatives, rejection or a limit. | Continued availability for later development is a separate question. |
| Chédin et al., [co-designing movement-generation models with Voguing and Dancehall dancers](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791515) and [repository copy](https://ualresearchonline.arts.ac.uk/id/eprint/26884/) | Dancers and researchers curated movement material and developed model and interface variants through improvisation and revision. Dancer-Y used outputs of differing fidelity for different purposes in the final comparison. | Use this finding within that case. A wider fidelity ranking, style authority or prevalence claim needs other evidence. |
| Ableton Live 12, [Comping](https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/comping/) | Retaining and auditioning takes while keeping the source material. | A take lane can preserve takes for comparison. Establish their continued availability for the intended use and any subsequent selection from the relevant evidence. |
| Timing examples in the [Dance profile](#mdpereference72---dance-making-movement-usable-for-its-participants) and the local Balboa cases | Compare continuous movement, discrete articulation, perceived timing centers and timing that the partner can read. | Use the examples to design or compare teaching and movement variants. Evidence of a repertoire or cultural retention has a different scope. |
| Shimon project sources in `MDPE.14` | Configuration-specific observations of gesture, timing, attention, noise and control in robotic music. | Compare studies only for claims and conditions they can support. Wider cultural continuation needs evidence at that scale. |

Reconsider current availability when a relied-on source premise, configuration, population, right or intended use changes. An older record can remain adequate when the conditions still hold. Apply any actual deadline or warranted review policy. For a historical question, use the conditions at that time.

### MDPE.16:9 - Relations

| Related result | Use here |
| --- | --- |
| `MDPE.8` | Identify the subject and intended use when uncertainty about them changes which alternatives belong in the comparison. |
| `MDPE.9` | Use candidates or observations from a performance comparison. Wider membership and later availability require grounds for those questions. |
| `C.17`–`C.19`, `G.5` and `C.11` | Use their results for characterization, archive or front stewardship, pool policy, selection or a local choice, where those issues matter. |
| `MDPE.13` | Use a recognition or selection arrangement to establish how a rule, incentive or observed selection affected or could affect availability. |
| `MDPE.14` | A conflict assessment or decision can identify separate uses or a requirement to keep alternatives available. |
| Relevant domain method, including music, dance, teaching, capability development, archives, rights, events, production, tools, operations or engineering | Use it for needed upkeep, reconstruction, access, permission, skill, configuration, rehearsal or trial work. Establish what it actually supplied and how that affects the branch. |
| `MDPE.7` | Use the supported alternatives and their limits for a finding about an earlier choice, comparison of feasible work, recommendation or authorized decision. |
| `MDPE.20` | Use the alternatives and their conditions when comparing possible developments. A sufficient existing availability finding can be used directly. |
| `MDPE.17`, `MDPE.18` and `MDPE.19` | Use them for a receiver's performance, cultural memory or historical and current continuation or loss, as the question requires. |
| Direct composition, choreography, improvisation, repertoire, teaching, rehearsal, curation, event, tool and engineering methods | Perform the relevant domain work when needed, or use its existing result. |

### MDPE.16:End

## MDPE.20 - Forecast How a Music-or-Dance Practice May Develop

> **Status:** Stable

> **Type:** DPF pattern body
>
> **Primary working result:** a forecast for a specified music or dance practice, population, place, period and horizon. Explain the plausible developments, their grounds and limits, and which implications distinguish any competing explanations. To examine an earlier forecast, identify what was known when it was made. For an empirical update, identify the observation used and its bearing on the forecast. Give a recommendation when requested. Make a decision only within the authority granted for it.

### MDPE.20:0 - Use This When

Use this method to forecast how a music or dance practice may develop, or to examine an earlier forecast on its original grounds or compare it with subsequent evidence. Different changes can fit the same current observations. Establish which possibilities matter to the question. A project may also need to prepare, choose what to teach, publish or change, or decide what to retain or test.

Typical reasons to examine a forecast include the following.

- one popular rhythm, movement, performance format, teaching form, or platform trend is called the future;
- a geometric prototype, statistical cluster, reconstructed lineage, prevalence estimate, or repeated transmission result is presented as evidence of a dynamical attractor without a model of change;
- one creator, book, school, competition, festival, platform, or technical tool is credited with determining later culture;
- a team assumes that current recognition, streaming, enrolment, or press visibility establishes future reproduction;
- a style-switching or style-mixing observation is explained by one memory or learning model without rival explanations;
- one local success is expected to spread through a scene despite unknown teaching, partner, venue, recognition, selection, and retention relations; or
- a project proposes an intervention without explaining what the forecast depends on or which findings would count against it.

Ask about the development the evidence supports.

> Which developments remain plausible under the relevant conditions? What differs among their implications? If the project needs to act, which response is justified on those grounds?

The result can be a conditional forecast, a comparison with a past prediction, or an empirical update based on an observation newly taken into account. If a choice depends on it, identify what is justified across the remaining possibilities or what would change that choice.

Use a suitable existing forecast or the direct field method when it already answers the question. Use MDPE.20 when the explanation still needs the particular performers, materials, structures, transmission, recognition tasks, scene conditions or observations that distinguish the developments in question.

For related tasks, start with the direct method.

- Use `MDPE.9` to compare candidates for a local performance.
- Use `MDPE.18` for a lineage or source question.
- Use `MDPE.19` to establish continuation or loss in a specified population and period.
- Use the relevant domain method to carry out one chosen local change.
- Use the applicable modelling method for a geometric, rhythmic, statistical or active-inference model when the question concerns the represented structure or mechanism itself.
- Use the dated account directly when the only question is what an earlier prediction said. Compare its conditions and implications when the question concerns its basis, adequacy or later outcome.

#### MDPE.20:0.1 - Working Distinctions

| Claim or subject | What it establishes |
| --- | --- |
| possible trajectory | A conditional account of how a named practice or distribution may change. Evidence of the later practice can test its implications when it concerns the right population, time and conditions. |
| geometric prototype or centrality | Position in a specified representation and candidate space. A claim about attraction over time also needs a model of change. |
| statistical cluster | A grouping in observations or in their representation. More than one process can produce the grouping. |
| reconstruction bias | A tendency for material to change in a particular direction as people perceive, remember, imitate, teach or reproduce it under stated conditions. To explain population selection, examine how that tendency affects who receives or reproduces variants. |
| changing prevalence | A change in how common a characteristic is in the specified population and period. State what was counted and how the sampling supports the population estimate. Retention, stability, value and cause have their own grounds. |
| lineage or reconstructed ancestor | A historical relation or hypothesis. Forecasting from it requires assumptions about what may happen next. |
| dynamical attractor | Under `A.3.3`, specify a state space, transitions or a law and the conditions and evidence for a basin or stability. Recognition of a style is a separate observation. |
| project choice | A decision by a holder with the applicable authority. Wider recognition, selection, transmission, retention or loss depends on what happens in the population. |
| publication of a forecast | Making it available can affect attention and later observations. To claim an effect, examine who encountered the forecast, what changed and the grounds for the connection. |

Identify who or what supplies each contribution to the forecast. Dancers, teachers, organizers, curators, human teams, robots and AI participants can act where their agency for the work is established. An instrument, floor, venue or platform can constrain or support that action. Use `System` for a physical or operational whole meeting its conditions and `C.2.1` when the identity of recorded content affects the forecast. Distinguish the recording and playback equipment from the observations, instructions or claims they make available.

### MDPE.20:1 - Problem

Performers vary materials and methods. Bodies, instruments, robots, venues, tools and media can make particular variants easier to use. Teachers and peers can transform what they receive. Partners, audiences, judges, curators, platforms and communities select different features. A variant can spread, split, combine with another, survive locally or disappear. Publishing a forecast can itself affect attention and copying.

The same present pattern can therefore arise from different mechanisms. A rhythm family may become concentrated because listeners reconstruct it toward familiar ratios, performers prefer what their bodies can coordinate, teachers simplify it, a platform amplifies it, a competition rewards it, or the sampling method sees only one scene. Selective transmission and biased transformation can also fit similar population observations.

An observation may establish that a rhythm is central in a representation, a creator influenced a particular work, a clip spread or a learner recovered a familiar movement. To forecast from it, explain which development it supports, which other developments remain plausible and what would distinguish them. A project contemplating action can then examine what it could change and who would bear the cost.

A long list of scenarios can leave the question unresolved. Give the serious mechanisms, conditions and expected observations that distinguish the outcomes. Some may remain indistinguishable with the available evidence.

### MDPE.20:2 - Forces

| Force | Tension to preserve |
| --- | --- |
| Action and uncertainty | The same limited preparation can be justified across several developments when a project needs to act. |
| Domain detail and overfitting | A different performer, partner, scene, instrument, medium or teaching arrangement can change the scope of a forecast. Ground wider claims in evidence for the wider setting. |
| Structural regularity and mechanism | A useful representation can expose a regularity without explaining how practice changes. |
| Individual and population change | Recovery of a movement by one performer can identify a local capability. A scene trajectory requires evidence about the relevant population and how the relevant practice spreads, changes or disappears, where that affects the forecast. |
| Local choices and cultural change | A team may control a school, event, tool or publication. Wider use depends on what the relevant performers, groups, services and institutions receive and reproduce. |
| Forecast and its possible influence | Publishing or teaching a prediction may change the practice or affect its measurement. Establish whether that happened when the claim depends on it. |
| Informative probes and participant burden | Better discrimination can require performers, partners, teachers, audiences, venues, or communities whose time, consent, and risk matter. |
| Useful alternatives | Consider drift, branching or absence of a stable attractor where they fit the evidence. Retain the differences that matter to the forecast or choice. |

### MDPE.20:3 - Solution

Identify the practice, population, period, horizon and question. Use applicable observations, models or qualified estimates, including an existing forecast where it suffices, to assess or develop the serious trajectories and their implications. Include drift, branching or absence of a stable attractor where relevant. To assess an earlier forecast on its original grounds, use the information available at the time. To test what happened subsequently, compare the dated expectations with relevant later observations. For an empirical update, identify the observation taken into account and what it supports, weakens or leaves open. A forecast can be complete on existing grounds. If a decision is requested, assess the feasible actions. Select further observation only when its expected contribution is worth its cost and delay.



#### MDPE.20:3.1 - Name what may change and why the forecast is needed

Identify the parts of the forecast that matter to its use.

- The changing subject, such as a practice, a family of variants, repertoire, a performance form, a teaching arrangement or an event.
- The population or scene, place and period covered by the starting evidence.
- The forecast horizon and the scale of the claimed change.
- What may change, such as the material, the distribution or recognition of variants, participation, how the practice is reproduced or retained, or whether it branches, hybridizes or disappears.
- The question to answer and any decision or preparation that depends on it.
- The authority, permissions and affected participants for a proposed intervention.
- The point beyond which further inquiry would no longer serve the question.

For a choice about two teaching arrangements in one school next season, use that school's population and horizon. Extend the forecast to a wider community only on suitable grounds.

#### MDPE.20:3.2 - Establish the evidence for the starting conditions

Use results applicable to the population, time and claim that can affect the forecast or a decision relying on it. Examples include

- the bounded practice and project focus from `MDPE.8` and `MDPE.1`;
- observed or proposed variants and the evidence of their availability from `MDPE.9` and `MDPE.16`;
- performer capability and context sensitivity from `MDPE.10`;
- observations from `MDPE.12`;
- recognition-and-selection arrangements from `MDPE.13`;
- evidence of practice conflicts, their consequences or decisions about them from `MDPE.14`;
- evidence about access, receiving performance or transmission from `MDPE.17`;
- cultural memory and lineage evidence from `MDPE.18`;
- evidence of continuation, change or loss in the specified period from `MDPE.19`, and
- support arrangements from `MDPE.22`.

A lineage account, catalogue, enrolment figure, streaming or competition record, press report, syllabus or expert estimate can support a particular claim. To estimate how common actual performance was, identify the population, sampling and performance evidence. For continued reproduction, examine that activity over the relevant period.

When direct evidence is absent or too costly to obtain, a qualified estimate can support a forecast or a bounded choice if its basis and uncertainty are adequate. Identify what would change the estimate. Where the evidence leaves the question open, report that limit. For a decision, compare a narrower or reversible response, worthwhile inquiry and stopping.

#### MDPE.20:3.3 - Choose structures and representations for the forecast question

Identify the practice being represented. A rhythmic question may concern musical material, ongoing movement, discrete events, positions or timing relations. A movement question may turn on partners, contact, phrases or specific performances. For a scene, identify its participants, events, schools, media, variants and the evidence of reproduction, change or loss that the forecast uses.

For the comparison, identify

- the selected structure and characteristics;
- the representation—such as notation, timing trace, video annotation, geometric rhythm space, movement features, repertoire relation, interaction graph, distribution, or historical tree;
- the operations it supports;
- the distinctions preserved and lost; and
- the population and observations to which it is tied.

Representations make different relations visible. In a geometric display, centrality, symmetry, distance and a local optimum concern the represented structure. A claim about a basin of attraction also needs a state space and dynamics. Identify those assumptions even when the same picture illustrates both.

#### MDPE.20:3.4 - Develop trajectories from plausible mechanisms

Identify credible explanations and the developments each would support. Different mechanisms can predict the same outcome under the conditions examined. For example,

- **perceptual or reconstructive:** listeners, dancers, teachers, or imitators systematically transform material toward familiar or easier structures;
- **motor, bodily, instrumental, or robotic:** coordination, effort, morphology, control, latency, or instrument constraints make some variants easier to perform and reproduce;
- **contextual retrieval and interference:** cues, partners, music, venues, body state, or transition history change which learned repertoire is expressed;
- **capability development:** teaching, rehearsal, feedback, context variation, and transfer change who can enact or recognize the variants;
- **motivation and interest:** some challenges, surprises, identities, affiliations, or rewards attract attention and repeated practice under a named population and use;
- **material and ecological:** floors, venues, instruments, media, tools, schedules, cost, access, and safety change feasible Work;
- **mediation and network:** teachers, peers, events, recordings, platforms, recommendation, and network topology change exposure and reconstruction chains;
- **recognition and selection:** partners, audiences, judges, curators, schools, organizers, and communities amplify or reject different features;
- **transmission, retention, and loss:** variants reproduce with transformation, remain locally available, split across populations, or cease to be enacted; and
- **drift, branching, or no stable attractor:** change has no stable basin under the selected horizon, or several branches remain viable.

Retain serious rivals when they affect the forecast or its use. Different developments can still justify the same preparation.

For each serious trajectory give its mechanism, conditions, expected direction or distribution, uncertainty and observations it makes more or less likely. Use `A.3.3` for an actual state-space and transition-law claim, and `C.28` when the question depends on attributing a causal contribution.

#### MDPE.20:3.5 - Derive observations that distinguish the trajectories

What observation would count differently under these explanations? Relevant cases include changes across imitation chains, return after a cue or partner changes, differences in recognition or performance across tempi and venues, continued enactment at later events, and the fate of variants after a teaching, access or selection rule is withdrawn. Identify an observable implication at the scale and under the conditions the claim requires. Select new work only if an observation is needed and feasible.

First use any adequate observation already available. To obtain another, establish that the expected result justifies the design, acquisition, participant effort and delay and that capability, consent, access, resources and timing make it feasible. For a selected observation, specify

- which prediction the observation tests and whether rival trajectories make its possible outcomes more or less likely,
- who or what will supply the observation, the relevant work and the music, dance, research, event, platform or engineering method needed to obtain it,
- the population, setting, comparison, representation, and time window,
- the sampling, measurement, transfer, consent, and burden limits,
- what each result would imply for retaining, narrowing, rejecting, replacing or adding a trajectory, and
- any decision that could change as a result.

For a comparison between mechanisms, prefer an observation whose outcomes differ in likelihood across them. Identify its source, time, interpretation and limits. Use `A.10` when a source-to-claim connection is unclear or must be recoverable by another reader, `C.16` for a needed measurement method or interpretation and `C.27` for a material timing question. A comparison can remain inconclusive. State what the comparison establishes or leaves unresolved. Further observation depends on the remaining question and its cost.

#### MDPE.20:3.6 - Use the forecast and obtain further evidence when it is worth the work

A forecast can be returned on its existing grounds. If ongoing work requires a next action, use `A.15.7` within the current method or `C.11` for a bounded choice among feasible options. Compare the expected information from another observation with the total cost, delay and displaced work. If the relevant performer, access, authority, resources and time are available and the inquiry is justified, obtain the observation through its domain method. Use the result to revise or retain the forecast. If it changes the grounds of a decision, identify what the authorized holder should reconsider.

A project may compare events under different teaching, network or selection conditions, prepare for developments that remain plausible, maintain alternatives through `MDPE.16`, choose a reversible response through `MDPE.14`, change an environmental condition through `MDPE.22`, or stop when further work would add too little. Use an adequate existing finding for the question it covers.

For a proposed intervention, identify the subject, purpose, who may authorize the work, affected participants and systems, burdens, intended local result and possible wider consequences. State which observations would strengthen or weaken any causal claim relied upon. A later effect needs evidence of what happened.

#### MDPE.20:3.7 - Include the forecast's possible influence

Publication, teaching, funding, distribution or endorsement of a forecast can change attention, recognition, imitation, selection or measurement. Include that possibility when it could affect the forecast, its interpretation or a decision.

Identify what the forecast said, how it was published or taught, who could access it, who encountered it and what subsequently changed, to the extent relevant to the claim. An effect attributed to publication needs evidence connecting that exposure to the change.

#### MDPE.20:3.8 - Return the forecast or its empirical update

Identify the forecast, its basis and conditions. For an empirical update, identify the observation and what it changed, confirmed or left unresolved. Add the practical response when that is part of the assignment.

```text
Practice, population, starting period, horizon and question:
Supported trajectories, their implications and any observations that could distinguish them:
Available evidence or qualified expert-estimate basis, conditions, and uncertainty:
For an empirical update: obtained observation, direct Method or source, source-to-claim relation, uncertainty, and transfer limits:
What the available evidence or update supports, weakens or leaves open:
Preparation, intervention or stop when a practical response is wanted:
Holder of authority and who bears the costs for a proposed or actual action:
Conditions that would change the forecast or a decision relying on it:
```

Retain trajectories the evidence supports within their conditions. Narrow their population, horizon, representation or mechanism when appropriate. A distinguishing observation can defeat an explanation, and a new mechanism can justify adding a rival. For a historical comparison, preserve the dates and scope of the earlier forecast and any subsequent evidence used. A new publication date alone leaves the underlying grounds unchanged.

A result can be qualitative or inconclusive. State the subject, relations, scope, evidence and uncertainty that support it. A finding from another population can limit a hypothesis or suggest a local comparison while leaving the grounds for intervention open.

### MDPE.20:4 - Worked Cases

#### MDPE.20:4.1 - A rhythmic family: complete one forecast update

During its current term, a city social-dance school notices that one rhythm family appears increasingly often in adult beginner and intermediate classes and social events. It must decide whether to standardize a central pattern for the next term, keep teaching several variants, or first change how it observes transmission.

It starts with four serious trajectories:

1. reconstruction during listening, remembering, singing, drumming, or teaching pulls variants toward population-specific rhythmic priors;
2. performer, tempo, partner, or instrument constraints select variants that are easier to enact;
3. network topology, teachers, event programming, and media exposure interact with which variants are selected and how they are reproduced; or
4. the apparent center is local branching or sampling drift rather than a stable attractor.

Toussaint's geometries describe rhythmic structures, equivalences, distances, transformations and neighborhoods. Several of the school's trajectories can produce the same central pattern in a chosen representation. That centrality alone gives no reason to prefer one curriculum on the proposed mechanisms. A curriculum can still be justified on grounds shared by the surviving trajectories.

**Published observation and its use in the forecast.** Marjieh and colleagues studied people who chose and sang melodies received through controlled social networks. Differences between network topologies diminished when selection or reproduction bias was removed. The result supports interaction among topology, selection and reproduction in those singing networks. The constructed school can use it as external support for the plausibility of its third trajectory. It still needs local grounds to say that the mechanism explains its dancers' rhythm family.

Suppose two short teaching-chain sessions fit the school's schedule, the team has authority to arrange them, participants agree, and their expected value justifies learner and teacher time and displaced teaching. The team chooses to compare selected and reproduced variants, partner readability and performer burden under two peer-exposure arrangements. The external finding informs the comparison. The team can commission it under the stated local conditions. Its local results will depend on what happens in the sessions.

The published result supports the interaction trajectory in the experimental setting. Reconstruction, performability, branching and sampling remain possible explanations for the school. Reconsider a curriculum decision if a local observation or change of population, representation or other premise affects it. If the trial leaves the explanations unresolved, the existing grounds may still justify keeping several variants. Further sessions depend on what they could establish.

Suppose instead that no extra sessions fit this term and their missing result leaves the limited teaching decision supportable. On the same evidence and qualified teacher judgement the school can keep the supported teaching scope and decline the larger festival investment. That is a complete bounded decision. A change in the learner population or an actual venue or rights deadline could justify reconsideration. An older copy of the same applicable forecast can still be used.

#### MDPE.20:4.2 - Multidance switching: separated styles, blending, loss, or context-bound expression

In a constructed planning case, a school observes learners switching between two specified partnering
tasks taught in its tango and kizomba classes. Some keep the requested movement organization. Others
blend the sequences or do not carry a selected torso cue into the second task. The school wants to plan
next term's teaching. Identify the actual instructions, recording, tempo and partner in each task.

For a first comparison, use the A and B movement instructions from `MDPE.10:4.2`
with the same usable recording, tempo and partner. A second comparison can change
the recording while keeping the task. When both the task and recording change, a difference could reflect
either change or their interaction. Specify the receiving
conditions before adding an urban-kiz class, another recording or a new event.

Serious rivals include:

- capabilities for the specified movement tasks remain available but latent-context inference gates their expression, so the earlier coordination returns under earlier cues;
- a target coordination was never developed robustly enough, so changed context exposes a capability limit rather than retrieval;
- music, partner, cue, or transition history creates interference;
- dancers deliberately develop a hybrid practice that receiving partners and events may recognize or reject; and
- teaching and event arrangements select clean switching, blending, or dominance of one branch over time.

The COIN model supplies one hypothesis about how people create, express and update sensorimotor memories under contextual cues. For the school, consider earlier capability, interference, deliberate blending and scene-level selection. A suitable earlier observation can support a bounded teaching decision. If further evidence is worth obtaining, use `MDPE.10` to compare the same person's performances across `A → B → A` under the relevant cue and order conditions, or examine partners, teaching and events for a wider claim. One recovered movement cannot identify a whole scene's trajectory.

Depending on the finding and the task, the school may vary practice, develop a missing coordination, change a partner cue, retain a hybrid branch or alter its event. The observation about one dancer remains useful within that scope.

#### MDPE.20:4.3 - Short video: discovery aid, selection pressure, or measurement artifact

A dance school sees short camera-facing clips gaining views while its partner-response and long-form improvisation material appears less often in classes. It considers increasing short-form production.

The clips may aid discovery, favor camera-facing movements, or reach a different population from social dancers. Teachers might counter their influence with uncued partner work. Comparing views with actual performance might also account for the apparent change in practice. Identify what each explanation predicts under the school's conditions.

Look for distinguishing observations in classes and on the social floor, partner recognition, curriculum, continued performance or comparable settings with different exposure. Use existing records, or obtain more when it is feasible and worth the effort. The forecast can finish there. If the school chooses to act, `MDPE.22` can address the support environment and `MDPE.14` a proposal to separate uses. Establish any cultural effect from evidence of what happened after implementation and the grounds for attributing it.

#### MDPE.20:4.4 - Live coding and Algorave: a label does not forecast a practice

A team sees tools, live-code performances, a manifesto, events, recordings, teaching, and an audience community developing together. It asks whether a local Algorave series will become a continuing practice, merge with another electronic-music scene, remain an event format, or disappear after organizer and venue support ends.

Consider access to the tools, performer capability, recognition in live settings, event operations, publishing and reproduction by other practitioners. Independent new performers, recurring events without the original team and recognizable changed methods would support some trajectories more than others. Check which of these developments have actually been observed.

A new name, manifesto or successful series can identify what people called a series, proposed in a manifesto or performed at events. Those facts alone leave its identity as a cultural whole and its later development open. If the answer depends on whether the local series formed a new whole or continued a branch or event format, use `MDPE.24`.

#### MDPE.20:4.5 - Constructed feedback: teaching can change what selection recognizes

In the [shared-practice case](#mdpe2551---a-complete-constructed-case-the-evening-that-became-a-qualification-course), Mara and Ren prepare the next three events. Partners value a small pause-and-response variant which fails the challenge's large-visible-change entry rule. Extending the earlier selection pattern would favor large visible changes if the criterion and observers’ recognition stay fixed.

Compare two explanations before committing the programme. In a **fixed-preference account**, observers can already distinguish the relevant partner recovery, but continue to value visible display more highly for this event. Better instruction or a closer view need not change their selection; separate display and social opportunities may remain useful. In a **learning-and-selection feedback account**, observers initially miss the small recovery relation or judge it through the display task. Teaching the contrast and making it observable can change which variants they recognize as successful; changed eligibility then gives those variants more encounters, from which performers may construct further variations. This is a conditional loop, not a prediction that teaching inevitably reforms taste or a whole scene.

The two explanations imply different longer-term programmes. Both support keeping the social task, explaining what its challenge recognizes, preserving the prepared display for its audience and deferring a season-long investment based on an assumed change in taste. Sol can use the existing clinic, and Ren the allocated briefing. Attendees remain free to value the display or decline instructional work.

Suppose the same observers first reject the compact variation under the large-change rule. After a demonstration, they view the recovery close up, hear partners' reports of comfort and consider it under revised criteria. Some still prefer the larger display. They now recognize the small recovery and admit the variant. Ren can reject an account predicting that their recognition and selection would both stay unchanged. The observations establish that some still preferred the larger display. They leave the stability and distribution of preferences open. Because teaching, viewing position, criteria and invitation changed together, this comparison does not isolate their contributions. The local result supports keeping both opportunities. Persistence across a population needs later evidence.

If observers recognize the compact response but performers cannot reproduce it with their partners, further publicity will not supply the missing skill. Keep the finding about recognition and use an appropriate practice task if development is wanted. If the observers still prefer display, two occasions may remain valuable. If an expensive expansion depends on identifying the mechanism, specify the competing accounts, their differing predictions and an attainable comparison. Use the existing programme decision when it is sound under both accounts.

### MDPE.20:5 - Recognition and Assurance

A complete forecast or historical assessment answers the questions relevant to its use.

1. What practice, population, place, period, horizon and question does the forecast concern?
2. What structures and representations underlie the observations at the time in question, and what do they lose?
3. Which mechanisms support the serious trajectories, including drift or absence of a stable attractor when plausible?
4. Which distinguishing implications make the serious trajectories different, and what available basis or possible observation could narrow or defeat them?
5. Which observations, models or qualified estimates support the forecast? For an empirical update, which obtained observation changed or preserved which conclusion and within what limits?
6. Which developments does the evidence support, weaken or leave unresolved? What changed relative to an earlier forecast, if one is being compared?
7. When a response is wanted, which preparation, intervention or stop follows under the conditions? What could alter it?

Check the distinctions that matter to the claim.

- Identify whether the claim concerns an individual change, a population distribution, prevalence, retention or loss.
- prototype, centrality, cluster, reconstruction bias, lineage, increasing frequency, and dynamics attractor remain different claims;
- Establish the relation between the relevant practice, its representation, the forecast, observed events, any decision or intervention and its possible effects.
- Give conditions and distinguishing implications for the serious trajectories. Retain warranted rivals when available observations do not settle them.
- an empirical update cites the observation actually obtained, its direct Method or source, evidence basis, source-to-claim relation, population, setting, uncertainty and transfer limit;
- Identify which trajectories and, when applicable, which decisions the evidence warrants. Qualified retention, a preparation common to several futures, a stop or an inconclusive result can complete the question.
- Identify the music or dance performers, material, structures, methods and setting, and any recognition task or probe that matters to the forecast.
- expert estimates show basis, uncertainty, and update condition;
- Use publications, standards, curricula, media or platform measures for what they document. For a claim about how common performance was, examine the relevant performances and sampling basis. For continued reproduction, examine the activity across the period.
- For a proposed intervention, identify decision authority, permission, affected participants and systems, and who bears any displaced work.
- Give a numerical probability only with a model and evidence adequate to that claim.

### MDPE.20:6 - Common Failures and Repairs

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| “This rhythm is central, so it is the attractor.” | Identify the representation and meaning of centrality. A dynamical attractor needs appropriate transition and stability grounds. Consider reconstruction, performance, selection, branching or drift where plausible. |
| “The style is popular, so it will persist.” | Name population, sampling basis, reproduction relations, horizon, and evidence of continued reproduction. If changing a pressure would distinguish the forecasts, identify what could be observed and use suitable earlier observations where available. |
| “The creator caused the culture.” | Identify evidence of creation, publication, recognition, copying, transformation, selection or retention. Attribute a contribution at the scope the causal evidence supports. |
| “COIN explains style evolution.” | Keep COIN as one bounded sensorimotor-context hypothesis and preserve relevant capability, interference, partner, teaching, selection and population rivals. Choose additional tests by their actual contribution and whole cost. |
| “The model predicts 72%.” | Identify the variables, population, horizon, calibration and evidence that give 72% its meaning, and the question it answers. Use a qualitative forecast when the evidence supports only that. |
| “We have many scenarios.” | Give the supported mechanisms, distinct implications, evidence and remaining uncertainty. Include a practical response when required. An empirical update uses an observation actually obtained. |
| “Publishing the forecast will make it true.” | Treat the forecast's influence as a possible cause. Identify evidence of exposure, any later change and the connection between the two. |
| “Our intervention selects the future.” | Keep project choice separate from distributed cultural recognition, selection, transmission, retention, and loss. |

### MDPE.20:7 - Consequences

A practitioner can use the comparison in the following ways.

- Compare a popular prediction with other developments that have a credible basis.
- structural, perceptual, motor, teaching, media, recognition, selection, and retention mechanisms can compete without being collapsed;
- drift, branching, and no-attractor possibilities remain visible;
- Select a new observation or intervention when the result it could supply is worth its burden and the work is feasible.
- expert judgement remains usable with its limits distinguished from population measurement;
- forecasts can prepare a project for several developments; and
- Use the relevant music, dance, teaching, research, event, platform or engineering method for the work required.

Costs and limits:

- several trajectories require more thought than one extrapolation;
- observations can be slow, distributed, ethically sensitive, or confounded by the forecast itself;
- a bounded project rarely measures a whole cultural population;
- some mechanisms remain observationally hard to distinguish;
- interventions can move burden or change the practice being studied; and
- A forecast concerns a stated horizon. Extending it requires applicable grounds, which may already exist. Reconsider a dependent conclusion when a premise changes, a warranted review is due or a real rights, resource or use window ends. The date on an unchanged copy does not by itself change the forecast.

### MDPE.20:8 - Rationale and Source Use



| Source | Contribution | Scope of the finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FPF `B.5`, `B.5.2`, `A.3.3`, `C.28`, `A.15.7`, `C.11`, `A.10`, `C.16`, `C.27`, `C.29` and `C.36` | Develop rivals, examine dynamics or causal claims, choose a current action, and trace evidence, measurement, time, representation and cultural relations. | Use domain grounds for the actual practice, trajectories, observations and intervention. |
| Buskell, [What are cultural attractors?](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5491627/) | Distinguishes uses of *attractor* for transformation tendency, a cluster, increased frequency and equilibrium. | Identify which use fits the available observations and what explanatory mechanism is proposed. |
| Alex Mesoudi, [Cultural selection and biased transformation: two dynamics of cultural evolution](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8126458/) | Selective transmission and biased transformation can fit similar population observations. | Identify evidence bearing differently on the two processes before attributing the distribution to one of them. |
| Deffner et al., [Bridging theory and data: A computational workflow for cultural evolution](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11621747/) | A research method connecting generative assumptions, estimands, checks on simulated data and empirical comparison. | Use it when the unresolved mechanism calls for that design. A qualified local forecast can be sufficient on existing grounds. |
| Jacoby et al., [Cross-cultural comparison of rhythm priors in 15 countries](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-023-01800-9), and Ravignani et al., [Musical evolution in the lab exhibits rhythmic universals](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-016-0007) | Supply iterated-reproduction evidence for structured, population-sensitive rhythmic reconstruction. | Laboratory reconstruction is not the whole historical or social selection process. |
| Spiech et al., [4/4 and more](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-025-00360-0) | In three experiments with Western listeners, groove ratings peaked at moderate complexity in 4/4. Simpler rhythms elicited the highest ratings in the other tested meters. | Familiarity was inferred from cultural background. Enculturation and a possible innate preference for binary organization remained explanations. Reports of wanting to move and of pleasure concern those listeners and excerpts. Partnering and later development need suitable evidence. |
| Toussaint, *The Geometry of Musical Rhythm*, 2nd ed. (2020), especially chapters 8, 17–18, 36, and 39–42 | Supplies rhythm representations, metrics, transformations, similarity, complexity, genealogical hypotheses, and transmission cases. | The constructions do not constitute a universal rhythm ontology or causal theory of cultural attractors. |
| Heald, Lengyel and Wolpert, [Contextual inference underlies the learning of sensorimotor repertoires](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04129-3) | A model of how context affects the creation, expression and updating of human sensorimotor memories. | Treat extension to other music and dance tasks, cognition, robots, software or population change as a hypothesis with relevant alternatives. |
| Marjieh et al., [Characterizing the Interaction of Cultural Evolution Mechanisms in Experimental Social Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12847) | In controlled singing networks, differences across topologies diminished when selection or reproduction bias was removed. The result supports considering the mechanisms together. | Use the stated population and melody-choice and singing tasks. To assign the same mechanism to another practice, examine evidence from the receiving conditions. A forecast can retain it as a plausible explanation while that attribution is open. |

Choose sources and models for the evidence and assumptions relevant to this practice and horizon. A novel or popular model may suggest a rival. Prefer it over a grounded local explanation when its account or evidence improves the forecast for this case.

### MDPE.20:End

## MDPE.7 - Choose the Next Music-or-Dance Development Work

> **Status:** Stable

> **Type:** DPF pattern body
>
> **Primary working result:** a recommendation, an authorized choice of further music or dance development work, or an account of an earlier choice. Use the `C.11 ChoiceResult` or applicable domain decision where available. State what the evidence establishes about a previous choice and its grounds. For a recommendation explain which action, probe, rejection or change of question the comparison supports. Identify the actual chooser and authority for a claim that an authorized decision was made. Describe the work and its conditions if work was selected. Establish what was carried out separately.

### MDPE.7:0 - Use This When

Use this method when music or dance observations leave a choice about further work, when advice about possible work is requested, or when someone asks how an earlier choice was made. A performance, class, event, tool or intervention may have succeeded or failed while several different responses remain possible.

An authorized chooser may select a feasible option, choose a further probe, reject the set when no option survives, or identify a different question that needs an answer. Rejection, a change of question and a condition for revisiting an issue describe the outcome of considering the options. A concrete inquiry or reconstruction can itself be a work option when someone can carry it out.

For a present choice, identify its `DecisionSubject`, the options that answer the same development question and whether each is feasible under the relevant conditions. For an earlier choice, use evidence of the options, conditions, recommendation or decision at that time. Bring in other results when they materially affect the comparison or establish the history.

For example, the decision can be stated in these terms.

> Who is deciding or decided? Which options were considered or could address the named practice and use? What evidence, constraints and costs bear on the choice, and what could change an ongoing decision?

For a new comparison, apply the `ChoiceRule` that relates the options and their consequences to the `ChoiceResult`. For an earlier choice, recover that rule when the question requires it and the evidence permits. New information can change the comparison. A practitioner without authority to decide can recommend a course of action to the holder. Where authority is unknown, identify the recommendation or reported decision the evidence supports and the limit on claiming an authorized choice. Permission, capability and provision for carrying it out are separate matters.

For selected work, identify the intended result, performer, resources, permission and entry conditions it needs, including any condition still missing. A good performance may justify continuing on the tested stage. A failed trial may justify a narrower use, repair or stopping. Determine which response fits the actual options.

Use `A.15.7` when new facts change the next action within work already under way by an identified method. Use the existing result of a domain choice directly when it answers the question. Other useful entry points follow.

- Use `MDPE.8` when the practice subject or question needs identification.
- Use `MDPE.9`, `C.18` or the direct method when the task is to generate alternatives.
- Use an applicable `C.11 OptionSet`, domain rule and choice already made when they supply the answer.
- For planning or tool calls after a choice, use `A.15.2` or `C.24`.
- Use `MDPE.15` to carry out or investigate a selected local change.
- Use `C.36` or the relevant domain method to establish cultural recognition, transmission, retention or loss.

#### MDPE.7:0.1 - What counts as a choice of work

| Term | What to establish |
| --- | --- |
| *next development Work* | The bounded activity proposed for this choice, its intended result, the capability and conditions it needs and any identified performer. Use `U.Work` for an actual performance when its occurrence matters. |
| *development* | The particular change sought in material, method, capability, configuration, evidence, repertoire, teaching, recognition arrangements, cultural understanding or continuation. It can be a repair, reduction or suspension. |
| `DecisionSubject` | The agent that makes the bounded choice. Establish the basis of its authority separately and identify who could carry out any selected work when that matters. |
| *practice-developing Agent* | Who performed the development work. Use `E.10.ROLE` when role wording is ambiguous, `A.2.1` for an actual assignment of a specified kind, and `F.6` for precise attribution of dated work under that assignment. For a claim about a dated work occurrence, establish the performer’s agency under `A.13` and the work under `A.15.1`. Check ability, authority and permission where the claim relies on them. |
| *authority* and *permission* | Identify who has authority for this choice and what permits the action for the specified subject and time. Use `A.2.8.PER` for permission or non-prohibition. A performer's skill or an audience's support can inform a recommendation while the decision belongs to a different holder. |
| `ChoiceResult` | Under `C.11` the result may select an option, reject the set, select a further probe or identify another current question and its applicable method. Determine separately who authorized, committed, planned or carried out any work the choice occasioned. |
| *recommendation* | Advice about what to choose. Its author may have suitable expertise. To report an authorized decision, identify the actual choice and the holder’s decision right. An archive can support a narrower report when authority is unknown. |
| *revisit condition* | A change in evidence, configuration, capability, authority, cost, consequences for participants or intended use that would justify reconsidering a continuing choice. |

Identify what the decision concerns, such as an account, material, method, capability, performing system, event arrangement or specific work. If the intended subject or deciding body changes, identify it at the new scope.

### MDPE.7:1 - Problem Frame

Fluency reported by a performer, a cue read by a partner, a technical reading, applause, a competition result, a class performance and a surviving source can each be evidence about something different. Identify how each bears on this question.

A project may repeat its last successful activity, publish a promising result before learning whether it transfers, or abandon a branch that remains playable with another performer. A visible trend can displace local repertoire. Investigating an interesting lineage can consume the time needed to make a choice it would not change.

Connect the evidence that matters to the options, criteria and authority for the particular choice.

### MDPE.7:2 - Problem

Common mistakes include the following.

1. Treating the latest success, failure, measurement or opinion as a sufficient rule for selection.
2. Gathering every framework result even when most would leave the choice unchanged.
3. Giving the performer, human or robotic, the right to choose the project's work merely because it performed.
4. Reporting a technically well-founded recommendation as an authorized decision.
5. Presenting the team's choice of work as an already achieved change in what a population recognizes, selects or reproduces.

These mistakes can waste preparation time, prompt premature expansion or leave others unable to establish who chose the work and why.

### MDPE.7:3 - Forces

| Practical question | What matters |
| --- | --- |
| **Evidence and timely action** | For a discretionary probe, compare what an attainable result could add to the decision with its cost, delay and displaced work. Include any qualification required for the intended use. |
| **Local result vs wider horizon** | An occurrence can guide a later trial. To establish transfer or retention, relate it to the earlier performance and the relevant change or interval. A trajectory concerns a series. |
| **Creative exploration vs bounded commitment** | Creative exploration can generate further possibilities. Compare the finite `OptionSet` available for the particular choice. |
| **Expert judgement** | A qualified practitioner can recommend on limited evidence and decide when authorized. State the basis of the judgement, uncertainty and consequences, and identify what would affect continued reliance. |
| **Performing and deciding** | A performer may operate autonomously while the decision about further development belongs to the project team, a service with delegated authority or another holder. Establish the local arrangement. |
| **Coordinating the work** | Results from several methods can inform a choice. Use the ones that can make a material difference. |
| **Local action and cultural development** | Work selected locally can change an event or available variant. Identify what it establishes at that scale and use population evidence if wider uptake or loss is at issue. |

### MDPE.7:4 - Solution

For a present choice, identify the finite options addressing one music or dance development question and the criteria for comparing them. The rule and options together determine which `C.11 ChoiceResult` the comparison supports. The authorized holder may make the choice. An analyst may report a supported earlier decision or give a recommendation, even when someone else has authority to choose. For a historical question, use the decision and other evidence of what was considered, under which conditions and with what outcome. An adequate record can finish that task. For intended work establish its own permission, capability and resources. Use `A.22.CGUS` when the branching or return structure itself needs to be selected, recorded or compared.

#### MDPE.7:4.1 - Name the chooser, subject, and decision extent

Identify what the claim about the choice requires.

- The `DecisionSubject` and scope of its decision, including `DecisionSubjectGranularity` for a formal comparison.
- Who performed or would perform the development work, and any assignment needed for its attribution.
- The music or dance practice and its configuration at the time in question.
- The intended consequence and affected participants or systems.
- The horizon and resource limits for the choice.
- Relevant authority, permission, consent, safety and ways to decline, or material uncertainty about them.

Identify a role or assignment when the attribution depends on it. A dancer may speak for a pair, a bandleader for an ensemble or a service for its users where the arrangements give that authority. Use the basis for the particular scope before attributing a wider decision to a teacher, founder, robot, platform or majority.

#### MDPE.7:4.2 - Identify evidence that matters to the comparison

Possible contributions include the following.

| Source | What it can establish |
| --- | --- |
| `MDPE.8` development focus | subject, scope, affected Systems, or current question |
| `MDPE.1` creation basis | intended use, material, performer, style-bearing constraint, or creation decision |
| `MDPE.9` candidate dispositions | which material or performance branches remain feasible |
| `MDPE.10` capability evidence | which performer-involving Work is feasible or what development is needed |
| `MDPE.3` performing configuration | whether constituents, interfaces, timing, space, sensing, or coordination support the option |
| `MDPE.11` performed-result and `MDPE.5` occurrence results | what was proposed, prescribed, performed or presented, and the conditions and evidence for each claim |
| `MDPE.12` observations | which technical, bodily, partner, audience, recognition, or cultural claims change the comparison |
| `MDPE.13` recognition and selection | What an existing rule admitted, what a proposal would admit, any observed use and what a rule change would affect. |
| `MDPE.6` change of use | Whether material or a method works under changed conditions, how earlier use went and what reuse, revision, branching, testing or stopping would require. |
| `MDPE.14` conflicts among results | What conflict was established, its consequences, and what supports a selected change, preserving the tension, separate uses, another observation or rejection of the set, including who bears a shifted burden and what remains unresolved. |
| `MDPE.15` local change | What changed or failed, what evidence supports the result and any later question that still matters. |
| `MDPE.16` alternatives | Which branches were, are or could become available for this use, what remains uncertain, and what repair, testing or retention would require. |
| `MDPE.17`–`MDPE.20` | Evidence about receiving performance, source and lineage, continuation, loss or possible development for the period and population concerned. |

Use an adequate existing result directly. Seek a missing contribution when the answer depends on it and the work is justified. Otherwise state the limit or leave the immaterial question aside.

#### MDPE.7:4.3 - Identify the options for this decision

For a current decision, identify the proposals and assess whether the decision holder can select or test them under the actual conditions. Identify any requirement a proposal fails or any feasibility question that remains open. To examine an earlier choice, establish which options were then available or considered and which remain unknown. Typical work options include the following.

- continue or vary creation Work;
- investigate a specific uncertainty through performance, an existing observation or a feasible trial,
- develop a named capability for representative Work;
- reconfigure a performing whole, Method relation, interface, or event arrangement;
- make one selected local change;
- retain, repair, suspend, or remove a development alternative;
- teach a method or arrange suitable receiving practice,
- change the criteria or arrangements for recognition and selection,
- repair a lineage or continuation account;
- undertake bounded reconstruction, teaching, archival work or retirement when warranted by the available findings,
- run one trajectory-discriminating probe;
- perform or present one bounded Music-or-Dance occurrence under its direct Method;
- make a chosen edition of a claim or other account available for a particular use through `E.24.PUB`,
- stabilize an identified practice subject in a named configuration, or make that subject available for a named use under the applicable direct Method and relation.

For each proposed option, identify the work, intended result, required performing capability, any identified performer, material conditions, cost, affected participants or systems, and any needed stopping or rollback condition. Identify the method and support on which implementation depends where these change feasibility. A bounded inquiry can be an option if the work to answer it is specified. Keep options belonging to different choosers or different decisions in separate `OptionSet`s. Rejecting a set and identifying another current question are comparison outcomes.
